' My Lords and Gentlemen*

I have postponed your Meeting to this Time, that I might consult your private Convenience, as far as was confident with the Occasions of the Publick. The Continue ance of the present Tranquillity has afforded me an Opportunity for the former, and rendered the latter less press-

Iwg. Since the last Session, my Care and Attention have been constantly employed in improving this Situation: And I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that I have concluded a Treaty with my good Brother the King of t Spain; whereby such particular Differences, as, from the

I Nature of them, could not be settled in a general Treaty,

" have been amicably adjusted, without the Intervention of

[j any other Party; and the Commerce of my Subjects with

", that Country re-established upon the most advantageous

and sure Foundations.

In the Progress of this Work, I have received such Affurances of the sincere Disposition of the Catholick King,

*. to cement and maintain the most perfect Union with me, - as leave no room to doubt of its good Effects being felt

in all Parts; and there is the greatest Reason to hope, that the ancient Friend ship, and good Correspondence, between the Two Nations, which had been long unfortunately in-d terrupted, will, from mutual Interest and Inclination, be

-< now effectually restored.

1 have also, in Conjunction with the Empress-Queen, v* - / and the Scates-General, concluded a Treaty with the Elector of Bavaria; and am taking such further Measures*

as may belt tend to ftr&i'gthen andfecure the Tranquillity of the Empire, support its System, and timely prevent such Events, as have been found, by Experience, to in-danget the common Cause, involve Europe in the Calamities of War,ahd Occasion the Loss of much Blood and Treasure to toy own Kingdoms.

Both these Treaties shall be laid before you; and, as I have told you the Vrews with which I have entered into them, I mud do Justice to all the other contracting Powers, in the definitive Treaty of Aix la Chapelle, by acquainting you, dhat I have received from them the most full and clear Declarations of their Refolurion to prefcrvc the general Peace. 1

That nothing might be wanting for these salutary Purposes, I have taken Care to strengchen and consolidate the Tics of Union and Friendship between me and my Allies; the better to secure our mutual Interests, maintain the Peace already subsisting, and to prevent the Occa^ori of any future Rupture: And that there might remain no.

Doubt of the Uprightness and Sincerity of my Intentions*

I have made the proper Communications of the Measures I have taken, and the Principles on which they have been founded.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered Estimates to be laid before you, for the current Service of the Year. I desire only such Supplies, as shall be necessary for your own Security, and making good such Engagements as have been contracted, and arc now communicated to you. , The successful and happy Progress which has been made in the Reduction of the Interest of the national Debt* does great Honour to this. Parliament, and adds much to our Reputation in foreign Countries. So little of this greatWork remains unfinished*. that I make no Doubt of your completing it this Session* in the most just and equitable mariner.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have nothing further to recommend to you in particular. Let me exhort you, in general, to make the best use of the present State of Tranquillity, for improving the Trade and Commerce of my Kingdoms; for enforcing the Execution of the Laws; and for suppressing those Outrages and Violences, which are inconsistent with all good Order and Government; and endanger the Lives and Properties of my Subjects; whose Happiness, and flourishing Condition, I have entirely at Heart*

Haldane, Mr. Mostyn, Mr. Henry Vane, Mr. Lajcelks; Mr. Legge: And they are to meet upon Monday Fortnight, at Five of the Clock in the Afternoon, in the Speaker's Chamber; and to fit cyery Wednesday, Friday, and Monday, in the AfternoonAnd dll that come are to have Voices: And they are to take into Corisideration all such Matters as shall or may come in question, touching Returns, Elections and Privileges; and to proceed upon double Returps in the First Place; and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinions thereupon, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that will question any Returns, are to do it within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee are to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and* Records, for- their Information: And all Members who1 are returned for Two or more Places, are to make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall come in question touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members, returned upon double Returns, do withdraw, till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to.give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Sadsfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed, with the utmost Severity, against such Person.

Resolved,\That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof,

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any Cafe, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall fee, or be informed of to be in the House or Gallery, while the House or any Committeeof the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker's Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and chat he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall, shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmtn, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High-Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters, directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post-Office to this House, or feme other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster-General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon; and for Two Hours, at the lead, immediately after the Rising of the House; and also on every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, from Five of

the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their knpwn Servant or Servants, or Others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Fofl-master-General.

Ordered, That when any Letter or Packet, direfred to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame; and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to the House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going to Prayers, give Notice thereof to all Committees: And that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker: And that he do appoint the printing thereof: And that no Person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petitions for private Bills after the Seventh Day of March next.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, to be heard at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Petitioners do, by themselves, or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed either by the House or the Committee of Privileges and Elections, as the Matter to be heard shall be before the House or the said Committee, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lifts of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving in the said Lifts the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to: And that the Sitting Members do, by themselves, or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Mr. Horatio Walpole, of Callington, reported from the Addrefsoa Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address the King’* to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had Speech, drawn up an Address accordingly; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our sincere and hearty Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We beg leave to congratulate your Majesty on your safe and happy Return to these Kingdoms; and to express the warmest Acknowlegements of our Gratitude for your Majesty’s unwearied Endeavours to establish the prefect Tranquillity upon the surest Foundations.

We congratulate your Majesty on the Conclufton of a Treaty with the King of Spain, by which the particular Differences, that remained to be settled between your Majesty and that Crown, are amicably adjusted; and we feel the most real Satisfaction at the Reason there is to hope, from the Assurances which your Majesty has received of the sincere Disposition of the Catholic King, to cement and maintain the most perfe£t Union with your Majesty, that the ancient Friendship will be restored, and an uninterrupted good Correspondencefubfift between the

14 Geo. II*

Two Nations, to theii1 mutual Advantage and Happi-hess.

We refipeftfully acknowlege your Majesty's great Wisdom and Forefight, in taking the best Measures timely to prevent such Eyehts, as might hereafter involve Europe in the Calamities of War: And we have the belt grounded Hopes, from the full and clear Declaration of all the contracting Powers in the Definitive Treaty of Aix la Cha-selle, as well as from your Majesty’s Care and Attention to strengthen the Ties of Union and Friendship between your Majesty and your Allies, that we shall long enjoy the Bleffmgs of a general Peace.

We allure your Majesty, that we will chearfully raise such Supplies as shall be found necessary for the Security of your Majesty's Government, and to make good the Engagemenrsentered into by your Majesty for the publick Benefir, and, according to youf gracious Intention* communicated to this House.

Your faithful Commons beg Leave to express their Sense of the Happiness they enjoy Under your Majesty’s Government; and to allure your Majesty, that they are determined to give all possible Attention to whatever may promote the Trade and Commerce of these Kingdoms; and that they will endeavour to render the Laws more effectual, by enforcing their Execution, thereby todifeou-rage and suppress the Outrages and Enormities committed in Defiance of them.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We,your Majesty's rhoft dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our sincere and hearty Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on your safe and happy Return to these Kingdoms; and to express the warmest Acknowlegements of our Gratitude for your Majesty’s unwearied Endeavours to establish the present Tranquillity upon the surest Foundations.

Wc congratulate your Majesty on the Conclusion of a Treaty with the King of Spain, by which the particular Differences, that, from the Nature of them, could not be settled in a general Treaty, are now amicably adjusted; and we feel the most real Satisfaction at-the Reason there

Vol. 26.

1

is to hope, from the Affuranbes which your Majesty has received of the sincere Disposition of the Catholick King v to cement arid maintain the most perfect Union with your Majesty, that the ancient Friendftiip will be reftorfed; and an uninterrupted good Correspondence subsist between the Two Nations, to their mutual Advantage and Happiness.

Wc respectfully acknowlege your Majesty's great Wisdom and Forefight in taking the best Measures, timely to prevent such Events as might hereafter involve Europe in the Calamities of War; and we have the best grounded Hopes, from the full and clear Declaration of all the con-trading Powers in the Definitive Treaty of Aix la Cha-pelle, as well as from your Majesty's Care and Attention to strengthen the Ties of Union and Friendffiip between your Majesty and your Allies, that we shall long enjoy the Blessings of a general Peace.

We assure your Majesty, that wd will chearfully raise such Supplies as shall be found necessary, for the Security of your Majesty's Government, and to make good the Engagements entered into by your Majesty for the publick Benefit, and, according to your gracious Intention^ communicated to this House.

It is with the greatest Satisfaction that we receive your Majesty's gracious Approbation of the Progress already made towards reducing the Interest of the national Debt; and we assure your Majesty, that we will use our immediate Endeavours to finish that great Work with Justice and Equity.

Your faithful Commons beg Leave to exprest their Sense of the Happiness they enjoy under your Majesty’s Government; and to assure your Majesty that they are determined to give all possible Attention to whatever may promote the Trade and Commerce of these Kingdoms j and that they will endeavour to render the Laws more effectual, by enforcing their Execution, thereby to discourage and suppress the Outrages and Enormities committed in Defiance of them.

A Petition of several of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act for repairing the Road between Stamford and Grantham, in the County of Lincoln; and also of several Gentlemen, Clergymen, and Freeholders, and other principal Inhabitants, living near the said Road, whose Names are thereunto respectively subscribed; was presented to the House, and read; feceing forth. That by an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of his present Majesty (intituled, An Act for repairing the Road between Stamford and Grantham, in the County of Lincoln), several Tolls and Duties were granted and made payable for the'Repair of the said Road* and several Powers were given, which were respectively to take Place, and have Continuance, only from and after the Twenty-fourth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty-nine, for and during the Term of Twenty-one Years; and that by virtue, and under the Authority, and on the Credit, of the said Act, the Petitioners, the Trustees, have borrowed the Sum of Two thousand Pounds, which, together with the Income of the said Tolls and Duties, have been duly applied towards the repairing of the said Road; and the same principal Sum of Two thousand Pounds doth now remain wholly due and unsatisfied: and that the said Toils and Duties, and the Money so borrowed, have not been sufficient to complete the Repair of the said Road, which is Twenty Miles in Length; and that the Petitioners are satisfied and convinced, chat it will be impossible to complete the Repair of the said Road, and keep the same in Repair, and pay off the Sum borrowed, as aforesaid, unless the Term and Powers given by the said Act be enlarged, and the Tolls and Duties thereby granted be augmented: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be 2

Mr. Fane also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to (it again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

which hath been continued by several subsequent Acts to the First Day of ' yune One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-one, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, when the same will expire; several Regulations were made for the Benefit of Trade and Navigation ort the said Rivers, and the Power of the Commissioners thereby appointed, was extended as far as the said Town of Cricklade, in the said County of Wilts; and that, though the said Acts have been found very useful and beneficial, yet they have not answered all the good Ends for which the same were intended; but divers Abuses have heretofore been, and (till are, committed by the Owners of thefeveralTowing-Paths, and other Passages on the Banks of the said Rivers, and by the Owners of the Locks, Weirs, Turnpikes, Dams, Flood-gates, and other Engines, in and upon, or near adjoining to, the said Rivers; and also by the several Barge-Masters, and their Servants navi-: gating thereon; by reason whereof, and other Exactions,

the Price of Water-Carriage on those Rivers hath of late Years been very much raised; and the Petitioners are apprehensive, that, upon the Expiration of the said last mentioned Act, in case no new Law be made for the due Regulation of the Navigation on the said Rivers, the Abuses already experienced will greatly increase, and divers other Irregularities and Abuses be committed, to the great Damage of the said Navigation, and to the Detriment of the said Petitioners, and the Publick in general: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better carrying on and regulating the Navigation of the said Rivers of Thames and Isis, from the said City of London, Westward, to the said Town of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts\ whereby such proper Rules, Orders, Constitutions, and Regulations, may be made for the Benefit of the said Navigation, or other-

A Petition of the several Burgesses and Inhabitants of Westminster the City and Liberty of Westminster, whose Names are Election, thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several other Burgesses and Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Right Honourable Granville Leveson Gower Esquire, commonly called Lord Trentbam, having, by Acceptance of the Place of One of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, vacated his Seat in Parliament for the said City and Liberty; he, and Sir George Vandeput Baronet, on the Twenty second Day of November 174.9, being the Day appointed for the Lleftion of a Citizen or Representative in Parliament, offered themselves as Candidates at the said Eieftion; and that the Right of Eieftion having been invariably fixed in, and confined to, the Members and Occupiers of Chambers in the several Inns of Chancery within the said City and Liberty, and to the Inhabitants within the said City or Liberty paying Scotland Lot; and the Parish Books being the most proper Evidence of the Rights of the Electors, Sir George Vandeput, his Voters and Friends, pressed the High Bailiff, when they found he had neglected so to do, to apply for, and procure, the Parish Books to be brought to the Place of polling, that they might be referred to in the Course of taking the Poll, as a Means to enable him, as Returning Officer, to do that Justice, with Expedition, which he was bound to do; and that the Use of Cheque Books being expressly given by Act of Parliament, at County Elcft ions, and Inspectors being usually appointed at Elections for Cities and Boroughs, and the Electors for the City and Liberty of Westminster being equal in Number to the Freeholders of most of the Counties in this Kingdom; jnd as Inspectors would be fruitless, without the use of Cheque Books, Sir George Vandeput, and several other Persons intitled to vote at the said Eieftion desired that they might have the Use of such Books; but that the High Bailiff (as appeared from the whole Tenor of his Behaviour during the Eieftion) having determined to return Lord Trentbam in all Events, as also to render the Eieftion, as much as possibly he could, subservient to his own lucrative Views, absolutely refused to apply for, or procure, the Parish Books, or permit any Cheque Books to be made use of, as the only effectual Method of prolonging the Eieftion, and thereby extorting Money from the Candidates, and rendering his own partial and corrupt Con-dust less liable to be observed upon, in order thereby to avoid the Justice and Censure of this House; and that, during the whole Course of taking the Poll, the High Bailiff having refused the Parish Books, or any other Evidence to be produced, when Objections were made to the Votes of particular Persons, in order to quiet the Parties who made such Objections, constantly assured them, that he intended to grant the Candidates a Scrutiny, after the Poll was taken; and that that would be the most proper Time to settle all Questions touching the Rights of the several Voters; and that he would go on, then, to take

as also to gain to himself a greater Power and Influence over the Election, and a better Opportunity <ff extorting Money from the Canvlidates, contrary to the Duty of his Office, and in manifest Defiance of all Law and Justice: And further setting forth, That great N umbers of idle and difTolute Persons, who were hired for the Purpose (One or more of the Ringleaders of which were then, if not (till, Chairmen, or otherwise in the Service of Lord frentbam, or his Friends), armed with Bludgeons, and other offenGve Weapons, did, in so outrageous a Manner, insult andabufe the Electors, that were distinguished as Voters on behalf of Sir George Vandeput, that they were thereby greatly deterred and obstructed from giving their Votes; and great Numbers of Persons, from thence, were readily admitted through the Church to the Hustings, to poll for Lord i'rentharh; whilst the lawful Voters, in the Interest of Sir George Vandepul were totally excluded from, and denied, such Accel's; and that the High Bailiff having, by his Behaviour during the Time of taking the Votes, rendered a Scrutiny absolutely necessary, there having, iri Effect, been no Poll properly taken at all; granted a Scrutiny upon closing of the Poll, in order, as he then declared, to do Justice to the Parties; he having, as he then said, admitted several Votes to be taken down, on a Confidence that a Scrutiny would be had, wherein Justice might and should be done, or to that Effect: And that, having thus procured a Scfii-tiny, the High Bailiff then artfully insinuated to the Candidates, that the Scrutiny would be attended with unavoidable Expence and Loss of Time to him, and gave them to understand, that he expected to be paid for the fame; and, under that Pretence, obliged them to depbfit large "Sums of Money in his Hands, and by that means extorted to the Amount of Four Guineas a Day from each of the said Candidates during the Scrutiny, which lasted upwards of Ninety Days; all which said Sums of Money, thus taken, were under the specious Pretence of making him a Satisfaction for his Trouble and Expence; though his real Expence (if any) was very inconsiderable; and that the High Bailiff, being determined from the Beginning to have a Scrutiny, as the only proper Time to exercise an arbitrary Power over the Poll and Election, without Cheque or Controul, during the whole Course of the Poll, industriously avoided (as far as he could) determining or giving his Judgment upon the Rights of Election, in order to reserve to himself the greater Liberty of varying the true and ancient Right, and introducing such new and pretended Rights, as, upon Irfpeftion of the Poll, privately by himself, he should find would belt serve the Interest of Lord *irentbam, and vary the true Majority of legal Votes; and that, for this End, after the Scrutiny was granted, the High Bailiff gave the Candidates and Eleftois to understand, that the previous Step necessary to be taken, would be to settle the several Rights of Election within the said City and Liberty, and, under that Pretence, he contrived that the ancient Rights of voting, which had never before been so much as questioned, but by the uniform Practice, not only of his Predeccffors in all former Elections, and by himself in former, nay, in the Course of this very Poll, had always been confirmed, and submitted to, should be litigated and disputed; and therein spent Eight Days,which put the Petitioners to a most heavy and burthensome Expence in examiningMul-titudes of Witnesses, who all confirmed those ancient Rights: And that the High Bailiff after this pretended Enquiry, or Scrutiny, into the Rights of voting, declared, Vol. z6.

and that, in particular the High Bailiff, during the Course of the Poll, intimated his Opinion to be, that such Inhabitants, whole Landlords had been rated to and paid the Parish Taxes, and who had paid an advanced Rent or Money to their Landlords equal to such Taxes, had virtually, and in Effect, paid the Taxes, and therefore ought to be considered as Inhabitants paying Scot arid Lot; Translation of the Treaty concluded and signed at Madrid, on the 5th of October, 1750, N. S.

Whereas, by the 16th Article of the Treaty of Aix la Chapelle, it has been agreed between their Britannick and Catholick Majesties, that the Treaty of the Afliento for the Commerce of Negroes, and the Article of the annual Ship for the Four Years of Non-Enjoyment, flvould be confirmed to Great Britain upon the same Foot, and upon the same Conditions, as they ought to have been executed before the lateWari and the respective Ambaffactors of their said Majesties having agreed, by a Declaration signed between them on the 44-ch o(June 1748, to regulate, at a proper Time and Place, by a Negotiation between Ministers named on each Side for that Purpose, the Equivalent which Spain should give, in Consideration of the Non-Erj6yment of the Years of the said Afliento of Negroes, and of the annual Ship, granted to Great Britain by the Tenth Article of the Preliminaries signed at Aix la Chapelle, on the 44th of April, 1748:

Their Britannick and Catholick Majesties, in order to fulfil the said Engagements of their respective MinisterF, and to strengtnen and perftCt more and more a iolid and lading Harmony bfiwien the Two Crowns, have agreed to make the prefern particular Treaty between themselves, without the Intervention or Participation of any Third Power, so that each of the contracting Parties acquires, by virtue of tfe Cessions which that Party makes, a Right of Compensation Irom the orher reciprocally 3 and they have named their Ministers Plenipotentiaries for that Purpose 3 viz. his Britannick Majesty, Benjamin Keene Esquire, his Minister Plenipotentiary to hi* Catholick Majesty 5 and his Catholick Majesty Don Joseph de Car-Vtijal and Lancaster, Miniller of State and Dean of his Council of State 3 who, after having examined the Points in question, have 2grecd upon the following Articles:

His Britannick Majesty yields to his Catholick Majesty his Right to the Enjoyment of the Afliento of Negroes, and of the annual Ship, during the Four Years ftipulatrd by the 16 th Article of the Treaty of Aix la Chapelle.

II.

His Britannick Majesty, in Consideration of a Compensation of One hundred Thousand Pounds Sterling, which his Catholick Majesty promises and engages td Cause to be paid, either ac Madrid or London, to the Royal Afliento Company, within the Term of Three Months ac latest, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of this Treaty, yields to his Catholick Majesty all that may be due to the said Company for Balance of Accounts, or arising in ahy Manner whatever from the said Atliemo, so that the said Compensation shall be efletrmed and looked upon as a full and entire Satisfaction on the Part of his Catholick Majesty 3 and shall extinguifft, from this present Time, for the future, and for ever, all Right, Precension, or Demand, which might be formed, in cor.sequence of the said Afliento or annual Ship, directly or indirectly, on the Part of his Britannick Majesty, or on that of the said Company.

in.

The Catholick King yields to his Britannick Majesty all his Prettnfions or Demands in consequence of the said Afliento and annual Ship, as well with regard to the Articles already liquidated, as to those which may be easy or difficult to liquidate, so that no mention can ever be made of them hereafter oh either Side.

IV.

His Catholick Majesty consents, that the British Subjects shall not be bound to pay higher or other Duties or upon other Evaluations for Goods, which they shall carry into or out of the different Ports of his Catholick Majesty, than those paid on the same Goods in the Time of Charles the Second, King of Spain, lei tied by the Cedulas and Ordinances of that King, or those of his Predecessors 3 and although the Favour or Allowance, called the Pie del Fardo, be not founded upon any Royal Ordinance, nevertheless his Catholick Majesty declares, wills, and ordains, that it shall be observed now, and for the future, as an inviolable Law 3 and all the above-mentioned Duties shall be exacted and levied now, and for the future, with the same Advantages and Favours to the said Subjects.

Y.

His Catholick Majesty allows the said Subjects to take and gather Salt in the Island of Tcrtudos, without any Hindrance whatsoever, as they did in the Time of the said King Charles the Second.

yI.

His Catholick Majesty consents, that the said Subjects shall not pay any-where higher or other Duties than those which his Catholick Majesty’s Subjects pay in the same Place.

VII.

His Catholick Majesty grants that the said Subjects shall enjoy all the Rights, Privileges, Franchises, Exemptions, and Immunities whatsoever, which they enjoyed before the last War, by virtue of Cedulas or Royal Ordinances, and by the Articles of the Treaty of Peace and Commerce, made at Madrid in 16675 and the said Subjects shall be treated in Spain in the same Manner as the most favoured Nation, and consequently no Nation shall pay less Duties upon Wool, and other Merchandizes, which they shall bring into or carry out of Spain by Land, than the said Subjects shall pay upon the same Merchandizes, which they shall oring in or carry out by Sea: And all the Rights, Privileges, Franchises, Exemptions, and Immunities, which shall be granted cr permitted, to any Nation whatever, shall also be granted and p rmitteo to the said Subjects: And his Brhannick Majesty consents that the same be granted and permitted to the Subjects of Spain, in his Britannick Majesty's Kingdoms.

V1U.

His Catholick Majesty promises to use all possible Endeavours on his Part to abolish all Innovations which may have been intioduced into Commerce, and to have them forborn for the future 5 his Britannick Majesty likewise promises to use all possible Endeavours to abolish all Innovations, and to forbear them for the future.

IX. Their

ix.

Their Britannick and Cathoflck Majesties confirm, by the present Treaty, the Treaty of Aix la Chapelle, and all the ocher ^Treaties therein confirmed, in all their Articles and Clauses, those Articles excepted which have been derogated from by the present Treaty, as like wife the Treaty of Commerce concluded ac Utrecht in 1713; those Articles excepted which are contrary to the present Treary,which shall be abolished and of no Force; and namely the Three Articles of the said Treaty of Utrecht, commonly called Explanatory.

X.

All the reciprocal Differences, Rights, Demands, and Pretensions which may have subsisted between the Two Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, in which no other Nation whatever has any Part, Interest, or Right of Intervention, being thus accommodated and extinguished by this particular Treaty, the Two said most Serene Kings engage themselves mutually to the punctual Execution of this Treaty of reciprocal Compensation, which shall be approved and ratified by their said Majesties, and the Ratifications exchanged in the Term of Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Day of its Signing, or sooner, if it can be done.

In Witness whereof, Wc the above-mentioned Ministers Plenipotentiaries, that is to say, Benjamin Keene Esquire, in the Name of his Britannick Majesty; and Den Joseph de Carvajal and Lancaster, in the Name of his Catholick Majesty; by virtue of our full Powers, which we have mutually communicated to each other, have signed these Present?, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be put thereto. Done at Madrid, the Fifth of October 1750, New Stile.

(L. S.) B. Keene. (L. S.) Joseph de Carvajal

Transtation of a Treaty between his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesses the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, on the One Part; and his most Serene Highness the Elector of Bavaria, on the other Part; concluded at Hanover on the -Hth of August T75°-

Whereas his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, and their High Mightiness, the Lords the Stares General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, on the One Part; and his most Serene Electoral Highness of Bavaria, on the other Part; did conclude, in the Month of July 1746, for the Term of Four Years, a Treaty of Friendship, good Understanding, and Subsidy, which was signed the 21st of the said Month, at Munich, by their respective Ministers; and whereof the Tranquillity of the Empire, the Preservation of its Imerefts, and the Support of its System, made a principal Object: And whereas the said Treaty did expire the 21st of the Month of July of tljis present Year, the said High contradling Parties, feeling themselves always animated with the same Sentiments of Friendship One towards the other, and with the same Desire for the Preservation of the Tranquillity of the Empire, and for the Confirmation of its System, have authorized their respective Ministers to set about so salutary a Work; that is to say, his Britannick Majesty 'Thomas Holies, Duke of Newcastle, Knight of the most Noble Order of the Garter, and One of his Principal Secretaries of State; their High Mightinesses the Lords the States General the Sieur Hop, Lieutenant-General of Horse in their Service, and their Envoy Extraordinary to his Britannick Majesty; and his most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria, the Sieur Joseph Xavier, Count of Hajlang, his Chamberlain and Counsellor of State, Grand Commander of his Order of St. George, and Minister Plenipotentiary to his Britannick Majesty; which Ministers aforesaid being provided with the necessary full Powers, after several Conferences, have agreed upon the following Articles:

A. 1750.

Article I.

There shall be a sincere Friendship and most strict Union between his said Majesty, their High Mightinesses, and his most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria, so that each of them shall look upon the Imerefts of the others as his own, and shall faithfully use his Endeavours to promote them as far as possible; and mutually to prevent and avert all Disturbance and Prejudice.

Article II.

In order to give his most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria a Proof of the good Dispofi tion of the High Maritime Powers towards him, they grant him an annual Subsidy of Forty thousand Pounds Srerling, amounting to Four hundred Forty thousand Florins, current Money of Holland, which (half be paid every Three Months at the Hague, without the least Diminution; viz. Two thirds on the Account of his Britannick Majesty, and One-third on the Account of their High Mightinesses; which Subsidy shall commence from the 21st Day of July iaft, the Day of the Expiration of the last Treaty, and shall continue as long as the present Treaty shall remain in Force; provided that the Proportion of the Subsidy, which is to be paid by his Britannick Majesty, shall be paid in England, if his most Serene Eledloral Highness desires it

Article III.

In consideration of the Subsidy specified in the preceding Article, his most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria shall keep up a Body of Six thousand Foot, in the same State, and upon the same Conditions, as well in relation to the Requisition for the March, and to the Pay during their actual Service, as with regard to the Diminution of the Subsidy, in case of the said actual Service, which were stipulated in the Convention between his Britannick Majesty and the Landgrave of Hejfe, on the 9th of May 1740; the Articles and Clauses of which Convention, that are applicable to the Three Points above-mentioned, shall be understood as inferred here.

Article IV.

His most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria, having the Honour to be One of the most considerable Members of the Empire, solemnly protests that he will not separate himself from the said Empire in any fort; and that his Troops shall not be employed in any Manner against his Imperial Majesty, or against the Empire.

Article V.

His most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria, being persuaded that the Desires and Wishes of his Britannick Majesty, Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, with relation to the Affairs of the German Empire, tend solely to the Common Good thereof, and to the Preservation of its System, and feeling himself animated with a Desire of co-operating thereto in the same Manner, does not hefi-tate to promise, that he will second, by the Votes to him belonging, as well at the General Diet of the Empire, as at* the Assemblies of the Eledloral College and of the Circles, the good Intentions and Opinions of his Britannick Majesty relating to the Affairs of the Empire; and with this View it is therefore reciprocally stipulated, that the Envoys and Ministers of his Britannick Majesty and most Serene Eledloral Highness of Brunswick Lunenburg, and of his most Serene Eledloral Highness of Bavaria, who shall meet each other at the said Assemblies, shall consult together in Confidence, and act in Concert, as far as shall be possible, in the Affairs of Consequence chat shall relate to the Interests of the Empire.

Article VI.

In case that his most Serene Eledloral Highness should be attacked or disturbed in his Dominions, by any Power whatsoever,in Resentment of this Treaty, the High Maritime Powers shall do their utmost to procure him Satisfaction from the Aggressor, for the Damage which shall have been done to him.

Article VII.

ThisTreaty shall continue in Force for the Space of Six Years, £0 be reckoned from the a ill of July, of this pre-1 o sent

4 Geo. IL i° Jatiuarii.

*5

sent Year: And if the high contrafting Parties shall afterwards be disposed to continue, prolong, or alter it, they shall give each other Notice thereof, and treat about it, Three Months before its Expiration.

Article VIII.

This Treaty shall be ratified by thfe aforesaid high cbh-tracting Parties respectively, in the Space of Four Weeks from the Day of the Date thereof, or sooner, if possible; and the Ratifications shall be exchanged here at Hanover.

In Witness whereof, we* the aforesaid Ministers, have made Three Instruments of this Treaty, of the same Tenor which we, by virtue of pur full Powers* have signed* and thereunto fixed the Seals of our Arms.

Done at Hanover, the \\th Day of August, *750. holies Newcastle (L. S.) Joseph Xavier,

Transiation of a Declaration signed by the Miniftef*s Plenipotentiary of the Empress Queen of Hungary land Bohemia and of the Elector of Bavaria. Hanover, August -H, 1750.

Whereas, by a Treaty of Friendship concluded this Day between his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Eledlorof krunswick Lunenburg, and their High Migh-tindies the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, on the one Part, and his most Serene Highness the Elector of Bavaria, on the other, it is stipulated. that his Laid Majesty, and their High Mightinefies* should pay to his said most Serene Electoral Highness of Bavaria, an annual Subsidy of Forty thousand Pounds Sterling, during the Space of Six Years: And whereas the Prolongation of the Term of the said Treaty, from Four Years, which were at first proposed, to Six, is chiefly intended to serve as a Satisfaction, and as an Equivalent, for the Pretensions of his said most Serene Electoral Highness of Bavaria, upon the Duchy of Mirandola, and the Marqui-fate of Concordia. And whereas her Majesty the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia acknowleges. That, in Justice, the high Maritime Powers aforesaid should not be charged with that Equivalent; we the underwritten Henry Hy acini he. Count of Nay and of Richecourt, Chamberlain to their Imperial Majesties, and John Werner de Vorfter, Imperial Aulick Councilor, Ministers Plenipotentiary of her Majesty the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bobema, do, by virtue of our full Powers, declare that One-fourth Part of the said Subsidy of Forty thousand Pounds Sterling, viz. Ten thousand Pounds Sterling, by the Year, shall be duly and punctually paid, without any Charges, every Three Months, at Augsburg, by her said Imperial Majesty Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, to the Order, and for the Use, of his said most Serene Ele&oral Highness of Bavaria, during the whole Term of Six Years, that the said Treaty is to continue in Force. And I the underwritten Joseph Xavier, Count of Haflang, Chamberlain and Counsellor of State of his most Serene Electoral Highness of Bavaria, Grand Commander of his Order of St. George, and his Minister Plenipotentiary to his Majesty the King of Great Britain, do, by virtue of my full Power, declare, that provided the said Payment shall be duly made on the Part of her Majesty the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, her said Imperial Majesty shall be discharged of all further Demands on the Part of his most Serene Elc&oral Highness of Bavaria, of an Equivalent for his Pretenflons upon the Duchy of Mirandola, and the Marquisate of Concordia; it being, nevertheless, to be understood, that all the other Pretensions, either of her Majesty the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, or of his most Serene Electoral Highness of Bavaria, which are founded upon the Treaties concluded between them, shall be reputed to remain in their full Force, with- out their being anywise altered by this Declaration. And I do accept the said Declaration; and, by virtue of my full Power, I do discharge his Britannick Majesty, and their High Mightinefies, aforesaid, of the said Fourth Part of the Subsidy stipulated to be paid by them: And I declare, That the Three other Fourths of this Subsidy, VOL. 26.

which remain, are all that is expected or required, by virtue of the said Treaty, signed by me this Day, with the Ministers of his said britannick Majesty, and of their High Mightinefies the States General.

This Declaration shall be ratified by the aforesaid high tontradfing Powers respectively, in the Space of Four Weeks from the Day of the Signature, or sooner, if possible; and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged here at Hanover.

In Witness whereof, we the aforesaid Ministers Plenipotentiary, have made Four Instruments of this Declaration, of the same Tenor, which, by virtue of our full Powers, we have signed* and have put the Seals of our Arms thereto.

Done at Hanover, the Day of August,

J&s Naviga- Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, of the non. several Counties of Middlesex, Surry, Bucks, Berks, Oxford,

Gloucester, and Wilts} whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and other Persons interfiled in the Navigation of the Rivers of Thames and Ifiss from the City of London, West ward, to the Town of Crick-lade, in the County of Wills, was referred, That the Commitrefc had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place ind afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table*' Where the same was read* and is as followed!; viz.

A. 1750.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act passed in the Twenty-first Year of King James the First, for making the River Thames navigable for< Barges, Boats, and Lighters, from the Village of Bercotf in the County of Oxon, unto the University and City of Oxon: And also.

An Act passed in the Third Year of his present Majesty, for reviving an Act made in the Sixth and Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act to prevent Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Wears upon the said River of Thames, Westward, and for ascertaining the Races of Water-Carriage upon the said River: And also.

Several subsequent Acts; by which the said last mentioned Act had been continued till the id Day of June 17$ 1, and from thence to the End of the then next Sefo lion of Parliament* were severally read:

Whereby it appeared, that several Regulations were made by the said Acts, in regard to the Navigation of the said River; and the Power of the Commissioners, by the said Acts appointed, was extended as far as the Town of Cricklade, in the said County of Wilts.

Then the Committee examined Mr. Wm. Peace; who informed the Committee,

That he was a Barge-Master, and Inhabitant of the Towh of Reading; and has been employed in navigating Barges from thence to London for 40 Years last patl; during which time, the Banks in several Parcs of the River have beetl washed away; insomuch, that he knows several Places which w ere (in the Memory of the Witness) used for Paths for the Horses, and are now Ten Foot under Water: Thisobliges the Navigators to takefrelh Ground for their Towing-Paths; and the Owners of such Ground force them to pay what Sums they think proper, for the Liberty of Towing:

That he apprehends such Decay of the Banks is to be attributed to the Sett of the Stream, and not to the Track of the Horses, or Towing of the Barges.

That the Owners of Locks have rendered the Naviga- tion more dangerous, by letting the Sills, or Bottom of the Lock, Where the Tackle is fixed, in order to Unit? it, lie too high; and from not (hutting or drawing their Locks in a reasonable time:

That the Witness had a Barge in great Danger of sinking, about Six Weeks ago, by running against the Sill of a Lock; by which Ihe broke off all her Steerage: And other Barges have received considerable Damage at the same Place:

That the Lock, where this Damage was done, had been newly laid, and was placed higher up the Stream; and by that means was more prejudicial to the Navigation than formerly; though it had been always bad.

But, being aiked the Question, lie said, That the placing the Lock in <that manner was convenient for the adjacent Mills.

He further said. That the Barges now in Use draw no more Water than those -used 40 Years ago; that those Barges were as wide as the present, but not quite To long; and that the largest of the modern ones would carry 300 Quarters of Malt more than those Formerly used:

That the Barges draw four Foot Water; but by putting up what they call Wash-Boards, they can load them so as to draw Two Inches more; and he believes it has always been the Practice to put up Wash-boards; that he had them up at the time he received the Damage, as aforesaid; nor does he think the Navigation lafe without them; but at that time his Barge did not draw more than Four Foot Water; nor was it his largest Barge, he having One that would carry 1,400 Quarters of Malt; whereas that which was damaged, would carry no more than 900:

That 10 Quarters of Malt weigh about Twenty-Five hundred Weight; so that the largest Barges will carry 3,500 Weight, and are 125 or 126 Foot long, or thereabouts; but the length of the Barge does not render the Navigation more dangerous; on (he contrary, he appre-6 / hsnds

bends a short Barge to be in greater Danger than a long one:

That the Navigators pay greater Prices for passing the Locks, than formerly; that at the First Lock on the Thames at Sunning, the full-sized Vessels, which used to pay no more than j s. 6 d. now pay I2J. 6 d. and the idler Vessels in Proportion; that there has been nothing done to the Lock, to cause this increase of the Duty, it being rather in a worse Condition than formerly: But tinlel’s the Navigators will comply with the Demands of the Occupiers, the Matters of the Locks won’t supply them with Flalhes of Water in the dry Seasons.

Being asked the Question, he laid. That the Bargemen had lometimes sent their Servants to pen and draw the Locks, on such Occasions; but that those Proceedings were unwarrantable.

He further said. That a Barge would often lie aground, and other Barges running foul of her, would frequently obstruct the Navigation of the River; but if, when there 'arc many Barges in Company, they were obliged to keep in a right Line, one after another, it would prevent that Inconvenience:

That the Price of Water-Carriage is already advanced i s. for everyTwenty-five hundred Weight; whichisaboue 10 per Cent.: And if the said Act should not be continued, andfomefurtner Regulations made, it will be greatly detrimental to the Navigation of the said River.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for the better carrying on and regulating the Navigation of the Rivers of Thames and Isis, from the City of London, Wtftward to the Town of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts: And that Mr. Pcwney, Sir James Dashwood, Sir George Oxenden, the Lord Barrington, Mr. Bathurst, Mr. Moreton, and Mr. Pye, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of Sherard Wimberley, Post-Master of Post Witham, in the County of Lincoln, and others, whose Names are thereunto set, being Inhabitants, Land-Owners, an<d Occupiers of Land there, was presented to the House, and read* setting forth. That by virtue of an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, an Act for repairing the Road between Stamford and Grantham, in the County of Lincoln; alleging, that the same is the ancient and great Northern Road, arid common Post Road, the Commissioners therein named are impowered to erect Turnpikes, and take certain stipulated Tolls of all Traveller?, Carriages, and Cattle, passing through the fame, towards the Repair of the said Road; and to the End that no Dispute might arise, touching what Part of the Road, intended to be repaired, should be first amended, the Trustees were to order and direct the Road, from a certain Place or Close called Butchers Piece, on Wish am Common, and so through the said Common to the North End of Stretton Lane (being the most ruinous), to be repaired in the first place; and after such Part of the Road shall be sufficiently amended, the Trustees, cr any Seven or more of them, are impowered and required to order and direct the Money, arising by the said Act, to be laid out and applied in repairing the other Parts of the said Roads; and that the Money arising from such Toils has not only hitherto been insufficient for the Repair of the said ancient and great Northern Road, and common Post Road, but even fallen short for a sufficient Repair of that Part of it only from Butchers Piece, on Witham Common, to Stretton Lane\ and that Pattengers travelling with Coaches, Chaises, or on Horseback, go daily upon the Common both Winter and Summer, equally the same as before any Turnpikes were erected, to the great Loss and Damage of the Petitioners, and all ocher the Inhabitants of Post Witham aforesaid; Report on the Sir William Tenge, according to Order, reported from Contempt of the Committee, appointed to consider and report to the Mr. Murray. House, what Methods may be proper to be taken by the House, in relation to the Contempt of the Honourable Alexander Murray Esquire; who being, in pursuance of a Resolution of this House, brought to the Bar of this House, to receive his Sentence there upon his Knees; and who, being by Mr. Speaker directed to kneel, refused to be upon his Knees, as required by the said Refo-. lution 3 That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s TableWhere the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appears to your Committee, upon searching the Journals of this House, that many Persons, as well Strangers, as Members, have either, in pursuance of the ancient Practice of this House, or by special Order, been required to receive their Sentence, and in feme Cafes, their Charge, on their Knees, at the Bar (Instances of which appear in the Cafes referred to in the Margin*); and chat r.o Person, as far as your Committee can discover, hath ar any time refused so to do, except David Jenkins, who being, according to Order, 21 Feb. 1647, brought to the Bar by the Serjeant at Arms, to answer to his Charge, and being required to kneel, did absolutely refuse.

Your Commitre observe, that the House hath, by a Variety of Punishments, enforced Obedience to their Orders; and that a Breach of Privilege, committed in one Session of Parliament, hath been, and may be, punished in another; and that, when an Order of the House, made in one Session, hath been difubeyed in the Whole, or in Part (even in Cafes of Contempt, much less injurious to the Honour of the House than the present, such as Absconding or Refusing to pay Fees, &c.) the same Order hath been renewed in the next Session.

Your Committee also observe, that it is a {landing Order of the House, made 4th April 1707, That when any Person, ordered to be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, shall either abscond from Justice, or, having been in Custody, shall refuse to pay the just Fees, in either of cnefc Cafes, the Order for Commitment shall be renewed the Beginning of the next Session of Parliament; in consequence of which (landing Order, many Persons were ordered to be taken into Custody in the xufxt Session.

And your Committee observe, that this Handing Order hath lince been executed in several Instances.

Your Committee further observe, that the most usual Method taken by the House, to enforce Obedience to their Orders, against Persons already ordered to be taken into Custody, or to be committed to Prison, hath been by adding to the Severity of their Restraint.

A remarkable Instance of whicty appears in the same of John Trenche, the Warden of the Fleet, who, for his ob-

ftinate Refusal to deliver the Body of Sir Thomas Shirley, a Member of this House, detained a Prisoner in the Fleefl was committed close Prisoner to the Tower* 8th May 1604: Being sent for by the House, was by Mr. Speaker, by Order of the House, terrified with the Prison of Little Eaje\ and (the House finding him (till perverse) received this Judgment (1 1 May 1604) " That, as he did increase his Contempt, fothe House thought fic to increase his Punishment, and that he should he committed to the Prison called Little Eaje, within the Tower f from which Place the House (after having taken effectual Care that theirjudg-ment should be put in Execution 12th and 14th May 1604) did not release him until 17th May 1604, after Sir Thomas Shirley was delivered, and until he (the Warden) had been an humble Suitor to the House for his Liberty, and had expreflfed his Sorrow for his Offence, and his Hope that, upon this Acknowledgment of his Fault, the House would be pleased to pardon his Error, and receive him into their Grace and Favour.

After which Application so made, he was ( t; of May 1604) ordered to be brought to the IJoufe, and acknow-lege his Offence at the Bar, and humbly pray Favour of the House upon his Knees; and in the mean time was ordered to be freed from the Dungeon called Little Eaje.

On the 19th of May 1604, being called in, he, on his Knees, at the Bar, confessed his Error and Presumption; and professed, that he was unfeignedly lorry that he had so offended this House.

Upon which Submission, Mr. Speaker, by Direction of the House, pronounced his Pardon and Discharge.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee humbly fub-mit to the Consideration of the House, that it highly concerns the Dignity and Power of this House to vindicate its Authority in this Instance; and though your Committee cannot but oblrrve, that, notwithstanding the additional Restraint which the House hath already laid Mr. Murray under, he hath not yet thought fit to make any Submission: Your Committee desire Leave further to propose, that, in Indulgence to him, he be again brought to the Bar, by Order of this House; and that, in Conformity to the Precedent before-mentioned, Mr. Speaker be directed to put him in Mind of the Greatnels of his Contempt, and of his continued Contumacy; and to acquaint him, that if he doth not submic forthwith to the Order of the House, such further Punishment will be inflicted upon him, as this House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Doctor Lamond do attend this House \ upon this Day Seven-night.

Ordered, That Mr. Cooke, the Apothecary who was admitted to resort to the said Mr. Murray in Newgate, do attend this House upon this Day Seven-night.

Stamford, Sir John Cust reported from the Committee, to whom &c. the Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Road. passed in the Twelfth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for repairing the Road between Stamford and Grantham, in the County of Lincoln, and for making the same more effectual, is committed, and to whom the Petition of Sherurd IVimberley, P oft-Matter of Post- With aw, in the County of Lincoln, and others, whose Names are thereunto set, being Inhabitants, Land-Owners, and Occupiers of 1 and there, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him ro report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners examined Mr John Wimberley, who informed the Committee, That the Road through Post-Witham is, and always has been, the Poll Road; and the Poll Office has always been kept at that Town; that Six Mails come there every Week, Three of which arrive in the Night; and the Badness of the Road makes the Carriage of them both hazardous and difficult; that the Inhabitants of Post-Witham have endeavoured to amend the said Road; and, besides a yearly Rate for that Purpose, have constantly performed Four Days Srarute- Work out of Six, upon the said Road (being obliged to perform the other two Days Statute-Work on the Turnpike-Road); and finding themselves unable effectually to repair the fame, they desire that some Part of the Toils, to be granted by the aforesaid Bill', may be appropriated towards the Repair of the Road mentioned in the Petition.

Being alked, What Sum he thought would be necessary’ ro repair the said Road, and whether, if such Sum were to be detiufted out of the present foils, the Remainder would not be insufficienc to repair the Roads already directed to be repaired; lie laid, he was no'Judge of that; having never made any Calculation of the Eixpence of amending either the one Road or the other.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred back to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

And the said Petition was read; alleging, That the Petitioners think it their indcfpenfible Dity, to represent the Mischiefs which they apprehend will flow from the Bill, depending in the House, for a general Naturalization of foreign Protestants, if pa fled into a Law; and that the Petitioners, as Citizens of London, will be particularly affected by such a Law, in the Decrease, if not total Loss, of the Duties of Package, Scavage, Portage, and Balliage, of the Goods of foreign Merchants, granted by many Royal Charters, and confirmed by several Acts of Parliament; and expressing the Apprehensions of the Petitioners, that a general Naturalization of foreign Protestants is more likely to increase the Poverty, than make any Addition to the Wealth, of this Nation; for that neither the Rich, nor the Industrious, amongst them, need any such Inducement 5 as the latter never want Encouragement, nor the former the very Privilege in question, when they apply to Parliament for it: And further alleging, that a like Law being attempted in the Reign of the late King William, it was rrjefted, on such national Considerations, as is presumed can new escape the Attention, nor lose the Regard, of this House; and that when the Experiment was actually made, by paffmgaLaw for that Purpose, in the Reign of the late Queen Anne, it was found so detrimental to the publidk Interest, that it was shortly afterwards repealed, and not without some Reflections on the Mischiefs it had produced; and that the Petitioners apprehend the fame, if tiot greater, Mischiefs, may accrue by this intended Indulgence to Foreigners; who, being unacquainted with the legal Rights /ind Liberties peculiar to the British People, and though Protestants, yet differing from the established Church of this Nation, and bred under arbitrary Government, may not only want that Zeal and Affection necessary for the Support of our Civil and Religious Rights, but may be more easily tempted to invade them: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, Until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

and that great Part of the said Road between Tadcaster and Halton Dyal aforesaid, from the Narrowness thereof in several Places, and/from the Nature of the Soil, and by reason of the many heavy Carriages passing through the fame, is become very deep and ruinous, and, in some Seasons of the Year, impassable for Wheel-Carriages, and dangerous for Travellers; and the same cannot, by the ordinary Course and Method authorized and appointed by the Laws now in being, be effectually amended, and kept in good Repair; and alleging, that the Gentlemen, Owners, and Occupiers of Lands, lying near, and contiguous to, the said Roads, and the Merchants and Trades-men inhabiting and residing in that Part of the Country, are satisfied and convinced, that the said Roads from Selby and Tadcaster respectively, to the Town of Leeds aforesaid, might be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, in case competent Tolls and Duties were to be granted, and properly collected and applied, and communicated to both the said Roads; and that the Repairing and Amending of the said Roads would tend greatly to the Improving of the Trade and Commerce, and to the Eafe and Benefit of the Inhabitants of that Country: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem

A Petition of Samuel Baker was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Daniel Huger Esquire, of South Carolina, is now, and long has been, possessed of Eight thousand Pounds Old South Sea Annuities, (landing in his own Name, the Dividends for which the Petitioner has constantly received, by virtue of a Letter of Attorney; and that immediately after the passing of the Vote of this House of the 29th of November 1749, whereby such of the Publick Creditors as should, on or before the 28th Day of February 1749, signify their Consent to the Terms then proposed, were not to be liable to be redeemed till after the 25th December 1757, the Petitioner applied to the South Sea Company, in behalf of the said Mr. Huger, that he might be a Subscriber to the Terms then proposed; but as the Petitioner had only Power from Mr. Huger to receive the Dividends, he could not be admitted thereto $ and that Mr. Huger being informed of the said Vote, which the Petitioner had transmitted him by the very first Opportunity, he signified to the Petitioner his Desire to be admitted to the Terms thereof; and at the same time sent a Memorial to the Lords of his Majesty’s Treasury, requeuing the fame, and annexed thereto an Affidavit, purporting, that he, the said Mr. Huger, had no Knowkge of the said Terms, until the 3d Day of April last, when he drew up and signed the said Memorial; and that the Petitioner laid the said Memorial and Affidavit before the Lords of his Majesty’s Treasury; to which the Petitioner has received for answer, that they can give Mr. Huger no Relief: And therefore (forasmuch as Mr. Huger, had he been in Great Britain, would have accepted the Terms offered the publick Creditors, and did actually signify his Desire to be admitted thereto, so soon as he knew thereof), praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the said Eight thousand Pounds Old South Sea Annuities, belonging to, and (landing in the Name of, Dairiel Huger Esquire, may have the Benefit of the Offer made the Annuitants, by the Vote of the House of 29th November 1749; or that the House will grant such other Relief, as they shall fee meet.

A Petition of the Merchants of London, trading to his Colonial Bill* Majesty’s Colony of Rhode Island, whose Names are oi Credit* thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and of many of the most considerable of the Inhabitants of the said Colony, was presented to the House, and read; alleging,

That the Currency, or Medium of Commerce of a Country, being the Standard and Measure by which the Worth of all Things bought and sold is estimated and determined, it ought to be fixed invariably; otherwise Property can neither be ascertained nor secured, by any Plan or Method whatsoever; and setting forth. That the Currency of the Government of the Colony of Rhode Island \s so far from being fixed, that it has funk in its Value above One-half within these last Seven Years; whereby the Petitioners, and all the other Creditors of the Colony, have been greatly defrauded; and all those who reside in the said Colony, whose Effects or Estates have confided in Money, or Bills of Publick Credit, so called, amongst whom are Numbers of Widows and Orphans, have been grievously injured, oppressed, and almost ruined; and that the said Colony of Rhode Island hath now outstanding the Sum <^525,335/. in Bills of Publick Credit, emitted at several times, partly upon Loan, and partly to supply the Colony Treasury; and that the Sum upon Loan is 390,000l. the Value of which, at the Times of issuing, was 78,111/. Sterling, and the present Sterling Value is but 35,445/. as appears by a particular State thereof, to the said Petition annexed; and further alleging, that the Bills emitted to supply the Treasury, by Acts of Assembly, ought to be funk, or drawn in by a Tax; but that the Government of the said Colony hath hitherto delayed the Execution of these Acts, no Tax having yet been levied for that Purpose:

And further setting forth, That several Petitions for a new Bank, or another Emission of Paper Bills of Publick Credit, have been lately preferred to the present General Assembly of the said Colony, and the House of Deputies there, though a Number of Petitions, from the most considerable Inhabitants of the said Colony, were presented against it; and the same were strongly opposed by some of the Deputies in the said House, as being totally unne-ceflary, and in no respect wanted, as tending to depreciate greatly the large Quantity of old Bills then outstanding; and as the same might be destructive to the Privileges and Interestof the Colony, and subject them to the Royal Displeasure; notwithstanding all which, and notwithstanding the Address of this House to his Majesty, in the Year 1740, in relation to the large and frequent Emissions of Paper Currency in the Bricifh Plantations in America, and the Royal Pleasure signified thereon to the Governor of Rhode Island, by the then Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations; whereby they were acquainted, that his Majesty, in pursuance of the said Address of this House, had sent circular Instructions to the several Colonies, more immediately under his Government, not to pass any more Bills for the issuing of Paper Money, without a Clause inferred therein (as proposed by the said Address) to suspend the Execution till his Majesty’s Pleasure should be signified thereupon; and were at the same time admonished and advised to pay all due Regard to his Majesty’s Intentions, and to the Sense of this

A Petition of the Mayof, Aldefmen, Sheriffs, Citizens, Uncofo and Commonalty, of the City of Lincoln, in Com- Small Dcbl,< mon-Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the City of Lincoln is an ancient Corporation, and a County within itself, of considerable Extent; and having navigable Rivers to the Towns of Hull and Boston, carries on a Trade to those Parts; and that great Numbers of Artificers, and Handicraft People, are employed within the said City, and County of the said City, who cannot support themselves without Credit; and great Numbers of Dealers, from the adjacent Counties, attend the Fairs and Markets held in the said City, and rent Stalls therein, and seek their Livelihood; by vending their Wares and Merchandizes in the said City, and from thence are obliged to give Credit to many of the poor Inhabitants and Refiants within the said City; and that the said Artificers, and Handicraft People, are frequently put to great Difficulties, irt obtaining Credit; and the Dealers, who frequent the Fairs and Market^ lie under great Discouragement, from giving Credit for (mail Sums to the poor Inhabitants and Refiants within the said City, and Liberties thereof; by reason that many Persons, obtaining such Credit, evade the Payment of their just Debts, presuming on the Expence and Delay which attend the Recovery thereof, being confined to the ftrifl Rules of die Common Law; and suggesting, that the Petitioners apprehend that the giving of such Persons as enconirage the said Artificers, and Handicraft People, and such Dealer* and others, an easy nd speedy Method for recovering their just Debts, at a small Expence, will greatly tend to the promoting Industry, supporting useful Credit, and be of great Utility to the said City: And praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the said City, and County of the said City, and the Liberties thereof.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Bitu. Tradesmen, Householders* Shopkeepers, and Refiants* within the City of Lincoln, and County of the said City, whose Names afe thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others inhabiting within the said City, and Liberties thereof, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, in the course of their Dealings, frequently advance Money, and give Credit to the poor Artificers and Manufacturers, who seek a Livelihood within the said City, who would often be otherwise subject to great Distresses, and totally unable to carry on their different Occupations; and that the Petitioners very often suffer great Lofies, by reason that many Persons decline the Payment of the Debts they contract, as the Petitioners cannot obtain the Recovery thereof unless by due course of Law; which hath been found of little Advantage to the Creditors, and greatly burthen* feme to the poor Debtors; and alleging. That if *' proper Court of Judicature should be creeled for the Recovery of small Debts in a summary way, it would be of great Service to the said Artificers and Mami-fadurers, and many other industrious poor Persons, who, by having their Wants timely relieved, by finding Credit, might be preserved from utter Ruin and Destruction:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the said City, and County of the said City, and Liberties thereof; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

Honiton Ar- A Petition of the Persons, whose Names are thereunto

rear of Taxes, subscribed, on behalf of themselves and others, being great Sufferers by the late Fire in the Town and Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon, was presented to jthe House, and read ? setting forth, That on Sunday the 19th Day of July 1747, a hidden and most dreadful Fire happened in the Town and Borough of Honittn aforesaidi whereby great Part of the said Town was burnt down, which bccafioned a great Deficiency both in the Land Tax, House-Tax, and Window-Tax, within the said Town and Parish; and that a great many of the said Houses, which were burnt down, are not yet rebuilt, and many of those that are built are under some Mortgage or Mortgages, or some other Incumbrance, but notwithstanding which are liable to be rated to the Land Tax, Church, and Poor, and have been so rated ever since the said Fire; but that this House, upon a former Petition prefenced to them, commiserating the unhappy Circumstances of the Petitioners, remitted their Land Tax, and House and Window-Tax, from Midftummer 1747 to Christmas 1748; and that from Christmas 1748 to Lady-day 1751, there will be due and in Arrear for the Land Tax the Sum of £.128. 14J. o d. and for the House and Window-Tax, for the farqe Time, the Sum of £.31. 5s. 3d. as appears by the Schedule to the said Petition annexed, which the Petitioners are not well able to pay, for the Reasons before-mentioned: And therefore praying, That the House will take the unhappy Circumstances of the Petitioners into Consideration, by once more commiserating their great Calamity and Sufferings, and by ordering a Clause in such Bill, as the House may think most proper, whereby the Petitioners may be forgiven home to Lady-day 1751; and alluring the House, that the Petitioners will not again, upon this Occasion or Misfortune, any further trouble the House, but will, for the present Concdlion, be extremely thankful.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1751, is committed.

Ordered, That it he an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to receive a Clause or Ciaufes for the Relief of the Petitioners, as to the Arrears of Land Tax, and House and Window Taxes, as desired in the said Petition.
