Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom the Iflingtoa Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and other Inhabi- Church, tants, of the Parish of Saint Mary Ifltngton, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame* as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as foftoweth; viz.

To prove what is alledged in the said Petition, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. John Lane, Mr. Thomas Burton, Mr. Thomas Meek, and Mr. John Benton; who, being severally examined, said, That the Church of Saint Mary Ifltngton is an ancient Fabrick, and the Petitioners have for many Years past, been at a continual expence in repairing and keeping up thcChurch; and the said Mr. Benton{who wasChurch* warden of the said Parish in the Year 1748) further gave Evidence, that the Repairs of that Church in that Year amounted to 50/. and upwards.

And, in order to prove the Condition of the said Church and Tower, the Petitioners called

Mr. Benjamin Tinibrell, Mr. James Steere, and Mt-Geof-ge Ufford, Surveyors; who were, by an Order of Vestry of the Parish, iappointed to survey the Church and Tower, as to the Condition thereof; and they being severally examined, laid, That they did, in October last, view and examine the Condition of the said Church and Tower; and found the Walls of the Church out of an Upright and very ruinous, and some Part of the Walls «were Eighteen Inches out of an Upright; and that the Timber of the Roof is decayed and extremely bad, and the Pavement of the Church is very much under the Surface of the Ground and Road adjoining to the Church-yard. And the Witnesses further said, that the Church is not capable of being repaired, and should have been pulled down many.

Years ago; and that it is extremely dangerous for any Person to attend Divine Service therein.

And the same Witnesses being examined, as to the Condition of the Tower of the Church, said, it was not so feeble as to be in immediate Danger of falling; yet it is necessary' the same should be taken down and rebuilt at the same Time the Church is rebuilt, in regard the same will be buried in respect to the new Church; that the Bond Timber will not hold; and that no. substantial Work can be made in rebuilding the said Church unless the Tower be likewise rebuilt.

The Witnessfes last nailed being asked, What the Expence of rebuilding the said Church and Tower would amount to ? they said, That the Whole would amount to 7,000l. or thereabouts.

And, upon the whole, it appeared to the Committee, That the said Church is in a very ruinous and decayed Condition; and that there is a Necelfity for rebuilding the fame.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Parishioners of the Parish of Saint Mary IJling-ton, in the County of Middlesex, to rebuild the Church of the said Parish: And that Mr. Cooke, Mr. Lowndes, Sir William Beauchamp Proctor, Mr. West, Mr. Willes, and Mr. Gray, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Foreign Pro- A Petition of the several Merchants, Traders, and :estants Nat. others, residing in or near the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Increase of People being the most certain Means of advancing the Wealth and Trade of a Nation, the Petitioners have, with the greatest Satisfaction, observed, by the Votes of this House, that a Bill hath been brought into Parliament for

a General Naturalization of Foreign Protestants; and alleging, that the Petitioners have been by long Experience thoroughly convinced, that the passing of the said Bill into a Law will be of the greatest Utility to this Nation, as it hath a natural Tendency to increase the Number of Manufacturers, and reduce the Price of Labour, whereby the Merchants of this Kingdom will be enabled to export the Manufactures of this Country to foreign Markets cheaper, and in greater Quantities, than they have been able to do, by reason that this Nation is under-worked, and consequently under-fold, by foreign Manufacturers: And therefore praying the House, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

The Names subscribed to the said Petition were also read.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for naturalizing foreign Protestants be read a Second time.

and that a very considerable Trade in striped and chequered Linen Goods, made mostly of Irish Yarn, and manufactured in the said Towns and Parishes of Manchester and Wigan, and Parts adjacent, hath for many Years last past been carried on and flip-ported by the Petitioners, and others concerned in that Manufactory, and large Quantities of such striped and chequered Goods of the Value of Six Pence, and not exceeding the Value of Twelve Pence, per Yard, have been yearly exported to the British Colonies and Plantations, and other foreign Parts, without the Aid of the said Bounties, which do not extend to any Linens exported which are striped or chequered; and that a Duty of One Half-penny per Pound is laid by the Parliament of Ireland upon all Linen Yarn exported out of that Kingdom, amounting to 5/.per Cent.oi thereabouts,upori an Average, Which Duty the Petitioners are the less able to bear, forasmuch as the Expence of Factorage, and bringing thdr Yarn from Ireland, is a further Charge of 5 /. per Cent. at the lead, upon the Yarn bought there, which other Manufacturers of Linen Goods are not liable to; and that, by the Aid of the said Bounties, and by the Encouragement given from the Lineri Board in Ireland, to their Manufacturers of coarse Linen Cloth, they are enabled to give, and do now give, higher Prices for Yarn than the Petitioners, under the Disadvantages before set forth, can afford to give; and that the Petitioners, finding a sensible Decay in their Trade, will be obliged to cease from making several Articles in the Linen Way, which have hitherto contributed very greatly to the Employment of the many Poor Families in that populous Country, and have been generally allowed to makeup a valuable Branch of Trade, that may, as the Petitioners apprehend, fall into the Hands of the French, or other Foreigners, unless some Method is taken by Parliament to ease the Petitioners, with respect to the above-mentioned Disadvantages they lie under in providing Yarn from Ireland, and for the Encouragement of the Exportation of striped and chequered LinenGoods manufactured in this Country: And therefore praying the House, to take the P remits into Consideration; and to give such Relief therein as the same of the Petitioners requires, and as to the House shall seem meet.

so that the Passage through the said River will, in all Probability, be entirely loft in a little Time, or rendered so dangerous, that few or none will venture to pass through the fame; and that the said Fords are the great and common high Road leading from the Towns of Uvet poole, Qrmjkirk, and other South-weft Parts of the said County Palatine, unto the Towns of Preston, Lancaster, and other the North and North-weft Parts of the same County, and so on to Kendal, Carliftle, and to Norib Britain, which Road is greatly tiled, and through which many Land Carriages pals; and that the Petitioners conceive, that the only Method of keeping and preserving a convenient and safe Passage over the said River, will be by erecting a publick County Bridge over the said River, between the said Townships of Preston, and Penwortham, near a Place called the Fifth Houfte, where there is a good and firm Foundation for a Bridge; but that although the erecting of such a Bridge will be of general Advantage to the said County, andofgreat Benefit to the Persons travelling that Road, and, in all Probability, will preserve the Lives of many of his Majesty’s Subjects, yet the said Bridge cannot be erected, or Money raised for that Purpose, or for the Repair of the fame, without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That a Bill may be brought in, for erecting a publick County Bridge over the said River, at such Place as shall be thought most convenient, and for raising Money for that Purpose, by such Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

And it further appeared to your Committee, That on the said Day Alexander Stewart Esquire, proposed to take a Lease of the Estate, as described in the said Particular, for the Term of Three Lives and Sixty-one Years, to commence from the ift Day of November 1755, at the yearly Rent of 420/. And it likewise appeared to your Committee, That the Company are willing and desirous to carry the said Agreement into Execution, and Mr. Stewart is willing to accept the said Lease, and pay the Fine; but as the Trustees named in the said Deeds refuse to act, and the said Act only authorizes the Company to demise and lease the Premises in Ireland, so contracted for as aforesaid, for Sixty-one Years in Possession, or for Sixty-one Years in Possession, and for the Lives of any Three Persons, and the Life of the longer Liver of them, it is apprehended, that the Contraft and Agreement, made with Mr. Stewart, cannot be carried into Execution, nor a good Lease made to him of the Premises so contracted for, unless the Power of leafing be explained, amended, and rendered more effectual.

And your Committee observe. That the Power granted to the Company by the said Act, for letting their Estate in Long Acre upon building and repairing Leases, is defective; and as their other Estates in the City of London, and County of Middlesex, comprised in the said Deeds, confilt chiefly in Houses, many of which are out of Repair, and others require to be rebuilt, it would be for the Benefit of the said Estates that the Company should he enabled not only to grant Leases for Twenty-one Years, but also to grant repairing Leases for Forty-one Years, and building Leases for Sixty-one Years, as Occasion shall require, without taking any Fine for the same; but the Powers given by the said Act are not sufficient for that Purpose.

That by an Account produced to your Committee, it appeared, That the managing the said Trust Estates, for the Benefit of their Annuitants, and keeping the Variety of Accounts of and relating thereto, is necessarily attended withaconsiderable Expence, which the Company are not able to defray any other ways than out of the Rents and Profits of the respective Estates; but are very willing to accept of such Allowance in respect thereof, as shall be from time to time, annually settled and agreed to at an Assembly of their Annuitants and Creditors, to be held, pursuant to publick Notice in the Gazette, for that Purpose; which cannot be effected without the Authority of Parliament.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it will be for the Benefit of the Annuitants and Creditors of the said Company, to enable the Petitioners to confirm and make effectual the Agreement they have made with Alexander Stewart Esquire, for the Lease of their Irjftj Estate.

Creditors to explain and amend the said Act of the lift Year of his present Majesty, with respect to the Powers of granting Leases of their respective Estates in the City of London, and County of Middlesex, which are comprised in the respective Deeds of the 3d and 4th of October 1699, and of the ift and 2d of June 1741.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a reasonable Sum be allowed the Company, to defray the necessary Charges of the Execution of the several Trusts reposed, and intended to be reposed, in them.

That the Road from Tadcaster, over Brambam Moor, through Kidhall-Lane, over Winn Moor, and through Sea^ croft to Leeds, is Part of the High Road from York to Leeds, and between which Two last mentioned Places a great Trade is carried on, and which falls into the High Road from Selby to Leeds, at a Place called Halton Byal, Two Miles from Leeds; that the said Road between Tadcaster and Halton Byal, is in many Places lo narrow, that Two Carriages cannot pass; and, by reason of the Nature of the boil, and the many heavy Carriages passing the fame, it is become very deep and ruinous, and dangerous for Travellers; and that the same cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, by the Methods appointed by the Laws now in being.

Mr. John Gibjon, being examined, said, He had surveyed the Road from Tadcaster to Halton Byal; and confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Edmund Lodge, with regard to the said Road.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, Foreign Proof the Borough of Thetford, in the Counties of Norfolk testants Nat and Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; expressing the Apprehensions of the Petitioners, That the Bill depending in the House, for the general Naturalization of foreign Protestants, if passed into a Law, will be more likely toincrease the Poverty, than add to the Wealthy of this Nation; for that neither the Rich, nor the Industrious amongst them, need any such Inducement; and representing to the House, That a like Law being attempted, in the Reign of the late King William, it was rejected, on such national Considerations, as is presumed can never escape the Attention, nor lose the Regard, of this House;. and that when the Experiment was actually made, by passing a Law for that Purpose, in the Reign of the late Queen Anne, it was found so detrimental to the Publick Incereft, that it was afterwards repealed, and not without some Reflections on the Mischiefs it had produced; and that the Petitioners apprehend the fame, if not greater Mischiefs, may accrue by this intended Indulgence to Foreigners: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Southwell reported from the Cdiiimittee, to whom Champion’s the Petition of William Champion, of the City of Bristol\ Manufacture Merchant,was referred. That thfe Committee had examined 0 ?cltcr,( the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them* to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appeared to your Committee, That the Petitioner had closely applied himself, for a great Part of his Lifej to the Study df Mineral Productions, and Metalick Operations; and he finding, that the supplying of Toutonege, commonly called Spelter, depended chiefly upon the Importation thereof from the East Indies, wherfcby the same was rendered a fluctuating Commodity, and the Persons making use thereof in their Manufactures, were frequently disappointed and distressed, and the Manufacturers embar-tasted from the exccfiive Prices the Ingrossers, at Times, advanced it to, particularly in the Year 1731, when Spelter got up to so high in Price as 260/. per Ton; whereupon the Petitioner tried for a Discovery of the Arc and Mystery of making Spelter, that there might be a con-stanc and regular Supply thereof in England, on moderate Terms and Prices; about that Time the Petitioner entered into lohg Trial of Experiments, and pursued the same Six Years successively, with great Study, Application, and Expence; and having in the Year 1737 overcome the principal Difficulties, the Petitioner applied to his present Majesty for his Letters Patent, for the foie Exercise of the Art and Mystery of making Spelcer* which his Majesty was most graciously pleased ragranc accordingly, the §ixth of July, in the Twelfth Year of his Reign*

which Patent was laid before, and read to, your Com-hmtee; whereby it appeared, that the fastne Was to be in force for the Term of Fourteen Years.

Upon obtaining the said Letters Patent, the Petitioner erected large Buildings, and made other useful Conveniences, for the effectual carrying on the making of Spelter; wherein he expended and laid out 7,000l. or thereabouts, and made about 200 Tons,which he, from time to time, exposed to Sale; and when it came to Market, it had the Preference of any that had been imported.

It appears by the Evidence of several Persons examined before your Committee, That the Petitioner had laid out large Sums of Money in erecting Works and Buildings for making of Spelter; and those Wicnefies said, that thty had perused his general Accounts of the Profit and Lofsarifingfrom the Undertaking; whereby it appeared, that the Petitioner has been, and is to this Time, near Four thousand Pounds Loser, in bringing the Art of making Spelter to Perfection in England, arising principally from the great Fall in the Price of Spelter, from 260/. to 48 /. per Ton.

A Certificate from several Venders and Consumers of Spelter in this Kingdom was produced, and laid before your Committee, whereby they certify, That they have, for some Years pad, fold and used considerable Quantities of Spelter, made by the Petitioner; and that they find it, to all Intents and Purposes, as good for our Manufactures as what comes from Indian and, in some respects, preferable thereto.

It appeared to your Committee, That no Spelter is now imported from India, by reason that which was last imported from thence, was sold at a considerable Loss.

That the Benefit accruing to the Manufacturers in this Country, from the Petitioner’s Undertaking, is well known; and that it hath prevented Monopolizers from advancing the Markets in the extravagant manner they formerly did, which was much to the Prejudice of the Consumers and Workers of Spelter.

And your Committee was informed, That several Persons in Birmingham and Wolverhampton used great Quantities of Spelter; and they say, that the Petitioner’s Spelter was as good in Quality as any Spelter brought from the East Indies.

Upon the whole, it appears to your Committee, Thit the making of Spelter in England, will be very useful in manufacturing of several Sorts of Goods and Wares in this Kingdom.

Wardens, and Assistants, hath been made, pursuant to the said Law, but the said Company have ever since ceased to act; and that the Body of Fishermen are now under no Government or Regulation, the Times and Seasons of Fishing are frequently broken into, too small and^iin-sizeable Fish are constantly taken, new Methods*of unlawful Fishing aredevifedand practised, the EnCourage-ment for the Sale and Destruction of the young Fry is encreased, and the present legal Means for apprehending and punishing Offenders are defective; in consequence of all which, the Fry and Spawn of Fish are destroyed, the Price of many Sorts of Fish i« become excessive, the Fishermen in general are greatly impoverished,the publick Utility, intended to be provided for, is defeated; and the said Abuses cannot be prevented or redressed, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given for bringing in a Bill for the more effectual preventing the Destruction of the Fry and Spawn of Fish in the said River of *1 homes, and for the better regulating the Fishery thereof, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the Gitv of Bristol, under their common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend the Increase of our People will always be the Means of advancing the Wealth and Strength of the Nation, which is not only verified in other Countries, but has been sensibly experienced in our own, were, by the Industry of the foreign Procestants, w!k> have fled to us for Refuge, or introduced themselves amongst us, several new Manufactures have been let up, and others improved, to the great Advantage of the Trade and Commerce of the Kingdom; and that, at a Time when the neighbouring Nations, our Rivals in Trade are ttrongly exerting themselves in the Enlargement and Improvement of their Commerce; and expressing the Desire of the Petitioners, that the Bill depending in the House for the Naturalization of foreign Protestants, which appears to the Petitioners so justly calculated to answer that valu: ablePurpose to this Kingdom, may meet with ehedefired Success: And therefore praying the House, That the said Bill tnay pass inco a Law.

A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, A Aidants, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Adventurers within the City of Bristol, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend many important Advantages will arise from the Bill now depending in the House for the Naturalization of foreign Protestants; and that the Petitioners conceive it an undeniable Maxim, that the Strength and Riches of a Country consist in the Number of its People, and that such a Law, by introducing useful Traders and Manufacturers, would be exrremely beneficial to Trade and Navigation, as their Industry will give fresh Spirit to our Commerce, and inhance the Value of Lands; and that the Petitioners are the more desirous of encouraging foreign Protcftarrts to settle in this Kingdom, as pad Experience evinces that they have, on all Occasions, fopported with Zeal and Affection our prefenc most happy Establishment: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Devizes, &c. A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Road. Clothiers, and other Persons, living in and near the Towns of Bradford and Trowbridge, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the direct Road from the great cloathing Towns of Froom, Bradford, Trowbridge, and many Hamlets, adjacent, in the Counties of Wilts and Somerset, leads to the Green Man, in the Parish of Seend, and from thence to the Devizes; but that, through the present impafiable Condition thereof in Winter, and often in Summer, Wheel Carriages from those Parts are obliged, in going to and returning from London, to pass some-times Eight, sometimes Ten Miles extraordinary, round about; and not only so, but that this last Road is often impassable, by the Overflowing of the River Avon, by means whereof the Clothiers Goods frequently lose their Market, and are much damaged, to the great Discouragement of the Manufacture; and alleging, that the Petitioners conceive, the Bill depending in the House for repairing the Road from the Devizes to the Green Man in Seend, will be altogether inefficient to open a Communication for Wheel Carriages between the manufacturing Towns aforesaid and the Devizes, prevent any of the above-mentioned Inconveniencies, produce any Benefit to the Woollen Manufactures of those Parts, or answer any of the valuable Purposes specified in the said Bill, for that the Road leading from a Place called the Ragged Smock, in the Chapelty of Semington, in the said County of Wilts, to the Green Man in Seend, being in Length about Two Miles, and Part of the Road leading from the aforesaid cloathing Towns to the Devizes, is in a fpunderous and ruinous Condition, and almost impassable for Wheel Carriages in the Winter, and cannot be effectually amended and kept in sufficient Repair, by virtue of any Laws in being: And therefore praying, That an Amendment may be made to the said Bill, and that the Road may be repaired from the North End of the Borough of the Devizes to the Place called the Ragged Smock, in the Cha-pclry of Semington aforesaid; and that the Extent of the Reparation of the said Road may not be limited to the Green Man, according to the present Purport of the said Vo*. 26.

Bill; or that the Petitioners may have such further Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem truer.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Parish Clerk* Brethren, of the Company of Parish Clerks of the Cities Caaner*. of London and Westminster, Southwark, and Parishes adjacent, within the Bills of Mortality, was presented to ihe House, and read; setting forth. That the Company of Parish Clerks hath for many Years been incorporated, and had several Royal Charters and Privileges granted to them; and that, in pursuance of their Charters (the last of which was granted in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the First) they are obliged, and still continue, to render weekly and yearly, to the King and the Lord Mayor of London, an Account of the Christenings and Burials in their respective Parishes, together with the I 'if-eases and Casualties, whereby the State of Health in these grear and populo $ Cities may at all times appear; and alleging, that notwithstanding their Charter enjoins all Parish Clerks within the Bills of Mortality to observe the Directions and Orders contained therein, yet many of them refuse to comply therewith, and neglect to fend an Account of the Christenings and Burials within their Parishes; and that, notwithstanding all Sextons and Grave-makers, where no Clerk is, at all exempt or private Burial Grounds, are ordered by the said Charter to make Report weekly, of all Burials within their respective Burial Grounds, to the Company of Parish Clerks, yet, for want of sufficient Powers and Penalties to enforce their Charter, no Report is made at all, whereby the Account rendered to his Majesty, the Lord Mayor, and the*

Public, is become very deficient and imperfect; and that the said' Company of Parish Clerks are at a very great Expence in maintaining an Hall, Clerk, Printer, and Beadle, for performing this Service, and have no sufficient Estate, or other Means of supporting the Charges thereof, but the Profit that arises from the Sale of their weekly and yearly Bills, which, by reason of the aforesaid Defect and Imperfection, and the Prejudice and Damage they receive from the Printers and Publifiiers of News-Papers, who print and publish the material and essential Part of their Bills, is so reduced, that the Company will be in no condition of performing the Service required of them, and must be dissolved, and the laudable Ends and Purposes of their Incorporation entirely defeated; and that if the said Company were enabled to inlarge and make their Accounts more perfect, by having Power granted them to register in their respective Parishes the Births or Christenings of all Children born therein, in order that they may be inserted in their weekly and yearly Bills, a9 also to publish, weekly and yearly, as well the Deaths as Burials, together with the Casualties and Diseases, which shall anywhere happen within the Bills of Mortality, and to restrain all Printers and Publishers, except such Printer and Publisher as is appointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury and Bishop of London, agreeable to their Charter, from printing and publishing all or any Part of the said Bills, they would then be capable of performing this Service of publishing an- exact and perfect Account of all Births, Baptisms, and Deaths, within the said Bills of Mortality: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give Leave that a Bill may be brought in for the Purposes aforesaid, and to grant the Petitioners such further Powers and Privileges as shall seem fitting to the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideracion of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Upon the first-mentioned Petition;

Your Committee do find, that the said Mr. Thomiinfon did purchase Bank Annuities at 4/. per Cent. to the Amount of 11.328/. which, when the Subscription for the Reduction of Interest took place, was, and is at this Time, in the Names of Charles Apthorp and John Erving, both residing in Boston, New England-, viz 5,328/. in the Name of Apthorp, and 6,coo/, in the Name of Erving-, and Powers were given him by both of them to accept and receive the Interest thereof for their separate Uses, but no Power to dispose of the fame:

That on the First Subscription at the Bank he offered to subscribe the said Annuities, which was not admitted; being then informed, that his said Powers were not thought sufficient; but an Entry was made, by way of Memorandum, of such his Offer in the dubious Book: That, upon such Refusal, the said Mr. Thomiinfon did, by the First Conveyance for New England, acquaint the said Mr. Apthorp and Mr. Erving the rewith; who, in Return, by their separate Letters, dated Boston, June 5th, 1750, which were produced, not only approved of the Subscription, but fenc him Permits, which were produced, for subscribing the fame; and as it was impossible at that Season for them to know of such Subscription, and the Permits not arriving before the Time of subscribing the same was expired, they are deprived the Benefit of the Offer made the Annuitants of 29 November 1749, unless some further Provision be made by Parliament for that Purpose.

Upon the Second mentioned Petition 5 Your Committee find, that Daniel Huger Esquire, of South Carolina, has been long possessed of 8,000l. Old South Sea Annuities, (landing in his own Name, the Dividends whereof have been constantly received by Mr.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read 5 setting forth, That the City of Carlisle, in the County of Cumberland, and the 1'own of Newcastle upon Tyne, in the County of Northumberland, are situate on the Two principal Passages from the Northern to the Southern Parts of this Kingdom, the one near the Irish Channel, the other near the German Ocean, at the Distance of about Sixty Miles; and that the Road between them is for the most part through a Country uncultivated, and Wry thinly inhabited, frequently unpassable, and at all times very inconvenient either for T roops or Carriages; and that it has been found by Experience, as well during the late Rebellion, as on former Occasions, that the said Passages cannot be properly guarded without a free and open Communication for Troops and Carriages at all Times of the Year, between the said City of Carlisle and Town of Newcastle; and that the Want of such a Communication has been attended with great Inconvenience and Danger to this Kingdom, and that a Road proper for that Purpose cannot be laid our, or the Expence thereof defrayed, but by a National Assistance, and the Aid and Authority of Parliament! And therefore praying, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for laying out, making, and keeping in Repair, a Road proper for the Passage of Troops and Carriages between the said City iof Carlisle and Town of Newcastle, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Excessive Use A Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Com-of Spirits. monalty, of the City and County of Norwich, in Common-Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; complaining of the great Decay of Industry, Piety, and Virtue, amongst the common People of the said City; and alleging, that a manifest Change appears amongst the said common People in their Habitations,

Cloathing, and Manner of Living, from hiring Houses by the Year, and having suitable Furniture of their own, being decently cloathed, and appearing at Places of publick Worship on Sundays, to taking Lodgings by the Week, miserably and unwholesomely furnisheef, being wretchedly cloathed, neglecting all Places of publick

Martii. A. 1750.

Worship, and being guilty of Drunkenness, Debauchery,

Imbezzlements,*Robberies, and other gross Immoralities i and that the Petitioners have observed these things to grow upon the said common People as the Custom of drinking Geneva, and other spirituous Liquors, hath obtained amongst them, and fear that nothing will reclaim them, so long as they can be so easily supplied with those intoxicating Liquors: And therefore praying the House, to provide such a Remedy against this increasing Evil, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and Inha- ExcefiyeUle bitants, of the Parish of St. Anney within the Liberty of 0 pints' Westminster, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and other Parishioners of the said Parish, was also presented to the House, and read; complaining of the immoderate Increase, which has been made of late Years, in the Number of Gin-fellers in that, as well as in the neighbouring Parishes in the City of Westminster, and of the extensive and complicated Mischiefs which attend the customary Use of spirituous Liquors amongst the lower Class of People, extinguishing all Regard to common Decency, depraving their Morals, inflaming their Passions, wafting their Means of Livelihood, making them prone to every Wickedness, enervating all their Powers both of Body and Mind, and rendering them unhappy in themselves, and equally unfit either for the Service of God or their Fellow Creatures; and alleging, that the Mifehiefs complained of are not confined to the present Generation, but, as the Petitioners apprehend, must be found equally fatal to the future Welfare and Security of their Country; it appearing, by undoubted Experience, that the Number of Births are thereby much diminished. Multitudes of poor Children destroyed in their Infancy, and consequently the Number of those useful Hands greatly lef-iened, which, by their Vigour, Industry, and Labour of every kind, are most confeflcdly one of the principal Sources of the Wealth and Strength of the Nation: And therefore praying the House, to take the Grievance complained of into Consideration, and apply such Remedy to it, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common-Council assembled, relating to spirituous Liquors, is referred.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, the Committee examined

James Pickering; who said, That he is perfectly acquainted with that Part of the Kiver Ribble, which lies between the Townships of Preston znAPenwortbam, having been employed as a Fisherman there for these Forty Years last pad; and that the Fords lie in the great Road between Livapoole and Preston, and between Preston and Ormskirk:

That he is well acquainted with the Fords, the Passage whereof is very dangerous; and that he remembers above Twenty Persons being drowned, in attempting to pals the fame; and at the Time when the Frclhes and Tides rife, there is no Possibility of passing them:

That the said Ford has been Three times removed wi:hin these Eight or Ten Years; but the new Fords, by the frequent passing of Carriages, are soon worn into Holes, and become deep and dangerous; and the Ford now in use is already very bad:

That the Ford (hists with the Tides and Frelhes; and that he apprehends them to be in danger of being totally loft.

Mr. Robert Porter said, That these Fords lie in the common High Road from Liverpool, Ormskirk, and the South-weft Parts of Lancashire, to Preston and Lancaster, and so on to Kendall, Carlisle, and Scotland; and that many Persons carry their Coals that Way:

And he confirmed the Evidence of James Pickering, with respect to the Danger of the said Fords; and added. That there was no other Way of passing the River, without going over the Bridge at Preston, which is Five Miles about, through a very flat, dangerous, and rotten Road, which is impracticable for loaded Wheel-Carriages;

And that a great part of the Country (he believes Forty -or Fifty Miles in Circuit) is supplied with Fuel by Carriages drawn over the said Ford; and that the erecting a Bridge there would be of great Advantage to the County in particular, and to Trade in general.

Mr. Henry Sejton said. That he was a Mason, and had been employed to survey the said River, and draw a Plan of a Bridge; in pursuance whereof, he had drawn a Plan, which he laid he would give Security to finish, and uphold Vol. 26.

for Twenty-one Years, for the Sum of Three thousand Pounds.

Mr. George Grey informed your Comrtiittee, That he had taken a Level of the River, between the old Bridge and the proposed new one, and finds the Fall of Water to be Twelve Feet.

And to prove the intended Bridge would be no Inconvenience, as to (topping the Current, he said, That the River is 274..... broad, where the said Bridge is intended to be built, and only 152 below; so that afeer the said Bridge shall be erected, there will be a greater Passage for the Water through the Arches, than there is below.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge over the River Ribble, between the Townships of Preston and Penwortham, near a Place called the Ftfb House, in the County Palatine of Lancaster:

And that the Lord Strange, Mr. Bold, and Mr. Fazakerley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Representation and Petition of the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia in America, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that his Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Representation and Pedtion, recommends it to the Consideradon of the House, to do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Representation and Petidon was brought up, and read; setting forth, That in Execution of the Trust reposed in the Petitioners, by his Majesty’s Charter, they have applied their principal Attention to make the Province of Georgia subservient to the Interest and Trade of Great Britain; by raising such Produces as are raoft wanted, for the carrying on of our Manufactures, and which that Part of America is capable of raising; and that, in pursuance of this, the Petitioners have (as far as they were enabled by the House, by the Aid granted for the Year 1750), promoted the Culture of Silk in the said Province, by promising and appropriating proper Sums for Premiums on the producing of Silk Balls, and on the Silk wound from those Balls; which Premiums are to be paid on the Pound both of Balls and Silk, according to their Value; and that they likewise give Rewards to encourage the Women to acquire the Art of winding the Silk from the Balls; and that, without these Encouragements, this useful Produce would probably have been crushed in the beginning; but that, by these, the Trustees have great reason to believe it will be; considerably increased this Spring; in which Season this Work is begun and completed; and that the Trustees were induced to promise these Encouragements, from the ample Testimonies given by our Merchants and Manafafturers, that tht American Silk is equal inFineness and Goodness to the best Italian Silk, and from the great Demands in England for Raw Silk, for want of which (there not being a sufficient Supply by foreign Importation) many of our Mills for organizing were become in a manner useless, and great Numbers of our Looms, and greater Number of our Manufacturers, were in danger of (landing idle, for want of Employment; and that another Produce of Georgia, viz. Indigo, (though the first Essay) appeared upon the Sale thereof, soon after the Importation of it, in September last, to be little inferior in Quality to the French Indigo, and bore as high a Price as any which is now raised in the British Colonies; and that by proper Returns made by the Magistrates, the Number of white People in the Province amounted to 1,619 at Midsummer 1749; since which Time, 61 foreign Protestants were sent in juJy 1749, and more were fentin July last; and that then (as the Trustees have been informed by the Magistrates) there were 349 working Negroes in the Province, besides Children too young for Labour; and that thcTrustees have supplied the Detachments of Soldiers, doing Duty in the Province, with such Provisions, as it was thought proper they should undertake to do; and representing to the House, that the Trustees have maintained a Civil Government in the Province; that the Magistrates, and other necessary Officers, receive certain annual Sums, agreeable to an Estimate sent over to them, which the Trustees have always regularly paid; and that on a Stop of such Payments, the Government mud immediately cease(the Inhabitants being at present unable to bear the Expence thereof) the Consequeners of which need not be described: And therefore, as the Trustees are not able to make such Payments, or grant Encouragements for the further promoting the Culture of Silk, without the Aid and Assistance

Yymple, Advocate, Ruling Elder, Commissioners from the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, was pre-fenred to the House, and read j fecting forth, That by the Laws of Scotland, before the happy Union of the Two Kingdoms, Provision was made for the Maintenance of the Ministers of the Gospel in their respective Parishes of that Kingdom, by appointing, from time to time, parliamentary Commissions for Plantation of Churches, and Valuation of Tythes, who were impowered to appoint and settle a constant and local Stipend to each Minister, to be paid out of the Tythes of each Parish; and also, to grant Augmentations to Ministers, not already sufficiently provided for; all the Powers of which Commissions were, by an Act of the last Parliament of Scotland,\ vested in the Court of Session; and that great Numbers of the Ministers of the Church of Scotland, who are not sufficiently provided for, have not hitherto applied for, or obtained any Relief, with respect to the Augmentation of their Stipends or ProviGons, which by Law the said Court of Session is impowered to give them; which hath been in a great measure occasioned by the great Expences that the Ministers must be at in carrying on Processes before the Court of Session, as Commissioners for Plantation of Kirks, for obtaining such Augmentations; which few Ministers, in their narrow Circumstances, afe able to bear; and alleging, that such Processes too frequently occasion unhappy Differences betwixt the Minister and his Parishioners 5 which, if properly settled, would be for the mutual Benefit, Ease, and Satisfaction, of both Minister and Parishioners; and that the Clergy in Scotland fa fat greatly, by not having their Stipends punctually paid; and that, although they have the Law in common with other Subjects, yet rigorous Prosecutions against their Parishioners might tend to alienate the Minds of their People from them, and consequently to make them less useful in their sacred Function; which if put under proper Regulations, might be recovered, without such Prosecutions; and that in Scotland there are sundry Churches, so near one another, and the Parishes so small, that they cannot afford a suitable Maintenance to their respective Minister; and many other Parishes are so extensive, as to be too great a Charge for any One Minister; and such Parishes being properly united or divided, as the same should happen, would tend very much to the Benefit of that Country; and that these Inconveniencies having been taken into Consideration by the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, which met *x. Edinburgh in May last, they came to a RefoJution to make humble Application to Parliament for Relief, and appointed the Petitioners their Commissioners f6r that Purpose: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar-Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies, was presented to the House, «nd read; feuing forth, That by the Act of Navigation, passed in the 12th Year of King Charles the Second, it is enacted, That no Goods shall be imported into, or exported out of any Territories belonging to the King, in Asia, Africa, or America, in other VeflTels than such only as belong to the People of England, Ireland, Wales, or the Town of Berwick, or are built in the British Plantations, and owned by British Planters, and whereof the Master, and Three-fourths of the Mariners, are English, on pain to loft such Goods and VefiTel; and Commanders at Sea, having Commissions from the King, are impowered and required to bring in, as Prize, Vessels offending contrary to this Act; and in case of Condemnation, One Moiety shall be to the Use of such Commanders, and their Companies, and the other Moiety to the King; and that by the same Act, it is further enacted, That no Goods of foreign Growth or Manufacture, brought into England, IrelandWales, Guernsey, Jersey, or Berwick, in English or other Shipping belonging to some of the said Places, and navigated as aforesaid, shall be brought from other Places than those of the Growth and Manufacture, or from those Ports, where they can only, or have usually been shipped for Transportation, on pain to forfeit such Goods and Vessel; and that by another Act of Parliament, passed in the 15th Year of King Charles the Second, it is enacted, That no Commodity, of the Growth or Manufacture of Europe, shall be imported into any of the King's Plantations in Asia, Africa, or America, but what shall have been shipped in England, Wales, or Town of Berwick, and m English-built Shipping, navigated as aforesaid, and carried directly thence to the said Plantations, upon pain of Forfeiture of the Goods and Vessel; and alleging, that in the making of these Laws (always looked upon as the Bulwark of the British Commerce) the Legislature of Great Britain had, as the Petitioners conceive, Two great and important Objects in view. One thelncrease of Naval Power, by making Britisls Shipping, and British Subjects, the foie Carriers of the whole British Commerce, the other the apjpropriating and securing to Great Britain all the Emo-

luments arising from the Trade of her own Colonies; and so jealous has the British Legislature been of guarding these Two great Sources of her Wealth and Power fronji any Invasion, that it was no sooner perceived that One of these great Views was like to be crofted and defeated, by a Trade beginning to be carried on between the British Northern Colonies in America, and the French, and other foreign Colonies there, by which the British Subjects in North America served themselves with foreign Sugar, Rum and Melasses; and, by so doing, transferred to Fo* reigners the Benefit of a Trade, which, in its natural Channel, properly belonged to Great Britain, and which was in the same Degree advantageous and beneficial to th£ foreign Sugar Colonies, as it was prejudicial and hurtful to our own; then an Act was passed in the 6th Year of his present Majesty, by which a Duty was laid of Five Shillings per Hundred upon all foreign Sugars, Nine Pence per Gallon on all foreign Rum, and Sixpence per Gallon on all foreign Melasses, that should, after the 25th Day of December 1733,* be imported or brought, into any of his Majesty’s Colonies in America, which it wa* then generally^pprehcnded would as effectually-put a Stop to that Trade, as an actual Prohibition; and that the laying of this Duty shewed, in the strongest manner, as the Petitioners apprehend, the Sense of the Legifiatufe of the pernicious Nature of this Trade, and that it ough; not to be any longer endured; but that, notwithstanding all the Care hitherto taken by the Legislature to preserve and guard these Two important Branches of her Commerce, of inestimable Value to Great Britain, from the Encroachments of Foreigners, the British Traders ip North America forgetting all Ties of Duty to his Majesty, the Interest of their Mother-Country, and the Reverence due to its Laws, have, as though they thought themselves independent of Great Britain, for some Years past, carried on a very large and extensive Trade, not only with the foreign Colonies in America, but also with the French and Dutch in Europe, directly in Violation of the said Acts; which, if not speedily prevented, by some more effectual Provisions than have hitherto been made, will be attended withConsequences fatal to the British Sugar Colonies, and greatly detrimental to the Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain itself; for that a settled Course of Traffic!* has been carried on for several Years past between forme of his Majesty's Subjects in North America, and the Ports of Marjeillcs and Toulon; and their Ships have gone thither laden with Pitch, Tar, Train-Oil, Oak, Timber, Knees, and Planks, for building Ships; Masts, Spars, Staves, Rice, Logwood, Beaver, Martins, Deer and Elk Skins, and Furs, and Naval Stores, carried directly to the Arsenals of France-, and for which they have taken in Return Goods of the Growth and Manufactures of France, or other foreign Countries, confiding chiefly of French Silks, of several Sorts, Silk Stockings, Gold and Silver Lace, Twist and Wire, Velvets, Gloves, Oils, Olives, Capers, Soap, Spices, Drugs, and Earthen Ware; A Petition of several Merchants, and other Dealers, Duties on within the City of London, concerned in the Cotton Linen Yarn. Trade, and in the Manufactures ofcoarfe,checqued, and striped Linen, and of Linen mixed with Cotton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That very considerable and extensive Manufactures of coarse checqued and striped Linen, and of Linen mixed with Cotton, have been carried on for many Years past in this Kingdom, whereby our Home-Consumprion hath not only been entirely supplied, but also very large Quantities of the said Manufactures have been annually exported to foreign Markets, and to his Majesty’s Colonies in America; and that the said Manufactures are* chiefly worked up with coarse Linen Yam imported from Ireland, and upon which a Duty of One Half-penny per Pound1 Weight is paid upon the Exportation thereof from that Kingdom 5 and that very large Premiums have been lately allowed upon coarse Linens exported from Ireland, and very considerable Bounties given upon the Exportation of coarse, brown, white, and dyed Linens, from this Kingdom; whereby the Manufacturers of checqued and striped Linen, and of Linen mixed with Cotton (which are not intitled to the said Bounties) have been subjected to great Disadvantages, as the Manufacturers of brown and white*

Linens both in Britain and Ireland have been enabled to purchase Yarn at x higher Price than the Persons concerned in the checqued, striped* and Cotton Trade, cart afford to give, and the Price of the Yam has accordingly advanced at least 20 L per Cent. and that, under these Disadvantages and Discouragements, the Exports of our coarse checqued and striped Linen, and Linen and Cotton Manufactures, have of late been very consider- ably decreased, and there is great Reason to apprehend, that this Trade must, in a very short Time, be totally ingrossed by the French 2nd Dutch, who can be supplied with coarse Yam at as moderate a Rate as the same has been usually fold for in Ireland, and from which Supply the British Manufacturers are in a Manner excluded by the present high Duties upon foreign Yarn; and that the Manufacturers abroad are also enabled, by the low Price of foreign Linen Yam, to purchase Cotton at an advanced Rate, and to manufacture the same with Linen, and to vend such Manufactures at foreign Markets, upon more reasonable Terms than Manufactures of the same Fabrick and Species can be sent from this Kingdom, and that by this means the Cotton Trade is in a great Degree fallen into the Hands of the French and Dutch; and alleging, that unless some Provision be made for relieving the said Manufactures from the Difficulties they at present labour under, these important and valuable Branches of Trade must be inevitably loft, to the Ruin of many Thousand Manufacturers employed therein, and to the great Detriment of his Majesty’s Colonies in America, particularly to such of the said Colonies as are concerned in the Growth and Culture of Cotton, and also to the great Prejudice of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, especially to the Mediterranean and Levant Seas: And there- fore praying the House, to take this Matter into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief as to the House shall appear necessary.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions;

An Act made in the T wentieth Year of his present Majesty's Reign was produced, whereby it appeared, that several Tolls were granted for repairing the Road from Catherick Bridge to Tarm, in the County of York, and from thence to Stockton, in the County of Durham, and from thence through Sedgefield to the City of Durham.

Mr. Cuthbert Readjhaw and Mr. William Dixon, were examined; and said, That in pursuance of the said Act, great Progress had been made in repairing the said Road; and that, if Provision was made for continuing and repairing the said Road to the Town of Lancaster, it would be of great publick Utility, as the shortest Communication would be thereby opened between the Two Seas, and the Expence of conveying Goods and Manufactures to and from the Counties of York and Lancaster much leffened, and the Trade of that Part of the Kingdom greatly increased:

And that many Parts of the Road, leading from the Termination of the Road directed to be repaired by the said Act to the Town of Lancaster, are very narrow and deep; and that the said Road is also in many Places almost impassable for Wheel Carriages, and cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course appointed for the Repair of Highways.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road leading from the East End of Brump-ton High Lane, in the County of York, to the Town of Richmond, and from thence, to and through the Towns of AJkrig and Ingleton, in the said County, to the Town of Lancaster, in the County of Lancaster: And that Mr. Comptroller, Mr. John Yorke, Mr. Reynolds, and the Lord Downe, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Motifon reported from the Committee, to whom Lincoln the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriffs, Citizens, Small Debts, and Commonalty, of the City of Lincoln, in Common-Council assembled; and also the Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Tradesmen, Householders, Shopkeepers, and Refiants, within the City of Lincoln, and County of the said City, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and others, inhabiting within the said City and Liberties thereof; and also the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Tradesmen, and Inhabitants, of the Close and Bail of Lincoln, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, were referred; That the Committed had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Two first-mentioned Petitions, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. John Garmfton and Mr. Francis Barnard, who, being severally examined, said, That the City of Lincoln is an ancient Corporation, and a County within itself, of a large Extent, and has Rivers, which are navigable to the Towns of Hull and Boston, and a considerable Trade is carried on to those Parts:

That Numbers of Artificers and HandicraftPersons are employed within the said City, and County of the fame, who cannot support thtitvselves without Credit; and Numbers of Dealers come from the adjacent Counties to attend the Fairs and Markets held within the City, who rent Stalls, and gain a Livelihood by felling their Goods and Merchandize, arid frequently give Credit to many of the poor Inhabitants residing therein:;

And they further said, That those poor Artificers are / often under Difficulties to obtain Credie, and the Dealers who keep the Fairs and Markets are greatly discouraged from giving the fame, for small Sums of Money, to those poor Persons, by reason that many of them who gain Credit, evade the Payment of their just Debts, prefum-ing on the Expence and Delay which attend the Recovery thereof:

And they both severally said, That if an easy and speedy Method for recovering of just Debts, at a small Expence, should be granted, it will be a means to promote Industry, support useful Credit, and be of great Advantage to the said City.

And to prove the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition the following Witnesses were examined;

Mr Garmfton and Mr. Barnard, who severally said.

That the Close and Bail of Lincoln are Districts, situate within, and surrounded by, the City of Lincoln, but are in the County of Lincoln, and, upon Account of che said Situation, the Inhabitants thereof are, and ufuaJJy have been, taxed to the Land Tax as Part of che City, and Tub-je£t to the Commissioners for the said City, and County of the fame, and not to the Commissioners for the County at large; and unless some Provision be made for the Inhabitants of the said Close and Bail, they will, by means of their continual Intercourse and frequent Dealings with the Inhabitants of the City, be subject to great Inconveniencies in suing, and being sued for small Debts:

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee' came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petitions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the more speedy and easy Recovery of small Debts within the City of Lincoln, and County of the same City, and the Liberties and Precincts thereof, and within the Close and Bail of Lincoln, within the County of Lincoln.

CarlifleRoad. Sir William Myddleton reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Nobility, Gentry, Clergy, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Counties of Cumberland and Northumberland* was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fa& contained in the said Petition * and had directed him to report a State

thereof Co the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth * viz.

The Committee find the Matter of Fa& contained in the said Petition to be as follows:

That the City of Carlifte, in the County of Cumberland» and the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, in the County of Northumberland* are situate on the Two principal Passages from the Northern to the Southern Parts of this Kingdom, the first near the Irish Channel, the other near the German Ocean, at the Distance of about 60 Miles one from the other:

And Major-General Cholmondeley informed your Committee, That during the Time of the late Rebellion, he marched with the Troops from Newcastle, which were ordered to Carlifte to intercept the Rebels: That on the First Day the Troops set out at Seven in the Mornings and it was Eleven at Night before they arrived at Oving-bam, which is only Eight Miles from Newcastle; and the next Day they set out at the same time, and marched to Hexham* where they did not arrive till Eleven of the Clock at Night, and the Carriages did not come in till next Day:

That the Distance from Newcastle to Hexham is no more than Sixteen computed Miles; and in good Road an Army will ra^rch Sixteen Miles in Eight Hours j that the Reason of this Delay was the Badness of the Road* which was almost impafiable for the Carriages, and quite so for Artillery.

Colonel Seabright* Aid de Camp to the late Field* Marshal and Captain Morgan* federally confirmed the Evidence of General Cholmondeley 5 and Colonel Sear bright added. That if this Road was passable for Troops and Carriages, an Army might march from Newcastle, to Carlifte in left Time than they could from Edinburgh to Carlifte: And all the aforesaid Witnesses agreed, that ig was of great Importance to open a Communication between the Towns of Newcastle and Carljle, for the commodious Passage of Troops and Carriages on any future Occasion.

Mr. Thomas Sayer informed your Committee, That he is well acquainted with the Road from Carlifte to HexbamB which is mostly through an open Cotmtry, with very feyf Houses, not One Part in Ten of the said Road being through inclosed Grounds: That the Country is rocky* mountainous, and boggy, and absolutely impaifable, both in Summer and Winter, for heavy Carriages; and there are several Waters in the said Road, which frequently overflow and render it impafiable.

And it appeared to your Committee, That it is im* possible to repair the said Road by the ordinary Course of Law, nor even by the erecting Turnpikes thereon, ic being open in some Parts for Twenty Miles together, so that the Payment of the Tolls might easily be evaded; but could they be collected, the Country having little Commerce, and being uncultivated, a very small Income would arise therefrom, the Inhabitants for Twenty Miles together, not being able to furnifti Forty Carriages towards the Repair of the said Road; there being in some Parts no House to be seen for Ten or Twelve Miles together.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of several Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others, Inhabitants of East Greenwich, and Places adjacent, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants, was presented to the House, and read; fetcing forth, That in the Parish of East Greenwich, and within a Quarter of a Mile, or thereabouts, of the Town, in which there is a Royal Palace, and that well known fu-perb Building, the Royal Hospital for Seamen, there is a Storehouse or Magazine, wherein are frequently kept very great Quantities of Gunpowder; and that, besides the great Danger which must attend all Places of this kind, this Magazine (lands in an open Field, not inclosed with any Fortification whatever, whereby it is exposed to Treachery, and every Accident; and that the Petitioners have made Application to his Majesty’sBoardkjf Ordnance, to have the said Magazine intirely removed; to which the Board have replied, That it is not in their Power to remove the King’s Magazine, or to make a Purchase of Land, and ered another elsewhere; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners apprehend, if through Treachery, or by Lightning, or any other Accident, the said Magazine should take Fire, among many great Mischiefs which would follow, not only the Lives and Properties of the Petitioners, but the said Palace and Hospital, the King’s Yards and Stores at Deptford and Wodwich, and the Banks and Navigation of the River ‘Thames, and the Ships failing and at Anchor therein, would be inevitably destroyed, and almost inconceivable Damage accrue to the Cittesof London and Westminster: And therefore praying, That the said Magazine may be entirely removed to

such a Distance from their Habitations, as that the Lives and Properties of the Petitioners may be preserved, and the several other Mischiefs before-mentioned may be prevented, in such manner as the House shall think fit.

Sir Henry Erskine Baronet, (a Member of this House) delivered to the House a Complaint, in Writing, relating to General Philip Anstruther, (also a Member of this House) lare Lieutenant-Governor of the Island of Minorca.

Ancf the said Complaint was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The same of Sir Henry Erskine Baronet.

In the Year 1742 Lieutenant-General Philip Anstruther, at that Time Lieutenant-Governor of the Island of Minorca, was Commander in Chief of his Majesty’s Forces there, and Sir Henry Erskine was then a Lieutenant in the Regiment of Foot, commanded by Brigadier General Offarrell, in Garrison in that Island.

In the Month of May, in that Year, Sir Henry Erskine being sent for by the said Lieutenant-Governor to Mahon, was put in Arrest, by his Order, without any particular Crimes being laid to his Charge.

In consequence of this Arrest, the said Sir Henry Erskine was kept in Confinement in Fort St. Philips, for Three Weeks, and upwards; and in that Time, before any Charge was exhibited against him, or any Coiirt-Martiai appointed for his Trial, was carried before the Court of

Royal Government, and there required In the Presence of the said Lieutenant-Governor, to be examined, upon Oath, in a Cause of Complaint exhibited into that Court against Two other Persons, in relation to Memorials which had been presented to Brigadier Paget, Commander in Chief in the said island, during the Absence of the said Lieutenant-Governor, complaining of the said Lieutenant-Governor’s CondudV; the being concerned in composing which Memorials, was afterwards made, by the said Lieutenant-Governor, Part of the Charge against' the said Sir Henry Erskine, before the Court-Martial after-mentioned.

After Sir Henry Erskine had remained upwards of Three Weeks, under this Arrest, without any Charge, on the 18th June 1742, a Copy of Accusation was transmitted to him, by the Lid Governor’s Secretary, and Notice sent to him to prepare for his Trial, before a General Court-Martial, to be held upon the Wednesday following, being the 2 2d; which Charge confided but of Two Articles, the First, for having co-operated and afiifled in composing and dispersing several false and calumnious Libels, injurious to the Character of the said Lieutenant-Governor, and others; the Second, for having refused to answer, upon Oath, some Questions put to him in the said Court of Royal Government, in relation to the Memorials before mentioned, when carried thither as a Prisoner, after the Arrest as aforesaid; so that one Part of his Crime arose after his Confinement; and the other, had it been true, would have been notorious, and might have been proceeded upon without Delay.

The Court-Martial appointed to try the said Sir Henry Erskine was conflicted in an unusual Manner; some of the Witnesses brought by the said Lieutenant-Governor, to support the Accusation, were then in Confinement, at his Instance, and under his Order; they were by him refused to be set at Liberty, as required by the Court-Martial, that they might give their Testimony freely; and the Reason alleged for fuchRefulal, by the said Lieutenant-Governor; or the Perfun employed by him to manage the said Prosecution, was, because the said Witnesses were notorious Rogues. They were twice rejected by the Court; and the Lieutenant-Governor, although he refused to release them before they had thus given their Testimony, sent an Ecclesiastick of Distindbion in the Island, to allure one of the Witnesses of future Liberty, and the Friendship of the Lieutenant-Governor, if he would give Evidence against the said Sir Henry Erskine; as the Person so sollicited has since declared.

The Court-Martial having rejected these Witnesses, the Lieutenant-Governor, who was himself the Prosecutor, before the said Court had gone through their Proofs of the Accusation, ordered the Judge-Advocate, when the Court was not fitting, to deliver up the Proceedings of the said Court to him; but this the Judge-Advocate refused to do, without an Order from the President; and the President refused to give such Order, without an Authority from the Court assembled.

The Lieutenant-Governor, finding he could not get the Proceedings themselves into his Hands, or make out his Charge, threatened to dissolve the Court, and call a new one, but being diflliaded from absolutely dissolving the said Court, who were to have met the next Morning, by their own Adjournment, he arbitrarily 3nd illegally adjourned the same fine die, ordered the President and Members to repair immediately to their respective Garrisons, and continued the said Sir Henry Erskine in his Confinement, without a Possibility of obtaining his Liberty, or clearing his Character, by making a Defence.

The Court-Martial was upwards of Threc Weeks under this Adjournment; during which Time the said Sir Henry Er/kine remained in Arrest.

The Lieutenant-Governor was at length prevailed on, by repeated Letters from the said Sir Henry Erskine, to rc-assemble the Court. It met; and after having heard his Defence, and several Witnesses on his behalf, pronounced Sentence; which he has been since informed was in his Favour.

Sir


24 Geo. II. 11 ° — 120

IX7

Sir Henry Erskine was continued in Arrest many Days after the Sentence was past; and the Proceedings and Sentence were delivered to the said Lieutenant Governor, who received the same; but the said Lieutenant-Governor has neither made them publick, or ever signified, either to the said Sir Henry Erskine, or to the President or Judge-Advocate, whether the said Sentence has been approved of or not.

The said Sir Henry Erskine was at last discharged from his Arrest, and ordered to his Duty, in his proper Garrison, in the said Island, by the said Lieutenant-Governor; which Order, signified to him by the Fort Adjutant of Saint Philips, contained not the smallest Intimation of the Sentence; of which he has never been able to procure any Copy from the said L eutenant Governor, or prevail on him to pubiifh the fame, notwithstanding Application has been made to him for that Purpose.

Sterling in England; and by the Sinking of the Value of the Currency so much, the Creditors of the said Colony, and all Persons who reside therein, whose Effects or Estate have confided in Money, or Bills of publick Credir, have been greatly defrauded:

Thar what affects tire Exchange between Great Britain and any One of the Four Colonies, will affect the Exchange of all the rest:; '

' That, in his Opinion, it is not poflibl^ to prevent the introducing Rhode Island Bills in the other Three Colonies, nor to prevent the Government of Rhode Island making fresh Emittion of Bills, without an Act of Parliament:

That he knows many Persons, possessed of large Effects in the said Colony, who designed to come to England to live, but were prevented by the depreciating the Value of their Money, by the Increase of Bills of Credit; and . have been thereby rendered incapable of paying their Debts here:

That no general Tax has been levied, for paying off or sinking the Bills of Treafiiry, for upwards of 20 Years pafl, which ought to have been done, except One in 1744, for 10,000l. their Currency, which is less now than I,oco /. Sterling.

Then he laid before your Committee a Journal of the Proceedings of the General Assembly of the Colony of Rhode Island, which was transmitted to him, with a Petition to his Majesty, from the most considerable Merchants, and Persons of great Eftares, in the said Colony; in which is an Account or State of the Paper Currency*of the Colony of Rhode Island, &c.; which, upon comparing it with the Account or State to the Petition annexed, they agreed in every Particular.

Your Committee observing, that in the said Account 176,964/. 6 s. 10 i d< is said to be paid in, and burnt, at several Times, Mr. Grant said, That that was mostly paid with Money received from England, granted upon Account of the Canada Expedition:

’ That in the said Journal are several Petitions, dated June ijth, 175c, and Third Monday in August 1750,-signed by a great Number of Persons, 10 the General Assembly, against emitting any more Bills of Credit; and in the said Journal is also a Resolution of the House of Deputies of v: the said Colony, dated August 24th, 1750, That the Sum of 50,000 /. in Bills of publick Credit, of a new Tenor, be emitted by this Colony, to be let out upon Loan; and a Bill was ordered to be prepared for that Purpose; which 50,000l. is equal in Value to 400,000 /. Bills of Credit, of the old Tenor.

Then the Journal of the House, of the 25th of April 1740 (That an humble Address be prefenced to his Majesty, humbly to desire him that he will be graciously pleased to require and command the respective Governors of his Colonies and Plantations in America, punctually and effectually to observe his Majesty’s Royal Instructions, not to give afient to, or to pass, any Acts, whereby Bills of Credit may be issued in lieu of Money, without a Clause be inserted in such Act, declaring that the same shall not take Effect, until the said Act shall be approved by his Majesty), was read: In pursuance of which Address, a Letter from the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, approved by an Order of their Excellencies the Lords Justices, in Council, dated 14 August 1740, was, with a Copy of the said Address, fenc to the Governor and Company of Rhode Island, signifying to them, that by the said Address they might perceive how much the House of Commons apprehend the.Commerce of Great Britain to have been affected by the large and frequent

1750.

Emissions of Paper Currency, in his Majesty’s Colonies in America, in which Rhode Island has had too large a Share; and that his Majesty in pursuance of the said Address, had fenc circular Instructions to the several Colonies more immediately under his Government, not to pass any more Bills for the lfiuing of Paper Money, without a Clause inserted therein, to suspend the Execution till his Majesty’s Pleasure should be signified thereupon; and admonishing, and advising them to pay all due Regard to his Majesty’s Intentions, and to the Sense of the House of Commons, upon this Occasion.

Then the Journal of the House, of the 29th of May 1749 (That an humble Address be prefenred to his Majesty, that he will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that there be laid before this House, in the next Session of Parliament, an Account of the Tenor and Amount of all the Bills of Credit which have been created and issued in the several British Colonies and Plantations in America, as well those under Proprietors and Charters, as under his Majesty's immediate Commission and Government, that Shall be then outstanding, distingnishing the Amount of the same in each Colony or Plantation, and the respective Times when such Bills, so outstanding, were issued, with the Amount of the said Bills in Money of Great Britain, both at the Times when such Bills were issued, and at the Time of preparing the said Accounts, and also the Times fixed for the Calling in Sinking, and Discharging, such Bills, and the Funds appropriated for that Purpose), was also read: In pursuance of which Address^ his Grace the Duke of Bedford, one of his Majesty’s.Principal Secretaries of State, on the 19th of July 1749, wrote a Letter to the Governor and Company of Rhode Island, signifying the said Address to them, and his M.ajcity’s Pleasure thereon, that they should order the Accounts, mentioned in the said Address, to be transmitted to him, in order to their being laid , before the Parliament j which Account was transmitted to his Grace accordingly; and being pro duced to your Committee, and compared with the Account or State of the Paper Currency of the said Colony, to the Petition annexed, it agreed therewith.

Upon the whole, your Committee came to the following Resolutions

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Value of Silver, in the Colony of Rhode Island, hath, between the Years 1742 and 1749, varied from 28 s. or thereabouts (the Value in 1742) in 6oj. per Ounce, or thereabouts (the Value in 1749); and that in 1742 the Exchange between England and Rhode Island was from jod/. to 550/. Rhode Island Currency, for 100l. Sterling, and in the Year 1749 the Exchange was from 1,050/. to 1,100l. Rhode Island Currency, for 100l. Sterling in England.

Resolved, That in the Four Governments of New England \ viz. the Massachusetts Bay, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and ConneRicut, the Bills of Credit issued in One Government have a promifeuous Currency in the other Three Governments; and Experience has shewn it to be impradicable to prevent the Introduction of Bills of Credit issued in One Government, into the other Three, without an Act of Parliament of Great Britain.

Resolved, That the great Rife in the Value of Silver, and in the Exchange, occasioned by the repeated Emiftions of Paper Bills of Credit (particularly in Rhode Island) hath been the Means of defrauding the Creditors, in all the Four Governments, of great Part of their Property; and, by introducing Confusion into Dealings, hath proved a great Discouragement to the Trade of these Kingdoms.

Resolvedy That, notwithstanding repeated Notices of the Senle of this House, the said Colony of Rhode Island, on the 3rd of August last, passed a Vote for emitting of JO,000/, in Bills of publick Credit, of a new Tenor, equal to 400,000l. Currency, to be let ouc upon Loan, in Contempt and Defiance of the Authority of his Majesty, and this House, contrary to the Representations and Remonstrances of many of their own Inhabitants, to the further Depreciation of their Currency, and the defrauding of the Creditors of all the Four Colonies.

A Petition of the Merchants, principal Inhabitants, Foreign Pro-Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and Artificers, of the City of tcstants Nat-Bristol\ whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House,

That though, from the Titles of the Two Petitions, which have been presented to the House (the one in the Name of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their common Seal; and the other in the Name of the Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchant Adventurers within the same City) praying, that the House would pass the Bill for the general Naturalization of foreign Protestants into a Law, it might be reasonably inferred, that the Sense of all the Citizens of the said ancient and opulent City appears thereby, yet that in Fact there were not more than Forty individual Persons consenting to both the said Petitions; and that the Petitioners, who are some of the most considerable Merchants, Tradesmen, and Artificers, within the said City, were no-ways consulted thereon, or privy thereto; and that the Petitioners (notwithstanding what is suggested by the said Petitions) conceive, that should the said Bill pass into a Law, the fame, instead of being an Advantage to the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom, would be highly prejudicial to the Interest thereof, for that it would not only tend to the depriving of many thousands of the industrious Artificers and Poor, from procuring a sufficient Support for themselves and Families, and thereby, of confluence, in crease the Poor Rates, but that besides, the Introduction of such a number of Foreigners, instead of being a Support to the present happy Establishment, might endanger the Subversion of our Constitution; and that the Petitioners also apprehend, that should this Bill pass into a Law, the fame, instead of increasing our Manufactures, would, in the End, tend greatly to the Diminution thereof, in regard that many Foreigners, under the Umbrage of such a Law, would come and reside amongst us'for a time, in order only to inform themselves in the Nature of the several Methods and Managements of our Manufacturers and Artificers, and, after having made themselves Matters thereof,return again into their native Countries, and there carry on or assist in the carrying on. Manufactures of the like kind, to the Detriment of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
