stortMeach Mr. Berkeley reported from the Committee, to whom Road. £he Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of North-leach, in the County of Gloucefi&, on behalf of them-felwes, and many others, travelling the Road leading from the Top of Crickley Hill to a Place called Frogg Mill, and from thence to Burford and Witney, and so on through the Parities of Hanborough and Bladen, int;o the great Road leading from Woodfiock to Oxford at Campsfield, in the Parish of Kidlington, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered k in at the Clerk’sTable; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition;

Mr. Richard Ricketts said, That the Town of North-leach is an ancient Market Town, where formerly a considerable Trade was carried on, which of late Years has very much decreased, and is now almost loft; that it lies upon the ancient Road from Gloucester to Oxford, is a Post Town, and formerly Stage Coaches uftd to go through the Town, and Horses for Stage Coaches were kept in the Town; that in the said Town are Four Pumps, Plenty of running Water, and many good Houses of Entertainment, and is very conveniently situated for the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Parishes to lodge Goods and Parcels carried between Gloucester and Oxford:

That Horses for the Stage Coaches have not been kept 3n the said Town for upwards of Thirty Years past; the Coaches generally since that Time having gone another Road upon the Hill, about a Quarter of a Mile from the Town: That he apprehends the Reason the Stage Coaches did not continue to go through the Town, was the Bad-ness^of the Road; and the Loss of the Trade, he apprehends, was owing to Persons travelling the other Road, apd the Want of a Market in the said Town:

Mr. William Robins said, That from the turning out of the Road through Northleach into the Road again is only Four Miles and Sixty-six Lugg; and the Road now used, from the turning out to the coming into it again, is Four Miles:

That the Road through Northleach may be easier amended than the Road upon the Hill; the former lying through a shallow Soil and rocky Ground, and Stone much easier got, and at a cheaper Rate, and the latter is a deep miry Clay; that he has computed the Expence of repairing both Roads; and the Road through Northleach will cost Four Pounds per Furlong less than the Road upon the Hill:

That the Road through Northleach being the hardest Road, Waggons in Winter frequently go that Way; and twice this Winter he has seen the Stage Coach go through Northleach:

That the Road upon the Hill is the flatter Road, though the other is but a little up Hill and down, going into and out of the Town of Northleach; and that, were both the Roads amended, a Carriage would be but a Quarter of an Hour more going through Northleaeb than the other Road:

That at Northleach are many good Houses of Entertainment, several Pumps, and a constant Supply of running Water, which is very convenient for Cattle travelling; whereas, in the other Road, there is only Qnc Von. 26.

House of Entertainment, oh any Water, but at One Place; to be had in dry Seasons for many Miles together; and in a very dry Summer there has been so great a Want of Water there, that he has been obliged to go Half a Mile to fetch Water: That this happened about Twelve Years ago; but he has known the like happen for Two or Three Years together, till the Ponds there were altered; the last of which was finished about Two or Three Years agoi

That if the Road through Northleach was amended, and Carriages went that way, Passengers would have the.

Advantage also of passing by the aforesaid House of Entertainment and watering Place.

Mr.Jujliman Lovefy said, That the Road through Northleach is capable of being amended cheaper than thd. other Road, by reason hard Stone is easier to be got for the Repairs thereof th^n for repairing the Road upon the Hill; and the Road through Northleach being a light and rocky Ground, the other a deep miry Clay:

That at Northleach is plenty of Water, but on the other Road there is only One Place for many Miles together, to water Cattle at; which is private Property, and is generally attended with Expence to the Driver:

That on the Hill Road Five Parishes. are obliged to do Statute-work, and on the Road through Northleach only Four; but for the effectual Repair of either Road, more is to be depended upon from what will arise by a Toll than from what the Inhabitants can do.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing the Road from the Top of Crickley Hill, in the County of Gloucester, to Frogg Mill, and through the Towns of Burford and Witney, and Parishes of Hanborough and Bladen, to Campsfield, in the Parish of Kidlington, in the County of Oxford; and also the Road from Witney, through Ensham, Cumner, Wigh-tam, and Botley, to the City of Oxford; is committed;

That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, for repairing the Road from Frog Mill through North-leach, to Burford and Witney.

and setting forth, That the Charges of building and finishing the said proposed Bridge, with necessary Ramparts or Wings, will amount to a very large Sum of Money, which the Petitioners are informed is intended to be levied and raised by a Tax to be laid upon all the Lands in the said County Palatine; and that the Place where the said Bridge is proposed to be fixed and set does not lie in the Post Road from London, leading to the North Part of the County of Lancaster, and from thence to the several Counties of Westmorclotid, and Cumberland, or in any other Post Road; and that there is an ancient Stone Bridge, of Five Arches, over the said River, within a Mile, or thereabouts, of the Place where the intended Bridge is proposed to be built, which has been always repaired at the Expence of the said County, and which is now in good Repair, and (lands in the great Post Road leading to the North Part of England and Scotland, and within less than a Mile of the Borough of Prefon; which Road takes in the South-East, and a great Part of the West Side of the said County Paiatine of Lancaster; and that, adjoining to the South End of the said Bridge, there is a Road called Walton Ccpp, of Half a Mile in Length, which has also been always repaired by the said County, at a very great Expence, and is now incomplete Repair; and that there is a Ford at Penwortham, near the Place where the intended Bridge is proposed to be built, which is always passable, except in Tides and Land-Floods; and there is a good Ferry for Horse and Foot, within a very little Distance of the Place where the intended Bridge is proposed to be built; and alleging that the said intended Bridge will be of very little, if of any, Use to the North, North-East, Sourh, or Middle Part, of the said County Palatine (except the Borough of Vreston, and a small Part of the Country adjacent thereto) and that all Passengers and Carriages, to or from Liverpool to Preston, may avoid the Ford or Ferry ^Penwortham,at all unfealon-VoL. 26f

able Times, and have the Benefittff a Turnpike-Road, by going over Ribble Bridget which is very littte more than Two Miles about; and1 that the Petitioners conceive such intended Bridge, if erected, will not be of so general Use and Service, as to intitle the Gentlemen Promoters of the Bill, or to give them any reasonable Pretence to call upon the County to make good the Expences of building and maintaining the fame, with proper Ramparts and Work: And therefore praying. Foreign Pro- A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Afilstants, of testants Na- the City of Rochester, in Common-Council assembled, was uialijauon. presentcc| to tjjC House, and read; alleging, That the I VOL. 26.

Petitioners apprehend, and verily believe, the Bill depending in the Houie- for naturalizing foreign Protestants, in case the same should pass into a Law, will be attended with many bad Consequences and Inconveniences 5 and be a grear Discouragement, not only to the natural-born Subjects of this Kingdom, but likewise.a Detriment to the Trade and Wealth thereof; particularly, as the Petitioners have great Reason to think, that it will only induce the poorest and most indigent foreign Protestants, and their Families, to come and settle amongst us, in order to their being better provided for, and maintained, by the several Parishes in which they may reside: which will be a further Increase of the Poor of such respective Parishes, already so much over-burthened, that they are even now with great Difficulty, provided for; and that daily Experience convinces us, that the industrious Foreigners never fail of receiving proper Encouragement, from the constant Employ they meet with amongst us; and that if any Persons of Fortune, or any tolerable Ability, should be desirous of partaking of those inestimable Privileges, so peculiarly the BlefTing of the natural-born Subjects of this Kingdom, they may, upon their Application to Parliament, be intitled to the same; and that many Foreigners (probably some of them Roman Catholics) who will perhaps never so much as think of refining amongst us, may; notwithstanding, fend over their Servants, or Agents; in order to receive the Benefit of such a Law; that they may make use of his or their Names, in carrying on their Trade} and submirting to the judgment of the House* how far it may prejudice, if not totally frustrate, the Intent of having our Navigation carried on byTHree-fourths of the Mariners being English (which, if this Bill should pass into a Law, may be wjiolly performed by Foreigners, who may never reside Here longer than to obtain their, being naturalized); and expressing the Apprehensions of the Petitioners, that so great an indulgence to Foreigners; although Protestants, as they differ very much from the,

Religion of our Country, and have not a true Sense of those great and valuable Privileges this Nation enjoys, under our present happy Establishsnent in Church and State, may be so far from strengthening and improving that Zeal and Affection, every Britiftj Subject has and ought, at all times, to shew For his native Country, that it will rather greatly rend to the weakening, if not invading, of our Civil and Religious Rights: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And the said Answer was read; and is as followeth; toiz.

Answer of Lieutenant-General Anstruther y to the Complaint exhibited against him in the HonourableHouse of Commons by Sir Henry Erskine Baronet. Lieutenant-General Anstrutlftr returns his most humble Thanks to the House, for the Copy sent him of die Complaint exhibited against him by Sir Henry Erskine*

To an Accusation, alleging nothing, and insinuating every thing that was villainous, it was difficult to answer; but the Honourable House has obliged his Accufcr to reduce his Charge into Writing* and to that Lieutenant-General Anstruther most readily, and conformably to the strictest Truth, answers as follows:

Lieutenant-General Anstruther allows. That in the Year 1742 he was Lieutenant-Governor, and Commander in Chfef in the I (land of Minorca:

That Sir Henry Erskine was then a Lieutenant there, in Colonel OjfareWs Regiment:

That in the Month of May or June he was put in Arrest; and, in consequence thereof, remained not in any Fort or Cattle, as is insinuated in the Charge, but in an Officer's Quarter in the Town of St. Phillip's; where any Body might have, and had, Accefe to hito:

That he continued there some time before the Charge was delivered to him; that he was called upon by the Court of Royal Government, and there required to give his Evidence, upon Oath, in a Cause there depending, according to the Laws and Customs of that Island* but Lieutenant-General Anstruther denies, that it was alleged against Sir Henry Erskine as a Crime, that he refused to answer Questions that might relate to himself: And fays. He then told Sir Henry Erskine, that if any Question should be put, which he thought might affect himself, he was not to be deftred to answer it; which Sir Henry Er-yfoV/^acknowledgts in the Proceedings of the Court Martial; but does say, that it was alleged against Sir Henry Erskine as a Crime, that he refused absolutely to answer, as he ought to do* according to the Laws and Customs of that Island.

Lieutenant-General Anstruther begs Leave to observe. That the Court Martial did not fit till the 24th of June 1742, which was Six whole Days after Sir Henry Erskine had his Charge delivered to him and that the Delay, between the putting Sir Henry Erskine into Arrest and bringing on his Trial, was not with aoy Intention to distress him, but arose, amongst other Reasons, from the Time taken to persuade a Person of the Rank and Character of Lieutenant-General JJ^ndafyd to be President of the Court

Martial; who, however,being an elder Officer than Lieutenant-General Anstruther, could not be persuaded thereto; and the Crime being of a very dark and intricate Nature, it required some time to collect Evidences, though the General had good Reason to believe the Fadts were true; and say?, that had Sir Henry Erjkirit, when called lipon by the Court of Royal Government as an Evidence, candidlV declared what he knew of the Transactions in the General's Absence to His Prejudice, that he would not have ihfifted upon bringing him to a Court Martial.

Lieutenant-Genei-al Anstruther denies, that the Court Martial appointed to try Sir HenrJ Erskine was cdnstituted in any uhusual Manner.

He fays. It is true, thafc Two of the Evidences offered by him to the Court, were under a Sentence of the Court of Royal Government; but, in regard to their being re* fused to be set at liberty, as required by the Court Martial, and the Reason alleged to be given for such Refusal, namely, <c That they were notorious Rogues ,*' it is so fat from being true, that, in fact, the Court Martial never made any such Request, as by their Proceedings will appear; and he begs Leave here, in general, to observe once for all, that he is only One of Three Members who compose the Court of Royal Government; and that the Or- ders and Sentences there given are not his, but the Orders and Sentences of the Court; and fays, if the Witnesses above-mentioned were under any Reftrainc, it was by Order of the Court, and not by his Order.

With Regard to his fending a Message to one of these Witnesses, or to any other Person, inducing them to give false Evidence, he utterly denies it: To procure false Evidence is a Crime of* so heinous a Nature; as he trusts this Honourable House shall never find the least Reason to suppose him guilty of; it is the very Crime Sir Henrf Erskine was accused of, and which was positively sworn against him by James Xemenes, as will appear in the Proceedings of the Court Martial.

The General owns, That before the Prisoner had begun his Defence, he desired the Judge Advocate to bring him' a Copy of the Proceedings, that he might fee what had been said by the Evidence against the Prisoner; which he thought was the more requisite as he was the Prosecutor, and, con6deringhis Station, could not attend the Court.

He likewise owns, That he desired a Copy of the Proceedings from the Court Martial; which he ftiil beg» Leave to think was a reasonable Request: But fays. That he never threatened to dissolve the Court, and call a new one but he did adjourn the said Court; which he did consider to be neither arbitrary nor illegal, because frequently practised in military Business, and at that time extremely necessary for the following Reason, which he begs Leave to lay before the House:

One Mr. Murray, who had been employed by Sic Henry Erskine to write in his Office when Secretary to Brigadier Paget, and whom the General relied upon as. One of his principal Evidences, was secreted, that disappeared, or was sent privately out of the Istand, a. few Days before this Trial was to come on, without General Anstruther's Knowledge, but not without the Knowledge and Privity of Sir Henry Erskine, though then in Arrest, as he himself owned, and as will appear in the Proceedings of the Court Martial.

Upon Inquiry, Mr. Rancon, One of General Anstru-ther's Secretaries, acknowledged, That he had given One of General /Instruther's Paffporcs to this Mr. Murray* without the General's Knowledge; for which Action the General instantly dilmifted him from his Service, and never afterwards employed him; and the General fays, the First Notice he had of this Transed&orv came from. Sir Henry Erskine.

The General fays, He had some Intelligence of rhls, Mr. Murray, and was in Hopes of being able, during this Adjournment, to produce him; but, having used all- his Endeavours for that Purpose, was disappointed and he fays, he believes it is very unusual, if ever pradlifcd, to liberate a Prisoner during the Adjournment of a Court Martial,

A Petition of the Hop Planters in the County of Essex, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Hop Planters are at very large Expence in the Planting and Stocking their Hop Grounds with Poles, and Management of tjiem, before any thing can arise, amounting at lea-ft to Forty bounds an Acre, which remains a dead Stock; many of which Grounds will hold but few Years, and other fresh Grounds are to be raised in their (lead at the like Expence; and that, after the said Grounds are got into such Order, there is a very great annual Expence in keeping up the Stock, and cultivating the said Grounds,before the Crop is grown; and after grown, in picking, drying, and inning the fame, besides a Duty of One Penny per Pound; in Confederation of which Expences, the Proprietors of the Tythes did at first, and for many Years, accept of a moderate Composition, in lieu of those Tythes > but that of late Years, they have in general, from time to time, largely raised those Compositions, and many of them actually taken the Hops in Kind, and in divers Places (though in itself the hardest Tythe that ever was paid) have, contrary to all other Tythes (which are to be taken . as soon as fevered) obliged the Planters to pick the Tythe Hops, the fexpence of which alone is often more than the Value of the Rent of the Land; and that it has occasioned many expensive Law Suits, some now depending, and many more likely to be commenced; and that the Petitioners have great Cause to apprehend, that the Method of taking Tythe of Hops in Kind (oppressive as it is) will become general, unless the House will take into Consideration the Hardship of their same; and representing to the House, That the taking of the Tythe of Hops in Kind must necessarily occasion a great Diminution of their Plantations, by rendering many of the Planters unable to&ear the Expence, and by greatly aif-couraging the Industry of others; and that great Numbers of poor Families are at present wholly, or in a great mea-. sure, supported, by being employed in Hop Grounds, who otherwise, for want of Employment, must become burthen some to the Parishes; and that not only Wood-Lands in particular, will be of much less Value, but the Rents of other Lands lowered by so greatly increasing the Parish Rates; and the publick Revenue must be considerably diminished as to that Duty: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give such Relief therein as to the House shall seem most fit and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole Hou'e, to whom the Petition of the Hop Planters, residing in and near the City of Canterbury, a&d other Places, in the County of Kent, on behalf of themselves and others; and also the . several other Petitions relating to the Tythe of Hops; are referred.

Sir William Stanhope reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Noblemen, Gentlemen, arid others. Inhabitants of Eafi Greenwich, and Places adjacent, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of che said Petition, Witnesses were called > vix Mr. Abraham Allen and Mr. Thomas Moore; who, being severally examined* said. That they are well acquainted with the Parish of East Greenwich; that there are large Buildings in and about the Town, as also a Royal Palace, and an Hospital for Seamen 5 and within a Quarter of a Mile of the feme, adjoining close to the River Thames, there is situated in an open low Place, a Storehouse or Magazine for Gunpowder, in which, there is frequently kept about 4*000 Barrels; which, if by *Accident of Lightening, or otherwise, it, should be set on Fire, the Houses and Buildings in and near the said Town would be destroyed.

And they further said, That Application had been made by the Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants of the said Town, to the Board of Ordnance, requesting that the said Magazine might be removed; to which an Answer from that Board had been returned, dated the 14th Decern for 1750, in the following Words; viz. " That it was not " in their Power to remove the King's Magazine, or to " make a Purchase of Land, and erect another elsewhere."

Mr. Thomas Furnace, many Years Storekeeper of the said Magazine, being examined, said, That the same is fenced round with an open Palisade of about Eight Feet high, and a constant Guard of a Serjeant, Corporal, and Nine private Men, do Duty there Night and Day for the Safeguard thereof; that the Quantity of Powder at this Time kept therein is about 8,000 Barrels (which is the largest Quantity he ever knew); but that, on aMediurh, One Year with another for many Years past, not more than 3 or 4,000 Barrels of Powder is kept there; and all possible Care is taken when it is received into the fame, or delivered out.,

Mr.....Skinner, Engineer belonging to the Board

of Ordnance, being examined, feid. That the Magazine lying so low makes it the more dangerous; for if the same should be set on Fire by any Accident, it would overset the Houses and Buildings in and near Greenwich, and tear up the Banks of the River Thames adjoining thereto; but doth not apprehend it could have any Effect on the Houses and Buildings at Deptford or Woolwich: And he added. That the Magazine is in pretty good Repair at present; but, as it is situated, there is no Pofii-bility of making the same so safe as where the Foundation is firm, and where Arches may be turned for Security of the Powder, as all Magazines should be, to prevent Accidents by Lightening, or otherwise:

That, by Order of the Board of Ordnance, the Witness, with several other Persons, had been down the River Thames, in Search of a Place whereon to erect a Magazine, and the only One they found proper for that Purpose was at Purjleet; it lying so high, and being Two Miles from any Village, no Damage can happen, if che same should be blown up.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, that he will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that an Estimate be laid before this House of the Expence of removing the Magazine of Gunpowder, now being within a few Paces of the Town of Greenwich, to some more convenient Place, and further Distance from the said Town, and Cities of London and Westminster.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most Honourable Privy Council.

That King Charles the First, by his Letters Patent, in the Twelfth Year of his Reign, by the Advice of his Privjr-Council, constituted certain Commissioners therein named, to view and survey the River Avon, in the Counties of Warwick, Worcester, and Gloucester, at the Expence of one William Sandys, and to do as therein is mentioned* to make the same navigable, in the Counties aforesaid, for the better supplying of the said Counties with Wood, Iron, Coal, and other Commodities, which they then wanted; and that, in Recompence of his great Charge therein, the said William Sandys, but not his Heirs or Executors, was thereby intitled to the Benefit of the Water-Carriages thereon, as in such Cases is usual; and the said Commissioners were to report their Progress and Proceedings therein, from time to time, to the said Council, that such further Measures might be taken by the said Council, as to them should seem meet) but that the Usurpation corning on, no further Orders were made for settling the Trade, or any other Matters relative to the said River; and that, during the Usurpation, it was in the Poflfcflion of one William Say, upon whose Attainder it became forfeited; after which, by a Grant now recorded in the Rolls, 16 September, 13 Charles ad, all the Manors and Estates, of Persons attainted, and therein named (amongst whom William Say was one) were, in most general Words, without particularly describing them, or even saying in what Counties they were, granted to Lord Berkley, and others, in Trust, for James Duke of York, who, in the Month of June 1664, in Consideration of 500l. assigned over all his and their Term therein (but how long that was, the Petitioners are entirely ignorant) to an Anccftor of the present Proprietor, who, by virtue thereof, has leased out the Profits thereof, at various Rents; and his Tenants, or their Agents, have, time after time, in consequence thereof, varied the Rates of Tonnage thereon, at Pieafure; and, under Pretence of its being a private Property, the said Tonnage is now become arbitrary, and, by Means thereof, a heavy Load upon the People, instead of the publick Good, which it was at first intended to be; and that, though by a Clause in an Act passed in the 14th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, the said Navigation was ordered to be continued and preserved, and Commissioners were thereby appointed to settle all Disputes relating thereto, without mentioning to whom the Navigation then belonged, yet it does not appear, that the said Commissioners, or any of them, acted or did any thing in the Premiles, but that the Owners and their Tenants have ever since acted and done as they pleased, and have not only monopolized the Coal-Trade thereof, and fixed such unequitable and high Rates of Tonnage thereon, which now equal the Freightage upon Corn and Goods, called Merchandize, passing upon the said River, as greatly to prejudice the Vol. 26.

Trade in general, and the Petitioners in particular; but have likewise made various other Exactions on People navigating-up and down the said River; aria used such arbitrary Methods of proceeding, that the comttion Metfiods of Law, for Redress, could not with; Safety-be fiftefby Persons aggrieved; and that the same appears to the Petitioners to be such, that nothing but parliamentary Aid can give Redrds: And therefore pteying the , House,

Avon Navi- A Petition of Herbert Lord Viscount Windsor, in the gation. Kingdom of Ireland, Baron Mountjoy of the Isle of Wight, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner and his Ancestors have been for many Years past, the Owners and Proprietors of the Navigation of the River Avon, running through the Counties of Warwick, Worcester, and Gloucester, formerly made navigable by William Sandys, Esquire, at an Expence of 20,000l. or thereabouts; and that the Petitioner and his Ancestors have expended many Thousand Pounds in supporting and maintaining the said Navigation, and have, by themselves or Tenants, received the accustomed Tonnage, and other Duties, for all Vessels navigating on the said River; and reciting Part of a Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, capital Burgesses, and other the Inhabitants of the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester; and observing, that Two other Petitions from the Towns of Parjhore and Chipping Campden, and other Villages and Parishes near the said River of Avon, have been also presented to the House, in relation to the said Navigation; and alleging, That the Petitioner is advised, that the Clause in the Act of Parliament of the 14th of King Charles the Second, relating to the River Avon, mentioned in the said Petitions, is in the First of the said Petitions mifiepresented, for that the Commissioners, by the said Act appointed, had only Powers to determine Differences between the Proprietors of the Navigation and the Land-Owners, touching the cutting and making navigable of the said River, but not in relation to the Tonnage and Duties payable to the Petitioner, and those under whom he claims. Proprietors of the said Navigation; and that the Petitioner apprehends, his Property may be affefted by the Bill, prayed by the said Petitions to be brought into this House: And therefore praying, That the House will give Leave that he may be heard before the Committee, to whom the said Petitions are referred, against the said several Petitions, or that the House will give the Petitioner Rich other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confident ion of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, capital Burgesses, and other the Inhabitants, of the Borough of Evesham, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Com- McmlcsCoal mittee, to whom the Petition of Michael Menzies Esquire, Machine, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition;

William Lambton Esquire, informed your Committee,

That he had seen the said Machine or Engine, mentioned in the Petition, made use of; that it is worked by the Weight of Water only, and did draw up the Corf of 1 8 Pecks of Coals, which is about 500 Pound Weight, from the Bottom of a Pit of 50 Fathom, in a Minute and a Half: That it is a very expeditious Way of drawing up Coals from the Bottom to the Mouth of the Pit; which Evidence was confirmed by a Member prefenc, who had also seen the said Machine worked.

Mr. John Craufurd said. That he has seen a Model of the said Machine, which he thinks a very fine Invention; and is of Opinion^that it will draw Coals from the Walls where they are dug to the Bottom of the Pit, and from thence to the Pit’s Mouth, and so to the Heaps and Staiths, in a more expeditious and cheap Method than any other Engine he has ever seen.

Then Letters Patent, dated the 9th Day of February, in the 2 3d Year of the Reign of his prefer.t Majesty,were produced, which invest the sole Use and Benefit of the said Machine, in that Parc of Great Britain called England, in the said Michael Menzies, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, for the Term of Fourteen Years:

And also Letters Parent, dated the 19th of October 1750, for the like Use of the said Machine, for that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, for the Term of Fourteen Years,

Then Mr. Craufurd informed your Committee, That Mr. Menzies had spent a great deal of Time in inventing the said Machine, and in crying Experiments of the fame; and had also been at great Expence in obtaining the said Letters Patents:

That the said Mr, Menzies was bred a Counsellor in Scotland, and had practised as such for several Years;

which

24 Geo. II. 25° Martii.

which Business he has almost totally quitted, in purfuitof the said Invention:

Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioner hath fully proved the Allegations of his Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill, for vesting the lole Property of the said Machine in the said Micbae^Menzies, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, for such further Term as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for vesting, fora certain Term of Years, in Michael Menzies Esquire, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Property of a Machine, by him invented, for conveying of Coals from the Places where they are dug to the Heaps at the Mouths of the Pits; and, in some Cafes, from the Heaps to the Staiths, or Places where they are put on board Ships or Keels: And that the Lord Advocate of Scotland and Mr. Andrew Mitchell do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Bridge, subscribed, Gentlemen, Land-Owners, and Farmers, in behalf of themselves, and many others, in the Hundred of Blackburney in the County Palatine of Lancaster y was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That there is a Petition presented to the House, praying for Leave to bring in a Bill for erecting a publick County Stone Bridge over the River Ribbley between the Town-ships of Penwortham and PreJlony in the said County Palatine, at or near the old Fords and Ferry; and setting forth, That the Charge of building the said proposed Bridge, and making a Rampart necessary for a Passage thereto, which will amount to a very large Sum, is to be levied and raised by a Tax upon the said County Palatine; and that the said proposed Bridge will not be in the Western Port: Road to the Northern Countie-, nor of any VoL. 26.

149

Service or Convenience to the Petitioners, and the greatest Part of the said County; and that there are Three good Fords through the River Ribble, near where the said Bridge is proposed to be built, and, when the same are rendered impassable by Floods or high Tides, there is a good Ferry for Horse and Foot; and that Persons, who do not choose to go over the said Ferry, by going a little more than Two Miles about, come into the great Turn-pike Post Road leading from London to Preston, and any other Place Northward, and have a Passage over the said River at a large Stone Bridge, which is within a Mile, or thereabouts, of the said new intended Bridge, and is now in good Repair, being maintained by the said County Palatine at a very great Charge; and representing the Injustice of an Attempt to burthen the Petitioners, or their Estates, with any Part of the Charge of building the said Bridge, as the Value of their Lands is greatly diminished by the Mortality amongst the horned Cattle, and they can receive no Benefit or Convenience from such new Bridge: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill.

A Petition of several of the Aldermen, Gentlemert, and others, in the Borough of Wigan, and Land-Owners, and Farmers, in the Townships adjacent, in behalf of themselves, and many others, of the Hundreds of Ley-land and Derby, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; fetcing forth, That there is an ancient large Stone County Bridge over the said River Ribble, within the Distance of One Mile, or thereabouts, from the Place where the new intended Bridge is proposed to be built; and that there are several good Fords, pafiable for Carts and Horses over the said River, except in case of high Tides and Floods, and, at such times, a good Ferry for Horse and Foot near to the Place where the said Bridge is intended to be built; and that there are Two Roads leading froto Ormskirk, in the said County, to Preston aforesaid; the One over Bank Bridge, and from thence to the new intended Bridge at Preston, and the other, leading through the Townships of Eccleston and Walton in le Daley in the said County, over the said ancient County Bridge, to Preston; which last mentioned Road is the better Road, and only One Mile and Three Quarters Statute-Measure, or thereabouts, further than the Road over the said Bank Bridge; and alleging, that there is no Necessity for such new Bridge; and that the Petitioners conceive, the said new Bridge can only be a Conveniency to a small Part of the said County; and that it is a very oppressive Attempt to lay any Part of the Charges thereof upon the respective Estates and Properties of the Petitioners, who will receive no Benefit thereby; and alleging. That no Instance can be given where there are Two County Bridges so near each other: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill.

Greenock The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Harlou^ Committee, to whom the Petition of the Managers of the ur* Vol. 26.

5

Town of Greenock's Funds, in behalf of themselves, and of the Mailers, Ship-Masters, and others, the principal Inhabitants of the said Town, and Baronies of Easter and Wester Greenock, and Fimart, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. John Cathcart, and Mr. Archibald Maclean, said.

That the Town of Greenock is situate on the River Clyde* and is very convenient for carrying on a foreign and coasting Trade:

That Sir John Schaw Baronet, who is principal Proprietor of the said Town, did, in the Year 1705, by a voluntary Subscription of the Inhabitants, begin to make a Harbour there; which is, although not completed, the moll commodious Harbour in North Britain, and capable of containing near 200 Sail of Ships; but that several Works are necessary to be done, in order to complete and preserve the said Harbour:

That the said Town of late is become very populous; and that the Managers of the Town Funds have, with the Consent of the said Sir John Schaw, made a new Parish, wherein is a Meeting-House, which they have endowed with a competent Stipend, raised by voluntary Subscription of the Inhabitants:

That there is now extremely wanted, in the said Town, a new Church, a publick School, a House for the Reception of poor Inhabitants, with proper Market-Places; but that the fame, together with the necessary Works to complete the said Harbour, will cost a considerable Sum of Money; and that, from the small Revenue of the said Town, the said Works, though so extremely necessary, cannot be carried into Execution, without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for levying a Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or One Sixth Parc of a Penny Sterling, on every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer, which shall be brewed for Sale, brought into, tapped or fold within, the Town of Greenock, and Baronies of Easter and Wester Greenock, and Fimart, and Liberties thereof, in the County of Renfrew, for repairing the Harbour of the said Town, and for other Purposes: And that the Lord Advocate of Scotland, and Mr. Hope Weir, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Farmers, and Land- Ribble Owners, in the Forest of Ro/cridale, and Parts adjacent, Bn<tee> in the Hundred of Blackburn, on behalf of themselves, and many others of the said Forest, in the County Pa* latine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That there is a Bill depending in the House, for erecting a publick County Bridge over the River Ribbley between the Townfhtpsof Preston and Pen-wortham, in the said County Palatine, at or near the Fords in the said River, and a Ferry over the fame, and forraifing Money upon the said County, for defraying the Expence thereof, and of the Ramparts, belonging thereto; and setting forth. That there is an ancient large Stone County Bridge over the said River, within the Distance of One?

Mile, or thereabouts, from the Place where the new-intended Bridge is proposed to be built; and that there are several good Fords passable for Carts and Horses, over the said River (except in case of high Tides and Floods, and at such Times a good Ferry for Horse and Foot) near to the Places where the said Bridge is intended to be built; and alleging, That the Petitioners conceive the said new Bridge can only be a Conveniency to a small Part of the said County; and that it is a very oppressive Attempt, to1 lay any Part of the Chargesfchcreof upon the respective Estates and Properties of the Petitioners, who will receive no Benefit thereby; and further setting forth, That within Twelve or Fourteen Years last past the Petitioners have, at their own private Expence, built, within the said Forest, over the Fords and Rivers, in the publick Highways,

Twelve Bridges, which are now maintained at such their Expence, and no Charge to the Hundred or County, in regard the said Bridges are near or adjoining to their own Estates; and therefore further alleging, That if the intended new Bridge is to be built, it ought to be done at the Expence of such Gentlemen as will have an Advantage thereby, and not charged upon the whole County 5 and that no Instance can be given, where there are Two County Bridges so near each other: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be head by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Hop Planters residing in and near Tythcof the County of Suffolk, and other Places in the County HoP4-of Sujjolky on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners are at a very great Expence, in the Raising, Planting, Poling, and annual Cultivation, of their Flop-Grounds, and in picking and drying their Hops; and have, besides, constantly paid a considerable Duty of One Penny perPound, charged by Law upon all Hops, towards the publick Service; and that, by reason of these great Expences, the Petitioners are unable to pay the Tythes of Hops in Kind; and have therefore been accustomed to pay a yearly Composition in lieu thereof; with which the several Persons intitled thereto were always satisfied; but that of late Tythe in Kind hasactually been taken of several of the Petitioners, and demanded of others; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive this Demand will be infilled upon, and become general, if not prevented by the Legislature; and representing to the House, That the present Method of taking the Tythe of Hops in Kind, will not only be attended with the most fatal Consequences to the Petitioners, by ruining, in a great measure, their Plantations, but must also greatly discourage and diminish the Planting of Hops in general; whereby great Numbers of poor Families, who constantly depend upon, and are employed in the Hop-Grounds in this Kingdom, will be deprived of their Support; the V alue of a considerable Part of the Wood-lands, and other Lands of this Country, be greatly affected; and the Publick lose, in great measure, the Benefit of that, at present, very considerable Branch of the Revenue, arising from the Duty upon Hops: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give the Petitioners such Relief therein, as the House shall think just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Hop Planters, residing in and near the City of Canterbury and ocher Places, in the County of Kent, on behalf of themselves, and others, and also the several. other Petitions relating to the Ty the of Hops, are % referred. j

A Petition of William Bolan Esquire, Agent for his Majesty’s Province of Massachusetts Bay, in New England, was presented to the House, and read? setting forth. That by an Act passed in the 6th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, a Duty of $s. per Hundred was laid upon all foreign Sugars, Nine Pence per Gallon on all foreign Rum, and Six Pence per Gallon on all foreign Melasses, that should, after the 25th Day of December 1733, be imported into any of his Majesty’s Colonies in America ? and that the British Sugar Colonies do not produce Rum, Sugar, and Melasses, sufficient for the Consumption of Great Britain, and the BrUish Northern Colonies, and their Fisheries, and are not able to take off and consume the Lumber and Provisions which the British Northern Colonies have to spare; and that the Prices of British Rum, Sugar, and Melasses, have greatly increased since the passing of the said Act; and reciting Part of a Petition of the British Sugar Planters, and others, which hath been presented to this House, and which complains of the said Northern Colonies? and alleging, That the said Province of Massachusetts Bay, one of the Northern Colonies, hath not had any Opportunity of being informed of the said Complaint: And therefore, as the Petitioner is Agent for the said Province, praying the House, That he may be at Liberty to be heard, in Defence of the said Province, against the groundless and injurious Charges contained in the said Petition? and that the House will be pleased to take into tlfeir Consideradon the State of his Majesty’s Northern and Sugar Colonies, with respect to the said Act of the 6th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign 5 or that the House will give such other Relief in the Premises, as they shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies, is referred; and that the Petitioner be heard before the said Committee, Upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of the Merchants of Liverpool, and the Proprietors of Brine and Rock Salt, in the County of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That this valuable Commodity has produced great Wealth to this Nation, as well as a very considerable Revenue to his Majesty; and that great Quantities of Salt are exported from that, and other Ports in Great Britain, to Ireland, to our Colonies in America, as well as to foreign Parts; but that the Laws relating to the Exportation of Salt are very defective, and often attended with great Loss and Difficulties to his Majesty’s Subjects, particularly in these Articles, wherein there is no proper Provision made for Salt shipped to Ireland, and loft in the Port where it is shipped; nor for the fame, when Part is destroyed and loft by Stress of Weather at Sea; nor for Salt loft in Barges and Boats, that bring it down the Rivers where it is made, to be shipped for Exportation} nor for Salt shipped for foreign Parts, and loft in the Port where it is laden on board; nor for Salt shipped to foreign Parts, where a Ship meets with Damage at Sea, and is forced back; and that the Proofs, required by Law in case of such Loss, are attended with great Expence and Difficulty, and very often impossible to be complied with, whereby his Majesty’s Subjects are liable to great Losses and Ruin: Ant} therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Lawsrefpsft- S*r R*chard Lloyd reported from the Committee, aping Felonies, pointed to revise and consider the Laws in being which relate to Felonies, and other Offences against the Peace; and to report their Opinion thereupon, from time to time, to the House, as to the Defcdls, the Repeal, or Amendment of the said Laws; That the Committee had considered some of the Matters to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Vo l. 26.

Resolved, That it is the (Opinion of this Committee, That the Watch within the City of Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and such Parts of the Parishes of St. Clem&nfs Danes and St. Alary le Strand, as lie within the Duchy of Lancaster, and within the several Parishes of St. Andrew Holbourn above the Bars, St. George the Martyr, SI. George Bloomsbury, and St. Giles in thi Fieldsy is defective, either as to Number, Strength, or Diligence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there is not a sufficient Power to make and raise Rates for the Watch, within the Places above-mentioned.

Resolved, Thac it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Salaries paid to Watchmen are too small to induce able-bodied Men to undertake that Service; and th£ Watching all and every Night makes it impossible for industrious Handicraftsmen or Manufadhirers, to accept of being employed as Watchmen; but that, if the Duty and Pay were divided, it might be worth while for laborious People to undertake it, as it would not hinder them from following their own Occupations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision should be made for raising and enforcing the Payment of Money for maintaining an able Watch, with in the several Parishes and Places aforesaid, where there is not sufficient Power at present to raise Money for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in the Parishes, where they have Watch Rates by Acts of Parliament, it should. be lawful for the Justices, at their Quarter-Sessions, on Complaint made by a competent Number of substantial Inhabitants, that there is a Deficiency in the Number or Strength of the Watchmen, to order such additional Number as to them shall appear to be reasonable; and to order a Rate, not exceeding a certain Sum in the Pound, over and above what they are now impowered to raise by their Watch Acts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Watchmen be always ready to attend the Constable in going round the Parish, and to guard Ptifoners, over and above such as shall have particular Walks assigned them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Constables, Watchmen, or any of them, have Power, and be authorized, to take up, and secure in their Round-House, all and every suspicious Person or Persons, that they shall find loiteringand lurking about the Streets, Pafifages, and Alleys, and do not give a iatisfadlory Account of him, her, or themselves, though he, she, or they, are not actually in the Commission of any Breach of the Peace, and carry such Person or Persons, so taken up, before a Justice of the Peace, as loon as conveniently may be, who shall, irt case no satisfactory Account is given to him, commit him, her, or them, to the House of Correction as Vagrants.

Resolved, That it is the Opiniort^of this Committee, That in order to induce Parishes to do their Duty, in preventing the Outrages which have become so frequent of late, and are grown to so enormous a Height, that, in case any Robbery shall be committed, or any Person affaulted, with an Attempt to be robbed, in any of the Highways, Streets, Lanes, or other Passages, Fields, or other open Places, within the Bills of Mortality, that such Person, 1b robbed or foafiaulted, shall, without Delay, give Information thereof before a Justice of the Peace, who shall be required immediately to fend his Warrant to the Churchwarden, Overseer, or Constable, requiring him or them to publish and advertise, in some One of the daily Papers, for Two Days together, a Reward to be paid upon the Conviction of such Offender or Offenders or any of them, to the Person or Persons who shall take, or cause to be taken and convicted, such Offender or Offenders, in such Proportions as shall be directed by the Court before whom such Person or Persons shall be convicted; which Sum, together with the Charge of Prosecution, shall be paid out of the Poor Rates of the Parish, wherein such Robbery or Afiault shall be committed.

A Petition of the Trustees appointed by, and in pur- Surry fuance of, several Acts of Parliament, made in the 4th, Roads. 6th, and 10th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty*

King George the First, and in the 10th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for repairing the several'

Roads therein mentioned, in the Counties of Surry and Sussex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; reciting Part of a Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Tradesmen, of the Counties of Surry, Sussex, Kent, and Southampton, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making, widening, and keeping in Repair, the several Roads therein mentioned; and alleging, That the Petitioners conceive, the making, and keeping in Repair, the said Roads will be of great Benefit and Advantage to the said Counties, and the City and Liberty of Westminster, and to all Persons who shall have Occasion to travel that Way; but that the Petitioners are informed. Two Gentlemen have made Propo-fals to the Committee (to whom the said Petition is referred) for making, and keeping in Repair, the said Roads, upon having a Toll granted to them by Parliament, fora certain Number of Years, with Power to remove some of the present Toll-Gates, and to erect others, upon and near to the new Roads, and to receive to their own Use

Il* Aprilis. i6i

such additional Toll, which shall be granted by Parliament for the Purposes aforesaid; and that the Petitioners conceive, the Granting of such Powers would very much, lefTen the Toll already granted by Parliament, for maintaining and repairing the Surry and Sussex Roads, and consequently affect and prejudice the Lenders, to whom the Sum of Fifteen thousand Two hundred and Fifty Pounds is now due, upon Mortgages of the Tolls already granted, in respect of their Security; and that the Petitioners apprehend, in case such new Roads, as are proposed, were made, and proper Powers vested in the present, and such other Trustees as the House shall think proper, by Authority of Parliament, such Trustees would be thereby enabled to maintain and keep the said Roads in good Repair, without the Addition of any new Toll to those already granted, but that, if the necessary Sums for making such new Roads cannot be otherwise raised than by an additional Toll, the Petitioners conceive, such Roads may be made, and kept in Repair, under the Management and Direction of a Body of Trustees appointed by Parliament, at a less Expence to the Travellers and Passengers than by any private Persons: And therefore praying the House, ro grant the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Tradesmrn, of the Counties of Surry, Sussex, Kent, and Southampton, is referred: Acd that they do examine the Matter of this Petition, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

and that, as the Monies arising by the said Two Turnpikes are more than sufficienc for keep, ing the said Road in Repair, and paying off the Monies due on the Security of the said Tolls, the Petitioners, and all others travelling on the said great Post Road, have more Reason to hope for a Relief to themselves, and the Publick in general, by a Reduction of the said Tolls, than to expect a Continuance of them, for such new Purposes as are mentioned in the Petition of the said Trustees; and that (however necessary it may be thought to repair the Road from Stilton to Peterborough, leading, into the Fens of Lincolnshire) the same ought not to be done at the Expence of those who never travel thereon, which must be the same if such an Application of the Tolls arising at Saltree and Wansford aforesaid, is differed to be made by the said Trustees, as is aimed at by their said Petition; and that these Petitioners apprehend, the Principal Money due on the Security of the said Tolls is very inconsiderable; and that the fame, by the Monies already raised, and in the Hands of the Trustees, together with the Tolls to be collected, might be soon paid off and discharged, afrer which the Petitioners hope, that the said Tolls should cease and determine, according to Equity, and the Intention of the Legislature; but that the Petitioners cannot conceive, that by a new* Act of Parliament, not only the said Tolls should be continued, during the prefenc Term (of which Eleven Years, and upwards, are yet unexpired), but that the fame, or at lead so much thereof as is more than necessary to preserve the said Road between Alconbury Hill and Wansford, in its present good Repair, should be applied to the Making and Amending of foreign Roads, on which the Tolls are not collected; and even the said VoL. 26,

high Tolls be also continued to a further Term for the same most unprecedented and unreasonable Purpose, which, besides the extreme Injustice of the Thing, can, in its Consequence, tend to nothing less than the Decay of that Pari of the great Northern Road: And therefore praying.

Mr. Speaker informed the House, That the Deputy of the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, had something to communicate to the House, relating to the Exe* cution of the Orders Yesterday made, for removing Mr. Murray from his Majesty’s Goal of Newgate, into the Custody of the said Serjeant at Arms.

And the said Deputy Serjeant being called upon, aCr quainted the House, That he did Yesterday communicate to the Keeper of the said Gaol Mr. Speaker’s Warrants; for removing the said Mr. Murray; and that being thereupon admitted to the said Mr. Murray, he the said Deputy Serjeant did acquaint him with the Orders of the House, for his Removal; but that his Physician, Dr. Lamond, being present, and giving it as his Opinion, that it might be very improper to remove the said Mr. Murray that Night, and that it would be more adviseable to defer such Removal dll the next Morning, he the said Deputy Serjeant acquiesced therein, and accordingly did this Morning, together with Doctor Lamond, again attend the said Mr. Murray, and told him. That he, the said Deputy Serjeant, was ready to execute the said Warrants; but that the said Mr. Murray then said. That he thought such Removal would be of little or no Service to him; and that as the Application to the House was without his Knowledge, he chose, if it could be permitted, to remain where he was 5 that he also requested the said Deputy Serjeant to inform the House, That he was extremely thankful for the Favour intended him 5 and that the said Doctor Lamond likewise thought, that as his Fever had left him sooner than he apprehended, it was the best way not to remove him, as nothing but Air and Exercise could be of real Service to him.

And the said Deputy Serjeant being farther examined, also acquainted the House, That he found, from his Conversation with the said Mr. Murray, that he had been informed of the Steps which had been taken for the said Application to the House; and that he, the said Mr. Murray, expressed great uneasiness thereupon, and used some Words of Resentment towards One of his Relations, on Account of such Application being made; saying, That it was a mean Thing in him, to apply to the House, without his, the said Mr. Murray's, Content.

The House was moved, That the Minutes of the Information given by Dactor Lamond Yesterday, at the Bar of this House, and of his Examination consequent thereupon, might be read.

And the same were read accordingly;

And the House being informed. That the said DoCtor Lamond was attending at the Door;

He was called in; and, being examined at the Bar, gave the House an Account in what Condition he found the said Mr. Murray last Night, with his Reasons for thinking it improper to have Mr. Murray removed at that Time* and also acquainted the House, That the said

Mr. Murray does not desire to be removed out of Newgate, unless he could have the Benefit of Air and Exercise, and was dilfatisfied with the Application which had been made to this House; and that he, the said DoCtor, does not now perceive any Symptoms of the said Mr. Mur* ray's having the Gaol Distemper; but thinks him much better than he was Yesterday, although far from being wel}.

And then he withdrew.

Ordered, That the Orders made Yesterday, For removing the said Mr. Murray from his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate, into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, and the several Orders subsequent thereupon, relating to the said Mr. Murray, be revoked.

Ordered, That the said Mr. Murray do remain in the same Custody he was in, with the same Orders, in relation to him, as were subsisting Yesterday, before the said revoked Orders were made.

Ordered, That Mr. Prowse have Leave to make d Mo- Cowaimts. tion, it being after Three of the Clock:

And he moved the House accordingly:

and that it is well known, and can be proved, that the many proves of Cattle, which are reprelented as eloping from the great North Road, and using the Hamerton Road, are lean Beads, travelling from the North into Norfolk and Suffolk, and which have used that Road only since the Distemper among the Horned Cattle has been so rife in Lincolnshire; and that they have a nearer Way, by Thirty Miles, through Lincolnshire, and by Wisbech, to those Parts, which there is great Reason to believe they will use again, as soon as the said Distemper has ceased; and that the fat Beads, for the London Markers, from the North, and different Parts of Lincolnshire, use an open Road, where no Bars can be erected, and make their Way through the Counties of Northampton and Huntingdon, into Bedfordshire and Hert-fordshire, by Hemington, Luddington, Pburning., and Old-weston, and sometimes by Tarwell, Naffington, Elton, Warmington, Ashton, and Barnwell, without coming into the Wansford Road at all, or into the Oundle Roads, through any of the Villages mentioned in the said Petition, towards Alconbtiry or Huntingdonand that the greater Part of the loaded Carriages, and Droves of Cattle, travelling from Stamjord, and from Oundle, to Alconbtiry and Huntingdon, use an ancient publick Road leading through the several Parishes of Warmington, Hemington, and Lutton, in North-amptonshire, and Glatton, Great Giaing, Little Giding, and Steeple Giding, in Huntingdonshire, in their Way to Ha-merton V/ater Gate, which is an ancient Drove-Way, and a more spacious Road, being high and open, and in Part already mended, and more capable of being mended than that through Thurning, Winwick, and Hamertont which is low and narrow in many Places, and crosses Two or Three Brooks, which subject it to be flooded very deep; and that these Petitioners have expended great Sums of Money in mending the fame, and have also contributed their Assistance in supplying the Petitioners for the Bill with Carts, towards mending Part of the Road in Upton Field\ common to all these Petitioners; and that they are willing to do their Statute-Work upon the fame, which, if duly observed, and done by the several adjoining Parishes, will sufficiently keep all the said Roads in good Repair; and that the Matter alleged in the said Petition, that several large Droves of Beasts and Sheep, and also Wool-Waggons, and other Carriages, have, since the Erection, of another Toll-Bar at Wansford, using the Hamerton Road, so cut and torn up that Road, that the Farmers are often deprived of carrying their Grain to Huntingdon, is of no Weight; for that the Farmers of the several V illages, mentioned in the said Petition, can, whenever their Common Field Way to Alccnbury is very bad, find a short Way to go with their Waggons inro the great North Road; and that if a Bill should pass, according to the Prayer of the said Petition, a very large Sum of Money will be drawn

from the Revenues of the 'foll-BiarS on the great Road, to amend those Two Branches of collateral Roads (which will be intirely useless to those who travel on, and pay to the Support of, the said great Road) and more Money will be annually required to support the fame, and the Expences of the Bar-Keepers, which it is believed the Travellers on the said Road, paying at such Bars, will never enable the Petitioners to support; and that it will otherwise (and particularly by Barnwell) greatly lessen the Revenues arising from the Tolls on the great North Road, by turning off great Numbers of Horse Travellers from Stamford into the Barnwell Road, through which they will pass, for the fake of paying One Toll only, instead of Three; all which Hardships and Inconveniencies, these Petitioners apprehend, will so lessen the Income of the Tolls on the said great Road, that it will remain almost a perpetual Burden to the Parishes where the said Petitioners dwell, as well as to the Publick; whereas, in its present State, the Income of the said Tolls will, as the Petitioners have great Reason to brlieve, clear off the whole Debt of Nineteen Hundred Pounds, mentioned in the said Petition, in less than three Years; and the Tolls thereof; in consequence, being unnecessary to be continued at more than One-half of what is now paid, will so ease the Petitioners, and all others travelling, and carrying on Traffick, on the said great Road, that it will be an Encouragement to all Travcllers and Traders to use the fame; whereby it will always hereafter be able to support itself, at a very small Expence to the Publick: And therefore praying, That a Bill may not pass, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; but that these Petitioners may be relieved, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trullees, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution several Acts of Parliament passed in the 9th and 12th Years of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and in the 13 th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and in the 7th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the Roads therein mentioned, between the White Post on Alconbury Hilly in the County of Huntingdon, and Wansford Bridge, in the same County, being the North Division, and of others the Gentlemen of the said County of Huntingdon, and the County of Northampton, adjoining or near to the said Road, is referred, to examine the Matter of these Petitions, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of Richard Partridge, Agent for, and on Trade of behalf of, his Majesty’s Province of Penflvania, in Ame- American rica, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, omcs* That the Inhabitants of Penflvania in particular, and of North America in general, are very numerous; and from their Situation, in cold and severe Climares,do constanrly take off and consume great Quantity of the W oollen and other Manufactures of this Kingdom, and thereby contribute to the Wealth and Benefit of Great Britain, in its Trade, Navigation, and Revenues; and that the said Inhabitants are industrious in seeking Opportunities to remit Returns, towards paying the large Sums which they continually owe, as the Balance of Trade, to their Mother-Country; and that the Inhabitants in North America have given the most incontestable Proofs of their Zeal and Loyalty to the King’s Royal Person and Government, and of their Duty to their Mother-Country; and divers of them have sacrificed their Lives and Fortunes, for the Annoyance of the King’s Enemies, and for gaining the

most

24 Geo. II. i 6° Aprilis169

mod valuable Acquisitions frond ttiefrti *, and that those numerous Inhabitants are in want, for their necessary and daily Sustenance, and for many other Purposes, of large Quantities of Melasses, Sugar, and Rum, which the British Sugar Islanders cannot supply them with, in any Proportion to their Necessities; and for which they also demand fdch Prices, as the Circurrtttances of the poor industrious North Americans, and of their Trade and Business, cannot afford to give; and that the British Inhabitants in the Sugar Islands are reduced to a very small Number,the Ten Acre Men, who are or should be the Numbers and the Strength and Support of small Islands, being in great measure bought out; and the immense Produce and Wealch of those Islands is brought into the Hands of a few rich and opulent Persons, whose Plantations are in general extremely beneficial to them; and that the said few Sugar Planters have from time to time, contrived every specious Method to raise great Riches to themselves, by advancing the Price of their Produce upon their Fel-low-Subje£h $ by which means they have aimed wholly lod rhefingle Benefit which they might have rendered to their Mother-Country, by keeping open a Trade at foreign Markets, for a Part of their Produce, which by that Method is in effe<5l given up to their Rivals in the Sugar Trade, who greatly undersell them there; and that the said Sugar Islanders have, on all Occasions, endeavoured to represent themselves to be as useful as they are wealthy, and as if they were of equal, or even of greater Benefit and Advantage to their Mother-Country, than the very great Numbers of their Fellow-Subjects in North America, notwithstanding the known Nakedness of the Slaves in the Sugar Islands, the small Number of white Subjects there, and the great heat of their Climate; all which render it impossible for them to consume any thing like the Quantity of Woollen, and other British 'Manufactures, taken off by North America; and notwithstanding that the Balance of Trade between Great Britain and North America is always greatly in favour of the ' Mother-Country; but between Great Britain and the Sugarlflands, is apprehended to be as condantly in favour of the Sugar Islands, and against the Mother-Country; and it is apprehended, that if an Account could be dated of the great Expences and loss which this Nation fudains, in continually maintaining One Squadron of Ships of War at Barbadoes and the Leeward JJlands, and another at Ja-maicayfoT the Defence and Protection of those Islands, in Convoys for their Trade, in great Quantities of Ammunition and Stores of War supplied to them, and in Regiments and Companies of Land Forces sent and kept there, it might appear that the Sugar Islands are far from being of so much Advantage to this Kingdom as the Northern Colonies, more especially considering the great Number of useful British Sailors, which those Climates destroy; and that the said Sugar Planters, in the 6th Year ‘ of the present King’s Reign, applied for, and obtained, an Act of Parliament, for laying very high Duties on fpreign Sugars, Rum, and Melasses, imported into any of the British Colonies in America; and that it was apprehended, at the Time when such Duties were laid, that the same would necessarily produce Two Consequences; the Onethat che same would introduce Frauds, as every Community may afford a few bad Men; the other, That it would enable the Sugar Planters to tax and raise what Price they pleased for their Produce upon the British Subjects in the Mother-Country, as well as upon those in North America; and the Experience of Seventeen or Eighteen Years since that Act passed, has too well judi-fied those Apprehensions; and that of late Years, and since the Parting of that Act, the Produce of the Sugar Islands, particularly their Rum and Sugar, is evidently grown into far more frequent Use here than in former Times; the Prices of the same are also very greatly advanced j and the Sugar Planters contend, that they make far greater Quantities than they formerly did; and yet, as the Petitioner is informed, they have none left on Hand, but the Whole goes off at the present greatly advanced Prices, to the great Profit of a few Sugar Planters, who have, from time to time, been favoured with many Vol. z6%

and great Indulgences; notwithstanding which, they are dill unsatisfied, and are aiming at new Schemes of the highed national Import; which may leffcn and reduce the Trade, Commerce, and, of Consequence, the naval Strength of this Nation in America; may artld and make Navigation Laws for Foreigners; and may didrefs the British Subjects in North America; and all this, in order to the One great End always aimed at by the Sugar Planters, that they may raise what further Prices they shall think fit upon their Fellow-Subjects, more especially those in North America, for the Necessaries of Life; and that, in order to introduce a Scheme of so high, so dangerous, and so mischievous a Nature, the said Sugar Planters, on the 12th of March lad, presented to this House a Petition, signed by about Forty-two several Persons only, but filled the Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others, trading to, and intereded in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies; in which Petition, the British Subjects in the Northern Colonies are most injuriously charged with forgetting all Ties of Duty to his Majesty, the Intered of their Mother-Councry, and the Reverence due to its Laws, and with having carried on a Trade, as therein mentioned, as though they had thought themselves independent of Great Britain; and alleging, That the Petitioner apprehends, that such Forty-two Persons offer so injurious a Charge against the King’s most faithful, most loyal, and most useful Subjects, in North America (who have given such drong Proofs of their disinterested Duty and Loyalty to the King, and their Mother-Country) in order to mifre-present them, and bring them under the Displeasure of this House, the better to carry on the redlefs Desires and Designs of che Sugar Planters, for their own partial Advantage, to the great Hurt and Damage of the British Subjects in North America, and to the prejudice of this Kingdom in many other Respects > and that the Inhabitants of che said Province have had no Possibility of hearing of the said Charge, or of the dangerous Scheme projected thereon, which may affect every thing that is dear and valuable to them, and much less of defending themselves against the fame, or of shewing the pernicious Consequences which would attend the present Project of the said Sugarlflanders, as well as the many great Mischiefs which have ensued from the said Act of the 6th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign: And therefore, in behalf of the said Province, praying the House to take into Consideration the great Weight and Importance of the present Application, and not to examine into the fame, on any Representation to be made thereof by the Sugar Planters only, but to afford the Inhabitants of the said Province an Opportunity of knowing of the fame, and of indruding their Agent thereon, and of hearing him by his Counsel against che same; or that the House will be pleased to afford such other Relief in the Premises, and in such other manner, as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others trading to, and intereded in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies, is referred: and that the Petitioner be heard by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of the IVlayor and Commonalty of the City of New Sarum,in Common-Counci] assembled, was pre-

fented to the House, and read; alleging, That should the Bill lor a general Naturalization of foreign Protestants pals into a Law, the lame, instead of being an Advantage to the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom, will be highly prejudicial to the Interests thereof; for that it would not only tend to the Depriving ofmanyThoufands of the industrious Artificers and Poor from procuring a sufficient Support and Maintenance for themselves and Families, and thereby ofconsequence increase the PoorRates, but that the Introduction of'such a Number of Foreigners (Papilts, perhaps, under the Disguise of Protestants, Strangers to the Laws and Customsof this Country) may endanger our Civil and Religious Rights, and prove fatal to our present happy Establishment; and that it is greatly to be apprehended, that this Bill, instead of bringing over a rich and mercantile People, will pour in upon us none but the Poor, and Outcast of other Nations; and that instead of introducing new Arts and Sciences amongst us, it will be a Means of robbing us of such as we are already in Possession of; and that a like Law beina; made in the Reign of

J o o

Queen Armey it was found so detrimental to the publick Incereft, that it was shortly afterwards repealed, and not w ithout some Reflexions on the Mischiefs it had produced; and that the Petitioners apprehend the same (if noegreater) Mischiefs, may accrue, by this intended Indulgence: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Reading, in the County of Berks, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it will be far from being advantageous, and, on the contrary, will be very detrimental to this Nation, by dillrefling and increasing the Number of the Poor; and that in the Reign of Queen Anne a large Number of Poor, under the Denomination of Palatines, were introduced by the Favour of such a Law; who were so far from being of any Service to the , Kingdom, that they filled it with Poverty and Diseases; on which Account, among others, the Law was soon after repealed: And also expressing the Fears of the Petitioners, that the same Misfortunes would attend this Bill, if passed into a Law; and chat it might be made use of by evil Persons, to inllil Uneasiness into the Minds of his Majesty’s Subjects; and that the bringing into this Kingdom such Numbers of Protestants, of different Persuasions, would very much increase the Schisms, already too numerous in the Nation; and that the Persons,-who are likely to come over, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, seem to the Petitioners to be such, as would more probably join with the Enemies of the Kingdom, than with the real Friends of our happy Constitucion: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

That they will not grant an unlimited and immediate Rightof Naturalization to every Foreign Protestant, who shall think proper to accept of the fame; but will (at lead) confine the Benefit thereof under such Restrictions and Limitations, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.
