Avon A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, capital Burgesses, Navigajon. other the inhabitants, of the Borough of Stratford upon Avon, in the County of Warwick, andorthe Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the several Parishes of Old Stratford, Bint on, WelfordWeston upon Avon, Clifford Loxley, and Hampton Lucy, in the Counties of Warwick and Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, by reason of their Situation upon, or near to, the Banks of the River ill ’ Avon, running from Stratford upon Avon aforesaid, through the Counties of Warwick, Worcester, and Gloucester, are greatly concerned and interestec^n the Navigation carried on upon the said River; and thatntHe said Navigation hath been of late Years dii"couraged, and the good Ends and Purposes of a clause, contained in an Act passed in the 14th , Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, in favour of Persons having Occasion to navigate upon the said River, have, in a great measure; been frustrated, by reason that the Rates of Tonnage on Coals, and all Kinds of Goods and Merchandize, both up and down the River, hath been not only uncertain and various, according to the arbitrary Will and Humour of the Persons claiming stich Tonnage, but hath been exacted in an undue and exorbitant Manner; and that the Publick in general, and the Petitioners in particular, have been great Sufferers by the bad State into which the Navigation of the said River is reduced, by the Means aforesaid, and are likely to be still more so, unless by the Aid of Parliament the Rates of Tonnage upon the said River can be ascertained: And therefore praying. That the Cale of the Petitioners may be taken into the Consideration of the House; and some suitable Provision may be made for them, in case any Bill shall be brought in, in consequence of the fevc-ral Petitions already presented to this House, touching the Navigation of the said River, and the Fixing of the Rates of Tonnage thereon; and that the Petitioners may Vol. 26.

have Fuch further and other Relief in the Premises, ii to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, capital Burgesses, and other the Inhabitants, of the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester, is referred.

presented to the House from the Trustees, appointed for executing the Powers veiled in them by several Acts of Parliament made for repairing the Roads from Alconbury Hill, in the County of Huntingdon, to Wandsford Bridge, in the same County; and alleging, That the said Road from Alconbury Hill to Wandsford aforesaid, being the great Poll Road from London to the Northern Parts of this Kingdom, has been extremely well repaired by the Monies yearly collected at the Turnpikes at Saltree and Wandsford aforesaid, and Hill continues in such good Repair, that the Petitioners, in common with all others travelling on the said great Poll Road, conceive the same Tolls, instead of being continued for making and repairing the Roads from Stilton to Peterborough* and from Alconbury . Hill, to Barnwell Gate, being Roads quite across the Country, and no-ways belonging to the great Poll Road, at the Expence, and not for the lead Benefit of the Travellers on the said great Poll Road, ought to be reduced for the good of the Publick in general; and that, if the Bill prayed for by the said Trustees, should be established into a Law, it is manifestly evident, that the same will be to the entire Disadvantage of the said great Poll Road, and consequently to the great Prejudice of the many Inhabitants resident on the North Side of Wandsford aforesaid: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem just and equitable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution several Acts of Parliament, palfed in the 9th and t 2th Years of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and in the 7th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the Roads therein-mentioned, between the White Post on Alconbury Hill, in the County of Huntingdon, and Wandsford Bridge, in the same County, being the North Division; and of others, the Gentlemen of the said County of Huntingdon, and the County of Northampton, adjoining, or near to the said Road, is referred 5 and that they do examine the Matter of this Petition, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

In Support of the Allegations of the Four First-mentioned Petitions, the Agent for the Petitioners produced an attested Copy of an original Grant of King Charles the First, dated the 7 th of April, in the 1 ath Year of his Reign, and directed to Certain Commissioners therein named; which recites, thajt Hrilliam Sandys, of Fladbury, in the County of Worcester, Esquire, had undertaken, at his own Charge, to make the River Avon, from the Severn, to or near the City of Coventry, and also some other Streams falling into the fame, running through the Counties of Warwick; Worcester, and Gloucester, navigable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, for the better supplying the said Counties with Wood, Iron, Pit Coal, and ocher Commodities, which they then wanted; and that the said William Sandys had also been at great Charges, in purchasing Estates, and otherwise, for bringing the said Work to Perfection; in Recompence whereof, his Majesty was pleased to grant to the said William Sandys only the Benefit of the Water Carriages, upon the said River, as in such Cases were nfual and that his said Majesty well approving the Undertaking of the said William Sandys, tending so much to the publick Good of the aforesaid Counties, by opening a Passage by Water through an inland Country, whereby the Commerce of those Parts (which then, by reason of the Length and Foulness of the Ways, was much interrupted) would be greatly enlarged, did thereby appoint Commissioners to determine Differences, and to facilitate the said Work,so advantageous to the Publick; with such further Powers, as are therein mentioned; which Grant was to have Continuance, until his Majesty should think fit to revoke the fame.

Then aClause in an Act, of the 14th of Charles the ad. Was read; which cnafts. That the River Avon, then made navigable by the said William Sandys, should be continued, maintained, and preserved, and all Differences that might thereafter arise, were to be determined by the Commissioners therein named: But it doth not appear to your Committee, by whom, or for how long Time, the said Navigation was to be preserved or continued, nor in whom the Property thereof was vested; or that the Commissioners therein named (who have all been long since dead) had ever any Power to afeercain the Rates of Tonnage, i£c. upon the said River.

Thar, from the Want of Power to ascertain the Rates as aforesaid, frequent Disputes have arisen between the Pofllflhrs of the said Navigation, and the several Persons navigating the said River.

And, in order to shew the Nature of those Disputes, and the Inequality of the several Rates of Tonnage, and that m'jft Parts of the Coal Trade have been ingrossed by the Possessors of the said Navigation,

Edward Horne, a Millwright, said, That he knows the River Avon, and the several Locks and Weirs erected thereon; that the Number of Locks is 14, and the Weirs Six.

And being afleed, what he thought the Charge of keeping, the said Locks and Weirs he mentioned in Repair ? he said. He would support them, as well as they are, and have been supported for several Years pad, for 140/. per Ann.

And being afleed what Number of Mills there are upon the said River, and what Quantity of Flour he thought they sent down the River per Ann. ? he said, There are 13 Mills, besides a.small Mill at Fladbury, called Cropthorn Mill; and that he imagines 16,000 Sacks of Flour, or thereabouts, may be annually sent down the Navigation, and about 5,000 Weigh of Grain; and that the Number of Vessels that pass the several Locks in the same Time> may be about 400, of 30 Ton Burden, upon an Average.

And, being cross-examined, he was afleed, what Foundation he had for saying 16,000 Sacks of Flour were ary-nually sent down the River ? he laid, That such was the general Opinion of Persons concerned in the Trade, and of whom he was one; and that it was also the Opinion of various Persons, that 400 Vessels pass the Locks of the said River annually.

At Bredon 6d.\ at Eckington 12d.\ at Najford\ and so to Parfhore Bridge, 2 s.; at ParJboreTown, at Piddle, and at Fladbury, 2 s. 6 d.‘, and from Chadbury to Evejhafn 3 s; that the Rates he mentioned had been always the constant Rates, and that Jie never knew of any Alteration therein.

And being asked, if it was usual for Vefi^ls of 60 Tons to come up the said River 40 Years ago ? he said. It was for Vessels of 40 Ton; but that he. never heard of Vessels of 60 Ton.

Being cross-examined, he said, That he had been at Sea these 20 Years; since which Time he had never paid any Tonnage; nor had he ever paid any at Bredon himself, but had seen it paid once or twice.

And being aiked, to w hom those Payments were made, of that he mentioned to have seen at Bredon ? he said, To one Roberts (a Tenant to Mr. Rudge) to whom the Witness then fold the Coals.

And being asked, how he could possibly know what Tonnage was paid for those Coals, when Roberts (as Farmer of the Tonnage) was the Person who received it ? he said, That before he fold the Coals, he understood what Tonnage was to be paid} and that, to the bed of his Knowledge, it was paid.

And being asked, if he did not always consider, when he fold the Coals, w hat Tonnage was to be paid, and so fix the price accordingly ? he said, He always did; and that, as to the several Rates before-mentioned, it was the general Report they had been paid; and that, as to the lid. at Eckington, the Witness had paid that himself.

against which Commerce, the Petitioner apprehends there is now no prohibitory Law subsisting; and alleging, That the Petition, signed by about Forty-two Persons, which hath been presented to the House, as a Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies, is in-juriousin many Parts of it, to the dutiful Sentiments, and experienced Fidelity, of hifc Majesty’s loyal Subjrfts in North America, and to the Character of the British Traders there, who are ihdifcriminately charged with the Violation of the Acts of Trade and Navigation; with which Acts those Petitioners have vainly endeavoured to blend the Law of the 6ih of his present Majesty, hying a Duty on foreign Sugar, Rum, and «Melasses, though in its Scope and Nature widely different from that System; which by encouraging Trade and Navigation, raised the naval Power of Britain; and that the said Petitioners having thus attempted to give disadvantageous Impressions of their Fellow-Subjects, have, under Colour of redressing fbme Abuses, from which no trading Country can ever be wholly free, introduced a Scheme of private selfish Gain to-themselves (which the Petitioner hopes is not countenanced by so respectable a Body, as that of the Merchants of London in general) and not contented with the quick Acquisition of Wealth, which their valuable Sugar Plantations give them, nor with the constant Demand they have, and the high Prices they receive, for all that they are capable of producing, nor with the repeated Indul-gencies of the Lcglfiature in sundry Laws, passed for their Ease and Benefit, are now endeavouring ro obtain an unjust Prohibition, to prevent their Fellow-Subjects' receiving from others what they themselves do not furnish: and ic is apprehended they cannot supply, without diminishing the Quantity of Sugars brought to the English Market, and thereby enhancing their Value; which Prohibition, in its Consequences, would soon totally destroy all Trade between the Northern Colonies, and the foreign Settlements, to the utter Impoverishment of those Colonies, the intire Destruction of their Navigation, the grievous Hurt of the Eng'ish Manufacturers, and to the great Diminution of the naval Strength and Riches of this Kingdom-; and that the Prohibition aimed at would, as the Petitioner conceives, be the Means of throwing many profitable Vol. 26f

ranches of Trade, now in our Possession, into the Hands of our Rivals in Power and Commerce, from whom they might never be regained, and is big with many other Mischiefs; and that the Subject-matter of the present Application is of the utmost Consequence to the Well being and Profperiry of all his Majesty’s Colonies on the Continent of America, and particularly to the Inhabitants of the Colony of New York, who, ignorant of the Petition presented, and of its dangerous Tendency, have not had Time to be apprized thereof, and to furnish the Petitioner with what they may conceive necessary and proper to- be urged in their Defence, against so pernicious a Scheme!

And therefore; in behalf of the said Colony of ifkcv York, praying, That the Petition of the said Sugar Plante^, and others, may not be proceeded upon, until the Inhalants of the said Colony are made acquainted therewith, and have Time to give their Instructions thereupon; and that the Petitioner may be then heard by himself, or his Coun-JrJ* against the Application of the said Sugar Planter^; or that he may have such other Relief, as the House shall judge proper and expedient. I

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies is referred; and that the Petitioner be heard by his Counsel, before the said Committe, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of the Merchants, and others, trading to the Trade of British Sugar Colonies, to North and South Carolina, to ^uloa^ Virginia, to Maryland, to Penjilvania, to New York\ to

New England\ to Nova Scotia, to Newfoundland, to Germany, to Holland, to France, to Spain, to Portugal, and to Body, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; expressing the Apprenen-fions of the Petitioners, upon occasion of the said Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies, praying a Prohibition of the Trade carried on from our Northern Colonies, to the French and Dutch West India Settlements; and alleging, That the Petitioners conceive, and firmly believe, that, if a Law should be obtained for that Purpose, and can be carried into Execution, it will immediately defeat the Growth andlncrease of all our Northern Colonies, and in a short Time will destroy their Trade and Navigation, their Ship-building, their Cod, Whale, and other Fisheries, their Furand Peltry Trade, their Rice, Indico, and Tobacco Trades, their Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine Trades, and all their other Trades and Business, to the great Hurt and Damage of at lead Two Millions of his Majesty’s most useful and good Subjects, Inhabitants of the British Northern Colonies in America, whose whole Time, Substance, Labour, and Industry, are employed, both by Sea and Land, to furnish this Kingdom with Naval Stores, and other Necessaries, for our own Use, and also for supplying the Markets of Germany, Holland, France, Spain, Portugal, and Italy, with Furs, Tobacco, Rice, Fish, and other Commodities; the Produce of ail which, together with the Freight of their Ships, and generally the Ships themselves, is all returned to, and centers here, and is laid out in the Woollen, Iron, and other Manufactures of this Kingdom; and thereby adds greatly to the Riches and Strength of this Kingdom, by thus bringing in so great an Increase annually to the national Stock, and consequently is an Advantage to all Degrees of Men amongst us, to the Land-holder, the Merchant, the Tradesman, the Artificer, and the Labourer; so that this great Hurt and Damage will not be confined to his Majesty’s useful and good Subjects, the Inhabitants of the Northern Colonies, bur, in its Consequences, must extend to the great Hurt and Damage of the Trade, Navigation, Wealth, and Strength, of this Kingdom, and of every Individual ia

v

in it, and will finally distress our own Sugar Colonies; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, in the same Proportion that this Kingdom, and her American Colonies, suffer by the Loss of this most advantageous Branch of Trade, the Kingdom of France, and.her Colonies, will gain, to the vast Increase of their Trade, Navigation, Wealth, and Strength; and that by our chus forcing them upon supplying their own, and other foreign Sugar Co-' ionics, with Fish, Lumber, and other Plantation Necessaries, and the Markets of Spain, Portugal, and Italy, with Fish (and in their own Navigation); and also putting them upon finding a large Vent for their Rum, Sugar, and Melasses (also in their Navigation), they will engross the whole Fisheries in America, which at this Time, as the Petitioners conceive, employ a Thousand Sail of British Ships and Vessels, and are one of the bed Nurseries for Seamen which this Kingdom has; and further alleging, That the Article of Melasses is become of general Use in all the Northern Colonies, not onlyfor carrying on their Fiflhery, Fur, and Skin Trades, in Competition with their Rivals the French (and in their Navigation) and all their Trades and Business, but even to their Well-being and Subsist£nce, so that it must tend to the Ad vantage of this Kingdom, and those her useful Colonies, that they should be fully supplied therewith, and at as low a Rate as possible; that lince the Act of 1733, which laid high Duties upon Sugar, Rum, and Melasses, imported from foreign Plantations into any of the British Colonies, the Prices of those Commodities have risen to at lead double the Price they were then at in our own Sugar Colonies; and that of late Rum has become of so general Use, that even at the vad Price it has for some Years pad been and is now at, the Planters in most of the British Sugar Islands have such a Demand for all th^y can make, that they have distilled all their Melasses into Rum, and therefore would not, nor will they now, nor indeed can they, supply the Northern Colonies with near the Quantity of Melasses that is ablblutely necessary for their Subsidence, and if they could supply them with Melasses, or even with Rum, it mud be at such Prices as mud in Time destroy their Trade and Navigation, and the Benefit thereby to this Kingdom; so that they have been compelled to go to the foreign Sugar Colonies for what the English Islands could not supply them with; and the Duty thereon being so high, some few, in some of the Colonies, may have been adventurous enough, in Contempt of the Law, to run some small Quantities on shore, without paying the Duty, to the Hurt of the fair Traders in those Colonies, who at the same Time may have had upon their Hands Rum and Melasses, purchased at high Prices in the British Sugar Colonies: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their Consideration, and take such Measures therein as shall appear to be the most effectual for securing the Intered of Great Britain, and her Northern Colonies, from the said Attempt; and give the Petitioners such Relief as shall be thought proper, either by taking off the high Duty laid upon the Importation of foreign Melasses into the Northern Colonies, or such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants of London in general, and of the British Sugar Planters, Merchants, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies, is referred.

Lawsrc/pedt- Sir Richard Lloyd reported from the Committee, who

i«g Felonies, are appointed to revise and consider the Laws in being which relate to Felonies, and other Offences against the Peace; and to report their Opinion thereupon, from time to time, to the House, as to the Defers, the Repeal, or Amendment, of the said Laws; That the Committee had <tonfidered some other of the Matters to them referred, and had come to several other Resolutioits, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk^s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followetti; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That one Cause of the Increase of Thefts and Robberies of late is an Habit of Idleness, in which the lower People have been bred often from their Youth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Multitude of Places of Entertainment for the lower Sort of People, is another great Cause of that Increase, as they are thereby tempted to spend their small Substance in riotous Pleasures, and in consequence, are put on unlawful Methods of supplying their Wants, and renewing their Pleasures.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Gaming, amongst the inferior Rank of People, is another great Incitement to Theft and Robberies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the great Security^ and Encouragement Robbers meet with from Receivers of stolen Goods, is another, and a principal Cause of the Increase of Robberies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the advertising a Reward, with no Questionsafked, for the Return of Things which have been stolen or loft, is another great and principal Cause of the Increase of Robberies and Felonies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the general Licence of Pawnbrokers (whose Number increases to a dangerous Height) in caking in all Sorts of Pawns, without knowing or inquiring about the Pawners, is a great Cause of Security and Encouragement to Thieves.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the great Del^y and Expence, which attend Prosecutions and Tryals of Crimes, is a great Security and Encouragement of Offenders.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there is a Want of sufficient Powers in the Magis-trares, and others, to search for, and secure for a reasonable Time, suspicious Persons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there should be a speedier and more effectual Way of iupprefling disorderly Houses, than the Laws have at present provided.

Resolved, That it is‘the Opinion of this Committee,

That it would be reasonable to exchange the Punishment of Death, which is now inflicted for some Sorts of Offences, into some other adequate Punishment,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there are great Defects in, and Abuses of, the Houses of Correction.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it would be of Service to the Peace of the Kingdom, to have a more expeditious Way of proceeding in Cafes of Indictments and Preferments of Misdemeanours.-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Persons breaking, or attempting to break, any Prison, should be made liable to some severer Penalties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the refeuing, or attempting to refeue, any Person, committed by Warrant from any Magistrate, or seized, in order to be carried before a proper Magistrate for an.

Offence agafnft the Peace, be subjected to some severer Puniftiment than can, by the Laws now in being, be in-ffidfced.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it should be in the Power of the Court, before whom any Felon is tried, where the Circumstances of the Prosecutor require it, to order a reasonable Allowance to ifucfi Prosecutor, according to their Discretion, to be paid by the Treasurer of the County.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Reward should be given for the apprehending any Person returning from Transportation, to be paid upon Conviction 5 and that the Method of convicting of such Offenders should be rendered more eafyand less expensive.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon,' agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill or Bills, pursuant to the said Resolutions^ And that Sir Richard Lloyd, the Master of the Rolls, Mr. Bathurst and Mr. Hardinge, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, having it entirely at Heart, to secure the future Welfare and Happinels of his People, has maturely considered, that nothing can conduce so much (under the Protection of the Divine Providence) to the' Pfefervation of the Protestanc Succefllon in his Royal Family, and the Support of the Religion, Laws, and Liberties of thele Kingdoms (which have been always most dear to him) as the making proper Provisions for the Care and Tuition of the Perfen of his Successor, and for the regular Administration of the Government, in case such Successor should be of tender Years; by means whereof* their Safety, and princely Education may be secured, the publick Peace, and good Order, maintained, and the Strength and Glory of the Crown of Great Britain suffer no Diminution. For these Reafens, his Majesty, out of his paternal Affection and Tenderness for his Royal Family, and for all his faithful Subjects, earnCftly recommends it to both Houses of Parliament, to take this weighty Affair into their moll serious Deliberation; and proposes to their Consideration, That when the Imperial Crown of these Realms shall descend to any of the Issue of his Son, the late Prince of Wales, being under the Age of Eighteen Years, the Princel? Dowager of (Vales, their Mother, should.be Guardian of the Perfen of such Successor and Regent of these Kingdoms, until they shall attain such Age; with such Powers and Limitations, as shall appear neccftary and expedient for these important Purposes.

Ic excites in ua the most sensible Feeling of all those Blefiings which we have enjoyed during youraufpicious and gloriousdjcign; of the Miidntis and Benignity q{ ypur Government, and of that constant Protection which your Majesty has.always extended to our Religion, Lay/Ond Liberties; which you have demondrated by your Conduct, as well as declared, by youf Royal Words, to be’mod dear to you. Happy would it be for all your faithful Subjjeftfc* if Heaven, in Mercy to these Kingdoms, would graciously permit a Reign, so distinguished with every Marklof Goouness ib.it can endear a British Monarch to feislPcople, to be prolonged beyond the ordinary Date. To> look* forward to its period, anticipates a Grief whtch no Words can express. Your Majesty*5 Greatness of Mind, ihewn in your Message, has called upon us, and set us the example, to enter into such Consider ..lions as the high Inii portance of the Occasion requires.

Not content with being the great Indrument of-our Happiness, during your own Time, your Majesty has pointed out to us a generous Concern to provide for the Continuance of that Happiness (as far as human Forefight can do) after God shall have deprived us of the inedimable Blefiing of your immediate Care. In return for this paternal Goodness, permit us to assure your Majesty, that we will lose no Time in taking into our Consideratioa the weighty Affair laid before us in your Message.

We are truly sensible of the high and eminent Qualities of her Royal Highness the Princess Dowager of PFales; and we look upon what your Majesty has been graciously pleased to propose to our Consideration, as the Result of your Wisdom, and tender Concern for your Royal Family, and the Intereds of these Kingdoms; and we shall have the most dutiful Regard to what your Majesty has been pleased so wifely to recommend.

In our Deliberations on this important Sobjeft, we shall think it our Duty, as w'ell as our essential Intered, to have theftriCteft and most zealous Attention to the Preserva* tion of the Protestant Succession, as settled by Law, in your Royal Family; the numerous hopeful Branches whereof, formed by your Instruction, and led by your Example, we look upon as so many Pledges of the Security of our Religious and Civil Rights, to future Generations.

May it please the Divine Providence to grant your Majesty such confirmed Health, and Length.of Days, as may render those Provisions, which your Wisdom has fuggeded to us, on this Occasion, unnecessary in the Event; that we may very long enjoy the Benefits of your gracious Government, and your Majesty the dutiful and affefticnate Returns of a most obliged, loyal, and grateful People.

In Support of the Allegations of the ‘first-mentioned Petition,

An Act passed in the 9th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for repairing the Roads leading from Rjoyfton, in the County of Hertford, to Wandsford Bridge, in the County of Huntingdon, was read; by which Act several Tolls were granted for repairing the said Road, from the 24th . of June 1711, for the Term of 21 Years:

An Act passed in the 12th Year of the Reign of her said Majesty, for more effectually amending the said Road, was also read; whereby the said Tolls were continued for the further Term of 21 Years, from the 24th of June then next ensuing:

An Act passed in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the more effectual amending the said Road, wa§ also read; whereby several other Tolls were . granted for repairing the said Road, from 24 June 1727 for the Term of 2.1 Years:

An Act passed in the 7th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was also read; whereby the Tolls and Powers, granted by the said former Acts for repairing the Road from Alconbury Hill to Wandsford Bridge, were continued from the Expiration thereof for the further Term of 14 Years.

Mr. Robert Mitchell, Clerk to the Trustees, was examined, and said, Thathe was appointed to that Office in the Year 1734; and that, since that Time, about 3,000l. has been borrowed upon the Credit of the T oils: that there now remains due about 1,900l. besides some Interest; and that the Money raised has, ta his Knowledge, been duly applied.

By the Account-Book of the Trustees it appears. That on &he 23d Day of ORober lad (the Time the last Account was Audited) there was remaining a Balance in the Treasurer’s Hands of 461/. 12s. 2d.

Mr. Mitchell said. That of the Money collected since that Time, he believes there may be a Balance of 200l. after dedufting the Money paid, and to be paid, for the Repairs of the said Road, and other Expences attending the fame:

And he produced an Account of the Monies collected at the Turnpikes erected at Saltree and Wandsford, from the Year 1737 to 1750, both inclusive, whereby it appeared, that the Monies collected at Saltree Turnpike have annually exceeded the Monies collected at Wandsford; and that in the Year 1750 the Sums collected were as follows:

And he said, That the Reason why the Saltree Bar has produced more than the Wandsford n because Travellers frequently go another Road to avoid the Payment of the Toll at Wandsford.

Mr. John BaL’S was examined, and said, That he has been Surveyor of the Road from Alconbury Hill to Wandsford above Twenty Years; and that the said Road is in general in very good Repair, but that, as many heavy Carriages pass. through the fame, and the Spil thereof is in many Places’of a strong Clay, it will not long remain in the present Condition unless it be repaired; and that, as the Materials lie at a considerable Distance, he apprehends the necessary Repairs of the said Road will, one Year with another, amount to about 500l.; and that the Repairs have amounted to about that Sum annually for Six Years past.

Mr. Ralph Newton was also examined, and said. That he lives upon the Hamerton Road; that for some Years last past has seen great Number of Cattle and Carriages pal's through OundU, Barnwell, Aborning, IVinwick, and Hamerton, and formerly through Huntingdon, but lately through jBugdeti, and have thereby avoided the Payment of Tolls at the Stamford, Wandsford, and Saltree Toll Bars; and that, by these Means, the said Roads have been very much torn up, and are now in so ruinous a Condition, that the Inhabitants of that Parc of the Country are not able to get to Huntingdon Market without very strong Teams:

And he added. That Trespasses have been frequently committed by the Cattle which have been drove upon the said Road:

And being asked, Whether, if the Road through Oundle was repaired, moreTcople would not pass that Way? He said, That he believed there would be fewer, because they would then be subject to the Payment of a Toll: and that they would rather go through the great Road, as that is the nearest Way, though they paid Three Tolls; and that People enough go that Road to support the Expence of repairing it.

Mr. Thomas Kirby was also examined, and said. That upwards of 10,000 Head of Cattle came through* the Omdle and Hamerton Road the last Year; and that theyliave come that Way only for Three or Four Years last past: The said Mr. NIitcbeli said, That the Road from Stilton to Peterborough is a Branch of the great North-East Road, and measures about Five Miles and an Half, but is in a very ruinous Condition; and that great Droves of Cattle, which come in at Stilton, pass through the said Road: That the said Road is a shorter Way from London Xo the Eastern Parts of LPncolnshire than the great Road; but that there is a nearer Road than even the last mentioned; but very few People make use of it:

Being further examined, he said, That Travellers from Alconbury Hill to Peterborough pay Toll at Saltree, and have about Seven Miles of Turnpike Road; and that those who go from Alconbury Hill co Wandsford pay Two Tolls: That Carriages to Lincolnshire, when they are not able to get through the Peterborough Road, go the great Road, which he thinks is several Miles about; and that, if the Peterborough Road was in good Condition, he believes that many Carriages would leave the great. Road: And being asked. If a Bar was erected between Stilton and Peterborough, and the same Tolls collected there as at the other Gates, whether the Money collected would be sufficient to repair the said Road ? He said, He believed it would, but could not be certain:

The said Mr. Bales said. That Materials proper for repairing of the Road from Stilton to Peterborough, lie within Three Furlongs of it all the Way; that it is only necessary to repair Five Miles of it; and that under good Management, the same might be well repaired for about 3001, per Mile:

That rf the said Road was fn good Condition, mans Passengers would go that Way who do not use it now; and that it would induce some, but he believes not many* to leave the great Road:

And being asked, If the same Toll was collected upon this Road as at 'Saltree, whether it would be sufficient tQ repair it ? He said. He did not think it would be sufficient to repair it in 20 Years; and that the best Place to erect a Turnpike at was in WoodfonsLane; but that such Turnpike might be avoided, and particularly by all Passengers on Horseback.

To shew that the Taking-in of the Road from Stilton to Peterborough, in the Manner it is intended, will be . of Advantage to the great Road;

' Mr. Mitchell was again examined, and said, That if d Turnpike was to be erected on the Hamerton Road, and the Tolls on the great Road were lowered One-third, he believes that the most Part of thfe Cattle and Carriages would go through the great Road; and the Tolls collected at Saltree and Wandsford would, in his Opinion; be increased by this means about 50 /. per Annum:

That the Road from Stilton to Peterborough will cost, to repair it well in the Manner he would have it repaired, about 1,000l.; and that, if the Statute-work was performed, and the Road under good Management, it might be afterwards kept in Repair for about 5csl.per Annum: That if the Turnpike at Wandsford was removed ta Ncrmoncross Hilly which is about Half a Mile beyond the 75 Mile Stone, it would take in Passengers and Carriages to and from Peterborough, the Eastern Part of Lincoln* shire, IVittlefeay and several other Places, whereby the Tolls would be increased about aoo /. per Annum above what are collected at Wandsford.

Being asked, If the Wandsford Turnpike was removed to Normoncrossy whether Travellers from Peterborough to the great Road, might not come into the great Road between Stilton and Normoncross Hill without paying Toll? That the Road Irom Taxley to Stilton is in a very bad Condition; and that, if the Broyk was scoured fof about Half a Mile, Travellers could not pass, but would be obliged to go a Quarter of a Mile about to Normoncross Turnpike; or that a Side-Bar might be erected at the said Brook; but he owned, that the Road through Taxley to Peterborough is at present a great Road:

And he also said, That Travellers might miss the Bar at Normoncross Hill, by going through Stilton old Road: But he said, That if a Turnpike was erected at Stiltori TownEnd,he believed as much Money would be raised there as at any other Place; for that this Bar would take ,in all Travellers from Peterborough, and the Eastern Parte ' ‘of Lincolnshire, unless they went Five or Six Miles about; and that, if a Side-Bar was erected, it would take in alt Passengers from the adjacent Towns.

The Evidence produced in Support of the Allegations of the Petition of the Mayor of Stamford, &c. was as followeth:

Mr. John Newball was examined, and, said. That he is a common Carrier, and lives near Stamford; and has paid Tolls for the Repair of the Road from Alconbury Hill to Wandsford Twenty-three Years:

That from Alconbury Hill to Stilton was first repaired; and the other Parr, from Stilton to Wandsford, has teen repaired about Seven or Eight Years:

That before the Road was turned at Water Newton, it was in that Part in a very bad Condition and Persons were frequently obliged to go through private Grounds; but that the whole Road is now in good Repair:

That Travellers from Alconbury Hill to the other Side of Wandsford Bridge pay Two Tolls; and that, before the Road from Stilton to Wandsford was repaired, Persons Who travelled from Peterborough to Stilton, had near as much good Rqad for the Payment of One Toll, as those that went from Alconbury Hill to the other Side of Wandsford Bridge had for the Payment of Two; that those who do not go over Wandsford Bridge only pay One Toll for the Whole Road; and that a great Number of the Inhabitants of Wandsford have paid to both the Bars:

That Monies collected at the Turnpikes at Wandsford and , Saltree is more than sufficient to keep the Road in Repair; and that, if the Term is enlarged, as ic is proposed to be, he himself would take the Saltree Turnpike; with the Money now in Hand, and, would give Security to pay off the Debt and Interest, and thinks that he could also keep the Road in good Repair:

But, upon further Examination, he owned, That if the Wandsford Bar was entirely taken away, Passengers might go Fourteen or Fifteen Miles upon the Road without paying any T ell:

That not One Passenger or Carriage in T en, that travels upon the great Road, goes to Peterborough; and that therefore they would pay towards the Support of a Road that they have no Benefit of:

That Passengers and Carriages from Peterborough pay at Saltree Bar, but not at Wandsford; and they go about Seven Miles upon the Road, and the Remainder of the Road is about Eight or Nine Miles more:

Being a(ked, IF the Wandsford Bar was removed to Stilton Town End, whether all Passengers and Travellers muff not go through that Bar ? he said, That in that case Carriages from Peterborough, and the East Parts of Lincolnshire, would pay at Two Bars; but that he thinks, the Passengers on Horseback might avoid the Stilton Bar: That if Wandsford Bar was taken away, and no Bar fixed at any other Place, Passengers would not pay any thing from Stamford to Saltree, which is Seventeen Miles together; for that the Repairs of the Road from Wandsford to Stamford is independent of the Saltree and Wandsford Tolls, and is repaired by the Tolls collected upon the Stamford Road; and that the Bar on the North Side of Wandsford, belongs to the Trustees for repairing thfe, last mentioned Road:

Being asked If the Road from Stilton to Peterborough is Part of the great Road ? he said, That it leads to Crow-land, and some other Places; that he believes One-fifth Part of the Travellers from Lincolnshire to London do not now cOme through Peterborough, but more would use that Road if tt was repaired, for it would be the cheapefr, because they would avoid Two Bars at Wand ford; and that this would tend to the Decay of the great Road; but that if the Bar upon Wandsford Bridge was removed to the End of fyilton Town, he thinks they could not avoid die Payment of Toll without trefjpaffing.

which Expedition failed of Success, and was attended with the Loss of a considerable Number of Men; and the Charges thereof were so great, that the Inhabitants were unable to make Payment thereof in Money, and were thereby induced to issue Bills of Credit, to a considerable Amount, in lieu of Money, to their Creditors; and that, during the late War, the said Province issued Bills to a very large Amount, and they answered altogether instead of Money, to effect the publick Services, which were performed by the said Province.; and that the Credit of a People, in Cafes of fuel den Emergencies, is often the only means of their Preservation; and the said Province, as the Petitioner apprehends, has a natural and lawful Right to make.use of its Credit, for its Defence and Preservation; Sorrey A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Roads, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, dwelling in the Town iaricl Parish oi Lewifham, in the County of Ken*/was presented to the House, and readj setting forth. That the greatest Part of the Highways or Roads leading from a Place called Ho w's Miliy or the First Mill Pond at Southend, in the said Parish of Lewifham, to the Extent of the same Parish, next Bromley, in the said County, and in the Port: Road from London to Tunbridge Welhy and from the said Mill Pond at Southend, to the Extent of the Parish of Lewifham aforesaid, towardsBeckenham, in the said County (the said Roads being each of them in Length Half a Mile, or thereabouts) by reason of the many heavy Loads of Timber, and Carriages laden with other Goods, Stage Coaches, Passengers, and Droves of Cattle, which daily pass over the said Roads, and particularly by reason of the’ excessive Loads of Timber which frequently pals out of Sussex and Surrey, (through Beckenham aforesaid) over the lait-mentioned Road, to his Majesty’s Dock-yard at Deptford, and to Wharfs there, and at Greenwich, in the said County, and of the excessive Carriages oY Meal and Corn, which pass from Croydon, in the County of Surrey, over the same Road, to his Majesty’s Mill at Rotherhith, and to London, are become so very ruinous and founderous, that the said Roads are almost impaflfable for the Space of Five Months in the Year, and very dangerous to all Persons^ Horses, and Cattle, passing over the fame; and that the ordinary Course, appointed by the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, is not sufficient for the effectual repairing and amending the said ruinous and founderous Roads j nor are the Inhabitants of the said Parish of Lewifham of Ability to repair the fame, except some other Provision be ’made for raising Money towards putting the same in good and sufficient Repair: And therefore praying, That a Clause may be added to the Bill, which is ordered to be brought into the House (for widening the Road from the Stones End at Lambeth, to Newington, and for making a new Road across some Grounds into the Kentish Road, near the Lock Hospital, and for making other new Roads therein mentioned) for repairing, amending, and widening, the Roads from How's Mill, or the birjl Mill Pond at Southend, in the said Parish of Lewifham, to the Extent of the said Parish of Lewifham, next Bromley aforesaid, and from the said Mill Pond to the Extent of the said Parish of Lew-isham, towards Beckenham, as aforesaid, for so long Time, and in such manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

have been laid out and expended, and great Care and Diligence employed, in repairing the Highways in general, within the said Riding; but that, nevertheless, the same are become very ruinous and dangerous to Traveilers, occasioned by the many heavy Carriages passing upon the fame; and that, although great Care hath been taken, to fee the Laws now in being, for ascertaining the Weights of Carriages, and for preventing any Carriages weighing, together with their respective Loadings, above Sixty hundred Weight, from travelling on the Roads of this Kingdom, duly put in Execution j yet, notwithstanding all such good Endeavours therein, many Waggoners, Carriers. and others, having found out various Methods of evading the said Laws, do daily travel upon the said Roads with Waggons, Carts, and ocher Carriages, weighing, to gether with their respective Loadings, above Eighty hundred Weight, which the Number of Horses, by the Laws now in being, allowed to be employed in the Drawing of loaded Carriages, enables them to do; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that, unless some farther R^straint be laid on the Owners of Waggons, and other L Carriages travelling upon the Roads of this Kingdom,more

A Petition of the Gentry, Clergy, Merchants, Traders,* Manufacturers, and Inhabitants, in and about Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented s ways* to the House, and read; fecting forth. That of late Years very great Sums of Money, raised as well by the ordinary Course of the Laws made for the repairing the Highways in general, as by extraordinary Powers granted by Parliament, for repairing of sundry Highways in particular, have been laid out and expended, and great Care and Df ligence employed, in repairing the Highways, in general, within the said Riding; but that, nevertheless, the same are become very ruinous and dangerous to Travellers, occasioned by the many heavy Carriages passing upon the lame; and that, although great Care hath been taken to fee the Laws now in being, for ascertaining the Weights of Carriages, and for preventing any Carriages, weighing, together with their respective Loadings, above Sixty hundred Weight, from travelling on the Roads of this Kingdom, duly put in Execution; yet, notwithstanding all such good Endeavours therein, many Waggoners, Carriers, and others, having found out various Methods of evading the said Laws, do daily travel upon the said Roads, with Waggons, Carts, and other Carriages, weighing, together with

Prayers.

That the Petitioner should be forthwith discharged out of the Custody of the said Sheriffs, upoti the Petitioner giving a new Judgment to the said William Stead, for the said Sum of 1,604/. i6j. 6i. with Stay of Execution thereon,' for One Year, which was computed from the 17th Day of March 1749; and that the Petitioner entered into a Bond to the said William Stead, with Two Sureties, who were approved of by One of the Judges of the Court of King’s Bench, in (double the Penalty of the said Sum of 1,604/. 16s. 6d> with which the Petitioner then flood charged in Custody, with Condition that the Petitioner would not withdraw himself out of England, but would always be ready, either in London or Middlesex, at the Expiration of the said Year, to be subject to any Process the said William Stead should think proper to take out against him; and that the Commissioners, appointed by the said Act to examine into the Claims of the Creditors of the said Company, and to report to the House their Opinion fcof the Justness and Reasonableness of such respective Debts, have, m their Report made to the House, allowed the said Sum of 1,604/. i6j. 6d, to be due and awing, from the said Royal African Company, to the said William Stead; and alleging. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 25th Day of March 1752, the Duties, now payable upon the Importation of foreign Linen Yam, shall ceale and determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the said Duties, there be granted to his Majesty a Duty of One Penny for every Pound Weight, Upon all Raw or Brown foreign Linen Yarn, and also a Duty of Three pence for every Pound Weight of unwrought Incle, short Spinnel, and other whitened aijd bleached foreign Linen Yarns, which shall be imported into this Kingdom, after the said 25th Day of March 1752.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties be carried to, and made Parc of, the Aggregate Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the Duties and Revenues which were charged with several Annuities, and other Appropriations, the like Sum be charged upon the several Duties and Revenues, commonly called the Aggregate Fund, and made applicable to the same Uses and Purposes.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Capital Burgesses, Alconbury and other Burgesses and Inhabitants, of the Town or Borough of Stamford, in the County of Lincoln, was pre- s* fented to the House, and read; alleging, That by the Powers proposed to be given to the Trustees, to be appointed by the Bill depending in the House (for enlarging the Terms and Powers, and making more effectual several Acts of Parliament, for repairing and amending the Highways leading from Royfton, in the County of Hertford, to Wansford Bridge, in the County of Huntingdon, so far as relates to the Amending of that Part of the Road as lies between a Place called the White Post, on Alconbury Hill, in the County of Huntingdon, and Wansford Bridge, in the same County, called the North Division; and that the Toils taken at Saltree and Wansford Toil Gates may, from and after a certain Time, be lowered; and for repairing the Road leading from Stilton, in the said County of Huntingdon, to Peterborough, in the County of Northampton) to repair the Road from Stilton to Peterborough, out of the Monies arising by the Turnpikes of Wansford and Saltree,

Handing upon the great Northern Post Road, the Petitioners apprehend the Repairs of the said great Post Road will be neglected; and the Monies arising therefrom be applied to the Disadvantage of all Travellers thereon, and the Publick in general: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration; and give Leave, that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill’s passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be made from the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, if they think fit.

Ayon An ingrossed Bill* for the better regulating the Navi-Kifigation. gation of the River Avon, running through the Counties of Warwick, Worcester, and Gloucester, and for afc^rtaining the Rates of Water Carriage, upon the said River, was read the Third time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Rider, providing that this Act shall not extend to give Liberty to any Person to keep a publick "Wharf, or to la*de or unlade any Goods between Evesham and Harrington Sluices, except for private Use.

And the same was thrice read, and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Rider.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, to oblige the Occupiers of Mills to draw the Water for forwarding Barges up and down the River, upon Payment of a certain Sum.

And the same was twice read with a Blank, which was filled up.

And then the said Clause was read the Third time, and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Rider.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Rider, to oblige the Occupiers of Mills to draw' the Water for the Purpose of repairing any. Sluices or Engines belonging to the Navigation, upon the Conditions therein mentioned.

And the same was twice read with Blanks, which were filled up.

And then the said Clause was read the Third time, and*

upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by way of Rider.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, to restrain Bargemen from drawing any Flood-Gates, Dams, or Sluices, without the Consent of the Owners.

And the same was thrice read, and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Parc of the Bill, by way of Rider.

Vol. 26.

Another ingrossed Cliause was offered to be added t6 the Bill, providing that this Act shall not impeach any Contrafts between the Owners of the lower Part, and the Owners of the upper Part, of the said Navigation, nor determine any Leaies between the Owners of the Navigation and their Tenants.

And the same was twice read with Blanks, which were filled up.

And then the said Clause was read the Third time, and, upon the Question put thereupon^ agreed to by the House, to Be made* Part of the Bill, by way of Rider.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be,

An Act for the better regulating the Navigation of the River Avon, running through the Counties of Warwick,

Worcester, and Gloucester, and forascertaining the Rates of Water Carriage upon the said River.

Ordered, That Sir John Rufbout do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Thomas Stephens; were severally referred; That the Commitcee had examined the Matters of Fact contained in the said Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. tJpon the first-menrioned Petition,

Mr. Cadwallader Coker, Soapmaker, said. That great Quantities of Pot-allies are used in the soft Soap and Dying Trade; and also by the Whitfters of Cloth and Yarn; and that great Quantities of soft Soap are used in the Woollen Manufacture:

That the Quantity of the best Pot-alh used in a Barrel of Soap is 56 Pounds Weight, which Barrel of Soap weighs 256 Pounds; and that, within these Ten Years, Pot-allies arc advanced 50 per Cent.; that Pot-allies are extremely scarce at present, there being not above 50 Ton in the Merchants Warehouses; and that there used to be between 1,500 and 2,000 Tons; that the same Quantity of fine Allies do not come from Russia that uled to do: That there are Three Sorts of Allies imported; one from Russia, another from East Country, and a Third Sort from Naples; that the Price of English Allies has rofc within these Ten Years from about 16/. to 25 /. per Ton.

Mr. William James, Soapmaker, said, That annually about 1,600 Vats (which is about 800 Ton) of the best Russia Allies are consumed in the Making of Soft Soap; that the Czarina contrails with particular Merchants here, and none are imported from Russia but by them: 1 That the Second Sort of Pot-allies comes, from Riga, Conningsburgh, and Dantzick; these go under the Denomination of East Country Allies; and that, for the Two last Years, about 500 Ton each Year was imported:

That the Third Sort comes from Naples; of these not above 120 Ton per Arm. are consumed in England; and that none are used but in the Manufacture of soft Soap: That in February 1743 the'belt Russia Allies were only 35I. per Ton; but that ever since they have gradually advanced, and are now worth 55/. per Tonand that the Witness would be glad to have them et that Price, as there are not above 50 Tons at present in the Merchants Hands; and that upwards of 1,400 Tons are used per Annum in the Manufacture of loft Soap, all which are paid for in Specie: and that it is very apparent, the Manufacture of soft Soap mull be at a Stand, and, in conference thereof, the Woollen Manufacture, if more Allies are not imported this Year than the Merchants expect: That the Second Sort, or East Country Allies, which used to be about 10/. per Ton less than the best Russia, the Merchants say, cannot now be imported under 42 L a Ton:

That the Third Sort, or Naples Allies, are now worth about 40 /. per Ton; that they advanced 6 /. per Ton the last Sale:

And being asked. What the Duty on Pot-allies were ? He said, 6 s. 2 d. and 9-ioths of a Penny for every Hundred Pounds; and that it is the same on all Species of Pot-allies:

That at present One Merchant imports all the Russia Allies:

And being alked. To what he attributed the Advance upon the Pot-ashes ? He said. They are told by the Merchants, that it is owing to the Woods being burnt y but that, in his Opinion, it is owing to the unlimited Orders the Dutch, French, and Flemings have, to buy the East Country Allies:

That there has been of late much greater Demands by the French, Flemish, and Dutch Markets, for East Country Allies, than usual:

And that in England there used to be 15 or t,6oo Ton of East Country Allies (exclusive of the Russia) and now there is none at all:

And being alked, If English Allies would not make loft Soap? He said. He apprehended a small Proportion of English Allies are necessary, and rather make the Soap better, as they soften it, and if it was made of all Russia

Pot-alh it would be too hard } tHat the Price of English Afties now is 25 /. a Ton, and of Russia 55 /.; that they generally rife and fall in Proportion.

Mr. Houghmani Broker, being alked, What Quantity of English Allies are annually consumed in the Soap Manufacture ? He said about aoo Tons:

And being alked. What Quantity of Pearl Allies are used in England? He said, About 500 Ton per Annum, for which we now give 36 /. a Ton; and that about §even Years ago they used to be 30 and 32/. a Ton; that we import them from the North, Dantzick, Riga, Germany, and Uamborough\ that they are chiefly used by the Whitfters and Dyers.

Colonel Williams said, That he knows New York, Connecticut > and Massachusets; that there are great Quantities of Wood of various Kinds in chose Countries.

And Mr. Houghman being alked, What fort of Wood was proper for making Pot-allies of? said. That all Wood is made use of without DistinClion.

Colonel Williams being alked, What the Price of Labour was in those Places he had mentioned ? said, That, at a Medium, the Labour in Summer was from \%d. to 20 d. and in Winter from 14 d. to 16 d.:

That about Five Years ago, when the Witness was abroad, he, with some other Gentlemen, made about Ten Barrels of Pot-alh,. which they sent over to Bristol; and they received an Account from the Merchants, to whom they sent it, that it was a middling Sort; and the Reason they proceeded no further, was on Account of the Duty: -

And being alked, If the Duty had been taken off, he thought the People they employed had Skill to have improved it

He said. If the Duty had been taken off, they should have continued it: That the Wood, of which ic was made, was taken promiscuously:

And being alked, What those Allies fold for ? He said. He never heard:

And being alked, What Price he thought it might be afforded at ? He said. He could not tell.

Mr. James said. That, about Five or Six Years ago, he had received Pot-allies from New York, but they were not. so good as the East Country Allies; but if they had been well made they would have been good enough.

Mr. Michael impey said, He received about 8 Cwt. of Allies from Pensilvania in the Year 1735; and though they were not so good as the Russia, yet they were very good; and they cost him 30s. a Hundred, and the best Russia then were 36 s. y that he thought them as good as the East Country Allies.

Mr. James Abercrombie said, He had lived in Carolina; and that there are great' Quantities of Materials for making Pot-allies there:

And being alked, If he thought the Price of Labour such, that (if the Duty was taken off) People could make them there with Success ? He said, He had heard People had made Pot-allies there; but, on account of the Price of Labour, and the Duty, had left it off.

Mr. Robert Dinwiddle said, There is Wood enough in Virginia, Maryland, and Pensilvania, to make Pot-allies; but he has heard the People there complain of the high Duty upon Allies, which prevented them undertaking it; but said. He believed the Want of Skill to be as great an Hinderance to the Making it as the Duty is.

Mr. Bejwich confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Dinwiddle.

DoCtor Mitchell, being asked the Question, said, He thought there was not much Mystery in making Pot-ashes; and he believed, the Reason they do not make them in America is owing to the Price of Labour, and the Duty upon them; that the knowledge he has of the Art of making them is from Books and Experience; that he had made some in Virginia; and that, after he returned to England, he endeavoured to get the best Information about them he could from Sweden or Rtffia; that he had published five or six different Ways of make-ing Pot-ashes, but that he believes there may be other Ways; that the Witness had made 20, 30, or 40 Cwt. at a time, and believed them very good; but that he' kept no Account of the Expence of making them:

And being asked, If Fern would not make Pot-ashes ? he said, It would: but they are not near so good as Wood-ashes; for that in 1749, the Ashes made from Fern fold from 16 to 20s. a Hundred, and the Ashes xnade from Wood fold for 40 s.

Then Mr. Crockatt produced to your Committee a Parcel of Pearl Allies; which were shewn to several Persons present (killed therein, and who said they were very good of the Kind:

Mr. Crockatt said. That Mr. Stephens was the Person who made those Ashes he had produced; and that he had, before shewn them to several Persons in Trade, who had approved of them; and that he had fold them within 1 s. per Cwt. of the Price of the best Pearl Ashes that were then in London, and he never heard of any Complaint of them, and from that he concludes they were good.

Mr. Ehotnas, a Dry-Salter, who had bought Three or Four Calks of Mr. Stephens's Pearl-allies, said, They were very good, and not inferior to any others; that he fold them to the Whitfters, and had no Complaint of them; and that if more’ were to be brought, he should buy them again, and would give as much for tjlem as for any other PearL-ashes.

Mr. Crockatt said. He was convinced, if the Duty was taken off, it would encourage People to go on with the making them in South Carolina; that he knows the People there would have given Mr. Stephens a Reward to have instructed them in making Ashes, if the Duty had been taken off, and that they were in Treaty with Mr. Stephens about it; that he apprehended Mr. Stephens had a particular Art in making Pot and Pearl-ashes, which made them offer him a Reward:

That he knows Mr. Stephens has been at great Study, Labour, and Expence, in bringing his Method of making Ashes to Perfection:

That the Witness knew one Captain Hanning, who left off being Captain of a Ship in order to go to Carolina to make Pot-ashes:

That he accordingly followed the Making of them for Two or Three Years, and made several Thousand Weight; thataGentleman in London was concerned with him, and they loft a great deal of Money in the Undertaking:

That he did not know what their Ashes fold for, but that they were not near lb good as Mr. Stephens's:

And being asked, Why they left off the Trade? he said, He apprehended because they loft Money by it, which was owing to the high Duty, and want of Skill; but that, if they had had good Skill, he thinks they might have bore the Duty:

And being asked, What was the Price of Labour in South Carolina? he said, He could at any time hire a Negro for a Year at 50/. that Currency, which is about 7/. Sterling; but, besides that, you find him Victuals, which is about 20s. a Year more; that he has made a Computation, and that you will gain by each Negro 15 or 18/. Sterling per Annum:

And being asked, If he thought Negroes could make Ash ? belaid, They could do the laborious Part, which is the chief; that he was convinced, if the Secret of making Ashes was known in America, and the Duty taken off, it would reduce foreign Pot-ashes; and that he believes, if they had made them for a while, and was once (killed therein, they might be able to pay the Duty.

Mr. Houghman said, That he had consulted the Merchants who deal in foreign Pot-ashes; and that they say, they should be glad to fee an Encouragement given to bringing over Pot-ashes from America, for they were afraid they should not get Ashes enough to supply the several Manufactures.

Clause (A), and also Clauses (B) and (C), the Three next Amendments made by the Committee to the said Bill, being severally read a Second time, were postponed.

Papers, and itveral Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House, together with their Vot. 2.6.

Observarions upon so many of* the said Matters as they were directed by the House to make their Observations upon; and he read the Report in hisPlace; and afterwards delivered the same (together with an Appendix thereto) in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Reporc was read.

The said Report and Appendix are as followeth; viz.

As the Petition of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, on behalf of themselves, and the said Company, which complains of the Refusal of the Royal African Company of England to confirm the Agents, Factors, and Writers, appointed by the Committee of the said Company of Merchants, appeared to your Committee of the utmost Consequence, they thought it their Duty to enter immediately into the Examination of the Disputes between the Old Company and the Committee of the New Company; and, after several Examinations in regard thereto, and Propofals reciprocally made, the Two Parties at Length produced to your Committee Articles of Agreement, in which both Companies acquiesced, and declared themselves mutually satisfied.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine into the following Paragraph, in Captain Pye*s Letter to the Secretary of the Admiralty, dated the 18 th of March 1749 j viz.

" I should think I did not execute the Confidence re-posed in me by my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, did I not represent every Circumstance I thought essential for the publick Good; and must therefore declare to have heard a Gentleman, late one of the ChiefAgents at Cape Coast Castle, and esteemed a Man of Veracity, say. That he can prove the African Company to be Debtor to the Forts and Settlements near Fourscore thousand Pounds, out of the Monies granted at different Times by Parliament for the Maintenance and Support of the said Forts and Settlements." And, Captain Pye, being examined, informed your Committee, That he received the said Information from Mr.

\Thomas Chalmer; whereupon your Committee examined the said

Mr. Chalmer; who said, He had lived many Years at Cape Coast Castle, partly as Fafbor, and partly as Chief Agent for the Royal African Company; and he produced a Book, which he said was a Copy of the Account Current of the said Company, according to their General Books of Accounts kept at Cape Coast Castle, from the First Day of January 1736-7, to the 31st Day of December 1748; and he said, that this was the Paper on which he founded the Information he had given to Captain Pye:

And it appeared to your Committee, that, during the said Period, Why dab was separated from the Government of Cape Coast Castle for the Space of Six Years; and that he knew nothing of what Supplies were sent to fVbydab in the said Six Years, and nothing at all of what was sent to Gambia at any Time, so that his Evidence appeared to your Committee not sufficient to charge the Company with the Matcter contained in the said Paragraph.

Your Committee then proceeded to consider the Report of the Commissioners for examining into the Claims of the Royal African Company of England, appointed by, and in pursuance of, an Act of Parliament, passed in the last Session:

And, in going through the Remark on N° 2. observed, that the Commissioners have stated specially several considerable Sums in African Trust Stock, and in Money* which Charles Hayes Esquire, hath received of the Company: and so much of the said Remark, as related to the said Mr. Hayes, being read, your Committee received from Mr. Hayes a State of His Cafe, which is hereunto annexed in the Appendix N° 1.; and Mr. Hayes was examined; and your Committee observe, That the said Charles Hayes Esquire hath sworn before the Commissioners, that the whole Produce of the 5,000l. Trust Stock, so transferred to him, was by him disbursed or applied for the Service of the Company; and that the several Sums of 210/. and 3,6411, is. 11 d. were expended by him, at different Times, in the Service of the Company:

And your Committee find, That the said Services were in getting the best Information he could upon the Powers of the Company, and searching Records, and advising with Counsel thereupon, and in making the first, and the several subsequent Applications for a, Parliamentary Allowance, for the Support of their Forts and Settlements, and defraying several other necessary Expences relating thereto; and your Committee also observe. That, from the Nature of the Service, there must have arose very considerable Expences; and your Committee also observe, that the Paid Company hath never called Mr. Hayes to give an Account of the Particulars; and as for the 800l. which Henry Parjons Esquire, owed to the Company, at the Time of his Death, for 2,000l. Trust Stock, and which was discharged by a Transfer made by the said Charles Hayes, of 2,000l. Stock, together with a Dividend of 101, per Cent. on the fame, at a Time when the Market Price of African Stock was but 10/. per Cent.

Your Committee observe, That the said Charles Hayes hath sworn before the Commissioners, that he was no ways interested therein, or had any Benefit thereby; that the said Henry Parjons remained, at the Time of his Death, justly and truly indebted to the Company, in the Sum of 800l. for the said 2,000l. Stock; and that he the said Charles Hayes was a Trustee for the said Henry Parjons, for the Sum of 2,0001. Stock; and that, having that Sum in the Name of John Tyjoe, he directed the same to be transferred by him to the Trustees, in Satisfaction of the said Sum of 800l. which ought to have been paid by the said Henry Parjons*, from all which Circumstances your Committee beg leave to observe, That there is Efficient Ground ro believe, that the Value of the said 5,000l. African Stock, and the said Sums of 21c/. and 3,641 /. is. 11A. so received by him, were, bond side, expended by him in the Service of the Company; and that the said Charles Hayes Esquire, hath discharged himself of the said Sum of 800l. which was truly owing by Henry Parjons Esquire, deceased.

Who claims, as Executor of the last Will of Henry Turner, late Governor of William's Fort, Whydah.

And it appeared to your Committee, that the said Bracebridge was possessed of the Will about a Month before the Commission for settling the Claims of the Creditors of the Royal African Company was closed; but that the same was not proved till the 28th of March last; and that he laid no Claim before the Commissioners.

And it further appeared, that no Accounts had come from Whydah, since the Year 1745; and that therefore his Account with the Company could not be made up: And,

Mr. James Craick, late Chief Agent of Cape Coast Castle, said. That when he came from thence, last March was Twelvemonth, Mr. Turner being dead, no Account was found of the Expenditure offome Goods of the Company, which he had had in his Hands; so that they could not tell, upon the Coast, whether the Company was indebted to him, or he to the Company.

Uponall which Circumstances, vour Committee thought it improper to proceed any further in the Matter of the said Petition.

founded their Claims to Interest upon the following'Rea-fons:

That the Parliament granted several Sums to the said_ Company, for the Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements; which induced the Petitioners to trust the Company:

And they further urged, That the House has already resolved, that the Compensation to be given to the Royal African Company shall be, in the first place, applied to the Payment of the bond side Creditors of the said Company; and that therefore the Creditors ought to be paid their Interest, before the Proprietors can have any Part of the Compensation.

Upon which, your Committee observe. That the Creditors never took any Asignment upon the Supplies granted by Parliament:

That the Value of the Security, and the legal Right to Interest, are not to be considered but jointly with the Means of coming at them; and that the Ad: of Parliament not dirccting the Commissioners to compute Interest, seems to imply the sense of the House, at that Time, to have been, that Interest should not be allowed.

Your Committee then proceeded to consider the Petition of Alexander Grant, and Richard Oswald, of London, Merchants, for themselves and Company; and find the Matter of Fad: therein contained to be as follows:

Mr. Spence, Secretary to the Royal African Company, being examined, said, That the Fort on Bence Islandi formerly belonged to the Royal African Company; that it was loft in the Year 1728., by the ill Management of Walter Charles, Governor of the said Fort; who used the Natives so arbitrarily, that they rose upon him, and took the Fort.

Captain Boyce said, That when Mr. Charles was drove away by the Natives, they burnt down the-Hpufes, and, blew up the Magazine; that,he (the Wirness) bought*he Fortin 1744, of the King of that Country, for Mr'. George Fryer; and that he gave for it the Value of 100l. in Goods, as Entry-Money, and 120 Bars, value 5 s. Sterling each Bar, yearly, for the Space of Five, Years; and that he was to hold it as long as he pleased; that he put it into a State of Defence, rebuilt the Magazine, and made the Ramparts 30 Foot high; that he mounted Twenty-two Guns, Ten of which, being Nine Pounders, he found jin the Rubbish; and the others were smaller.

Being further examined, he said, That he had not the Consent of the Royal African Company, to make this Bargain with the Natives; that he knew the Fort had been theirs; and that he does not know that the Company was ever invited to come and settle there again; and that, when in April 1743, he sollicited the King of that Country for Liberty to settle upon the said I/land, he refuled his Consent; saying, That he believed he came from the Company, who, for their ill Ufige, he was resolved should never emoe there again; and that the said King would not let him settle there, till he made it appear, chat he belonged to Mr. Fryer; and that then he lent him Men, and assisted him in the Settling; and that, during this Treaty a French Ship came there, and offered large Presents to the King, to have Liberty to settle in that I (land: That he made this Purchase for the safe Keeping of his Goods, and for a Defence against the French in War Time; and that he carried on a Trade there, tinder the Protection of the Fort, between Four and Five Years.

That he apprehended the Guns belonged to the Royal African Company, but gave them no Information about them; and found no other Military Stores there:

That he never applied to the Company for their Con* sent, or informed them of this Bargain with the Natives; but that he took Possession of the Fort, for the Use of Mr. Fryer, for the better Keeping of his Goods; and had a special Order from him, to settle where-ever he pleased; and Mr. Fryer had the Benefit of the Trade carried on there.

Being further examined, he said, That the Fort is proper to be kept up for the Defence of the Trade; but he does not know, whether the Natives will let the new Company take Possession of it, as they declare very much against the old Company:

That he has seen many French Vessels trading upon that Coast, since the Peace; and that, if they should get Possession of the Fort, he apprehended they would get the Trade of that River, and the Coast adjacent, entirely to themselves; and that there is about 200 Ton of Redwood got there yearly, value about 32 /. a Ton; between 3 and 4,000 Negroes; about 15 Ton of Elephants Teeth, value 240 Guineas a Ton; but not much Wax, nor Gold, nor any Grain; the Grain Coast being a little below it:

That he has known English Subjects settle on the Banana Jjlcnds\ upon which he has heard the French had Intention to settle; but that the Fore would prevent them:

That the Company, during his Time, never claimed the Guns, or the Fort; and that this River is^a very safe Place for Ships; and will admit Ships of War, being not less than Twelve Fathom Water at the Entrance, and Nine where they anchor; and that a Ship of War, stationed there in Time of War, would be of great Service to scour and protest the Coast.

Then an Article of Bargain and Sale of the said Fort and Island, dated the 8th of July 1748, from Mr. Fryer to Mr. Oswald, was read.
