APPEND I X, N°. 1.

To the Honourable the Committee* -to whom the Report of the Commissioners, appointed to examine into the Claims of the Creditors of the Royal African Company, is referred.

The Commissioners, in their Report to the Honourable House of Commons, having stated specially the several Sums of Money which Charles Hayes, late Deputy Governor of the African Company, had expended, in Disbursements and Expences, in and about the Company’s Affairs, for Two and Twenty Years, viz, from 1726 to the End of the Year 1748, he humbly begs Leave to explain to this Honourable Committee the Reasonsand Occasions of such Disbursements and Expences.

And, First, as to the Sum of Two hundred and Ten Pounds, which was paid to him in the Year 1726, he begs Leave to inform the Committee, That many Gentlemen, then newly come into the Direction, being desirous -to know whether the Company had, by their Charter, a legal Right to the foie Trade to Africa, within the Limits thereof, exclusive of all others his Majesty’s Subjects, he was ddired to get the best Information he could, in rel&ion thereto 5 whereupon the Records of the Rolls were examined, and Copies of such Royal Charters as had been granted to former Companies, from the Commencement of the Trade of this Nation to Africa, were obtained, many printed Cafes, and feme Judgements upon Record in the Courts in Westminster-Hall; in relation to the Prerogative, were searched; and many Consultations with Sollicitors, and others, were had 5 and sundry Cafes were prepared, and laid before several of the most eminent Counsel at that Time, for their Opinion thereupon; and ‘ this Money was expended in Fees to Counsel and Sollicitors, and in defraying the other necessary Charges in and about this Affair.-

As for the Ten thousand Pounds nominal Trust Stock, which the Company themselves valued at 30 per Cent, (the current Price then at Market) in their own Books, and which the Court of Assistants, on the 23d Day of October 1729, directed to be transferred to Francis Lynn Esquire, to be disposed of, with the Privity of Sir B'tbye Lakey Charles Hayes> and Henry Parsons, without Account, the said Charles Hayes humbly begs Leave to inform the Committee, That the Company having, about that Time, an Intention to apply for an Allowance from the Publick, towards the Support of their Forts and Settlements in slfricdy which they well knew could not be done without a considerable Expence, and the Company being, at the same time, greatly straitened for Money for their other necessary Occasions, they judged this to be the best way they could take to make Provision for that Service j and as public Applications are always attended with great Expences, this was then thought to be a very moderate Provision for such a Service; and as no Man would have the Gentlertten intruded with the Application thereof, he African neither thought it necessary to keep by him any particular Company* Account of the Sale and Application of such of the said Trust Stock as come to his Hands; nor can he now, it this Distance of Time, give any particular Account thereof; but he doth very well remember, that One^half, or Five Thousand Pounds, of the said nominal Trust Stock, Was left to the Care and Disposalof the said Henry Parsons, and the other Five thousand Pounds, of the said nominal Trust Stock, was left to the Care and Disposal of the said Charles Hayes; that for more than Twelve Months preceding th£ said 2 3d Day of October 1729, the said Henry Parforts, toge> ther withhimself, had been at many Charges and Expences in Attendances upon the Ministry, in order to lay before them the Nature of the Company’s Cafe, the Hardships they laboured under, and their Inability to support the Charges of their Forts and Settlements any longer, without some suitable Aid and Assistance from the Publick *, that upon the Company’s Application,by Petition to Parliament/the Session next after the said 23d Day of October 1729; for Relief, the said Petition met with great Oppoftnon froth the then separate Traders,who had enjoyed the Protection of the said Forts and Settlements, for the Seventeen Years preceding, without contributing any thing to the Charge of them; and who were then apprehensive, that the o;d Act in 1697, which had laid a Duty of 10/. per Cent.

for 13 Years, on their Trade, might be again revived\ and therefore, in order to support the Company’s P re -tensions, it was found absolutely necessary to consult the Journals of both Houses of Parliament, as far back as the-Reltoration, to fee what had been done in former Parliaments, in relation to this Trade, to advise with Counsel upon such Difficulties as arbfe, to employ several Sollicitors, to print and give away great Numbers of Cafes, Estimates, and other Papers, fur the Information of the Members, to fumtnon, subsist, and defray the Charges of many Witnesses, who attended, from time to time, to be examined upon that Occasion, be Tides many other daily Expences, for Coach-hire, Coffee-houses, Taverns, and the like; and the said Charles Hayes humbly hopes, that when the Committee shall be pleated to consider that these and the like Ditburfements and Expences, were necessary and unavoidable, and that all other Charges and Expences whatsoever were borne and defrayed out of the Produce of the above-mentioned Ten Thousand Pounds nominal Trust Stock, without putting the Company to any other Expence, the Honourable Committee will be of Opinion, that the Gentlemen, who had the Conduct of this Affair* did not abuse the Confidence which the Company had reposed in them.

As to the Third Article, relating to his Disbursements and Expences, in and about the Company’s Business, for Eighteen Years running; viz. (from 1730 to 1748) which, ir> so long a Course of Time, amounts to a considerable Sum, when collected together, he must crave Leave to observe, that, as the Company were obliged to attend and sollicit for the same every Session, such an Expence could not be avoided; which he humbly hopes will be thought very moderate; and, more especially, as many other Expences, upon numberless Occasions, were included in the said Accounts of Disbursements, and no where else charged to the Company.

As to the Fourth and last Article oF Eight hundred Pounds, which Henry Parsons Esquire was in Arrear to the Company at his Death, on Account of Two thousand Trust Stock, Part of the large Parcel which he

The same of Mr. Hopcgood's Family, with relpeCb to the African Stock now remaining in their Names.

Andrew Hopegood Esquire, the Father, having a Demand on the Company, for Principal Money, really and bond side lent, and Interest, amounting together to the Sum of 7,384/. did in the Year 1712, subscribe the same into the Company’s Stock at Par, and thereby became intided to 7,584/. Capital Stock; which, although no Part of it has been alienated since the First Purchase, yet by the several Variations and Reductions the Company have fmee made in their Stock, notwithstanding all the Calls have been duly paid in upon the fame, yet is now reduced to 559/. Capital Stock; besides which, the said Andrew Hopegood, since the Year 1712, viz. in the Years 1720, 1722, and 1723, hath laid out in the Purchase of other Parcels of the said Stock the Sum of 7,211 /. none of which Stock cost less than 30 /. per Cent. and not any of the whole Sum alienated since the Time of first* subscribing or purchasing the fame, but through the like Variations and Reductions made by the Company; the Representativesof the said Hopegood have Credit in the Company’s Books for only 1,676/. for such Jaft pure ha fed Stock; but in regard that many other Proprietors may be under the like Circumstances, with respect to the last-

mentioned several Parcels of Stock, they waive any particular Claim in respe<5l thereto; but humbly hope, with respect to the first mentioned Sum, in which their same is singular, they may be intided to a DistinClion from the other Proprietors of Stock, and may be considered accordingly out of the Compensation to be allowed to the Proprietors.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Farmers, Ditto. Madders, Mcalmen, Shopkeepers, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, in and near the Towns 0 {Hit chin, Baldock,

Stevenage, Wellwyn, and Hatfield', in the County of Hertford, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That the Petitioners live in an inland Country, and that great Quantities of Wheat, Flour, Meal, and Malt, are sent weekly from all Parts of the said County, by Land-carriage, for the Use of the Cities of London and Westminster;

minster; and that the Petitioners are from thence supplied with divers kinds of Goods and Merchandize, for their necessary Use and Consumption; and that the Trade and Business of the said County are chiefly carried on by Land-carriage; and alleging, That should the said Bill pass into a Law, the Petitioners are greatly apprehensive the Price of Carriage mud be considerably increased; and the Petitioners have the more Reason to fear such Advance in the Price of Carriage, because, since an Engine for weighing Waggons has been erected at the Toll-gate at Whet-fione, in the County of Middlesex, through which the Petitioners are obliged to pass, in coming to, and returning from, the Cities of London and Westminster, the Price of the Carriage of Goods has been considerably raised; and should weighing Engines be erected at all the Turnpike Gates in‘ 1England, the Petitioners apprehend the Consequence of such Law would be a general Advance in the Price of Carriage all over the Kingdom j in which Cafe, the Petitioners would pay a large advanced Price on such Goods and Manufactures which they consume, as come by Land-carriage to London, and from thence are brought down for the Consumption of the Country; and that many of the Petitioners were so sensible of the inconveniencies arising to the Inland Trade and Business of the Country, from the Restrictions already laid on Land-carriage; that they were actually preparing a Petition to be presented to the House, 'praying a Repeal of the Act, passed in the 14th Year of his Majesty’s Reign, which impowers the Trustees of any Turnpike Road in England, to erect Engines for weighing Waggons; but that they dropt such their Design, on seeing by the Votes of this House, that the aforesaid Bill was ordered to be brought in: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill; or that they may have such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third time: And that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel against the faiU Bill, if they think fit.

lo of course the Petitioners will be under a Necessity of railing the Price of the Commodity in Proportion; which will not only bring very great Hard-ships upon the Consumers, and especially the lower Sort of People, but may also greatly affect, as the Petitioners apprehend, the Dairy Farms in those several Counties; For the Information and Guidance of the Committee, in considering the Matter to them referred, they have made the best Searches and Inquiries they could into the Journals of the House, and the Practice of the Officers* from whence they find, that the present Table of Fees has been in general the Rule for demanding and taking them ever since the Year 1700; a List of the Fees having been in that Year laid before the House, and entered in the Journals; which Lift was, by anOrder of the House, of the 22d Day of February 1731, fixed as a (landing Rule to the Officers of the House, for demanding and taking of Fees, for all Times to come; but, as in that Lift the Articles relating to private Bills and Clauses are expressed in Terms too indeterminate, they have given Occasion to many Difficulties and Disputes, concerning their true Meaning and Import, between the Parties concerned, and the Officer without-doors, who usually receives the Fee* for the rest. — Of the Kinds of these Disputes, an Accouni has been very fully and candidly set forth to your Committee, by the Clerk of the House,in a Paper hereunto annexed. In Obedience to your Order, I have prepared the bed Account I was able to collect, either from my own Observation, or from the Information of others, as well of what has been the Rule and Practice of the Officers of the House, in relation to the Fees for private Bills and Clauses, as of what Difficulties or Disputes have of late arisen thereupon

As to the Question, What are private Bills, within the Meaning of the Table of Fees ? or, in other Words, What Bills are liable to the Payment of any Fees at all ? The Rule observed by the Officers of the House, in their Demand of Fees, seems to have been this; where a Bill concerns the Inrereft, cr contained Provisions calculated for the Benefit of any particular Person or Persons, or of any particular Body of People, they haVe' always considered. themselves as intitled to Fees for such Bill.

Under this Article, the following Doubts have been made.

Where a Bill appeared to be of general Utility, although immediately, and in the First Instance, calculated for the Benefit of a particular Person, or Body of People, it has of late been sometimes argued, that such Bill was a publick one, and therefore not liable to pay any Fees.

Where a Bill has been brought into the House, upon Motion, without a previous Petition, or in consequence of a Report from a Committee of the whole House, it has been sometimes argued, that the Manner of bringing in such Bill proved it to be a publick one, and therefore not subject to the Payment of Fees.

This last Method of avoiding the Payment of Fees has been more particularly practised of late, with regard to the Continuances of temporary Acts.

Application is made to the Committee, appointed to consider of expiring Laws, to insert in their Report of Laws fit to be continued, such Acts as, in their own Nature, ought to pay Fees, and for which Fees were originally paid. — Now, as the Provisions directed to be made, in consequence of such Report, are usually inserted in some general Bill, the Persons incerefted in such particular Provisions are under no Necessity of appearing to solicit or follow such Bill; so that no Demand of Fees can be made; and the regular Method (and indeed in such Cases the only remaining one) of ipforcing the Payment of Fees, by objecting to the Progress of the Bill, is what the Officers of die House must be very backward to rn^ke use of, in relation to Matters which have the Appearance of being originally taken up by the House itself.

That the Petitioners apprehend the Method proposed to raise the Sum necessary to begin, complete, and keep in Repair, this expensive and unnecessary Work, will not only be very unequal, but lay the Petitioners under the greated Difficulties, by affcifh'ng their Properties; and the rather, as Two-thirds of the inhabitants of the said Street are Shopkeepers, Traders, and other Persons, whose whole Dependence is in Lodging Houses, and unable to bear so great a Tax; and that the Publick in general, not the Inhabitants in particular, will receive the Benefit (if any) of this great and heavy Burden, to be imposed upon the Petitioners; and that the Tax, intended by the said Bill to be laid upon the Petitioners, will far exceed the Expence they ever have been at about their Pavement, which they can keep in good Repair, at a moderate yearly Expence; and that as all, or the greated Part of the Inhabitants, have now Lamps at their own Doors, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, they will, notwithstanding, be obliged to continuethem, for their owri Security and Convenience: And therefore praying. A BILL for encouraging the Making of Pot-Afties and Pearl-A fhes, in the British Plantations in America, was read a Second time.

' Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House*

A Petition of William Lodge was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Pearl-Ashes are a Commodity extremely necessary for carrying on several Manufactures in this Kingdom; and for that Purpose great Quantities of them have formerly been imported from Germany, and other foreign Countries, at a great JExpence; and that the Petitioner having for many Years made it his Study to discover the Art of making Pearl-Ashes, knowing that in England there was Wood, and other Vegetables, for making more than suficient to supply the Demands for it in Great Britain, he, to the great Detriment of his Fortune, and at the Hazard of his Life, travelled into Germany, in order to discover the Art, and to set up a Manufacture thereof in England for the publick Utility; and that the Petitioner did thereby discover the Art of making Pearl-A(hes, and the Implements and Utensils necessary for that Purpose, and returned to England; and in the Year 1748 set up a Manufacture thereof, near Bury St. Edmonds, in Suffolk; and, in order to encourage the Petitioner therein, his Majesty, by Letters Patent, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, Jbearing Date the First Day of July 1749, was pleased to grant to the Petitioner an exclusive Power of making Pearl-A flies in England, and vending the fame, for the Space of Fourteen Years, according to the Statute in that same made and provided; and that, by the Terms of the said Letters Patent, the Petitioner was compelled to a Discovery of such of his Art, by inrolling the same in Chancery, for the Good of the Publick, after the Expiration of his Term, whereby all Persons are enabled to eome at the Knowledge of the Petitioner’s Secret; and that the Petitioner hath, from the obtaining of his Parent, carried on the Business of making Pearl- Ashes, which are in all Respects equal, and in some superior, to any imported from abroad; and doubts not but, before the Ex-Vol. 26.

piration of his Term of 14 Years, he shall be able to extend the said Manufacture greatly to the Benefit of this Kingdom, and thereby recompence himself for the great Trouble and Expence he hath been put to; and alleging.

That by the said Bill, should the same pass into a Law, without some Regard had to the Petitioner, his Majesty's most gracious Design, of granting the said exclusive Trade to the Petitioner, will be defeated, the Petitioner prejudiced in his Property, and all the Hopes of retrieving his Fortune, and compensating for his Labour and Danger, will be destroyed: And therefore praying the House to take the Petitioner’s same into Consideration; and that he may be heard, by his Counsel, at the Second Reading of the said Bill; and may have such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

LawsHpeft- $ir Richard Lloyd reported from the Committee, who ing Felonies, were appointed to revise and consider the Laws in being.

which relate to Felonies, and other Offences against the Peace, and to report their Opinion thereupon, from time to time, to the House, as to the Defects, the Repeal, or Amendment of the said Laws; that the Committee had considered some other of the Matters to them referred, and had come to several other Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as foliow-eth, viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Provision for the Poor of England, and Wales, is become a very great, and is at present an increasing. Charge on the real and personal Estates of the Subjects.

Rejohedy That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That one great Cause of this Expence, is, that the vast Sums raised for their Use are in general expended on their mere Maintenance only, and very little or no Care taken to provide for their Employment.

Rtfolvedy Tiv.it it is the Opinion of this Committee, That another great Source of this Expence, is, the Removals of poor Persons from one Part of this Kingdom to another, as to the Place of their legal Settlements, and the Numbers of Controvcrfies arising thereon,

Vol. 26.

Rjolvedy That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That another great Source of the Increase of Expence, is, that there is in general little or no Care taken to educate the Children of the Poor in Habits of Industry, so that when they grow up they are not able to pfovide £ Maintenance for themselves, and so live in Idleness, partly through Necessity; and consequently propagate a new Race of chargeable Poor, from Generation to Generation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That many Parishes are too small separately to raise a Stock sufficient wherewith to employ the Poor to any Advantage.

Rejohedy That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That it would, in all Probability, be a great Means of lessening, to a considerableDegree, the Charge of the Poor, and of greatly decreasing their Number, in a Very few Years, if some Method should be agreed on to maintain and employ the Poor by one common Fund in every County, although no Parish flhould be obliged to contribute more than they have usually paid to the Maintenance of their own Poor, at a reasonable Medium.

Resolved,\ That it is the Opinion of this Comteittefc, That after such Method shall be agreed upon, the Repeal of the several Laws concerning the Settlements and Removals of, and Certificates for, the Poor, would be a Saving of very great Sums now expended on those Occasions.

The Five first Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Sixth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Word " one," and inferring the Word " a " instead thereof;

And the Question being put. That the Word " one" {land Part of the said Refolurion;

It pa{fed in the Negatiye.

And the Question being put, That the Word " a *’ be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the said Resolution, by leaving out all the Words thereinafter the Word "County."

And the Question being pur, That the Words proposed to be left out (land Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

Rejohedy That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended. That it would, in all Probability, be a great Means of lessening, to a considerable Degree, the Charge of the Poor, and of greatly decreasing their Number, in a very few Years, if some Method should be agreed on to maintain and employ the Poor by a common Fund in every County.

The lad Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Sir William Tonge reported from the Committee, who were appointed to enquire into the Laws relating to Trade and Manufactures, and to report their Opinion, from time to time, to the House, as to the Repeal or Amendment of the fame; That the Committee had considered several of the said Laws; and had directed him to report their Observations thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee appointed to enquire into the Laws relating to Trade and Manufactures, and to report their Opinion, from time to time, to the House, as to the Repeal or Amendment of the fame, have very frequently met and made a considerable Progress in the Enquiry, for which they were' appointed; but they have found it a much more voluminous Work than they imagined, thot%h, ac the same Time, a very useful and necessary Employment and there-

a. 1751*.

fore have thought it proper only to rrprefenc to the House in general the following Observations.

They have gone through all the Laws relating to that Part of Trade and Manufactures usuallydistinguished under the Head of Drapery; a great Part of which they are of jfepi|Uon ought to be irltirely repealed; many, as being grown out of Use, and lcarce ever put in Execution, but on malicious and frivolous Pro*urions; others inti rely local; others, though perhaps well calculated for the Times jn which they were made, yet now become prejudicial to Trade, in its present State; others quite useless,. and particularly such as relate to the Aloage, now ac an End; and many others, to a great Number, an unnecessary Burthen to the Statute Book;

There are others proper to be repealed, though they may contain many useful and advantageousClauses, which, in the Opinion of your Committee, ought rather to be re-enacted in new Bills, unde^roper Titles, expressing the Contents, to avoid the gr£at Difficulty of finding them uhder several Heads; particularly in the Instance of (almost annual) Bills for continuing expiring Laws of various Kinds, many of the Titles- of which are deficient in the expressing the whole Contents; and others of which are of such different Natures, as to require great Attention, even in those who make the Law their peculiar Srudy, to reduce them under proper Heads* much more to J offices of the Peace, and others, who are entruftrd with the Execution of them.

Besides, there are several others of different Natures, well worth the Consideration of the House, particularly such as relate to the Reftrainrs laid on the Exportation of the Coin of this Kingdom; which may have a Tendency to prevent the Coining of great Quantities of the Bullion imported for the Balance of Trade from several Parrs, which lies dead, as being of moreVakie than coined Silver, by being capable of re-exportation for foreign and beneficial Trades; and if it were employed here, might be of great Use in Circulation, and would increase our Sterling Currency.

There arc other Laws of great Importance, which dr- serve Consideration; particularly such as require the serving an Apprenticeship for seven Yeats, before any Person can setup a particular Trade and Occupation, which were at first well intended, for securing the Goodness, and consequently the Value and Estimation, of our several Manufactures in foreign Parts, and to prevent the Disparage-meot of them, by unfkilfui Workmen; but fmcc the Improvement of Trade in general, it is found chat all Manufactures find their own Value, according to their Goodness; and that scarce any Prosecutions have been carried on upon these Statutes, but against such as have excelled in their own Trades, by Force of their own Genius, and not against such as have been ignorant in their Proft ffions; which is the Reverie of the Intent of such Laws, and a great Obstruction to Industry and Improvements.

These Obstructions arise partly from the Laws above-mentioned, and partly from particular Franchises and Byelaws of Corporations; but your Committee are of Opinion* if the legal Restraints were once removed, the particular Bye-laws would soon be reversed; as they cannot but observe, that the most useful and beneficial Manufactures are principally carried on, and Trade most fiouri thing, in such Towns and Places as are under no such local Disabilhies.

Your Committee also observe*, That a" Work of this Nature has been thought a properObjeft of Parliamentary Consideration, particularly in the First and Twenty-eighth Years of the Reign of King fames the First, and in the ThirdofKingCiwr/mheFirft,whenfeveral A 6ls,formerly passed, to a very great Number, were either confirmed, revived, altered, or repealed 5 but in so con used a Manner, as to require great Accuracy, and Attention, and frequent turning to the several Acts cherein mentioned, in order to know which of those Laws, and how much of each, remain in Force, and which of them are repealed; which Inconvenience may easily be avoided, in framing

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The advanced Season of the Year makes it necessary for me to put an End to this Session of Parliament; and I do it with the greater Satisfaction, as your diligent Application to the publick Business has brought it to lb happy a Conclusion. On this Occasion, I cannot but return you my hearty Thanks for the many Proofs you have given me of your Zeal and Affection for me and my Government, and the Care and Attention which you have exerted for the Interests of my People.

As Europe now enjoys a happy Tranquillity, very little Alteration has been made in the State bf^preign Affairs fmee your Meeting. My Resolution to preserve the general Peace is the fame; and I have the greatest Reason to rely on the like good Disposition in the Powers in Alliance with me, not only being continued, but confirmed and improved.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Readiness with which you have granted me the Supplies for the Service of the current Year demands my particular Acknowledgements; and the Prudence and Firmness you have shewn in completing the Reduction of the Interest of the national Debt is agreeable to me, as that Mjjrafure is essential to the Strength and Welfare of my Kingdom.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have nothing to desire of you, but effectually to consult your own true Interest and Happiness. Let it be your Care to maintain, in your several Countries, the publick

AM ESS AGE from his Majesty, by the Honourable Sir Henry Bellenden, Gentleman-Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And, being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, pursuant to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament* of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the-House; and is as foliow-eth* viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is with great Satisfaction that I meet you in Parliament at this Time, when the Continuance of the publick Tranquillity, and the flouriflhing Condition of my Kingdoms, leave us nothing to desire, but to secure and improve our present Situation. To this end all my Views and Measures have" been directed, both at home and abroad; and itjt this State of Things nothing can give me more real Pleasure, than to observe those solid Advantages which my good Subjects reap from it in their Tracts and Manufactures; some Branches whrrcof have also received considerable Benefit from the wife Provisions which have been made by this Parliament.

The Treaty lately entered into with the Elector of Bavaria was laid before you in your last Session, and I then acquainted you that I was taking such further Measures as might tend to secure the Tranquillity of the Empire, support its System, and timely prevent such Events as had been found by Experience to endanger the common Cause. I have since, for the same Purposes, in Conjunction with the States General of the United Provinces, found it necessary to conclude a Treaty with the King of Tolandy Elector of Saxony; which shall be communicated to you.

The unfortunate Event of the Prince of Orang/s Death has made no Alteration in the Srate of Affairs in Holland) and by the prudent and early Measures taken there the Quiet of that Country has been preserved, and their Government carried on upon the Foundation of the Settlement which had, with so much Fore fight, t^en previously established by Laws of the Republick. have received the strongest Assurances from the States General of their firm Resolution to maintain that strict Union and Friendship, which so happily subsist between me and those ancient and natural Allies of my Crown.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered Estimaces of the Expences of the ensuing Year to be prepared, and laid before you: And have no other Supplies to ask of you, but such as are re-quisite for those Services, and for making good such necessary Engagements as you are made acquainted with.

The Success which has attended your Firmness in reducing the interest of the national Debt will, I am confident, give you the greareft Satisfaction.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Experience I have had of your dutiful and (lead? Conduct makes it wholly unnecessary for me to prels upon you Unanimity and Dispatch in your Deliberations. But 1 cannot conclude without recommending to you, in the most earned Manner, to consider seriously of feme effectual Provisions to suppress those audacious Crimes of Robbery and Violence, which are now become so frequent, especially about this great Capital, and which have proceeded in a great measure from that profligate Spirit of Irreligion, Idleness, Gaming, and Extravagance, which has of.late extended itself, in an uncommon Degree, to the Dishonour of the Nation, and to the great Offence and Prejudice of the sober and4nduftrious Part of my People.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to Add-on his Majesty, to return the Thanks of this House to his Majesty, for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; ?’ec' to express our full and due Sense of the Happiness we enjoy under his Majesty's wife and just Government, and our well grounded Confidence, chat his Majesty’s View’s are, and ever will be, directed to no other End than to secure and improve the present flourishing Condition of his Kingdoms: That the Regard, which his Majesty is pleased 10 Certify for the Advancement of our Trade and Manufactures, is a signai Instance cf his Majesty’s constant and universal Attention to the Welfare of his Subjects; and that it cannot but be Matter of the utmost Satisfaction to this House, that the Provisions made for that Purpose by this Parliament, in pursuance cf his Majesty's former most gracious Recommendations, have produced the desired Effect: And to a ffure his Majesty, that wc will readily concur in all such Measures as tend to 6 fecufefc

Sir John Turner; And they are to meet upon Monday Fortnight, at Five of the Clock, in the Afternoon, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and to fit every Wednesday, Friday, and Monday, in the Afternoon: And all that come are to have Voices: And they are to take into Consideration all such Matters as shall or may come in Question touching Returns, Elections, and Privileges; and to proceed upon double Returns in the First place; and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinions thereupon, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that will question any Returns, are to do it within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee are to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information: And all Members who are recurned for Two or more Places, are to make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall come in Question touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or recurned a Member of this House, or endeavoured lb to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the Utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirediy, hath ehdeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

# Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall fee, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this

House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and IV^stminster, do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Scfilon of Parliament, the Paflfages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and Open; and chat no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall^oT the Paflfages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be noAnnoy-ance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen, attending the Members of this House, to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall. presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, That to prevent the Intercepting or Losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster-General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning, till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the rising of the House; and also on every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members, to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaster-General.

Ordered, That when any Letter, or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame, and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to the House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going 10 Prayers, give Notice thereof to all Committees; and that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do ap-

enjoy under your Majesty’s wile and just: Government, and our well grounded Confideflfcfv that your Majesty’s Views are, and ever will be, directed to no other End than to secure and improve the present flourishing Condition of your Kingdoms. The Regard your Majesty is pleased to certify for the Advancement of our Trade and Manufactures, as it is a signal Instance of your Majesty’s constant and universal Attention to the Welfare of your Subjects, demands our sincerest Acknow-legements. And it cannot but be Matter of the highest Satisfaction to us, that the Provisions made for char Purpose, by this Parliament, in pursuance of your Majesty’s most gracious Recommendation, have produced the desired Eflfcft.

We unfeignedly assure your Majesty, That we will readily concur in all such Measures as tend to secure the inestimable Blessings of Peace to us, by establishing more firmly the general Tranquillity in Europe.

Affected with the deepelt Concern, we condole with your Majesty on the unfortunate Event of the Death of the Prince of Orange; but, at the same Time, beg Leave to express the great Consolation we feel, from the strong Assurances given to your Majesty, on this Occasion, by the States General of the United Provinces; which Leave us no room to doubt of the Continuance of that strict Union and Friendship, so essential to the interests of both Countries.

Your faithful Commons, with the utmost Chearfulnels, promise to grant to your Majesty such Supplies as may enable your Majesty to fulfil the Engagements, and answer the several Services which shall be found necessary for the publick Good.

We cannot sufficiently acknowlege your Majesty’s Wisdom and Goodness, in recommending to our Consideration the Mischiefs and Dithonour which arise to this Nation, from the audacious Crimes, of Robbery and Violence so notorious of late to all the World; and we humbly assure your Majesty, That we will seriously proceed in revising and enforcing such Laws as may contribute to suppress those Enormities, by discouraging Irreligion, Idleness, Gaming, and Immorality, by promoting Industry, and establishing good Order, amongst your Majesty’s Subjects.

setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, several Tolls, Duties, and Powers, were granted for repairing the aforesaid Highways, and several considerable Sums of Money were borrowed on the Credit of the same Act; and several new Tolls, Duties, and Powers, were thereby granted for repairing the aforesaid Highways 5 and that the Trustees, by the same Act appointed, are thereby directed, out of the Tolls and Duties thereby granted, or out of the Monies to be borrowed by virtue Thereof, to pay the Monies which were lent on the Credit of the said former Act, and then remaining due; which Act of the Second of his present Majesty was to continue in Force for the Space of Twenty-seven Years, from the said 12th Day of May 1729, and no longer; and further setting forth, That the Tolls collected and received by virtue of the said last mentioned Act, have been duly laid out and applied according to the Directions thereof 5 and great Progress hath been made in amending the said Highways; but that the Sum of One thousand and Two hundred Pounds, and upwards, which was borrowed on the Credit of the said several Acts of Parliament, now remains justly due and owing to the Persons who lent the fame, or their Representatives; and that the same Highways cannot be effectually repaired, and kept amended, and that the Money borrowed on the Credit of the said Acts, and now remaining due, cannot be repaid, unless the Term and Powers, granted by the said last-mention^d Act, be further

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, Assist-anrs, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Wallingford, in the County of Berks, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the said Borough of Wallingford is a very ancient Borough, commodiously situated for Trade, on the Banks of the River Thames, and was formerly a very flourishing Town, with Two good Markets for Corn and Provisions every Week, to the great Advantage of the said Borough, and all the Country round about it; but that, by reason of theexceflive Badnels of the Roads leading to the said Borough, the same is of late Years fallen into great Decay, their Markets almost ruined, and their Trade entirely at a Stand; and that, in particular, the Road leading from thence to Wantage, and so on to Farringdon, in the County of Berks, is in many Parts become so deep and founderous, that for several Months in the Year it is very dangerous for Horsemen, and entirely impafiable for Carriages, and cannot be Jfofficiently repaired by any Laws now in being; and that the said Road lies through an exceeding rich and fertile Vale, in which great Quantities of Corn, Cheese, and Butter, are anndaily produced; but for want of being able to draw the same to Market in the Winter, the Farmers are very frequently impoverished, and rendered incapable to pay their Rents; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that in case the Roads above-mentioned were sufficiently repaired and amended, and thereby a Communication opened between the said Vale and the River of Thames, it would not only be an inconceivable Advantage to the Petitioners, and the Inhabitants of the said Vale, but also be a Means of supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with Malt, Meal, Cheese, and Butter, and other Provisions, at a much cheaper Rate than they can be supplied at present: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and make such Provision for repairing and amending the said Roads, as the House shall fee meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Berks, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed an Application is making to Parliament, for repairing the Road -from Wallingford, through Wantage, to Farringdon, in the County of Berks, which the Petitioners conceive would be a Work not only of great Advantage to the Towns through which the said Road pafies, and the Property of many private Persons, but of evident Utility to the Publick; and that many of the Petitioners are Inhabitants or Proprietors of the Vale of Berkshire; and that the same is an exceeding rich and fertile Vale, of great Extent both as to Length and Breadth, and producing annually immense Quantities of Corn, Butter, and Cheese, which, for want of good Roads and Markets, are rendered almost useless to the Publick; and that the Farms are thereby impoverished, and the Farmers very frequently ruined; but that the Petitioners apprehend, in case a good Road be made through the Vale, and an easy Communication opened to the River of Thames, and the Cities of London and Westminster, ic must necessarily be productive of good Effects, not only to the Vale of Berkshire, but many other Parts of the Kingdom: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, That the House will make such Provision for repairing and amending the said Roads, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and that they do examine the

Matters thereof, and report the fame, as they shall appear to them, to the House.

Woollen A PETITION of several Persons, \vh9fe Names are trade. thereunto subscribed, on the Behalf of themselves,

and other Merchants, Wool-ftaplers, Clothiers, Makers and Manufacturers of Worlted Yarn, Broad Cloth, Cam-‘ blets, Callimancoes, Stuffs/and other Woollen Goods, in the Town and Parish of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; ‘fetting forth, That there are great Quantities of Broad Cloth, Camblets, Callimancoes, Stuffs, and other Woollen Goods, made and manufactured in the said Town and Parish, which are fold and disposed of in most Parts of Great Britain, and exported to divers Places beyond the Sea9, whereby great Numbers of Families are main-stained and supported, and great Benefit and Advantage has accrued to the Nation in general; and that, for the -Working and Making up of the several Sorts of Woollen Goods above-mentioned, the Petitioners are obliged to purchase great Quantities of Fleece Wool of the Growth of divers Parts of this Kingdom; and that for several Years past % pernicious Practice has prevailed among the Wool Growers, laying upon the Fleece excessive Quantities of Pitch, Tar, or other marking Stuff, and a deceitful Method of wrapping up and winding within several of the fleeces of Wool, sold to the Petitioners, not only Pieces of coarse and unmerchantable Wool, but also GotsyDirt, and other Refuse, greatly tending to the manifest Loss of the Wool Buyers and Manufacturers, the Difreputation and Debasement of the Manufactures, and Prejudice of the Trade of this Kingdom; and that several 4 1

Laws &nd Statutes ihaVe formerly been made for the true Winding of Wool, but that some of them are become oblblete, and the rest of them, by reason of the Small-ness of the Penalties thereby inflicted, are ineffectual to prevent the fraudulent Winding and pernicious Practices afore-mentioned: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for. amending and rendering more effectual the Laws now.in being for the due Winding of Wool, and for preventing the pernicious Practice of laying on the Fleece excessive Quantities of marking Stuff; or to give such Relief to the Petitioners, in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants, Wool-ftapiers, and others, Manufacturers and Dealers in Woollen Go.ods, in the Town and Parish of Ilallifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That within the said Town and Parish of Hallifax, are manufactured large Quantities of Shalloons, Serges, Everlaftings, Callimancoes, Kerfeys, Long Ells, Stuffs, and other Woollens, by which not only Numbers of Families acquire a comfortable Maintenance, but, by the Exportation of such Goods beyond the Seas, die Nation in general is greatly advantaged and enriched; at)d that, in making the several Goods above, such of the Petitioners as are Manufacturers con fume Fleece Wool of the Growth of several Parts of this Kingdom; and that, of lace Years, the Growers of Wool have laid upon the Fleece excessive Quantities of Pitch, Tar, or other marking Stuff, whereby not only the Weight is greatly increased, but the Wool receives great Damage; and that it hath also been a Practice among them, to wind up within the Fleece not only Wool of different Sons and inferior Quality, buc also Dirt, Dung, and other Refuse, to the great Detriment of the Manufacturers and of their Manufactures; and alleging. That the fraudulent Winding of Wool is a Crime of ancient Date, and although the Wisdom of former Parliaments hath enacted several Laws and Statutes to prevent it, particularly that made in the 23d Year of King Henry the Eighth, yet most of them are become obsolete, and the rest not effectual to prevent the above bad Practices: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into their serious Consideration, and enact in such manner as to the House shall seem most likely to prevent and hinder the said Frauds and Abuses, and to extend and encourage thereby the Woollen Manufactory, so highly advantageous to these Kingdoms.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matters thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution so much of art Act of Parliament (intituled, An Act for repairing and enlarging the Roads from the Town of Hefty, in the West Riding of the County of York, to the Town of Leeds, and from thence, in Two several Branches, one through Bradford and Horton, and the other through Bowling and Wibfey, to the Town of Hallifax, in the same Riding) as relates to the surveying* ordering, amending* and keeping in Repair* that Part of the said Road which lieth between the said Towns of Leeds and Hallifax aforesaid, whose Names are thereuntofubferibed, was presented to the House, and read* setting forth, That by the said Act several Tolls and Duties were granted and made payable for repairing and widening such Parts of the said Roads as lie between the l ow ns of Leeds and Hdlltfax aforesaid, to take Place, and have Continuance, from and after the I ath Day of May 1741, for the Term of Twenty-one Years; and that the Petitioners, and several other Persons, in the said Act named, were appointed Trustees for putting so much of the said Act in Execution as relates to the surveying, ordering, amending, and keeping in Re*-pair, that Parc of the said Roads which lies between the said Towns of Leeds and Hallifax aforesaid; and the said Trustees were thereby authorized and impowered to fee up One or more Turnpike or Turnpikes, in, upon, across, or on the Side of the said Road lying between the said Towns of Leeds and Hallifax, provided that no Toil-gate or T urn pike should be erected upon or across any Fart of the said Roads, within Three Miles of any or the Streets of Bradford and Hallifax aforesaid; and divers other Powers and Authorities were granted to, and vetted in, the Petitioners, and the other Trustees, in the said Act named, for effecting and carrying into Execution the Purposes of the said Act; and that the Petitioners, in order to put the said Act in Execution, did cause several Turnpikes or Toll-gates to be erected upon and across the said Roads, in the most convenient Places, being above Three Miles distant from the said several Towns ot Bradford and Hallifax; and farther, by Virtue, and under Authority, of the said Act, and on the Credit of the Tolls and Duties thereby granted, borrowed, and took up, at interest, the^Sum of Thirteen hundred Pounds; and did apply the said principal Sum of Thirteen hundred Pounds, and also so much of the said Tolls and Duties as remained and exceeded after Payment of the Interest of the said Sum of Thirteen hundred Pounds, in repairing and widening the said Roads; whereby a considerable Part of the said Roads is very much repaired; but that in regard the Petitioners have not, by virtue of the said Act, any Power or Authority to set up any Gate or T urnpike, upon any Pan of the said Roads, being within the Distance of Three Miles from either of the said Towns of Bradford and Halifax% a great Parr of the Passengers and others travelling the said Roads have, by that Means, evaded the Gateiafid Turnpikes set up by the Petitioners, and have avoided the Payment of the several Tolls and Duties granted by the said Act; whereby the greatest Parc of the said Tolls and Duties, which otherwise might have been collected, have been loft; and the good Purposes intended by the said Act are, in a great Measure defeated; so that the greacer Parr of the said Roads between the said Towns of Leeds and Hallifax remains in a ruinous Condition, very dangerous for Travellers, and, in the Winter Season, almost impassable; and alleging. That the Petitioners are convinced that it will be impossible to complete the Repairs of the said Road, and keep the same in Repair, and pay off* the Sum borrowed as aforesaid, unless the Term and Powers given by the said Act be enlarged and the Tolls and Duties thereby granted be augmented: And therefore praying, Thar Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the said former Act, and encreasing the Tolli and Duties thereby granted, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Greenwich A Petition of the Commissioners or Governors of the

Hospital. Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, was presented to the House, and read; fetcing forth. That by an Act passed in the Eighth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign (intituled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl of Derwentwater, and Charles Radcliffe) the Commissioners or Governors of the said Hospital were required to contract and agree with able and sufficient Tradesmen, Artificers, or other Persons, for finishing and completing the said Royal Hospital in a Workman-like manner, on the easiest and most reasonable Terms, according to the Plan laid before this House, in that Session of Parliament; and that, in order to finish and complete the Building of the said Hospital, the House and Yard, and Twofmall Parcels of Land, hereafter mentioned, are necessary to be purchased, viz. a House and Yard on the West Side of the said Hospital, late in the Occupation of one Henry Stanley, a Carpenter (but now untenanted) commonly known by the Name of Stanley's House and Yard; containing, at the South End, Fifty-nine Feet; at the North End, Sixty-one Feet Two Inches; on the East Side, Seventy-nine Feet Seven Inches; and on the West Side, Eighty-five Feet Seven Inches, be the same little more or less; One Parcel of Land, on the same Side of the said Hospital, whereon a small House lately stood, in the Occupation of one Benjamin Hopkins, a Barber, and commonly known by the Name of Carr's House; containing, at the South End, Eleven Feet Six Inches; at the North End, Ten Feet Seven Inches; on the East Side, Fifteen Feet Five Inches; and on the West Side, Fourteen Feet Eleven Inches, be the same little more or less; and One other Parcel of Land, on the East Side of the said Hospital, whereon several Houses formerly stood, belonging to the Trustees of Morden College, and now in the Possession of the said Commissioners or Governors of the said Hospital; which, by reason of Infancy, and other Inabilities, the Petitioners have not been able to purchase; and that, by reason of such Inabilities, the Petitioners cannot finish and complete the said Royal Hospital, without the further Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to render all Contrafts and Agreements, which shall be made by the said Commissioners or Governors for the purchase of the said House and Yard, and Parcels of Land, valid and effectual, and for ascertaining the Recompence that shall be made for the fame, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Greenwich A Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Inhabi-hrialVauto. fants 0y r[ie Parilli of Eafi Greenwich, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne (intituled, An Act for granting to her Majesty several Duties upon Coals, for building Fifcy new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof, and for other Purposes therein mentioned), it is, amongst other Things enacted, That there shall be erected and built, of Stone and other proper Materials, Fifty Churches, with Towers or Steeples to each of them; whereof one shall be erected in the Parish of Eafi Greenwich, in the County of Kent; and that, by a subsequent Act, passed in the Tenth Year of her said Majesty’s Reign, for enlarging the Time given to the Commissioners for building the said Fifty new Churches, and for giving them further Powers for better effecting the fame, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, it is provided and again enacted, That one of the said Fifty new Churches shall be erected in Eafi Greenwich^ in the County of Kent, as in the former Act is directed; and that, by the last mentioned Act, it is further enacted, That no Burial shall at any time thereafter be in or under any of the Churches, by that Act intended to be erected: That a new Church hath been erected in the said Parish of Eafi Greenwich, pursuant to the aforesaid Acts; and that, the Liberty of burying under the said new Church being taken away by the aforesaid Act, the Parishioners have been obliged, at their own Charge, to purchase an additional Piece of Ground, which, together with the old Church-yard hath been constantly used for burying therein; and chat as well by the many Vaults and separate Brick Graves, which have of late been granted to particular Persons and Families, as by a considerable Increase of poor Inhabitants, and the frequent Burials consequent thereon, the said Church-yards are no longer sufficient for Burial-places for the Inhabitants; and that, before the Erection of the said new Church, a large Vault or Burial-place, under the old Edifice, was appropriated to the Use of the Parish for Burials, in which a Fee of Twenty Shillings was paid to the Churchwardens; and that the Petitioners have caused the said new Church to be carefully and diligently surveyed and examined by able and experienced Surveyors and Workmen, who find and report, that as the same is built on substantial Pillars of Brick, and arched, by erecting Brick Walls in the vacant Spaces between such Pillars, the same may easily a'nd safely be converted into separate Vaults for Burials, without digging or breaking up the Ground or Floor of such Vaults, or being any otherwise prejudicial to the Walls or Foundation of the said Church; and that by several Acts passed in his present Majesty’s Reign, Power hath been granted by Parliament for placing and depoficing Corps under many of the said new Churches (notwithstanding the former Prohibition) lb as the Ground or Floor of such VoL. 26.

Vaults be not broken or dug up: And therefore praying That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioners to place or deposit Corps in the Vaults or Arches under the said Church, and to ascertain the Fees that shall be paid for the fame, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof;' and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

As to the Inability of the Parties interested in the said Premises to convey the same to the said Commissioners;

Mr. Ellis reported from the Committee, to whom the Greemvich Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Inhabitants of Bur,alVaults, the Parish of East Greenwich, in the County of Kent, was referred, That the Committee bad examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations contained in the said Petition, Parc of Two Acts, the one made in the 9th, and the other in the 10th Year of the Reign of Queen dyne, for building Fifty new Churches in and abouc the Cities of London and Westminster, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, was read; by which said several Acts it was enacted, That one of the Churches thereby directed to be built Qiould be erected in the Parish 0VEast Greenwich, in the County of Kent; and by the last of ih$ said Acts it is also further enacted, That no Burial shall at any time be in or under any of the Churches by that Act intended to be erected.

William Rojs, being examined said. That a Church' having been erected at East Greemvich,in pursuance of the said ACh, upon thcGround whereon the old Church'flood, the Inhabitants, in the Year 1716, purchased a Piece of Ground contiguous to the old Church yard; which, together with the said Church-yard, has been constantly made use of for a Burial Place ever since.

Thomas Dawes, Sexton of the said Parish, said, That by reason of the great Encrease of the Inhabitants, and the frequent Burials conlequent thereupon, the present Churchyards are not futticient for that Purpose.

Then, in order to prove, That, before the Erection of the new Chur.ch, a Vault under the old Edifice was made use of for a Burial Place, a Table of Fees, dated in the Year 1705, and signed by the then Bishop of Rochester, was produced; whereby a Fee of Twenty Shillings was directed to be paid to the Churchwardens of the said Parish for every Corps deposited in the said Vault.

Thomas Ripley Esquire, being examined, laid, That he had carefully surveyed the said new Church, and finds that the same is built upon very substantial Pillars of Brick, and arched; and that if Brick Walls were erected between, and carried as low as the Foundation of such Pillars, the same would be a Security thereto; and the vacant Spaces might safely be converted into Vaults for Burials, without breaking up the Floor, or being in the lead prejudicial to ' the Foundation of the said Church. r

Then a Clause in an Act, made in the 2d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for making the Hamlet of Spittlefields, in the Parish of Saint Dunstan Stebunheath, alias Stepney, in the County of Middlesex, a distinct Parish, and for providing a Maintenance for the Minister of such new Parish; and also a Clause in another Act, made in the 3d Year of his Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for providing Maintenance for the Mini Iter of the/iew Parish Church of Saint Nicholas Deptford, in the Counties of Kent and Surry, and for making the same a distinct Parish; were severally read, in order to prove, that Power hath been granted by Parliament to bury under several of the said new Churches, notwithstanding the former Prohibition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Pariffiioners of the Parish of East Greenwich, in the County of Kent, to deposit Corps in the Vaults or Arches under the Church in the said Parish, and to ascertain the Fees that shall be paid for the fame: And that Mr. Ellis and Mr. Clevland do prepare, and bring in,

A Petition of the Serge Makers of Culmstock, in the Woollen County of Devon, was presented to the House, and TiatJc* read; complaining of Frauds committed by the Sellers of Wool, by winding Fleeces of Wool not sufficiently washfcd, and by winding, within Fleeces of Wool, Clay,

Lead, Stones, Dung, Sand, Tails, deceitful Locks,

Cot-gare, and many other Things, to make the Fleece the more weighty; and also by their excessive pitching and tarring their Sheep, and at such unseasonable Times in the Year, that, as far as they are pitched, the Pitch runs through the Wool, by which means it is wholly spoiled, and cannot be used in making any Cloth whatsoever; and alleging, That by the before mentioned Deceits and Frauds, which daily increase, the Petitioners continually sustain great Damage and Lodes; and that the same are so pernicious to the Serge Maker, and so prejudicial to the Woollen Manufacturers, that many are forced to leave off Business, to the undoing of themselves and Families: And therefore praying the House to inflict such

Penalty on those who shall be found guilty of such Frauds, that a final End may be put to such iniquitous Practices; and that the Action for the Recovery of the said Penalty may be tried in a furnmary Way, or in One of his Majesty's Courts of Judicature, at the Option of the Buyer; all which the Petitioners submit to the Consideration of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on the Behalf of thenilelvcs, and other Merchants, Wool-ftaplers, Clothiers, Makers and Manufacturers of Worded Yarn, Broad Cloth, Camblets, Callimancoes, Stuffs, and other Woollen Goods, in the Town and Parish of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York; and also the Petition of the Merchants, Wool-ftaplers, and others. Manufacturers and Dealers in Woollen Goods, in the Town and Parish of Hallifax, in the West Riding of the County of York; are referred: And that they do exa-, mine the Matter of this Petition; and report, the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of chemselves, and other Merchants, Wool-ftaplers, Clothiers, Makers, and Manufacturers of Worded Yam, Bays, and other Woollen Goods, in the ancient Town and Borough of Colchester, in the County of EJfiex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are great Quantities of Bays and other Woollen Goods made and manufactured in the said Town and borough, which are disposed of in most Parts of Great Britain, and exported to divers Places beyond the Seas, whereby great Numbers of Families are maintained and supported, and great Benefit and Advantage have accrued to the Nation in general* and that for the Working and Making up of the several Sorts of Woollen Goods above-mentioned, the Petitioners are obliged to purchase great Quantities of Fleece Wool of the Growth of divers Parts of this Vol. 26.

Kingdom; and that, for several Years past, a pernicious Practice hath prevailed amongst the Wool Growers* laying upon the Fleeces excessive Quantities of Pitch, Tar* or other markingStuff*, and a deceitful Method of wrapping up and winding within several of the Fleeces of Wool, sold to the Petitioners, not only Pieces of coarse and unmerchantable Wool, but also Cots, Dirt, and other Refuse, greatly tending to the manifest Loss of the Wool Buyers and Manufacturers, the Difreputation and Debafemenc of the Manufactures, and Prejudice of the Trade of this Kingdom; and alleging. That, although several Laws and Statutes have formerly been made for the true Winding of Wool, yet some of them are become obsolete, and the rest of them, by reason of the Smallness of the Penalties thereby inflicted, are ineffectual to prevent the fraudulent Winding, and pernicious Practice above-mentioned: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for amending, and rendering more effectual, the Laws now in being for the due Winding of Wool, and for preventing the pernicious Practice of laying on the Fleece exceftive Quantities of marking Stuff; or to give such Relief to the Petitioners, in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Wool-ftaplers, Dealers in Wool, and Manufacturers of Woollen Goods, in the City of London, Borough of Southwark, and other Places adjacent thereto, Whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are great Quantities of Wool brought in the Fleece from several Parts of the Kingdom to London and Borough of Southwark, and Places adjacent, and there broken and sorted into several Sorts, and sold to, and manufactured by, the Clothiers, Stuff Makers, and other Makers of Woollen Goods, in divers Parts of this Nation; and that there arc also great Quantities of Fleece Wool made up and manufactured into several Sorts of Goods, in the City of London and Parts adjacent; and that the Dealers in, and Manufacturers of, the said Fleece Wool have laboured tinder Very great Difficulties, and sustained very great Loss and Damage, by the exceftive marking and fraudulent winding thereof, whereby the Buyer has been very much deceived, in the Weight, and consequently in the Quality thereof, having frequently found, wrapped up in the Fleece, Pitch, deceitful Locks, Cots, Sand, Dirt, Dung, and other things, which by no means ought to be put therein; and alleging, That it is evident the fraudulent Winding of Wool was looked upon as a Crime of a heinous Nature long ago, from Two several Acts of Parliament, one of them made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of King Henry the Sixth, and the other in the Twenty-third of Henry the Eighth; which in those Times were, doubtless, looked upon as sufficient to deter Persons from so vile a Practice, but are at this time found by Experience insufficient for that Purpose: And therefore praying the House to take this Matter into Consideration, and give the Petitioners such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto fqbscribed, in behalf of themselves, and other Merchants, Wool-ftaplers, Clothiers, Makers and Manufacturers of Worded Yarn, Broad Cloth, Caroblets, Stuffs, and other Woollen Goods, in the Town and Parish of Wakefield, in the West Riding of the County of York, and the Villages adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Petitions of the Inhabitants of the Parishes of Leeds and Hallifax, in the County of York, presented to the House, complaining of the iniquitous Praftices of the Wool Growers of this Kingdom, in laying upon the Fleece excessive Quantities of injurious marking Stuffi and of winding up within the Fleece unmerchantable Wool, Dirt, and other Refuse, and praying for Relief therein; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend the several Allegations of the said Petitions from Leeds and Hallifax are true; and that the Grievances by them complained of call aloud for the Interpofttion and

A Petition o f the Commissioners of the Court of Re-queds of the Tower Hamlets, and of sundry other Inhabitants of the said Hamlets, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the ACb of Parliament, passed in the Twenry-third Year of the Reign of his present Majesty (intituled, An Act for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Tower Hamlets) hath been found very beneficial to the Publick, but defective in the following Particulars; for that it is doubtful, whether there be sufficient Authority given by the said Act, to compel the Appearance of Defendants, in case they refuse or neglect to appear to the Summonses of the said Court, and to proceed to Judgment, for want thereof; and whether certain Debts and Demands are cognizable in the said Court, particularly for Rent, for Goods detained, and otherwise, and likewise as to the Time of the Commencement of the Forty Days, for which Defendants are to be committed by virtue of the said Act; and whether Defendants, taken by virtue of the Process of the said Court, may be immediately carried to Prison, or not; and whether Attornies, resident within the said Hamlets, are subject to the Process of this Court: And there being no Directions in the said Act, that the Proceedings in the said Court should be taken Notice of in other Courts, Judgments have, for want thereof, been obtained in other inferior Courts agai nft Defendants, for the same Matter which had been already recovered against them in the said Court: And further setting forth, That the necessary Expences of carrying the said Act into Execution are, notwithstanding the utmost Frugality, so large (besides the settled Payments to the Marshalsea Counfei) that the clear Profits arising to the Officers of the said Court are thereby, and from the Number of Clerks, as well as from the Smallness of the Fees, rendered very inconsiderable, and greatly deficient of the Sums by the aforesaid Act thought; L io

j. 1752;

reasonable Allowances to the said Officers for their Services: And representing to the House, That it will be ex?* pedient that the Number of Clerks may, upon the Death, Resignation, or Removal of any of the present Clerks, be. reduced (which the Commissioners have not Authority to, do under the present Act); and also, that in order to raile a Fund sufficient for defraying the necessary Expences of carrying the said Act into Execution, some small Addition may be made to the Fees thereby already granted, which are lower than those in any orher of the Courts of the like Nature already establiffied; and that the Table of Fees be new regulated for that Purpose: And therefore, praying, That Leave may be given r6 bring in a Bill, to explain, amend, and render the said Act more effectual;, or that the House will be pleased to give the Petitioners such other Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion, thereupon, to the House.

And the same were read accordingly; and are as followed! i viz.

€i Resolved, That One Catife of the Increase of Thefts u and Robberies of late is an Habit of Idleness, in which " the lower People have been bred often from their Youth.

€i Resolved, That the Multitude of Places of Enter-€< tainment for the lower Sort of People is another great " Cause of that Increase, as they are thereby tempted to " spend their small Substance in riotous Pleasures; and <c in consequence are put on unlawful Methods of supply-<c ing their Wants, and renewing their Pleasures.

<c Resolved, That Gaming amongst the inferior Rank ff of People is another great Incitement to Theft and <c Robberies.

" Resolved, That the great Security and Encourage-<c ment Robbers meet with, from Receivers of ftokn Goods, is another and a principal Cause of the Increase " of Robberies.

" Resolved, That the Advertising a Reward, with no c< Questions asked, for the Return of Things which have c< been stolen, or loft, is another great and principal Cause <( of the Increase of Robberies and Felonies.
