A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Edinburgh Council, of the City of Edinburgh, in behalf of themselves, City, and the Community of che said City, was presented to the House,tmd read; setting forth, That the City of Edinburgh, being the Metropolis and Seat of the Government of Scotland, was thereby subject to all the Alterations and Changes of the State, which, with its remarkable Zeal, ever fmee the Reformation, in supporting the Protestant Interest, and many other unavoidable Occasions, hnd involved it in considerable Debts, far beyond what the common Revenue of the City could discharge; and char, in order to its Relief, an Act was passed in the Parliament of Scotland, in the Year 1693, giving to the said Town and Community, and to the Magistrates and Council, and their Successors in Office, for their Use and Behoof, an Imposition of Two Pennies Sects, or One sixth of a Penny Sterling, over and above the King’s Excise, upon the Pint of all Ale and Beer, either brewed, brought in, or vended, tapped, and fold, within the said Town, Suburbs, and Liberties thereof, commencing from the First day of July 1693, not exceeding the Space of Thirty Years; and that before the Expiry cf this Grant, an Act was passed in the Third Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, continuing che said Duty for Nineteen Years, from and after the Expiry of the former Grant, for carrying on a Variety of publick Works, to the Benefit of the City, and that Part of the united Kingdom; and that another Act passed, in the Ninth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, extending the said Duty over the Parishes of St. Cuthbert's, , Cannongate, South and North Leith, and adding Nineteen Years more to the Term granted by the Act of the Third Year of his said Majesty’s Reign, appointing the Produce of the said Gift, arising by the Duties within the City and Liberties and said Parishes of St. Cuthbert's, Cannongate,

South and North Leith, during the Space of Thirty-eight Years, from the First of July 1723, to be applied for carrying on the many great and useful publick Works that had been begun by the City, and for many other Uses and Purposes at length contained in the said Act of the Ninth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign; and alleging,

That although the Money borrowed, in virtue of these Acts of Parliament, chargeable upon the Granr, and the Duties arising from the Grant itself, have been carefully applied in the manner directed by these Laws, at the Sight of che Overseers therein named; yet, through the remarkable Decrease of that Duty, and the pundual Performance of the many annual Prccftations with which it was charged, it will be impracticable to carry on and finish the many useful Purposes for which the Continuation of the Grant was made; and the capital Debts of the City, at the Expiration of the Gift, mud remain a Burthen far beyond what its ordinary Revenue can discharge, unless the Grant X

be continued for a further Term, or some other Provision be made by the Wisdom of che Legislature, for the Relief of the said City and Community, and carrying on the useful Purposes at length recited in the Act of the Ninth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and allow a Bill to be brought in for adding to the current Term a Continuation of the said Grant, for executing and completing such of the Purposes of che said Grant, as remain unfinished; or that the Petitioners may beotherwise relieved, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Peruke- A Petition of the Master, Governors, and Commonalty

makers and of the Mystery of Barbers of London, and of the Peruke-Barbers Com- makers, inhabiting in, and within Seven Miles of, the said pany‘ City, whose Names arc thereunto subscribed, was presented

to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act passed in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth (intituled, An Act for Barbers and Surgeons) the Barbers and Surgeons of London were united and made one Body Corporate, for ever, by the Name of the Mailers or Governors of the Mystery and Commonalty of Barbers and Surgeons of London; and that, by an Act passed in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, the said Union was difiblved; and the Petitioners, the said Master, Governors and Commonalty, were made a new and distinct Corporation; but, by the Separation of the Surgeons, are in danger of being unable to support themselves > and that the Petitioners, who exercise the Art of Peruke-making, in the Liberties and Neighbourhood of the said City, are not a Body Corporate, nor under any Order or Regulation; for want whereof, great Frauds are practised in the said Manufacture, to the Discouragement of the fair Trader, and manifest Injury of the Consumer:

And therefore praying the House, That Leave may be given for the bringing in a Bill for incorporating the Peruke-makers, as well within as without the Libertiesof the City of London, and within such Distance thereof as the House shall think fit, with the said other Petitioners, die Master, Governors, and Commonalty, of the Mystery of Barbers of London, in such Manner, and under such Limitations, for regulating the said Art of Peruke-making, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Coji-sideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Hevtefbury Colonel Acourt reported from the Committee, to whom and Knook the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other In-Road. habitants, of the several Parishes of Heytesbury and Knook,

in the County of Wilts, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Freeholders and Inhabitants of the said Parishes, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame,#as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the

Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and is as followech j viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Janus Frampton Esquire said. He knows the Road

leading from Heytesbury to the Top of Hill, which

is in a very ruinous Condition, occasioned by the great Number of heavy Carriages that have pasted thereon since the Commencement of an Act, passed in the ijrh Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the several Roads leading from the Town of Westminster, in the County of Wilts

Then a Clause in the said Act was read, whereby it appeared, That the Trustees thereby appointed, were authorized to layout such Sums of Money as they thought proper, arising by the Tolls thereby granted, in the Repair of the aforesaid Road from Heytesbury to the Top of Anjirow Hill.

And Mr. Frampton further informed your Committee, That no Money had ever been laid out by the said Trustees in Repair of the said Road.

Mr. John Everley said, He has known the said Road about Fifty Years, and that there never used to be any Pound Rate collected for the Repair thereof till the Commencement of the aforesaid Act; but that, since that Time, they have been obliged to make a Rate of sometimes Six Pence, and sometimes Nine Pence, in the Poundand that the said Road cannot be amended, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course of Law.

Ordered, That it be an Inflrudion to the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairingand widening the Road from the Town of tVirminster, in the County of Wilts, to the City of Bath, in the County of Somerset-, and also the Road from the Town of Frome, in the said County of Somerset, to the Town of Beckington, in the same County; is committed; That they have Power to make Provision therein, to compel the Trustees appointed by, or in pursuance of, Two Acts of Parliament, the one made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First (intituled, An Act for repairing the several Roads leading from the Town of in the County of Wilts) and the other made in the 16th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign (for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the said Act) ro amend the Road leading from the East End of the Parish of Heytesbury to the Top of Anftrow Hill,in the Parish of Knook, in the said County of Wilts.

Westminster A Petition of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the Coun-House. City and Liberty of Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Justices of the Peace of the said City and Liberty, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Justices have, for many Years, held their Sessions at the Town Court House, near Westminster-hall, upon Sufferance only, and paying for the life of the fame, and are liable at any time to be deprived thereof; and that the said Court House is very close, small, and inconvenient, and always very dark, but now made more lb by reason of feme additional Buildings, lately erected for the Conveniency of this House; and that, from the Heat of the Place in Summer, and the Stench of a common Sewer running under it, and the Dampness thereof in the W inter Season, occasioned by the Lowness of its Situation, as well as its being often affected by Spring Tides, the said Court House is rendered very unwholesome at all Seasons of the Year, and the Meanness of its Appearance tends greatly to abate of that Obedience and Kespect, which ought to be shewn to his Majesty’s Commission; and that it being necessary, upon every Gaol Delivery, to bring a great Number of Prisoners into Court from the Prifcns of the Vol. 26.

Gate-house and Bridewell, who, in the present Court House, (land so near to the Bench, as to endanger the Petitioners catching the infectious Diseases which often rage in those Prisons; thereby, and by the constant unwhole-fomeness of the Place, many Gentlemen in the Commission of the Peace are intimidated from attending their Duty; and that, were a commodious Court House ereCfed on a convenient and airy Spot of Ground, within the said City, where the Petitioners, and the rest of the Justices might aficmble, without Risque or Danger of their Health or Lives, it would encourage their Attendance in Discharge of the Duty they owe to their King and Country, and thereby not only support the Honour and Dignity due to his Majesty’s Commission, but also tend greatly to expedite Justice, and promote the Peace, Ease, and Safety, of his Majesty’s faithful and loyal Subjects within this great and flourishing City and Liberty: And therefore, in regard such Court House cannot be erected with-, out the Aid of an Act of Parliament, praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for erecting a Court House for the Use of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the City and Liberty of Westminster, at the Expence of the Inhabitants thereof; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief and Assistance as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several of the Inhabitants of the City and Westminster Liberty of Westminster, on behalf of themselves, and the Court-House. rest of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That the Town Court House, near Westminster-hall, where his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace have, for many Years, held their Sessions, is small, inconvenient, and dark; and, from the Heat thereof in the Summer, and the Stench of a common Sewer under it, and the Dampness thereof in Winter, occasioned by the Lowness of its Situation, as well as its being often affected by Spring Tides, is rendered very unwholesome at all Seasons of the Years and that a great Number of the Petitioners are, from time to time, lummoned to attend upon Juries for the T rying of Offences or Finding of Bills at such Sessions, and from the Inconveniencies of the Court, and the want of a proper Place for the Petitioners to withdraw into, for considering of their Presentments, Bills, and Verdicts, a great Delay of Justice has frequently happened; and that the Petitioners, for the Convenience and Safety of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, are willing and desirous to raise a Sum of Money, by an equal Pound Rate upon themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, for the purchasing or hiring a Piece of Ground, and erecting, finishing, and supporting, a new Court House, with necessary and convenient Apartments, for the more safe, easy, and regular Dispatch of BuGness: And therefore, in regard the same cannot be effected without the Aid of Parliament, praying the House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the purchasing or hiring a Piece of Ground, and erecting, fitting up, and supporting such Court House, at the Expence of the Petitioners, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, for the Reception of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, and others, attending their Duty at the Sessions of the Peace aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matters thereof; and report the fame, as they shall appear to them, to the House.

Bromyard A Petition of several Gentlemen and Inhabitants, and Roads, other Persons, living in the Town and Parish of Bromyard, in the County of Hereford, and also of several of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace of and for the said County, and other Gentlemen and principal Inhabitants of the several Parishes lying near to the said Town and Parish of Bromyard, and many other Persons who frequently travel through the Roads to and from the said Town of Bromyard, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the several Roads, hereafter particularly mentioned, that is to say, from the said Town of Bromyard to a Place called The Half-way Ash, in the Parish of Docklow, being Four Miles or thereabouts, and to a Place called Herefordshire Lake, in the Parish of Whitburn, being Four Miles or thereabouts, and to a Place called Perry Bridge, in the Parish of Stoke Bliss, being Four Miles or thereabouts, and to a Place called Sapey Wood, in the Parish of Upper Sapey, being Four Miles or thereabouts, and to a Place called Bishop's Froome, being Three Miles or thereabouts, and to a Place called Wooferwood Gate, in the said Parish of Bromyard, being Two Miles or thereabouts, and to a Place called Herefordshire Lake, in the said Parish of Bromyard, being Three Miles or thereabouts, by reason of the Soil thereof, and the heavy Carriages passing through the fame, are become so ruinous and bad, that, in the Winter Season, many Parts thereof are impafiable for Waggons and Carriages, and also for Horses laden, and other Parts are dangerous for Travellers; which said Roads cannot, by the ordinary Course appointed by the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, be repaired: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the said Roads, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Manufacturers, and others, concerned in the Making and Vending of Beaver Hats, and Hats made of Coney Wool, Goats Wool, and other Materials, whose Names are under-written, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the said Trade in Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Art and Mystery of making Hats in Great Britain hath arrived to great Perfection; and that considerable Quantities of Hats, manufactured in this Kingdom, have heretofore been exported into foreign Countries, all Europe having formerly been supplied with Beaver Hats from England> and that, of late Years, the foreign Trade has much declined, which the Petitioners attribute, amongst others, to the following causes$ viz. to the many Rival Manufacturers of late Years set up in foreign Countries 5 to the very great Rife in the Price of Beaver, which of late has advanced upwards of £. 75.^ Cent. owing (as the Petitioners apprehend) in part, to the annual Import of Beaver Skins being, of late Years, much decreased, and the Export thereof greatly increased, Beaver Skins drawing back on Exportation more than half the Duty paid on Importation; and to the annual Import of Beaver into France, by their Canada Company, being, as the Petitioners are credibly informed, much larger than all the Beaver annually imported into Great Britain, either from Hudson's Bay, or from his Majesty’s Plantations in America; and for that Beaver imported into France is, of late, prohibited from being exported under severe Penalties; and alleging, That the Price and Quantity of Beaver, for the Use of the British and foreign Manufactures, being thus greatly in Favour of the Foreigners, who have also the Advantage of Labour cheaper, they are thereby enabled to vend their riats, in foreign Markets, upon lower Terms than the British Manufacturers can do, which threatens the total Loss of the said Trade to the British Subjects, in consequence whereof many thousand Poor, now employed in, and depending upon, the said Manufacture, will inevitably lose their Employ, and become burthensome to their respective Parishes: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and grant such Relief and Encouragement to the said Manufacture, as the Credit and Importance thereof deserves, and as to the House shall appear needful to preserve the fame.

A PETITION of Alexander Grant and Richard Oswald, jTjl for themselves and Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That a Fort situated in Bance Island, now called George Island, in the River Sierra Leon, in Africa, formerly belonged to the Royal Africaft Company, and continued in their Possession till the Year 1728, when their Factors were entirely driven from thence by the Natives, their Fort demoliflbed, and the Houses burnt; and that, from the Year 1728, the Island continued in the quiet Possession of the King of the Country, and the Fort demolished, until the Year 1744, when Captain John Boyce, of London, being the re, and discovering that the French were then treating for the Purchase, bought it for Mr. George Fryer 5 who, at his own very great Expence, rebuilt the Houses and Fort, and furnished it with Artillery and Scores, for the Protection of Trade, and the Support of the British Interest in that River; but that Mr. Fryer, finding upon Experience,that the Maintenance of this Fort, in such a def’enfive State, was and would be too heavy an Expence for him singly to bear, in the Year 1748 fold the said Island, with the Fort, Storehouses, Artillery, Vessels, Slaves, and Merchandize, then built and lodged there, to the Petitioners; who purchased them with a Design to carry on an exten-five Trade at that Settlement, when the times would admit of it; and that the Peri dopers believed the Property of this Island to be fully and legally vested in them by this Purchase, as they bought it under the Tide of Mr. Fryer, arising from the Purchase of Mr. Boyce for his Account, at a time when the African Company had been entirely dispofiefled, and their Fort had beea demolished

by the King of the Country, near Sixteen Years; no Endeavours having been in that time made by the African Company to regain PofiVflion, nor any Claim of Right having been made on their Part in Opposition to Mr. Fryer's Purchase, or, duringhis Possession, in consequence of it; and that the Petitioners were greatly surprised last Year, to find this Island, now their Property, given into the House as belonging to the Settlements of the African Company, which had been maintained and supported at the publick Charge; whereas this had been kept entirely at the Charge of the Petitioners, who had been induced to go to a very considerable Expence, in maintaining this Fort, from the Hopes they entertained of its enabling them hereafter to pursue their intended Trade with greater Safety and Advantages and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, That the House will not judge it to be confident with Justice to supersede their Right*to this Fort, acquired by Purchase, and in the unexceptionable Manner they have described; but, on the contrary, will be pieased to confirm the rightful Possession of the Petitioners: or, if* it should be the Opinion of the House, that the Petitioners have a clear Right to this Fort, but, at the same time, that it will be convenient for the general Trade of Africa, that this Fort should be vested in the CoQnmittee appointed to manage the Trade to Africa, in common with the other Forts belonging to the African Company, that, in that Cafe, the Petitioners shall be reimbursed their Charges, and that the Recompence for this Fort will not be assigned to the late African Company, whose Property it is not, and who have not for so many Years had the Possession, or been charged with the Maintenance of it.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Wool Growers, and Manufacturers of Woollen Goods, in the Forest of Pendle, and in the Parishes of Colne, Burnley, Padibam, Downham, Clithero, and Whaley, in the County of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That large Quantities of Wool are grown within the said Forest, Parishes, and Parts adjacent; and that great Quantities of Woollen Goods are also manufactured within the same, not only from the Wool grown therein, but from Wool brought from distant Parts; and alleging, That the Petitioners are well assured, that the Grievances relating to the Marking or Branding of Sheep with Pitch and Tar, and the false and deceitful Fleecing and Winding of Wool, for Redress whereof, the Petitioners are informed, Application is made to Parliament, are real and great in many Parts of this Kingdom; and that Sheep may be sufficiently marked without Pitch and Tar, or with only a small Quantity, and that laid on at dipping time only; which, being fixed upon the End of the Staple, rises therewith, and may be dipt off with more Ease, and less Danger of mixing with the Wool, before the Sheep are (horn, than after; and that the Fleecing of Wool with unmerchantable Locks, Dirt, and other things, therein, to advance the Weight, is downright Fraud, and a Loss to all heneft Dealers; and that the Country of the Petitioners is cold and mountainous, and it is found by Experience, the falving Sheep against Winter helps to preserve them through the fame, and promotes the Growth of Wool: And therefore praying, That no Restraint may be laid upon the Salving of Sheep: And further alleging. That, as to sworn Wool-winders or Fleecers, no such Vol. 26.

Officers have ever been appointed in the Country of the Petitioners; and that they think them burthensome and useless; and that the Grower is most proper to answer fur the Acts of himself, and his Servants: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Ccrnfi-deration, and so enact, as by the House may be thought most likely to prevent the Frauds and Abuses complained of, and to encourage the Woollen Manufactory, so highly advantageous to these Kingdoms.

Colonel Stephenjon confirmed the aforesaid Evidence; and added, That he has been informed, that Persons have plundered the Mines, and kept poffirffion of them by Force for a Night ora Day; and that they took the Opportunity, while their Comrades were trying at the last Assizes at Carlisle, to break open the said Mine.

Mr. Ireton, Mr. Giuifon, and Mr. Singlato, confirmed the above Evidence; and added. That he had heard, chat the Loss sustained by the Robbing of the said Mine amounted to £ 2,000. a Year.

Mr. John bowman informed your Committee, That he was Nephew to Mr. Shepheard's Steward; and that his Uncle -has tried to guard the Mine, but to no Purposei that the said Mine is fmiate in the Manor of Bor-rougbdale, but that he believes there is no Lord of that Manor; nor did he ever hear, that any Person claimed a Right to dig there, nor of any Conreft at Law about it: And he further laid. That, if the Robbers happen to get into the right Vein of Ore, they can get One thousand Pounds worth in Six Hours; which last Affercion was confirmed by Mr. Ireton.

Colonel Stepbenfon added to his Evidence, That he has frequently been upon the Grand Jury at Carlisle Assizes, and has always known Bills of Indnflment found against Persons for these Practices; and that there was an ln-di&menc found last Assizes against several Persons for (hooting at ihe Guard: And,

Mr. Ireton and Mr. Gunjon, being further examined, said, That they had known Prosecutions for Sealing Lead prove ineffectual from a Defect in the Laws.

Mr. Richard Gilpin, being examined, said, That he contracts with the Board of Ordnance for furnishing Iron Shot and Bomb Shells; and that Black Lead is used for washing the Inside of the Moulds, to prevent the Metal from burning and mixing itself with the Moulds; and that it answers this Purpose better than any thing yet found out.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Colony of A Representation and Petition of the Trustees for efta-

Georgia. blishing the Colony of Georgia, in America, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Representation and Petition, recommends it to the House to do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Representation and Petition.was brought up, and read; alleging, That the Trustees have hitherto supported the Colony of Georgia by the Assistance granted by this House, with such Success, chat they may presume to say, it will soon prove a beneficial Colony to Great Britain, not only on account of its Situation and Ports, but for its various Products, of great Utility to the Trade of this Nation, and especially the Produce of Silk, for which the Climate of Georgia is most particularly adapted: And, his Majesty having been graciously pleased to accept of the Offer of the Petitioners to surrender their Trust, praying the House to enable them to defray the Expences incurred by them since the last Grant.

Ordered, That the said Representation and Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

setting forth, That the Corporation of the Borough of Scarborough hath a prescriptive Right to certain Duties, from all Ships loading Coals at Newcastle and Sunderland\ for Repairing of Scarborough Old Pier, and, by an Act of the 37th of King Henry the Eighth, all the Lands and Houses within the Liberty of the said Borough are subject to the Payment of One-Fifth of tht ir Value, for the Support of the said Pier, in case the Produce of the Duties on Shipping should be insufficient for that Purpose; and that the Common Council of the said Borough have the Management of the said Revenue, Two of whom are annually chosen to superintend the Repairs of the said Pier, whose Accounts are audited by the rest of the Common Council only; lb that the Landholders, Freemen, and Inhabitants, within the said Borough, have not the Liberty to inspect the said Accounts, though their respective Houses and Lands are liable to be taxed to make good any Deficiency or Misapplication of the Revenue; that, in 1711, a Breach was made in the Old Pier by the Sea, and as no Surplus of the said Duties remained (though very large Sums might have been saved every Year) the Common Council of the said Borough mortgaged the Corporation Lands to repair the said Pier, and, from that time, to the Year 1736, a separate Account was kept of the Revenue of the Oid Pier, from the other Revenues of the Corporation, and the Money borrowed on such Mortgage paid off, and a considerable Sum saved out of the said Revenue, which ought to have been preserved in case of any future Accident; but that, fmee the said Year 1736, the said separate Account has been discontinued, and the said Savings, as well as what may have accrued since that time, entirely loft to the Publick; and that, by an Act of Parliament, of the Fifth Year of his present Majesty, for enlarging the Pier and Harbour of Scarborough, the Bailiffs and Burgesses of the said Town, or the major Part of them, assembled in Common Council, are intitled to receive by themselves, their Collectors and Receivers, divers Duties, by that Act appointed to be paid for the Purposes mentioned therein; and, pursuant to the Powers veiled in them, appointed a Treasurer, and other proper Officers, for carrying on the said Work; which, the Petitioners conceive, was prosecuted in a proper Manner till the Year 1744, at which time a certain Number of the Common Council procured a Vote of the rest for borrowing Three thousand Pounds on the Credit of the said Act, to carry on the said Work more expeditiously, and to pay off the Tradesmen’s Bills; which Two plausible Pretences induced other well-meaning Members of such Common Council to concur in that Measure; and that Three thousand Pounds were accordingly borrowed, on such Part of the Tolls as by the said Act are made payable at Newcastle; but no Part of the said Sum, so borrowed, was applied to the Purpose di-rested by the said Act; and that the Mortgagee, apprehending the Act might expire before he coidd receive his Principal and Interest, filed a Bill of Foreclosure in the Court of Chancery, and, in May 1749, obtained a Decree for Payment of Principal and Interest; by virtue of frhich Decree he is now in Possession of the Revenue so arising at Newcastle, so that no Part thereof can be applied towards the Support of the said Pier and Harbour; and Vol. 26.

alleging, That other Abuses have beeh Committed by divers of the said Common Council, in violation of the Trust reposed in them by the said Act; and that the Com-iriissioners, appointed by the said Act of the 5th Year of his present Majesty, did examine into, and discover the Misapplication of the Money raised for the aforesaid Purposes; but, from a Default in the said Act, they have not a sufficient Power to oblige any of the Persons, guilty of such Mifoehaviour, to make good or repay the Money so misapplied: And therefore praying, That the House will bepleased to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as may be just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as ic shall appear to them, to the House:

St. Albans A Petition of the Mayor and Aldermen, and several of

Small Debts. the principal Inhabitants of the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford; and also of several of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the Liberty of St. Albans, in the said County of Hertford, on behalf of themselves, and the rest: of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and Liberty, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That King Charles the Second did, by his Letters Patent, bearing Date on the 27th Day of July, in the Year 1664, amongst other Privileges, grant unto the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the said Borough, that they, and their Successors, might and should have a Court of Record, to be held weekly, if* manner as directed by such Letters Patent, for the Trial of all Pleas, Plaints, and Actions, personal or mixed, ordained by the Common or Statute , Law, arising within the said Borough, and the Limits Bounds, and, Liberties of the fame, not exceeding Fifty Pounds; and that the Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the said Liberty of Sain* Albans are always held at the Town-hall, within the said Borough, as well as the Quarter Sessions for the said Town; and also the said Court of Record, for trying such Causes as arise within the said Borough; and reprefendng to the House, That the Fees and Expences

are so great, in prosecuting Causes to Judgment and Execution, in the said Court of Record, or any superior Court; for the Recovery of Small Debts, under Forty Shillings, besides the Delays attending such Suits, that honest Creditors are thereby greatly discouraged from attempting the Recovery of such Debts; and by that means, many ill-disposedPersons,whohavecontractedSrnall Debts within the said Borough, and the Towns, Parishes, Wards; Hamlets, and Places, within the said Liberty of St. Albans, though able to pay, refuse so to do, and set their Credicors at Defiance; and alleging. That if a more easy, and less expen-five Method, were established, for the Recovery of Small Debts, within the said Borough, and the said Liberty of St. Albans, (as hath lately been done, by the Wisdom of Parliament, in divers other Places) ic would, as the Petitioners apprehend, greatly tend to the Promotion of Industry, and Support of useful Credit: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill* for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford, and the several Towns, Parishes, Wards, Hamlets, and Places, within the said Liberty of St. Albans', or that the Pciitioners may have such other Relief and Assistance in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meer.

Sajall De is. mon counc;i Qf the Borough and Corporation of Liverpool, in Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Town of lAverpool is a very ancient Borough, Corporation, and Port Town, and that its domestic and foreign Trade is very eXtcnfive and large, in which there are employed many Handicraft Men, Artificers, and Seamens and that the flourishing State of its Trade of late Years hath invited many Tradesmen and Dealers, Artificers, Seamen, and others, from Ireland, and other Places, to carry on a great Trade with the said Town, many of whom are now become settled Inhabitants therein; so that its Residents and Traders are now become very numerous and considerable, to the manifest Encouragement of Trade, and the public Wealth; and that, to sup-pert such a large trading Body, small useful Credit is found to be absolutely necessary among the Traders, Artificers, Handicraftsmen, and Seamen; by which means these Persons are oft enabled to prosecute their different Employments, to the Good of themselves, Support of their Families, and Increase of Trade and Navigation; but that now many dishonest Persons do presume to run in debt in the said Town, and Port of Liverpool, and Liberties thereof, in small Sums of Money, not amounting to Forty Shillings, upon a Confidence that their just Creditors will be deterred from going through the tedious and expensive Proceedings of a regular Suit at Law for Recovery thereof; by which base Practices the honest Creditor is greatly wronged, useful Credit ruined, and the poor honest Man, who rs obliged to make use of Credit, and who would pay, oft innocently falls a Sacrifice to the Resentment of some injured Creditor, through the Inconvenience of an expensive Suit, to the Ruin of his Family, the Loss of his Labour to the Publick, and the Burden of his Parish j and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that the giving of such Persons, as encourage the said Artificers, Tradesmen, Mariners, and others, in such useful Credit, an easy and speedy Method for recovering their just Debts, at a little Expence, upon such Plan as hath been lately granted to some other Towns or Places, will greatly tend to the promoting of industry, and supporting useful Credit, and be of great Utility to the Trade and Welfare of the said Town of Liverpool, and the landed Interest around its Neighbourhood: And therefore, on behalf of the Petitioners, and the Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants of Liverpool aforesaid, praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the said Town of Liverpool, and Liberties of the fame; A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, and principal Graziers, in that Part of the West Riding of the County of York, called Craven, and Places adjacent, was prefcnred to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners County is large, and moftty grazing Land; and that great Flocks of Sheep are kept upon the fame; and caking Notice, that Application is made to Parliament, for such Amendments and Additions to an old Act, relating to the Winding of Wool, and the Marking or Branding of Sheep with Pitch and Tar, and other Matters, as may be thought necessary to prevent Frauds and Abuses in the Wool Trade; and alleging, That the Petitioners are well assured such Frauds and Abuses, worthy the Attention of Parliament, are carried on by designing People, to promote their own private Interest, but to the Loss of all honest Dealers, and the Publick; and that Sheep cannot be fulliciently marked, so as to know them by Slits and Cuts in their Ears, and Brands upon rheir Noses and Horns, and Red or Wad laid upon the Wool; but that One or more Tar Marks are absolutely necessary; and that all imaginable Restraint ought to be laid upon the Practice of the Winding of Wool with Dirt, Locks, and other unmerchantable Things in it, to encrease the Weight; but that with relation to sworn Wool Winders, none such have ever been appointed in those Parts; but that the Wool Growers, or their Servants, do that Work themselves; and the Petitioners think the said Officers would be useless, and troublesome; and that the Petitioners Country is cold, and the Salving of Sheep found necessary, to preserve them through the Winter, and improve the Growth of the Wool: And therefore praying, That no Restraint may be laid upon Salving, nor further Restraint from marking with Tar, than that the Wool Growers dip off the Tar Marks from the Wool, before their Sheep be (horn, or the Wool wound up, or exposed to Sale; and that the House will take the Premises into their Consideration; andenaft such Redress therein, as to them may seem best.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, Merchants, Traders, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, of the Town and Port of Lancaster, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners conceive it would be a farther Improvement to the Woollen Manufacturee in the Northern Parts of this Kingdom, and of the utmost Consequence to the Increase thereof, to open other Ports for the Importation of Irish Wool, than, what are already allowed by Act of Parliament; and representing to the House, That the Town of Lancaster is very commodiously situated, for the Importation of Wool from Ireland, and for a more ready, and less expensive Land Carriage of the fame, when imported, not only to several manufacturing Towns in the said County Palatine, and the County of Westmoreland, but also to the very Seat and Center of the Woollen Manufacture, in the County of York, chan any other Port in those Parts; and that the Traders within the Port of Lancaster aforesaid do constantly employ great Numbers of Ships in carrying Goods and Merchandize to Dublin, and other Parts of Ireland; and that the said Ships do frequently return back empty, by reason of the present Ile-straint on the said Port of Lancaster, in regard to the Importation of Lift: Wool: And therefore praying, That Liberty may be given to any Person or Persons whatsoever, to import any Quantity or Quantities of Wool, and Woollen Yarn, from Ireland, to the said Port of Lancaster; and that a Clause may be inserted in some publick Act, for that Purpose, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer presented to the House, by His Majesty’s Command, Copy ot a Treaty between his Majesty the King of Great B? itain, and their High Mightinesses the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, on the One Part, and his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, on the other Part, concluded at Dresden, September 13th, 1751, and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and TranGation were read.

The said Copy is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said TranGation is as followed!; viz.

In the Name of the most Holy Trinity.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Elector of Brunswick Lunenbourg, and their High Mightinesses the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, having made known to his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, their sincere Disposition to tye more closely the Bonds offriendship, which have hitherto so happily subsisted between them by a Treaty of FriendGiip, of good Understanding, and of Subsidy, between his said Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesses, on die One Part, and his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, on the other Part, of which Treaty the Tranquillity of the Empire, the Preservation of its Interests, and the Establishment of its System, should be the principal Object; his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, feeling himself always animated with the same Sentiments of Fricndship towards his Bri-tannick Majesty, and their High Mightinesses, and having nothing more at Heart, than the Prekrvation and Interests of the Empire, has w illingly complied with this Overture, which is entirely conformable to his Intentions. With this salutary View, the High contracting Parties have authorized their respective Ministers; that is to say. His Britannick Majesty, Sir Charles Hanbury Williams, his Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary at the Court of his said Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, Knight of the Order of the Bath 5 their High Migh-tinelles the States General, the Sieur Cornelius Calkoen, their Minister Plenipotentiary to has Polish Majesty; and his Majesty the King of Poland, the Sieur Henry Count of Briihl, Baron of Forfte and of Pfoertben, Knight of Vol. 26.

371

the Orders of the White Eagle, of St. Andrew, and of the Black Eagle, his Prime Minister, Minister of the Cabinet of Conference, and of State, General of Foot, Grand Master of the Wardrobe, President of the Chamber of Finances, Director General of the Land Tax and Excise, Commissary General of the Ports of the Baltick, Commander of the Saxon Guards in Poland, Colonel of a Regiment of Light Horse, and of a Regiment of Foot, Pro-voft of the Chapter of Budijftn: Which Ministers aforesaid, being provided with necessary full Powers, after several Conferences, have agreed upon the following Articles;

1.

There shall be a sincere Friendftiip, and most strict Union, between his Britannick Majesty, their High Mightinesses, and his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony; so that each of them shall look upon the Interests of the others as his own, and shall faithfully ufc his Endeavours to promote them, as far as possible, and mutually to prevent and avert all Disturbance and Prejudice.

2.

In order to give his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, a Proof of the good Disposition of the High Maritime Powers towards him, they grant him an annual subsidy of Forty-eight thousand Pounds Sterling; viz. T wo-thirds on the Account of his Britannick Majesty, and One-third on the Account of their High Mightinesses the States-General; the Two-thirds shall be paid at London, and the One-third at the league, every Six Months, without the lead Diminution or Discount, the latter at the Rate of Five Dollars Eighteen Grqs, the Pound Sterling; the said Subsidy shall commence from Michaelmas, being the 29th of September 17 51; the h irft Payment of Twenty-four thousand Pounds shall be made on the 215th of March, and the Second on the 25th of September, in the Year 1752; which shall be continued from Six Months to Six Months, as long as this Treaty does last.

3-

In Consideration of the Subsidy specified in the preceding Article, his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, doth promiie, that, during the Continuance of this Treaty, in case that, contrary to better Expedition, a War should break out again in Europe, and that Great Britain, and the Republick of Holland, should be involved in if, he will not take Part either directly or indirectly against his Britannick Majesty, and the States General; and will neither give nor fend any Troops to such Powers, as shall be at War with his Britannick Majesty, and their High Mightinesses, or against the Two Imperial Courts; to which, in case either the one or the other should come to be attacked, his Polish Majesty will not fail to fend his stipulated Succours, conformably to the Engagements actually subsisting with them.

And, in case his Britannick Majesty, and their High Mightinesses the States General, should come to be attacked, his Polish Majesty will furnish them with a Body of Six thousand Men, or even more, if it can then be agreed on, in the same State, and upon the same Conditions, as well in relation to the Requisition for the March, and to the Pay during their actual Service, as with regard to the Diminution of the Subsidy, in case of the said actual Service; and to the fending back of the Troops, if his Polish Majesty should find himself attacked, which were stipulated in the Convention between his Britannick Majesty and the Landgrave of Hejfe, of the 9th May 1740; the Articles or Clauses of which Convention, that are applicable to the Four Points above-mentioned, shall be understood as inserted here.

4

His Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, being persuaded, that the Desires and Wifties of his Britan-nick Majesty, Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, with relation to the Affairs of the German Empire, tend solely to the common Good thereof, and to the Preservation of its

System;

16° Januarii.

37^ i 6° Januarii.A. 1752*

System; and feeiing himself animated with the same patriotick Sentiments, their Majesties mutually engage themselves to unite their Endeavours for the same salutary Purpose, and to consult together upon the Means of obtaining it; and with this View, it is therefore stipulatedon both Sides, that the Envoys and Ministers of their Majesties, who shall happen to be and meet each other, as well at the General Diet of the Empire, as at the Assemblies of the Electoral College, and of the Circles, shall consult together, in Confidence, and ad in Concert, as far as shall be possible, in the Affairs of Consequence that shall relate to the Interests of the Empire; the whole in Conformity to, and in consequence of, its fundamental Laws and Conllicutions.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, and their High Mightineflcs the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, engage themselves, that, in case his Po/ish Majesty should be attacked or disturbed in his hereditary Dominions, by any Power, or under any Pretence whatsoever, in Kefencment of this Treaty, they shall do their utmost to procure him Satisfaction and Indemnification from the Aggressor, for all the Damages which shall have been done to him.

6.

This Treaty shall continue in Force, for the Space of Four Years, to be reckoned from Michaelmas Day, of this present Year; and if the High contracting Parties shall afterwards be disposed to continue, prolong, or alter it, they shall give each other Notice thereof, and treat about it Three Months before its Expiration.

7*

This Treaty shall be approved and ratified by his Majesty the King of Great Britain, the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, and his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony; and the Ratifications shall be exchanged in due Form at Hubertjburg, in the Space of Six Weeks, or sooner, if possible.

In Witness whereof, the aforesaid respective Ministers Plenipotentiaries have signed the presentTreaty; and have thereunto affixed the Seals of their Arms. Done at Drejden the 13th Day of September, in the Year 17 51.

C. Hanbury Williams. Henry Count of BrubL

Lewes Roads. Mr. Sergi/on reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Sussex, and the several Persons usually travelling the Road from London to Lewes, in the said County, and from Lewes, to a Place called The Broil Park Gate, in the said County, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and haddirected him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. Samuel Ridge; who, being examined, said. That he knows the several Roads in the Petition mentioned, which are in a very bad Condition, and, in the Winter Season, Wheel Carriages cannot pass through the fame; and it is with great Danger and Difficulty that Pallengers on Horseback pass through the said Roads.

Mr. Anthony Nott and Mr. Richard Shadwell, being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Ridge, as to the Badness of that Part of the Road from the North End of Mailing Street to The Broil Park Gate.

And they added to their Evidence, That the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, through which those Roads lead, are incapable, by the ordinary Methods directed by the Law, to repair the same; but if the said Roads were amended, and made commodious for Travellers, it would be of general Advantage, and a great Conveniency to the adjacent Country; which cannot be done, without the Assistance of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road from the North End of Mailing Street, near the Town of Lewes, in the County of Sussex, to Uck-field, and from the North End of Mailing Street aforesaid to The Broil Park Gate, and from Offham, otherwise IVog-bam, to Sheffield Bridges, in the Parish of FI etching, in the said County: and that Mr. Sergi/on, Mr. Hay,

Sir Francis Poole, Mr. Thomas Pelham, and Mr. Henry Pelham, of Bramber, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Importing A Petition of the Master Printers of Silk, Silk Hand-Gum Senega. kerchiefs, Callicoes, Linens, and Stuffs, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the red of the Mader Printers of Great Britain of the Trade aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the printing of Silk, Silk Handkerchiefs, Callicoes, Linens, and Stuffs, employs a, great Number, not only of poor Men and Women, but Children, from Seven or Eight Years of Age, and upwards; and that the plain Silks, for the Use of the Printing Trade, are of our own manufacturing; and that the Flax and raw Cotton, of which the Stuffs are made, when spun and wove into brown Goods, yield three times as much as the prime Cod of the crude Materials; and that these, when whitdered, printed, and pencilled, yield from Thirty-five Shillings to upwards of One hundred Shillings; and that the Duty arising from this Manufacture produces a large Share towards the publick Supply, and, as the Petitioners are informed, is collected with a imaller Expence than most other Duties; and that the Laid Trade, on which the Livelihood of many Thousands of poor Families solely depends, cannot be supported and carried on without a sufficient Quantity of Gum Senega; notwithstanding which there is not (as the Petitioners are well informed, and thoroughly believe) in the whole Nation a Quantity sufficient lor above Two Months Consumption; and alleging, That as the Affairs of the African Company have for a considerable Time past: been so situated, that they have r.ot imported the necessary Quantity of the said Gum as heretofore, nor are, as the Petitioners have great Reason to believe, likely to import a sufficient Quantity thereof, within such a Space of Time as may relieve the Petitioners; and the said Trade being now, and for a considerable Time past having been,under the greatest Distress for want of an immediate Supply of the said Gum, it being the most valuable and uiefulDrug or Ingredient used therein, and the Price of that Commodity, for want of the Quantity usually imported, being advanced from 30 s. per Hundred Weight to upwards of Twelve Pounds per Hundred Weight, without any frofpeft (except from the House) of a Reduction of any Consequence, this valuable and most improved Branch of Trade, without same speedy Relief, wiil fall into the Hands of Foreigners, the numerous Poor employed therein become defti-tute and without Support, the publick Revenue greatly ldfened, and the Trade itself in Danger of being totally; ruined:, And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premiles into Confederation; and chat Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Importation of the said African Gum in BritiJfj Botcoms from any European Ports; or that the House will be pleased to give the Petitioners fuqh other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall teem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Coq-sideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

&c. between Taylors for advancing their Wages, or lessening the usual Hours of Work, are illegal, nuil, and void; and that Journeymen Taylors offending against the same Act, shall be committed to the Workhouse or common Gaol, for any Time not exceeding Two Months; that the Time limited for Journeymrn Taylors to work is from Six in the Morning nil Eight at Night, the Master allowing one Penny Half-penny a Day for Breakfast, and one Hour for Dinner, and every Journeyman to be paid Two Shillings per Diem, from the Twenty-fifth of March to the Twenty-fourth of June, and one Shilling and Eight Pence per Diem for the rest of the Year; and ic is further enacted, for the Reasons in the said Act contained, That the Justices for London and Westminster, at their Quarter Sessions, upon Application, may alter the Wages and Hours of Work; and Persons paying more than the Wages aforesaid, shall forfeit Five Pounds; and further setting forth, That the Petitioners have been always willing to comply with the said Act, and conform themselves in every Particular to the Contents thereof; but are now, and have been for some Years past, at times, threatened and terrified, and abused, by the Journeymen Taylors, for such their Compliance, in a riotous and tumultous Man-

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the said Petition be brought up;

Jt passed in the Negative, pa^uami£ Sir William Tonge reported from the Committee, ap-bioms. pointed to consider of Heads of a Rill for the more easy Con vision of Receivers of stolen Goods, and for the Regulation of Pawnbrokers, within the Bills of Mortality, That the Committee had considered the Matters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and areas folio weth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person, who shall, after a Time to be limited, exercise the Trade of a Pawnbroker, or Broker, dealing in Second Hand Goods, within the Bills of Mortality, shall take out a Licence for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Licences shall be granted, in like manner, as Licences for retailing spirituous Liquors are, by Law, directed to be granted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person be intided to take out such Licence, unleis he is an Housekeeper, and is rated, and pays, to Church or Poor, in the Parish where he carries on his Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person, taking out such Licence, shall pay for the same per Annum.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Pawnbroker, or Broker, dealing in Second Hand Goods, within the Bills of Mortality as aforesaid, who shall exercise such Trade, without such Licence, shall forfeit the Sum of and, for the Second Offence, the Sum of and for the Space of and, for the Third Offence,

be for the Space of such Forfeitures to

be levied in like manner as the Forfeitures for selling spirituous Liquors, without Licence, are to be levied.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person keeping a Shop or Room for the Loan of Money, or making a Trade of lending Money upon Pawns or Pledges, in any less Sum chan shall be

deemed a Pawnbroker.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person, who makes a Trade of buying and selling Second Hand Goods, shall be deemed a Broker; wich a Proviso, that no Person, who shall take Second Hands Goods in the way of his own Trade only, shall be deemed a Broker.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Pawnbroker and Broker shall put his Christian and Surname, and Trade, in legible Characters, over his Door.

ResolvedThat it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person, pledging or felling Goods to any one acting as a Pawnbroker, or Broker, who has not his Name and Trade so placed over his Door, shall forfeit the Sum of

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Pawnbroker, or Broker, shall keep a Book, Vol. 26.

in which he shall enter the Day of the Month on which he shall buy, or take any thing in Pawn; together with a Description of the Thing, the Sum paid or advanced thereon, and the Name of the Person, and the Place of his Abode, from whom such Thing was bought, or taken in Pawn.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Pawnbroker, or Broker, shall buy, or take any thing in Pawn, before Seven of the Clock in the Morning, or after Plight in the Evening, from the Twenty-fifth Day of March to the Twenty-ninth Day of September; or before Eight in the Morning, or after Six in the Evening, from the Thirtieth Day of September to the Twenty-fourth Day of March inclusive; in every Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Pawnbroker, or Broker, who shall buy, or take any thing in Pawn, which shall have been advertised to have been loft or stolen, and sufficiently described, in some one publick Paper, to be specified for chat Purpose, within the Space of Days preceding, shall be deemed guilty of

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thar any Pawnbroker, or Broker, who, having bought, or taken any thing in Pawn, which has been loft or stolen, shall not, upon such thing being, within the Space of Days next following, advertised, and sufficienrly described, in such Paper, forthwith give Notice thereof to the Person so advertising, shall be deemed guilty of

and such Pawnbroker, or Broker, so giving Notice as aforesaid, shall be intitled to the Reward of

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for encouraging Prosecutions against Pawnbrokers, or Brokers, so offending, it shall be in the Power of the Court to order all or any Part of the Fine, set upon such Offender, to be paid to the Prosecutor.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Pawnbroker, or Broker, who shall lufpe&any Person coming to his Shop to fell or pawn any thing, not to have come honeitly thereby, shall and may seize and detain such Person, and the Thing offered to be sold or pawned, in his Custody, till he can procure a Constable, or other Peace Officer, who shall forthwith carry such Person and Thing before a Justice of Peace; and in case, upon Examination, such Justice shall find Reason to suspect such Person of not having come honestly by such thing, he shall and may commit him for safe Custody for the Space of Days, and shall in the mean time order

such Thing to be advertised, and described, in the said Paper; and the Publisher of such Paper shall immediately insert such Advertisement without any Fee or Reward, and without paying any Duty for the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, if any Action shall be brought against such Pawnbroker, or Broker, on account of such Seizure or Detainer, he may plead the general Issue, and give the special Matter in Evidence, and shall be intitled to Costs.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, toencourage'Pawnbrokers and Brokers to stop such iufpected Persons, any Pawnbroker, or Broker, so (top* ping such suspected Person, shall, in case such Person be convicted, be intitled to a Licence for the ensuing Year, without paying any Duty for the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Pawnbroker shall, upon Pretence of Interest or Warehouse Room, or upon any other Pretence whatsoever, take above the Rate of per Week for every advanced upon any Loan, and so in proportion for any greater or less Sum, so as such Sum advanced does not exceed and, in case such Sum

Richard Spence, the proper Officer of the Company, for that Purpose; and that the said Royal African Company repaid 250/. of the 500l. and also paid thelnterest of the remaining 250/. to the 28th June 1743 $ and there being 59/. 2 s. 6 d. Interest, due on the re main -ing 250/. amounting, with the said 250/. to 309/. 2 s. 6d. they, on the 21st March 1747, issued their Bonds for the said 309/. 2 s. 6 d. bearing Date the 21st Day of March 1747, and numbered 486 for 100l. 487 for 100l. and 488 for 109/. 2 s. 6d.; and that no Part of the Principal or Interest of the said Bonds hath been paid; but the said 309/. 2s. 6d. and all Interest for the fame, is (till due; and that the said Mary Brookes died in the Year 1747, having made her Will, and the Petitioner one of her Executors. and the only acting one, and residuary Legatee, who is intitled to the said Bonds, and the Money due thereon; and that the said Petitioner, living chiefly in the Country, never heard, or was informed, of the A££ for appointing Commissioners to examine and state the Claims of the Creditors of the said Company; and therefore did not apply in due Time, to prove the said Debt; so that the same was not included in the Report of the Commissioners, delivered into the House the last Session of Parliament; and the further Time given by the Act of Jaft Session, to the said Commissioners, being only to enquire and state the Claims particularly mentioned in the said Act, the Petitioner will be now totally deprived of any Satisfaction for his Debr, which was so fairly contracted, and is so justly due to him, unless relieved by the House: And therefore praying the House to take the Petitioner’s same into Conficleration; and grant him such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of James Guthrie, for himself and Company, Merchants in Dumfries, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners did, in the Month of May 1750, enter for Exportation, at the Port of Kir-kudbright, 253 Hogsheads, containing 231,328 Pounds of Tobacco, for which the Duties had been duly paid and secured by the Petitioners, at Importation, according to Law; and which, after being regularly inspected by the proper Officers of the Customs, were fliipt on board the Ship Neptune, of Dumfries, James Sturgeon Mailer, for France; and that the said Ship, with the said Tobaccoes on board, after being finally cleared at the Custom-house, proceeded on her Voyage; but ijn going down tr.c River

You 26*

of Kirkudbright, and before die got without the Lirflits of the Port, (he (truck on a Rock, by which Accident (he Was overfer, and filled with Water; and that the Matter immediately acquainted the chief Officers at Kirkudbright of the Misfortune, and likewise delivered the Ship and Cargo into their Charge, so that the Tobaccoes might bd taken out in their Sight, and the Ship floated, and brought into a proper Place,where her Damage might be repaired; and that accordingly, wich the Consent of the said Officers/ and under their Inspection, the whole of the saidTobaccoeg were taken out of the Ship, and landed; but, upon Examination, were found to be so greatly damaged, that no more than 7,920 Pounds could be picked out of the whole, that was dry, and fit for Use, which was weighed and packed up by the Officers, and dill remains in their Custody; and that the Remainder of the Cargo, being 2 23,408 Pounds,was burnt at the Sight, and with the Approbation/ of the said Officers, the same being totally damaged, and unmerchantable; and that, notwithstanding the Petitioners proceeded in every Step of this Transaction in Concurrence, and under the Inspection, of the Officers; and also were at a considerable Charge, to prevent any Embezzlement of the damaged Tobaccoes, to the Detriment of the Revenue, by keeping, at their Expence, a Guard of near Twenty Officers, constantly during the landing and burning the said Tobaccoes; yet the Collector of the Customs at Kirkudbright refused to grant the Petitioners a Debenture,whereby they might be intitled to draw back the Duties on such Part of the Tobaccoes as had been burnt, unless he had an Order from the Commissioners of the Customs so to do; and when the Petitioners applied to the Commissioners for such Order, they refused the fame; alleging, That the Law allows of no Drawback, unless. the Goods are exported to foreign Parts, or loft at Sea, without the Limits of the Port where (hipt; so that the Petitioners are Itill unsatisfied for the whole Drawback of the Tobaccoes which were burnt, amounting to 5,878/. i8j. 10id. as well as for the Property of the 7,920 Pounds of found Tobacco, delivered to the Officers; and that, although the Law has made no Provision for this, particular Accident, yet in a similar Cafe, viz. That of Tobaccoes burnt in a Warehouse, by the Statute of the 12th of Queen Anne, the Drawback is allowed; but, in this Cafe, though the Merchant had done all in his Power to have the Tobaccoes exported in the manner prescribed by Law; and though they are certainly, to every Intent and Purpose,with regard to the Revenue, in the same same as if burnt in a Warehouse, or loft at Sea, yet here the Law provides no Relief: And therefore offering the same of the Petitioners to the Consideration of the House; and praying the y will grant such Relief, as they shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine and state to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition.

Westminster Sir Peter Warren reported from the Committee, to Court House. whom the Petition of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the City and Liberty of Westminster, w hole Names ape thereunto subscribed, in behalf of chemselves, and the rest of the Justices of the Peace for the said City and Liberty; and also the Petition of several of the Inhabitants of the City and Liberty of V/eJlminJltr, on behalf of chemselves, / and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty;

were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed!; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr. Wation was examined, and said, That the Justices VoL. 26.

of the Peace for the City and Liberty of Westminster have not of Right any Place to assemble in; and that they have, by the Permission of the Witness, who is Deputy Steward of Westminster, held their Sessions for several Years in the Town Court House, which belongs to the Burgesses and Courts Leet:

That the said Court House is very close, dark, and inconvenient, and is extremely damp and unwholesome; and that there is not sufficient Room for die Suitors, nor the great Number of Prisoners which are frequently brought to be tried at the Sessions:

That he has heard many of the Justices complain of the offensive Stench, and express their Apprehension of their Healths being greatly endangered by their Attendance in the said Place:

That a great many Persons are summoned to serve upon Juries, who are very much incommoded in their Attendance; and that there is not any proper Place for the Juries to retire to consider of their Verdicts, and other Matters:

That it would be for the Benefit and Advantage, not only of the Justices, but of the Inhabitants in general, if a proper and convenient Court House was erected; and that, in his Opinion, a Rate of 2d. in the Pound for One Year,upon the Inhabitants, would defray the Expence thereof.

Mr. Stephen Popham was also examined, with regard to the Expence of erecting the said Court House; and concurred in Opinion with Mr. Wation.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the purchasing or hiring a convenient Piece of Ground within the City of Westminster, and for erecting and fitting up a proper Court House for the Use of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the said City and Liberty thereof: And that Sir Peter Warren and Mr. Mundy do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That this is the nearest Road from Bristol to London, the other Road, through Bath, being, as the Witness was informed at the Post House, Seven Miles about:

That he apprehends the Stature Labour is insufficient to repair the Road; for that One Parish, in which there are but Five Teams, and but few Inhabitants, is obliged by Law to repair Two Miles of the woift Part of the Road. As to the Road mentioned in the Second Petition,

He informed your Committee, That it was worse than the other-; and that he passed it with great Difficulty about a Month ago on Horseback; and in some Parts of it Two Carriages cannot pass each other.

Mr. Cccke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners of the Court of Requests of the Tower Hamlets, and of sundry other Inhabitants of the said Hamlets, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the. Rcloltnions of the Committee thereupon, to the Hduft; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards-delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the Tower Hamlets, was read: And,

Matthew Dove Esquire, and Mr. James Savage, being severally examined, said, That they were Commissioners of the said Court; and that the said Act has been found very beneficial to the Publick.

Mr. Alexander Whitechurch, being examined, said, That the Commissioners doubt whether they have Autho- ' Tity to compel the Appearance of Defendants, and therefore have not caused them to be taken up on Attachments; but have ordered the Beadles of the Court to take their Engagement to appear; which has occasioned great Delay in their Proceedings.

Matthew Dove Esquire, being further examined, confirmed Mr. lVhitechurchys Evidence; and added, That Doubts have arisen whether the said Court has a Power to try an Action for Rent, or for Goods detained, and like-wife as to the Time of the Commencement of the Forty Days, for which Defendants are to be committed; and also whether Attorneys are liable to the Process of the said Court.

In order to shew the Inconvenience arising from want of the Proceedings of this Court being declared Evidence in other Courts,

Mr. Richard Venables said, That Edward Hadder sued his Wife, Bridget Venables (then Mrs. Greenacre) in the Court of Conscience, and recovered Five Shillings; for which an Execution was taken out, and the Money paid into Court; and that the said Hadder afterwards sued her in White Chcppel Court, and obtained a Judgment there for Four Shillings Damage and Costs, which he (the Witness) paid; and that his Wife offered Evidence there, that it was recovered in the Court of Conscience; but the Evidence was refused.

And he produced to your Commutee the Bill and Receipt for the Money pgid in the said Suit.

Mr. Robert Low, who receives the Money paid into the Court of Conscience, and pays it out, said, a Summons was issued out of the said Court against Bridget Venables, alias Greenacre, at the Suit of Richard Hadder; on which an Order was made 16th October 1750, for the Payment of 5 s. Debt, and Eight Pence Costs; that, the said Money not being paid into* Court, an Execution was taken out the 18th November following for 5 s. 8 d. Debt, and is. lid. Costs; in consequence whereof he the Witness received the said Debt and Costs; and that Three or Four Months afterwards he was subpoena’d to White Chappel Court, to prove that the said Debt was paid; but the Court refused to admit his Evidence, because the Court of Conscience was not a Court of Record.

Mr. John Joyce, being examined, said, That he was sued in the Court of Conscience by Matthew Lamb, for 1 /. i6i. 5 d. for Bread; and, on Hearing, he was ordered to pay the same at is. 6 d. per Month: That he made the First Payment on the 10th of May, and Three

him for 3 /. and upwards in White Chappel Court, the said Debt of 1 /. 16 s. 5 d. being Part of the Sum he was arrested for, to which the Plaintiff7 added Two Guineas which he pretended to have lent him; and that he (the Witness) would have produced Evidence upon the Trial, to prove the Recovery of the said Debt of 1 /. 16 j. 5 d. in the Court of Conscience; but was not admitted to do it; in consequence whereof, a Judgment was recovered against him for the whole 3 /. 1S s. 5 d. and Costs; which he has since paid.

Mr. Low, being examined as to the last mentioned Fast, said. That he was the Evidence called by Mr. Joyce, and accordingly attended with the Book of Orders, Ledger, and Cash Book, of the Court of Conscience, and was ready to prove, that the said Debt was recovered; but the Court were of Opinion, that the Court of Conscience not being a Court of Record, he could not be admitted an Evidence to prove the said Books, or himself to give any Evidence relating to the Transactions of that Court.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Refclvedy That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 23d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the Tower Hamlets, hath been found very beneficial to the Publick; but is defective in some Parts thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Method of compelling the Defendants to appear upon the Summons, has proved very inconvenient, and in many Respects insuffici^nt.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the enlarging the Powers given by the said Act, so as to include Actions of Detinue, and Debt for Rent, under Forty Shillings, where the Freehold does not come in Question, will be of Service to the Owners of Lands and Houses in particular, and to the Inhabitants in general within the Tower Hamlets.

In support of the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Mr. William Thompson said, That he knows the several Roads mentioned in the Petitions; that in general they are extremely bad, and particularly in some Places, owing to the Rottenness of the Soil, and also to the frequent Ovei flowings of Water; ’tis very often,with great Danger, as well as Difficulty, that Carriages do pass:

That at the Town o( Ripon there was formerly a great Market, for the Sale of Wool; but of late very little has been carried thither, which the Witness said he attributed to the very great Difficulty of the Carriage; and that there is also a very confideiable Trade for Lead and Butter at York, which is brought thither from Boroughbridge; but that Trade has met with great Interruption, chiefly owing to the Badness of the Roads;

The Governor and Co. of the Bank of England, humbly propose.

To advance the Sum of One Million, for Payment of Part of the Debt of the Navy, and other publick Services; and also the Sum of Four hundred thousand Pounds, charged on the additional Duties on Stamps, now carrying an interest at 3/. ioj. per Cent, per Annum; which, pursuant to Notice given the last Session of Parliament, are to be redeemed and paid off on the 24th Day of October 1752.

That Exchequer Bills be issued to them on or before the Times, at which the said Sums of One Million and Four hundred thousand Pounds respectively, shall be wanted, to be advanced, carrying an interest at 3/. per Cent. per Annum, to be charged on the Sinking Fund.

And they further humbly propose, That the said principal Sums of One Million, and Four hundred thousand Pounds, shall be repaid to them out of the First Excdles or Surplusses of the Sinking Fund, that shall be applied to the Payment of the Principal of the national Debt, next after the Remainder of the Sum of One Million One hundred and Ninety thousand and Forty-one Pounds Sixteen Shillings and One Penny, which has been advanced by the said Governor and Company, pursuant to an Act of last Session of Parliament, shall be discharged and paid off.

By Order of the Court of Directors,

Robert Lewin, Secretary.
