Ordered, That Mr. Dowdeswell have Leave to make a Motion, it being after Four of the Clock.

And he moved the House accordingly.

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

First, Your Committee caused the Report of the Com-xnifiioners to be read; and having examined Mr. James Poflethwaite, Accomptant to the said Commissioners, found that the Allowances made under N01. of their said Report, were the only true Sums in which the Company flood indebted to the several Claimants therein mentioned, the Enquiry and Examinations having been made in the same manner, upon these Claims, as upon the Claims of other Creditors by the said Commissioners enquired into, and reported to the House, in the last Session; but that there being very (lender Materials to support the Claims of Mef-sieur* Stockwell, Husbands, and Boteler, the Commissioners examined the Expence of maintaining the Forts for the preceding Year, and settled the Sums allowed to these Claimants, in proportion to that Expence; and that the said Commissioners were of Opinion, that the Claims contained under N° 2. of their Report, ought to be disallowed; and your Committee observe, that ttys Opinion

Vol. 26.

of the Commissioners was founded upon a want of Evidence to support the several Claims therein mentioned, or upon Account of Over-charges made by the several Clainv ants, or upon Account of the Deduction of 51, per Centum, which the Company usually made when any Money was paid in England, to the Officers and Servants of the Company, who had been employed in their Factories abroad.

Your Committee then proceeded upon the Petition of Joseph Philips, to them referred; and Mr. James Postlethwaite informed your Committee, That the Commissioners had Notice of the Three Bonds mentioned in the said Petition, which appeared to be outstanding; but were not claimed before the said Commissioners: Then the last W ill and Testament of Mary Brookes Widow, deceased, bearing Date the 26th Day of March 1747, together with the Probate thereunto annexed, were produced to your Committee, and read; and it appeared to your Committee, That the Petitioner, Joseph Philips, and one Job Jones,. were made, ordained, and appointed, joint Executors of the said Will; but that Letters of Adminifuation were granted only to the said Petitioner; and it appeared like-wife, that the said Petitioner was, by the said Will, constituted Residuary Legatee: Then Mr. Spence, Secretary to the Royal African Company, produced the original Subscription Book, N° 6. dated August the 27th 1739; whereby it appeared, That a Subscription was then opened by the said Company, for railing, by Loan, 20,000 /. to be employed in carrying on their Trade, with several Conditions therein mentioned; and to be repaid to the Subscribers at Four several Times, and by Four several Payments; that is to say, 25 per Centum on the 29th Day of August 1740, and 25 per Centum on the 29th Day of September 1740, and 25 per Centum on the 29th Day of October 1740, and the remaining 25 per Centum on the 29th Day of November 1740, with Incereft on each of the said Payments, after the Rate of 5 /. per Centum per Annum; and it appeared on the said Subscription Book, that Mary Brookes subscribed thereto the Sum of Five hundred Pounds; then a Receipt was produced, signed Richard Spence, and dated the 31st of August 1739; whereby it appeared, That Mrs. Mary Brookes paid to the said Richard Spence the Sum of Five hundred Pounds, in full of her said Subscription: Then a Receipt, signed by the said Petitioner, and bearing Date the 21st Day of March 1747 was produced, and read; whereby it appeared, That at that Time there remained due, on the said Subscription Receipt, the principal Sum of 250/. and 59/. 2s. 6 d. for interest thereon; and that new Bonds, N° 486, 487, and 488, were issued to the Petitioner for the said Sums, making in the whole, 309/. is. 6d.; and the said Bonds were produced, and read; and Mr. Spence informed your Committee, That no Part of the Money, due upon these Bonds, had been paid by the Company; and it appeared.

That the Petitioner lived chiefly in Berkshire; and that Mr. Spence acquainted him in JuJy last, and not before, with the Transactions relating to the Creditors of the Company; upost this your Committee observe, That 250/.

Part of the Sum claimed by the said Petitioner, is Principal Money due to him from the Royal African Company, and stands on the same Footing with several other Sums claimed by other Creditors, and stated by the Commissioners, under N° 2. of their Report by them made to Parliament, in the last Session; and that the Remainder, amounting to 59/. 2 s. 6 d. is interest Money, allowed to the said Petitioner by the Company, and turned into Principal; and therefore stands on the same Footing with the several Sums claimed before the Commissioners, and by them stated, under N° 7. of their said Report.

Stint Mar- Mr. Sdufbury reported from the Committee, to whom gam and the Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, St. John's Surveyors of the Highways, Scavengers, and other In-ParSh RatM habitants, of the United Parishes of St. Margaret and St. John the Evangelist, Westminster, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth 5 viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act of the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne was read; whereby it appeared, that the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, with the Vestry or principal Inhabitants of the said Parishes, are directed to meet annually, upon Tuesday in Easter Week, or ofeener, if Occasion require, and agree upon or ascertain the Monies or Rates to be afiefled within the Limits of the said Parishes for the Relief of the Poor, Repair of the Highways, and other Parish Rates, to be levied and collected by the proper Officers of the respective Parishes: Then,

Mr. John Feary, Vestry Clerk of the Parish of St. Margaret, being examined, said, That the Rate for repairing the Highway seldom exceeds One Penny in the Pound; which Persons who rent low-priced Houses, frequently refuse to pay; and that it cannot be recovered, without first summoning the Person, so refilling, to shew Cause for such Refusal; which if they neglect, or are unable to shew, and continue to refuse the Payment, the Method of Recovery of the said Rates is by Dvftrefs of the Offender’s Goods, the Expence whereof frequently amounts to Four Times as much as the Rate when recovered, and requires the Attendance of Three or Four Officers to make it: That, as to the cleansing the Streets, the Rate usually made for that Purpose is Four Pence in the Pound, which amounts to Five or Six hundred Pounds; but as this is collected by the Scavengers, which is an Office imposed on the Persons who serve it, it is seldom half collected; that the Assessment last Year amounted to 550/. ns.+d. and the Collection only to 280/. 10 s. 11 d. so that the Raker cannot half clean the Streets for the Money raised: That the Money collected for the Poor, the Scavengers, and the Highways, arc collected in Three different Rates; which enhances the Expence in making and collecting the fame; which would be considerably diminished if the same were reduced into One Rate.

Vol. 26.

In order to shew the Necessity of some Regulations, in regard to the Poor, the Witriefs produced to your Committee an Account of the Expence of the Poor, whereby it appeared, that the Expence of maintaining 344 Poor* in the Year 1742, amounted to 2,102/. 7s. 4! d and that, in the Year 1750, the Expence of 350 Poor amounted to 2,726/. 7s. 3id. fb that there is an additional Expence of 624/. 19/. 10Id. for maintaining an additional Number of Six Poor.

* Ellis Esquire, being examined, said, That he apprehended the Increase of Expence, incurred on account of the Poor, was occasioned by the Overseers having an unlimited Power of disposing of the Money collected, without being subject to any Check or Controul; and he said this was the general Opinion of the Inhabitants of the said Parishes.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Graziers* and Farmers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Occupiers of Lands, in the Parts of Kefteven, in the County of Lincoln, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Owners and Occupiers of Land in that County: And also,

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Graziers, and Farmers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Occupiers of Lands, in the Parts of Lind/ey, in the County of Lincoln, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Owners and Occupiers of Lands in that County:

Were severally presented to the House, and read; severally taking Notice, That Application has lately been made to Parliament, in order to obtain fomenew Law to enforce the Observation of the ancient Laws relating to the Winding of Wool, and to make the said Laws more efteftyal, by restraining the Marking of Sheep with Tar and Pitch, and for preventing all Deceit and Fraud in the Winding of Wool, for the future; and setting forth, That the County of Lincoln is of very great Extent, and hath lying within it large Quantities of rich Pasture Lands, whereon are de-pallured and kept great Numbers of Sheep; and that the Graziers, Farmers, and Occupiers of Land, in that County, do make some the whole, and others the greatest Part of the Rents and Profits of the Lands they occupy, by breeding and fattening of Sheep, and growing of Wool 5 and that the Occupiers of Lands, within the said County, have of late Years been at great Expence and Trouble in improving the Breed of Sheep 5 so that it is well known, that the Wool of that County is eLleemed the finest large Wool, and the properest Wool for making of the finest Crapes, Camblets, Damalks, and other fine Woollen Goods, of the like Nature or Kind; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend it is absolutely necessary, that Sheep should be marked with Tar Marks, in order to distinguish Property; and that, be Gdes this, where Sheep are depastured or fed on large Commons, or open Fields, it is usual, and, as the Petitipners apprehend, absolutely necessary, to mark such Sheep in like manner with a publick Mark of each Town; all which Marks are in a great measure washed out before the Sheep are clipped, though it is impossible intirely to clear the Fleecefrom such Marks,by walh-ing or rivering of them; and that, should the Mark or Marks be cut or clipped effectually from the Fleece, by the Grower, the Petitioners apprehend the First Buyer would, from thence, frequently take Occasion to object, that such Fleece was not a whole Fleece, and would refuse the fame; which would greatly depreciate the Value of such Wool, and put the Grower under great Difficulty to prove such Fleece was not a broken Fleece; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Buyers of Wool can easily discover whether any Frauds or ill Practices have been committed in the Washing and Winding of Wool, as all Wool bought by them, before it is delivered, is weighed in Parcels, not exceeding a Tod, or q8 Pounds, at One Weight 5 it being the Advantage of the Buyers to weigh in small Parcels, whereby

they get the Turn%f die Scale in every Parcel; and that, although by the Laws relating to the Weighing of Wool, it ought to be weighed by an even Balance, by Avoirdupoize Weight, yet the Buyers of Wool do, for the most part, insist to have an additional Weight of Half a Pound, and, in some Places, a Pound, over and above the legal Weight, in every Parcel so weighed; and that the Weigher of furst Wool, who is the Buyer, or his Agent, examines* very single Fleece, as the same comes to the Scale to be weighed, in order to fee whether it be or be nor a Cot; and in case he has Reason to fufpc& that any Fraud or ill Practices have been committed in the Winding of any Fleece, he may insist to open aiii examine it; and if such Liberty is denied him, the Petitioners apprehend he may lawfully refuse such Fleece or Fleeces* and that in the said County, and, as the Petitioners are informed, in some of the neighbouring Counties, it has ndt, within the Memory of Man, been usual for the Growers of Wool to wind their own Wool; but the same is wound or wrapped up by Persons profefting that Business, who are called Wool-winders; many of whom are appointed to that Office, pursuant to the ancient Statuce of the Staple, set forth in the 27th Year of King Edward the Third; and that, at the Time of the Appointment, such Wool-winders are sworn to the doe Exe--cucion of their Office, before the Mayor of the Staple, at Westminster-, and that the Petitioners apprehend it is for the Benefit of the Wool-growers in general, that the Wool should be washed and wound up clear of all Dirt, Soil, or Filth, and, as far as is possible (without cutting or clipping) from the Tar-mark*; since it is well known, that the First Buyers of Wool, under Colour of a Loss by such Marks, do generally expcCt and make greater Abatements in the Price of Wool, than the Weight of such Part of the said Marks, as remains after washing, does, upon a Medium, amount unto; and that the Petitioners are so truly sensible, that all Frauds and Mismanagemerics in the Washing and Winding of Wool, turn ^6 the Discredit and Disad vantage of the honest and fair-dealing Wool-growers, that theyfhould be glad some effectual Method could be found our, to prevent the like Practices for the future, withouc subjecting the innocent and honest Wool-growers in general to heavy Penalties, and frequent vexatious and expert-five Profecurions; and that all Difficulties, Hard-ships, or Penalties, laid upon the Growers of Wool, will, as the Petitioners apprehend, naturally tend to discourage the Growth of Wool, and lessen the Quantity; which, in the End, will hurt the Manufacturer, and Trade in general, and lower the Rents and Value of Lands throughout the Kingdom; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that, at the same Time that proper Laws are established, to prevent all AbufeSjMismanagement, and Fraud, being praCfifed by the Growers and First Srllers of Wool, like Provision will be m^de by the Legislature to prevent all Frauds and ill Practices in the First Buyers of Wool; and particularly to enforce the ancient Laws relating to the due weighing, and the Refafe or Re-fufals of Wools, and other Difficulties and Impo-ficions to which the Growers of Wool are often fuh-jected, in felling and disposing of their Wool, and in receiving and recovering the Money agreed ro be paid for the fame; for that, as the Laws now stand, the First Wool-buyers, by themselves, or Factors, do often come to a verbal Agreement with the Grower, for a Parcel of Wool, which, by the Agreement, is to be weighed up, and paid for at a particular Time, which the Buyer generally exceeds; and whether he does or does nor,instead of paying for the Wool, when it is weighed and delivered, generally gives the Seller Bills, payable at a future Day, which are often very irregularly paid, and sometimes not paid at all; whereby the Seller is put to great Trouble and Dif- ficulcy

faulty to recover the Value, as the Wool-buyers, for the qaoft part, live in remote Parts from the Seller; and further alleging, That where Wool-buyers have bargained lor a Parcel of Wool, at a certain Price, to be weighed,.delivered, and paid for, at a future Day, and it has happened, that, in the mean time, the Price of Wool has fallen, the Buyer, in such Case, has refuted to perform his Agreement; which, being usually verbal, the Grower has not any Method to compel him so to do, except by entering into a long andexpenfive Law-suit; and, at the same time, dares not dispose of his Property to another, left the First Buyer should afterwards demand a Performance of his Bargain, and infill it was not to be vacated or set aside, but by due Course of Law; by which means the industrious and honest Wool-grower is kept out of his Money, to his great Disappointment and Loss, and often to that of the Landlord; and that it frequently happens, that Part of the bell Fleeces are bruken, torn, or cut, from the Sheeps Backs, before the general Clipping in which Cale, it is necessary such Part of the Fleece as remains should be put into, and wrapped up wiih, a Fleece of equal Quality; for were such broken Fleeces to be deemed Refuse, a much greater Lois would attend the Grower than the Manufacturer, by accepting it; and that the Petitioners apprehend this Mai ter may be put under proper Regulations, by enjoining all Wool-growers not to Wind their own Wool, and obliging them to employ publick, licensed, and sworn Wool-winders, to wind the same (at least in the County of Lincoln, and such Places where Wool-winders have been usually employed) and by providing proper Laws and Rules for Licensing, Swearing, and Regulating, of Wool-winders: And theretore praying, That the House will take the same of the Petitioners inro Consideration; and provide such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Prayers.

Corn Bounty. A PETITION of the Merchants and Exporters of jtV Corn from the Port of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, whose Names are subscribed, was prefenced to the House, and read 5 reciting the several Provisions in an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, and in an Act, made in the 12th and 13th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, and in an Act, made in the Third Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for continuing the Duty on Malt, and by the several Malt Acts since, relating to the Bounty payable on the Exportation of Malt and Corn; and setting forth. That the Petitioners have in and since the Month of October 1750, at divers times, bought, put on Ship-board, and exported from the Pore of Great Yarmouth aforesaid, great Quantities of Wheat, Rye, Barley, and Malt, the said several Sorts of Corn being, at the Time of such shipping at the said Port, bought and sold under the several Prices mentioned in the said Acts; and, in consideration of the said Bounty, gave greater Prices to the Farmers for the said Corn, than the Petitioners otherwise should have done; and that the Petitioners, in shipping and exporting such Corn, have strictly observed and obeyed the Directions and Intentions of the said several Acts, and have procured Certificates, from time to time, from the Collector of the Customs in the said Port, of his

not having Money in his Hands, chargeable with the Payment of the said Bounty, sufficient to pay the fame; and have caused such Certificates, after being affixed to the Debenture of such Corn, to be produced to the Commissioners of his Majesty’s Customs at London, who have thereupon given Orders to the General Receiver, or Cashierv of the Customs, to pay the said Bounry-money, within Three Months, out of Monies in his Hands chargeable with the Payments of Money for the Exportation of Corn; and that the Petitioners, after the Debentures have become due, have applied divers times to the General Receiver, or Cashier, aforesaid, for the said Money; but have never been able to procure Payment of any Part thereof, the said General Receiver alleging.

That he had not, nor has, any Money in his Hands, chargeable with the Payment of the said Bounty-money, sufficient to pay the fame; so that there now remains unpaid to the Petitioners all the said Bounty-money for the said Corn exported by them as aforesaid, for upwards of a Year last past, amounting in the whole to a very large Sum of Money, great Parc whereof has been due these Twelve Months, and other Parts Eight or Six Months; whereby the Petitioners are greatly distressed in their Trade: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration, and make such Provision for the Payment of the Petitioners Bounty-money now due to them as aforesaid, and also for the better and more effectual Payment of such Bounty-money as hereafter shall become due by virtue of the said Act^ as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen vVoolleA of the Grand Jury, and other Gentlemen, Clergy, Wool- Trade, growers, and Manufacturers, at the General Quarter Sef-(ions of the Peace, at Kendall\ assembled, on Friday, the Seventeenth Day of January 1752, in and for the County of Westmorland, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That Application is made to Parliament, complaining of some bad Practices relating to the Salving of Sheep with Tar, and other Ingredients mixed therewith, the marking and branding the same with Pitch and

Tar, and the deceitful Fleecing of Wool with Dirt, and other Things therein, to advance the Weight, and for ap- pointing sworn Wool-winders, or Fleecers, to prevent the fame; and setting forth, That the Petitioners Country

is very cold and mountainous; and there are kept

great Flocks of Sheep; and that it is found, by Experience, that if the Sheep in those Parts were not salved with Tar, Butter, and Tallow, mixed, the Owners would, every Winter, lose the greatest Part of their Stocks; and, besides that, the Salving adds greatly to the Growth and Staple of the Wool; and that the usual Method of marking of Sheep is with Tar, and other Ingredients, as soon as the Fieece is taken off; which can do no Injury to the next Fleece, as it has a whole Year’s Time to spend itself, and no ways affects the Staple of the Wool; and the Sheep always, about a Month ’before Sheering, are well rivered or washed; and observing. That the Sheep in those Parts are generally very small; and, should it pals into a Law, that no Tail or Shank Wool should be wound up or fleeced, but to be cut off by the Owner of such.

Wool, the Grower would lose at least a Sixth Part thereof, besides the great Difficulty and Disputes which would, of course, arise between the Sellers and Buyers, about the aflbrtingand dividing the Tail and Shank Wool from the Fleece Wool; nor can the Buyers or Manufacturers of Wool, in those Parts, be hurt by the present Method of fleecing Wool, without a Wool-winder; the having'of which would also, in those Parts, not only be very expen-fiv«f, but troublesome, to the Growers of Wool: And therefore, as the Manner of Winding of Wool, now, and the Staple thereof, in every respect, is so well known, and which is chiefly manufactured into Coarse Goods, praying,

That no Restraint may be laid upon the Growers of Wool in those Parts, which may prevent them from falving or marking their Sheep as above-mentioned, or winding or fleecing their Wool as usual, nor any Profccurion against the Growers of Wool, for unfair fleecing thereof, after the Wool is delivered (as it afterwards is in the Power of the Wool-ftapler, or Carriers, to make use of unfair Means, in otaer to incur a Penalty upon the Seller, and as the Wool goes, in a general Way> upwards of Sixty Miles, by Land-

carriage,

424

A. 175-2.

carriage, and-through a-great many 'Hands, whereby/the hondt Wopl-grower may innocently suffer, from mali* cions and designing Persons) provided that no.Filth or pirt be wilfully wound therewith, to defraud the Buyers in Weight; and that no marking or branding with Pitch or Tar only be used above once in the Year; and that to be ifnmediately used after taking off the Fleece.

Ordered, That the said Petition dp lie upon the Table.

Saltish A PETITION of the Portreeves, Burgesses, and Water Jt\_ Inhabitants, of the ancient Town and Borough of Cnllomt. cTaviJlocky in the County of Devon, and the Inhabitants of the Parish of Tavistock, in behalf of themselves, and the neighbouring Parishes, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That the Corporation of Saltash, in the County of Cornwall, have petitioned for an Act of Parliament, for laying a Duty of Two Pence per Ton on all Goods, Wares, Merchandize, &?c. carried inVesselsup and down the River Tamar, which is navigable upwards of Twenty Miles from Plymouth 5 and representing to the House, That the said Town and Borough of Tavistock is a Place of very considerable and extensive Trade, and lies about Fifteen Miles North from Plymouth, which is the nearest Sea-port Town; but that the said River Tamar being navigable to within Three Miles of the said Town and Borough of Tavistock, most of their heavy and bulky Goods are brought up, and sent down, by the said River; andthatas the saidTownand Borough arc largely concerned in the Woollen Trade, and have likewise one of the best Markets in the County for Corn, Grain, and other Commodities, very large Quantities of which (especially Oats) are weekly bought in the said Market and Neighbourhood for Exportation, and sent down by the said River, the Petitioners conceive, if the said Petition should pass into a Law, it would greatly distress and clog the Trade of the said Borough and Parish, by considerably advancing the Freight of all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, as well exported and imported, as the Price of Carriage by Land, from the said Town and Borough, to Plymouth, is Twenty Shillings per Ton; whereas the Freight by Water, to within Three Miles of the said Town and Borough, is but Eighteen Pence per Ton; and the Land Carriage, for the said Three Miles, Three Shillings and Six PenceperTom making in all 5*. per Ton; and further representing to the House, That the chief Manure used in Improvement of Lands, in the said Parish of Tavistock, and the neighbouring Parishes, is Lime and Sea Sand; of whfch several Thousands of Tons are annually brought up the said R iver of Tamar, for the Use of the Farmers inhabiting within Ten Miles of the Banks of the said River; so that the Vot. 26. '

said Duty will greatly affect the Landed Interest, by enhancing the Price of Manure, as well as the Price of Corn and Grain, exported as aforesaid; to the Discouragement of good Husbandry, and the Prejudice of the poor Farmers; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the Corporation of Saltash have drawn up their Petition in a specious and artful manner, in order to mislead the House, and bring a very large Revenue to themselves, at the Expence of the industrious Tradesmen and Farmers: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleated, out of Regard to the Landed Interest and Trade of this Nation (both which will be considerably affected, should the Petition of the Corporation of Saltash be passed into a Law) to reject the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Free Burgesses, of the Borough of Saltash, in the County of Cornwall, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Merchants, and Exporters of4 Corn, Com from the Port of Ip/wich, in the County of Suffolk, whose Bounty. Names are subscribrd, was presented to the House, and read 5 reciting the several Provisions in an Act made in the First Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, and in an Act made in the 12th and 13th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, and in an Act made in the Third Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for continuing the Duty on Malt, and in the several Malt Acts since, relating to the Bounty payable on the Exportation of Malt and Corn; and alleging, That the Petitioners have, in and since the Month of October 1750, at divers Times bought, put on Shipboard, and exported from the Port of Ip/wich aforesaid, great Quantities of Wheat, Rye, Barley, and Malt; and that the Petitioners, in shipping and in exporting the fame, have strictly observed the Directions and Intention of the said Acts; but that the Petitioners have not been able to obtain any Part of the Bounty due to them for the said Corn and Malt, the Receiver General of the Customs alleging that he had not, nor has, any Money in his Hands, chargeable with the Payment of the said Bounty-money, sufficient to pay the fame: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and make such Provision for the Payment of the Bounty-money, now due to the Petitioners; and also for the better and more effectijal Payment of such Bounty-money, as hereafter shall become due, by virtue of the said Acts, as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by a Bill now depending in the House, it is intended to enable the Petitioners to purchase a House, and certain Parcels of Ground, for the finishing and completing of the said Royal Hospital; and that the Petitioners, in order to finish and complete the said Royal Hospital, may have occasion to purchase other Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments; but that the Owners or Proprietors thereof, though willing, may not be able to enter into proper and effectual Conveyances for that Purpose, by reason of Infancy, or other Incapacities or Disabilities: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill, to enable the Petitioners to purchase such Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, as shall be thought necessary by the Petitioners to be purchased, for finishing and completing the said Royal Hospital, and to enable Persons who may be willing to contract for the Sale of such Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, to convey the same to the Petitioners, for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill, to render all Contracts and Agreements, which shall be made by the Commissioners of the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, for the Purchase of a House, and certain Parcels of Land, for the finishing and completing the said Hospital, valid and effectual, and for ascertaining the Recompence that shall be made for the fame, is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instru#ion to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause or Clauses for enabling the Commissioners or Governors of the said Royal Hospital, to purchase other Houses, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, than are particularly de-cribed in the said Bill, and for enabling Persons who may

be willing to contract with them for the Sale of such Houses, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, to convey the same to the said Commissioners, or Governors, for the Purposes in the said Bill mentioned.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen of the Grand Jury, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held at Beverley, in and for the East Riding of the County of York, on the 14th Day of January 1752, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Growers of Wool, within the said East Riding, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That Petitions of several Persons, in the Towns and Parishes of Leeds and Haltifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, and other Places, have been presented to the House; complaining of Abuses pra#ifed in the Marking or Branding of Sheep, and in tnc Winding of Wool; and alleging. That the Petitioners apprehend, if such further Law should be made, in the manner prayed by the said Petitions, the same may be highly prejudicial to the Growers of Wool, and a great Discouragement to Persons keeping Sheep; for that if every Grower of Wool may be punished for his Servants small Omission in winding, or other Negle# complained of (though not wilfully done) and thereby incur a Penalty, and be in the Power of every vexatious Person to sue for the same, in one of the Courts at Law, whereby it may cost the Grower 40^. or 50/. which may be a means greatly to impoverish, if not entirely ruin, such Grower, it will thereby deter Growers from felling their Wool; and that if the Growers be distressed, by Profc-cutions at Law, they will not be able to pay their Rents; and the Landlords will suffer, and the Manufacturers like-wife; and that many Sheep will have very fine Wool upon the Shoulders, and Fore Parts of the Body, and the other Parts of the Body, and the Hind Quarters, will be very coarse, and little less, than what by some is called Cots j and cannot be separated from the Fleece, without breaking thereof; and yet by some Persons might be deemed Part of the Offences complained of; and that few of the Growers know howto distinguish the same; but that the Staplers, when they get the Wool from the Growers,usually divide every Fleece into Seven or Eight Sorts, or more, before they deliver it to the Manufacturer; and if any Manufacturer complains, it is generally charged on the Grower, though unjustly; and that sworn Wool-winders have never been appointed in the said Riding; and if any such should be, the same would be attended with great Charge and Inconvenience to the Growers; for that it frequently; happens, that some Thousands of Sheep, in the said Ride-ing, are dipt upon one and the same Day, and some at 20 or 30 Miles Distance; and a Hundred sworn Wool-winders could not possibly fee to the Winding of all the Wool in the said Riding; and that all Wool-growers are obliged to mark their Sheep, to distinguish one Man’s Property from another; because, in the said East Riding,1 there arc many large Sheep Walks, which lie open and contiguous one to another; and the Flocks of Sheep there are frequently straying and intermixing; and there are likewise many large Commons in the said Riding, which are (locked with Sheep of fiindry and divers Persons, in each Common, particularly a large Common, called Wallington, and Bishop Soil, extending in Length about Ten Miles, whereon the Inhabitants of Forty-eight Towns have Right of Common for Sheep, and whereon several Thousand Sheep are depastured and fed every Year; and that it isusual for those People, who have Right of Common there, to buy Sheep from other Places, at the Spring Time of the Year, to flock, departure, and feed on the said Common; and that the said Sheep have usually the Seller’s Mark upon them; and the Buyers are obliged to mark them with their own respective Marie, besides the Mark of the Seller, which they have on them when they so bought them, before they put them on the said Common, or ocher wife they could not know and challenge thqpi from others; and that without such marking, there would^ great Difpuces arise, and perhaps several Law-fuitsbe commenced; and that the Marking of Sheep with Pitch

That the Laws for branding and marking of Sheep, and the Winding of Wool, may (land as they now are, and unaltered; but if it shall be thought expedient for a new Lav* to be made, for inflicting or in-creating Pains and Penalties, that the same may extend to such Persons only as wilfully offend, with inrent to increase the Weight, or otherwise deceive the Buyer; and that all Complaints may be heard and determined in a summary Way; and that the Growers of Wool may not be distressed and ruined by vexatious Suits at Law, which may be attended with a great Discouragement to the Growers of W ool, if not to the greatly impoverishing or ruining of them; or that they may be protested, or otherwise relieved, as the House shall think proper.

Westminster Ferry, in the Parish of Lambeth, to New Croft, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That a Petition has been presented from several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many other Freeholders and Inhabitants of the Counties of Surry and Kent, and of the City of Westminster, relating to a Turnpike which has been erected upon the Road leading from Newington to Camberwell, in the County of Surry; and setting forth, That the Road from Newington to Camberwell, in the County of Surry, and from thence to Peckham Lane End, leading to New Cross, in the County of Kent, and from Camberwell Green, to the Fox under the Hill, in the Road leading to Dulwich, in the County of Surry, is in a very ruinous Condition, and in many Places very narrow and incommodious; and that the same cannot be effectually amended and widened by the Laws in being; and that some Doubts have arisen with regard to the Allowance directed to be made, by virtue of several Acts of Parliament, from the Trustees for the Repair of the Roads leading from the Stones End in Kent Street, in the County of Surry, to East Greenwich and Lewisham, in the County of Kent, to the Trustees for the said Cross Road; And therefore praying. That, in case the House shall think proper to order in a Bill upon the said last mentioned Petition, a Clause or Clauses may be inserted therein, impowering the Trustees of the Sussex and Surry Trust to erect a Turnpike on some Part of the Road leading from Newington to Camberwell, upon their making such further Allowance to the Trustees of the said Cross Roads, as shall be thought reasonable; and that such further Provision may be made therein for the more effectual repairing and widening the said Road, as to the House shall seem meet.

A PET ITION of the Mayor and Commonalty of the Borough of Dunbeved, otherwise Launceston, in the County of Cornwall, in behalf of them (elves, and other the Inhabitants of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Borough is an ancient Borough, and incorporated by several Letters Patents from his present Majesty’s royal Predecessors; viz. Richard the Second, Henry the Fourth, Henry the Fifth, Edward the Fourth, Henry the Seventh, Henry the Eighth, and Philip and Mary: by which Letters Patents several Immunities and Privileges are granted to the said Borough; particularly, that the Free Burgesses thereof shall be free of all Custom, Quayage, Pontage, and so forth, throughout his Majesty’s Dominions; and that the said Borough, in consideration thereof, pays annually a large Fee-farm Rent to the Crown, or those claiming under it 5 and that the said Borough is possessfed of Two Markets weekly, in which great Quantities of Corn and other Grain are fold, and from thence conveyed to the River Yhamar for Exportation; and that the Inhabitants of the said Borough are supplied by Means of the same River with all Sorts of Merchandizes, it being navigable within Twelve Miles of the said Borough; and taking Notice, That a Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Free Burgesses, of the Borough of Saltash, has been presented to this House, for an Impost or Duty of Two Pence per Ton to be laid on all Goods loaded and unloaded in the River Yhamar; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that, in case the same be carried into a Law, it will not only deprive the Petitioners of their Right as Free Burgesses of their said Borough, but also clog the Freedom of Commerce in general, and be an inexpressible Injury to the Petitioners and the neighbouring Inhabitants: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their ConGderation, and give the Petitioners l'uch Relief as the House shall think proper.

Tower Ham- And presented to the House a Petition of the several £ebtmall Poor Artificers and Manufacturers residing in Spittle

e ‘s* Fields, Shoreditch, Mile End, Newtown) and Bethnal Green,

within the Tower Hamlets, whose Names are thereunto subscribtrd, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Artificers and Manufacturers within the Parishes and Places aforesaid.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth, That, by the Bill now depending in the House, to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act, passed in the 23d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the Tower Hamlets, should the same pass into a Law, the Petitioners are informed the Fees, now payable to the Clerks and other Officers of the said Court of Requests, are intended to be increased; which the Petitioners apprehend would fall a heavy Burthen upon them, and a great Number of other useful poor Manufacturers, who, through a Stagnation of Trade, though industriously inclined, cannot get Employment in their several Occupations, by which Means many Hundreds are reduced to great Distress and N’eceffity, and thereby forced to contract small Debts; and, by reason of their Inability to pay the fame, are frequently summoned before the said Court of Requests, where the Fees now payable by Law put the Petitioners to great Straits and Inconveniencies, which are frequently increased by Fees extorted from them by the Clerks, not warranted by the said Act of Parliament; and reprefencing to the House, That the Petitioners are most faithful and loyal Subjects to his Majesty, as appeared by their great Zeal, in offering to take Arms for the Support of the Government, in the late unnatural Rebellion; and will be always ready to sacrifice their Lives in Support of the present Royal Family, and our happy Establishment; and expi effing the Hope of the Petitioners,

Vol. 26.

That they shall not be subjected to Hardships, for no,

other Purpose but an Increkfe of Fees to the Otfecers of the said Court; who, as the Petitioners are informed, have a very competent Satisfaction for their Trouble arising from the Fees at present payable by Law: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may have Leave to be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as tends to increase the Fees now payable to the Clerks and other Officers of the said Court of Requests, or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be heard,.by their Counsel, before the said Committe, upon the Petition.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admic Counsel to be heard at the same time in favour of the said Bill against the said Petition; and also against the Petition, referred to the said Committee, of the several principal Inhabitants, and other Householders, residing in the several Parishes within the Tower Hamlets, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said District.

Ordered, That Mr. Hay have Leave to make a Motion.

And he moved the House accordingly.

To ihew that the Manufacture of Printing employs great Numbers of Persons, and the Manner in which the Revenue arising by the said Manufacture is collected.

The Agent, on behalf of the Petitioners, called,

Mr. John Fenner, who said. That great Numbers of Persons, of both Sexes, and of different Ages, are employed in the Priming of different Species of Goods:

That the Duty paid on the said Manufacture, in Six Weeks time, by the Hotife where to the Witness belonged, was, upon an Average, for that Time, 400/, j which Duty is collected at the Printers Expence, and by their own Servants.

Then, to shew of what Importance the said Manufacture is to this Nation,

Mr. Robert Davis, Handkerchief Weaver, informed your Committee, That all plain Silks, made use of here in Priming, are of our own manufacturing: And,

Mv.Joseph Hague, a Warehouse-man, said, that Flax and Raw Cotton, of which Stuffs for printing are made, when wrought up,are of more than Four times the Value of the crude Materials.

Mr. Thomas li 'ebbc, Linen-draper, said, That the Value of a Piece of unwhitftered Linen, of 28 Yards, is about 35 s.; and when it is printed, and pencilled, it is worth from 42 j. to 5 /. 5 s. 0d.

Then, to shew to your Committee the absoluteNeceffity of Gum Senega, for the Support of the Manufacture of Printing, the Agent called,

The aforesaid Mr. Venner, who said. That the Trade of Printing cannot be carried on, without the Ule of Gum Senega; for that several other Gums had been tried, and had spoiled the Goods; that Gum Senega is used both in the pencilling and the printing Part of the Manufacture; and had rose within these Nine Years, from 35s. to 12/. per Hundred Weight.

Mr. James Plank also said, That Gum Senega is absolutely necessary in carrying on the said Trade; for that he finds no other Species of Gum that will answer the Purpose so well; and in the pencilling Part of the Manufacture, Gum Senega alone can be made use of:

That the Witness had tried to use several other Gums, in the printing Part; and by that means had spoiled the W ork: That the Sale of pencilled Linens, within these Three or.Four Years past, had greatly increased; and that the major Part of the Linens, sold at the House to which he belonged, are of chat Species; and the Demand for those Goods increaseth every Day; and that, as far as the Witness is acquainted with the Trade in general, this is the same at other Houses.

And being a(ked. What Quantity of Gum Senega would supply the whole Trade ? he said, About 120 Tons per Annum *, and that he made his Calculation from the Consumption at the House where to he belonged.

Mr. Edmund Farmer said, That, in some Parts of the Manufacture, no other Ingredient, except Gum Senega, will do; that he had made use of various Things in various Manners, in the said Manufacture, having tried, he believed, every thing that was glutinous in the vegetable Kingdom, but without Success:

That Brokers mix other Gums with Gum Senega; and for the Damage he once received, from a Small Calk so mixed, he was allowed Sixteen Pounds; and that Gum Senega, mixed with any other thing, is not fit for the Manufacturers.

And being afleed. If, by adding a large Quantity of Gum Arabick, it would not do in printing, as well as Gum Senega ? he said in some Colours it would not; that it would not do in Red or Purple; and in a Blue the Colour is much fainter than when Gum Senega is made use

of, and it will wash out; and that in the Colours he had mentioned, the House to which he belonged never dare mak<* use of Gum Arabick; and whoever does use it in those Colours, will lose his Reputation:

That, since the Conclusion of the Peace, the Price of Gum Senega had rose from j to 12/. per Hundred Weight; which he,thinks isowing to so little being imported of late; for that in 1741 the Price of that Commodity was only about 32 or 33 s. per Hundred Weight;

That the Witness never made any Computation of the annual Consumption of Gum Senega in this Kingdom; but he believed it to be about 120 Ton; as the House where to he belonged consumed about 8 or 10 Ton per Annum; and he thinks their House consumes about ryh Part of the Whole:

That there is a Manufactory in Hamburgh, and another in Holland; and he believed the French might supply the Hamburghers , that about Two or Three Years ago the Price of Gum in Holland was 30 or 32 s, per Ct. Weight; but what the Price was here, at that Time, the Witness could not tell.

Mr. John Cecil said, That he believed the Price of Gum Senega in Hamburgh now is 6/. 1 s. o d. per Ct. Weight.

Then he produced to your Committee, a Bill of Parcels, made out to Messieurs MauviUion and Company, dated 10th February 1744; by which it appeared chat the Price of Gum Senega here, at that Time, was 30/. per Cent. Weight, with a Discount of i \ per Ct.

And by a Bill of Parcels of Gum Senega, bought the nth February 1741, of the African Company, it appeared that the Price then was $<is.per Hundred Weight, with a Discount of 3 per Ct.

Then Mr. Cecil produced to your Committee, An Account of the Prices of different Species of Gums, which he had bought,from April 1743^0 November 1751; by which it appeared, That, from 174;, to September 1749, the Price of Gum Senega varied, from time to time, and had increased, upon the Whole, from 31*. to 52 s.per Hundred Weight; and from thence to November the 2d, 1750, to 5/. 17s. 6d.\ and from thence, to November the 2d, 1751, to ill. 10s. od.

Then Mr. Cecil informed your Committee, That there was a publick Sale of GumSenega the 29th oflaft Month; and that it then fold for 10I. per Ct. Weight:

That in the last Year there was only imported about 20 Ton; and that, upon a Calculation made of his own Business, he does not think less than 120 Ton per Annum would serve the whole Trade:

That he had tried Gum Arabick in his Business; but that in a Blue, Yellow, or Purple, it will not clo; but that he had used it in a Red, and in that Colour it did as well as Gum Senega; yet although in the House where to he belongs, they can make a good Red with Gum Arabick, there are other Houses deficient in that Art.

That for these Nine Years he had used 10 or 11 Hundred Weight of Gum Senega and Gum Arabick per Annum, Three Quarters of which were Gum Senega; that in the pencil Colours he uses about Six Tons of Gum Senega:

That the same Quantity of printed Goods are not exported as usual, though the Witness supplies some Places in Holland, where they print their own Goods.

And being asked, If the Hamburghers and Hollanders had the use of Gum Senega, and we had not, whether our Goods would be fit to meet theirs at Market? he said, If that was the Cafe, they would not:

That about Three Months ago he had received Advice from Hamburgh, that Gum Senega there was j /. per Hundred Weight; and Once that Time he had received another Account of its being 61. is. od. per Hundred Weight; and that he had contracted for Gum Senega at Hamburgh, at 61. is. od. per Hundred Weight, provided Liberty was given to import it.

That he imputes the great Rife of Gum Senega of late to a French Ship being burnt in September or October lad, Which had a Quantity of the said Gum on board; that the Witness had bought a few Tons of Gum Senega, and had shipped it for Dunkirk; and that it cost 9/. per Hundred Weight; and chat it then fold in Holland for 7 or 8 /. per Hundred Weight; but the Gum he bought, and shipped for Dunkirk, was sent to this Market again:

That the Hollanders allow of the Importation of Gum Senega from all the Parts of Europe , and that, as the Witness has been informed, a great Parcel has been bought at Amsterdam, and sent to Gibraltar, in order to be brought here

Mr. Marler was asked, Whether the Gum Senega, that was imported last August, was not offered to the Printers before it was put up to Sale ? he said, It was offered to him at 8/. per Hundred Weight; and he bought Half of it; but he could not afford to use it at chat Price; and was forced to fell it again.

Mr. George Potter was asked, How long Gum Senega had been at 9/. before the Importation in August ? he said, He believed Four Months; and a Year and a Half before that Time, it had been at 47 j.; and from that Time kept gradually rising.

Mr. Daniel Valentine said. There has been a general Prohibition these Three or Four Months of exporting Gum Senega from France, as he is advised by his Correspondent at Leghorn.

And Mr. Stevens said. He had been informed, that the Prohibition in France is to continue till February next.

And Mr. Potter added, that the Gum mentioned by Mr. Tor in, to have been returned from Dunkirk, he has bought ir here, since it came back.

M. Robert Kingscourt, a Druggist, said, That we should be glad to buy Gum Senega to fend abroad, at 7/. 10s. od. per Hundred Weight, or upwards; and that he daily ex-pected Orders, as far as 9/. ancj thinks the Scarcity is all over Europe:

That he would have been glad, at any Time within these Three Months, to have bought ic at that Price; and that, till within these Three Months, it was fold from 3/. ioj. to 4/.

And being asked, If any national Prejudice would arise from giving Leave to import Gum Senega from all Places whatsoever ? he said. He believed there would; and that, if Captain Lone had Success in the Voyage he is going to make, the Witness imagined Gum Senega would be at 3 or 4 / a Hundred Weight; yet he said, he apprehended, if all Ports were at Liberty to import Gum Senega, ic would not hurt the African Company.

Mr. George Potter said, That bethinks, if this Application to Parliament is attended with Success, it will discourage Ships from going to the African Coast, as the French can always fell Gum Senega somewhat cheaper than we; and the Consequence will be, that Trade will all get into the Hands of the French',

And added, That an African Trader can afford to fell Gum Senega at 40 s* a Hundred Weight.

Captain Lone, being examined, informed your Committee, That he opened the Trade for Gum Senega, on the Coast of Africa, in the Year 1748, after it had been long disused, and brought home that Year 38 Tons; that in 1749 he brought none home; but in 175 1 he brought 22 Ton, which he sold at 8/. a Hundred Weight; that he is now going again, and hopes not to get less than 50 Ton, and to return about May or June next:

That there was one Greenhall there last Year, who brought home 12 Ton; and that his Ship returned about Three Weeks ago; but he said, he did not hear of any Person going to the Coast of Africa this Year, besides himself.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Use of Gum Senega is necessary to the carrying to Per-

section the printing Manufactory of Silks, Linens, and Caliicoes.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Quantity of Gum Senega, imported *into this Kingdom, has, for some Years, greatly decreased; and that the Price thereof has of late advanced to an excessive Rate.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Gum Senega be allowed to be imported into this Kingdom, from any Place in Europe, under proper Limitations.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Confederation of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

ling’s Bench A Petition of the Prisoners in the Kings Bench Prison Moo. was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Prison in which they are confined is an old ruinous Structure, exposed to all the Inclemencies of Weather, equally during the Heats of Summer, and the Rigours of Winter* and at the same time so narrow and inconvenient, that the Petitioners are fometimescrowded to the Number of Seventeen in a Room; by which many Prisoners have died, for want of Attendance and Necessaries during their Sickness; which they cannot obtain, be their Distreflcs ever so great, or their Diseases ever so violent, in their present miserable Situation; and that, during the Heats of Summer, the Petitioners, through such crouding, are liable to pestilential Diseases, of which great Numbers of late have died; which the Petitioners, in some measure, attribute to the great increase of Prisoners of lare Years; by which the said Prison is become utterly unfit for the Purposes of a Gaol, and fatal to the Constitutions and Lives of the unhappy Petitioners; and that the Petitioners, upon applying for Relief to the Marshal of the said Prison, understood, that the Property of the Building belonged to the Publick; but that the Profits of the Prison went to private Persons, by virtue of a Mortgage of the said Profits, granted in the Reign of King Charles the Second, to William Lentkall Esquire, to whom, and his Heirs, the Profits of the said Prison were granted by the Crown, and which have been secured to the Afllgns of the Mortgagees, by subsequent Acts of the Legislature; and that, upon the whole, the Petitioners were cut out from all Benefit, but from Parliament; and that the Petitioners, as being the most distressed, and the most help-kfs Part of the Poor of this Kingdom, flatter themselves,

1 thatthey become hereby thcQbjects of the CarcsandCom-

passion of the House, especially at this Time, when the Relief of the Poor, is become the peculiar Consideration of Parliament: And therefore, under these most calamitous Vol 26.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act,passed in the 37th Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, was read, intituled, An Act for the Maintenance of the Pier at Scarborough, which directs, that Two Persons shall be annually elected by the Common Council of Scarborough, to be M afters and Keepers of the said Pier; who are impowered to levy a Fifth Part of the yearly Rent of Land, within the Corporation, for repairing, amending, building, and maintaining, the said Pier; with Power of Distress, in case of Non-payment.

And Mr. Timothy Otbie, Treasurer to the new Pier Duties, and One of the Capital Burgesses of Scarborough* informed your Committee, That several Tolls and Duties are granted for repairing the old Pier; which was confirmed by,

Mr. William Fowler, also a Capital Burgess of the said Borough, who had served the Office of Coroner; the Duty of which Office is to collect the Revenues for the / old Pier at Newcastle and Sunderland; which Duties amount to One Shilling and Four Pence on Foreign, and Eight Pence on Britifa Bottoms; and that the Chamberlains of Scarborough collect the Revenues on Lands; but the Witness does not know, that any Rate has been made in pursuance of the Act of Henry the 8th: That the Coroners, who are Two of the Common Council of the said Borough, have their Accouncs audited by the Common Council only.

But being alked the Question, he said. He could not tell whether any Owner of Lauds in Scarborough, charge- x able to the said Duties, might not be admitted to fee the Accounts:

That at the End of every Year the Coroners paid the Monies remaining in their Har.ds, of the old Pier Duty, to the Chamberlain of the said Borough* upon the Grccri Cloth, in the Town Hall, which is mixed with the rest of the* Town Revenues, in the Chamberlain’s Hands, and applied promifeuoufiy for repairing the Pier, paving the

Streets, paying Salaries, and other Services of the said Corporation.

Then an Act of the Fifth Year of his present Majesty was read, intituled, An Act to enlarge the Pier and Harbour of Scarborough, in the County of York; whereby it appeared, That federal new Duties were laid on Shipping, for enlarging, improving, and keeping in Repair, the said Harbour of Scarborough; which Duties were to take place the 24th of june 1732, and to continue till the 24th of June 1783; and the said ancient Duties are thereby continued.

And Mr. Otbie informed your Committee, That he was appointed Treasurer for the new Pier Duties; and that Collectors were appointed for the Receipt of the same at Sunderland, Newcastle, and other Places.

Mr. Vincent, Engineer to the said Pier, being examined, said, That the Works of the new Pier were properly carried on, and with great Success, till the Year 1744 j but afterwards were not prosecuted with the same Vigour} for that, before the Year 1744, they employed between Thirty and Forty Men, and afterwards not above Twenty on an Average: And he produced to your Committee an Account, by which it appeared, that less Money was expended in each Year, from the Year 174410 1751, upon the said Pier, than had been expended in any Year, between the Year 1735 and the Year 1744: That the Reason for employing so small a Number of Workmen, from 1744 to the present Time, was, that they had a greater Fund of Money in the First Period of Time than in the last; and that, in the Year 1744, he had an Order from the Common Council to make a Head or Finishing to the said Pier, though it was intended, by the Plan of the First Engineer, to be carried out Forty Yards further-;

That it was his Opinion, That if the Pier had been extended according to the Plan, it would have been more serviceable; but that his Opinion was not asked on that Occasion, nor did he know the Motives of the Corporation for (lopping the Work} but the Work was put a Stop to at the Time they borrowed Three thousand Pounds to carry it on; and that he received his Orders from the Bailiffs, which they gave to him in pursuance of a Vote of the Common Council.

That the Opinion of People is different in regard to the Utility of lengthening the Pier} but that it is plain the Work has already answered, since the Act of Parliament only proposed to gain Six Foot Water, and they have gained '1 welve.

Mr. Otbie, being further examined, said, That he was one of the Common Council in the Year 1744; but was excluded his Right of voting on account of his being Treasurer of the Pier:

That the only Motives urged for borrowing Three thousand Pounds on the said new Pier Duties were to carry on the Work with more Expedition, and pay off the Tradesmen’s Bills: That he believes 3,000l. was accordingly borrowed, he having paid the Interest due thereon; but not a Penny of the 3,000l. was applied for carrying on the Pier; and that, if it had been applied for that Purpose, it must have passed through his Hands.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City and Liberty Welhmnfter of W^eflminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed on CourtHouse* behalf of themselves, and the general Part of the other Inhabitants, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That a Bill is now depending for the purchasing or hiring a convenient Piece of Ground within the City of Westminster, and for erecting and fitting up a proper Court House, for the Use of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the said City and Liberty thereof; and alleging,

That such Court House is utterly unnecessary for the Purposes mentioned in the said Bill, inasmuch us there is already a good convenient and sufficient Court House adjoining to Westminster Hall, within the said City, with which ihc Justices lor many Ages have been content; and that no Obstruction or Inconvenience hath ever happened from the said Court House, neither, till now, was the same ever complained of; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, That, as they already labour under many Hard-ships, they shall not be further burthened with a new and unnecessary Tax; and further alleging. That the Petition, upon which the said Bill was ordered into the House, was carried about privately, and without any general Confutation or Consideration of the Inhabitants, with Intent, as is conceived, to impose on the Inhabitants* in general, as well as the House; 2nd submifting to the House, That in case the House. shall think fit to pals the said Bill, or any other for the Purposes therein mentioned (which the Petitioners hope they will not), the Trustees, for the Purposes in the said Bill mentioned, may be chosen by the Inhabitants in each Parish within the said City and Liberty, rn such manner as the House shall think fit; and thar the Justices may not be Trustees; and also that the Inhabitants may, in like manner, chuse the Collectors of the Rate* for the Purposes in the said Bill mentioned; and thar such Trustees as shall be chosen or appointed may be directed to take an Oath of Qualification, that they arc worth Pounds when ail their Debts are paid; and further expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, That, in case such Bill should pass, the House wi.l think it reasonable, that the Trustees may be liable to account; and in case of any Aggrievance or Oppression on the Inhabitants, that an Appeal may lie, in such manner as the House shall think fit: And therefore praying, That the Lid Bill may not pals into a Law; or that such Clauses, for the Purposes above-stated maybe inserted in such Law, and the Petitioners relieved therein, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed.

Mr. Burrell, according to Order, reported from the Performantt Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred of Quaran- to consider of the most proper and effectual Manner of tmc# performing Quarantine, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Manner of performing Quarantine, by airing Goods on board Hoys and Vessels, is not well calculated to prevent the Infection; and is inconvenient and expensive to the Merchant.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for the better and more effectual Performance of Quarantine, a Lazaret should be erected.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Chedney Hill, near the upper Part of Standgate Creek, in the River Medway, is a proper Place for a Lazaret.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the present Manner of performing Quarantine, by airing Goods on board Hoys and Vessels, is not well calculated to prevent the Infection; and is inconvenient and expensive to the Merchant.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That, for the better and more effectual Performance of Quarantine, a Lazaret should be erected.

The last Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itfelfinto a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to allow the Importation of Gum Senega into this Kingdom, from any Part of Europe, upon the Payment of a Duty;

The House was moved. That the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of James Guthrie, for himself, and Company of Merchants, in Dumfries, was referred, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly; and is as followed; viz.

The Committee examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; the State whereof is as follows.

Milward Rowe Esquire, Agent to the Commissioners of the Customs in Scotland, produced to your Committee the original Certificate of the Surveyor General, and Land-waiter, at the Port of Kircudbright; whereby it appeared.

That the Petitioners did, in the Month of May 1751, enter, for Exportation to France, 253 Hogsheads of Tobacco, containing 231,328 Pounds of Tobacco; for which the Duties had been paid and secured:

That the said Ship, in falling down the River of Kir-kudbright, was, on the 16th of June last, overset; whereupon the said Surveyor General, and Land waiter, attended the unloading of the whole Cargo, to prevent Embezzlement of the damaged Tobacco: That the said Surveyor, and Land-waiter, did attend accordingly, and saved 7,920 Pounds of dry Tobacco, which was delivered over, to them, and still remains in their Custody, and that the

A Petition of the subscribing Merchants of the City of Petition re-London,. in behalf of themselves, and all other Merchants of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; 12 0IU

alleging, That several Foreigners have, of late Years, beeri induced to come over into England, in order to obtain private Acts of Parliament, for their Naturalization, with a View to gain some Advantages to themselves, in point of Trade, and in particular to avoid the Payment of Aliens Duties on the Goods and Merchandizes which they transport from foreign Parts into this Kingdom; but having obtained such Acts, return back to their native Country, where they constantly reside* and cdnfequently bear no Part of the publick Taxes, nor in any manner contribute towards the Support of the State, or at all answer the Intention of the Legislature, which undoubtedly is, by grant* ing to Foreigners the Privileges and Immunities enjoyed by the natural-born Subjects of this Kingdom, and thereby encouraging such Foreigners to transport themselves and their Estates hither, to increase the Number of People, and advance the Wealth and Strength of the Nation; whereas there is great Reason to suspect, that these Persons, so na^ turaliaed, and returning to foreign Countries, out of thfe Jurisdiction of the Crown of Great Britain, frequently cover, under their Names, the Goods of Aliens, imported into this Kingdom; and riot being amenable to the Pro-cefsof the Courts of Justice here, are in no danger of irir curring the Penalties to which the Subjects, residing within this Kingdom, are liable, for such Offences: And there* fore, as it is highly conducive to the public Welfare, that Great Britain should be furnished with Merchandize by her own Subjects, ift the same manner as her Shipping is secured, by the Act of Navigation; and as it is manifestly inconsistent with the View of the Legidature, in granting the Benefit of Naturalization, that Foreigners, fd naturalized, should withdraw themselves out of the Lige-ance of the Crown of Great Britain, praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and to make Provision for preventing this Abuse of the Favour of Parliament, by restraining for the future, the Benefit of Naturalization to the Time during which Foreigners shall reside within this Realm, in such manner, and under such Limitations, as to the House shall appear fit.

And several of the Names subscribed to the said Petition were also read.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table*

Upon the whole, the Committee came to the;following Resolutions.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thar, in all future Acts of Parliament for the erecting or continuing any Turnpike, a Clause be inferred to oblige the Commissioners of such Turnpike, to take Security from their Treasurer or Receiver for the faithful Execution of the said Office.

Rejoived.\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in all future Acts of Parliament for the erecting or continuing any Turnpike, a Clause be inserted to prevent any Person, who shall be nominated a Commissioner/frorn acting or voting in the Business of the said Turnpike,'unless he shall be podefied of an Estate in Land, or of per-Tonal Fftate, to such certain Value as shall be specifitd in such Act.

Preventing Mr. Gybbcn reported from the Committee, appointed Kobberics, upon Friday last, to draw up Reasons to be offered to the Lords, at a Conference, for disagreeing to such of the Amendments, made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better preventing Thefts and Robberies; and for regulating Places of publick Entertainment, and punifiiing Persons keeping disorderly Houses; as this House hath disagreed to; That the Committee had drawn tip Reasons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Wrbere the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Commons disagree to the First Amendment made by your Lordships to the said Bill; Pr. 2. L. 9.

Because, so early a Commencement of the proposed Regulation, shay occasion some Hardship to the present Proprietors of Places of publick Entertainment, mentioned in the Bill; and can be attended with no great Utility to the Publick, as the Season between the First of August and the First of December, is that, in which the least Inconvenience is to be expected from these Places of Entertainment.

The Commons alto disagree to the Second Amendment made by your Lordships; Pr. 2. L. 13, 14.

Because, by this Amendment, the Remedy of a Mif-chief, which chiefly arises in the Cities of London and Westminster, or within Twenty Miles thereof, is extended to the whole Kingdom; and the Extension of this Provision beyond these Limits, may affect some Places, to which it may not be necessary that the Regulations, prescribed by the Bill, fhoilld be extended.

The Commons decline, at this Time, offering any other Reasons for disagreeing to these Two Amendments made by your Lordships; apprehending, tha: the Rea-lons already given, will induce your Lordships not to insist on the said Amendments.

To the Third Amendment made by your Lordships, Pr. 2. L. 15. the Commons do agree.

The Commons disagree to the Fourth Amendment made by your Lordships, Pr. 2. L. 16.

Because, the Michaelmas Quarter Session corresponds best with the First Day of Decembers which appears to the Commons to be the most proper time for the Commencement of this Piovision.

To the Fifth and Sixth Amendments made by your Lordships, Pr. 2. L, 26. and Pr. 3. L .3. the Commons do agree.

To the Clause marked (A) the Commons do agree, with the following Amendment; viz.
