King’s Bench Prison.

Lieutenant General Oglethorpe reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Prisoners in the King's Bench Prison was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had direifled him to report the fame* as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Wher? the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee thinks proper to reduce the Evidence brought in Support of the said Petition, under Three Heads.

First, That which tended to prove the present incommodious, unhealthy, and insecure State of tlje said Prison.

Secondly, The Nature of the Mortgage, under which the Marlhalship of the said Prison is now possessed and exercised.

Thirdly, The Inconveniencies arising, not only to the Petitioners, but to the Court, and Suitors in the Kings Bench, and to the Publick in general, from the said Mortgage

Upon the first Head, your Committee examined the Reverend Doctor Howard, Rector of Saint George's Parish, within which the Prison is situated; Mr. 1/aac Stapleton, Surgeon and Apothecary, who lives near the Prison, and has attended there for Twenty Years past; William Tew, Joseph Wingrove, William Bishop, John Lloyd, and others, who are, or have been, Prisoners within the Prison-house; and John Ashton Esquire, the present Marshal, with Mr. John Chapman, his Clerk and head Turnkey, and Messieurs Steere and Poultney, Surveyors and Master Builders, who have surveyed the Prison-house and Walls.

By the concurrent Testimony of all the above Persons, it appears to your Committee, That the said Building is old and ruinous; that, in its present State, the Prisoners are in the most miserable Situation for Want of Room; Seventeen being sometimes crouded into One Room, not above Fourteen or Fifteen Foot square; and that the Common Side is often overflowed with the Common Sewer, which occasions noisome Stenches: And the Reverend Doctor Hozvard said. That he once attended a Person in the Cells of Newgate, which he thought preferable to the Cabbins in which the Prisoners, upon the Common Side of this Prison, are lodged.

It further appeared to your Committee, from the Evidence above, That in the Summer Time infectious Diseases are apt to break out, for Want of Room and Air, amongst the Prisoners; that last Summer, particularly, Six or Seven Prisoners died of a Pefti-lential Fever; several have died of the Small Pox, and several of Spotted Fevers, within the Prison; and that," if the Marshal’s own Brother was confined a close Prisoner therein, he could give to him no Relief more than to the other Prisoners; and there is no Conveniency for separating the Sound from the Diseased, but One small Room, fit to contain One Person; and, that if the Prison should be suffered to remain the ensuing Summer in its present State, it may produce an Infcdlion amongst the Prisoners, and may be of the most fatal Consequence.

After this general Representation of the inside State of the Prison, your Committee will not trouble the House wi^h a great Variety of aflfedling Circumstances, that came out in the Course of this Evidence; which all concurred in proving the Place to be inconvenient, dangerous, and unhealthy.

And the said Mr. Poultney and Mr. Steere were of Opinion, that the same cannot be repaired.

Mr. William Soame, being examined, said, That there is a House and Garden, belonging to one Mr. Lyddal, near the said Prison, and within the Precincts thereof, which is very capable of being made an Infirmary; and may be made strong, and fit for the safe keeping of Prisoners, at the Expence of about £. ioo; that there are Eight large Rooms, and Four small ones, in it; and may be fitted up to contain Thirty-two Beds; and which the said Mr. Lyddal is willing to let at £. 25 a Year.

Under the SeconiHead of your Committee’s Inquiry, Vojl. a6.

they examined Mr. Brigs lock, Mr. Blackwell, arid Mr. Langmcre, Agents for the Mortgagees; by whom it appeared, That in February 16845 William Lentball Esquire mortgaged certain Lands, and the Fee-simple of the said Marlhalship, for a Sum of Money, to Sir John Cutler Knight, till the fame, and Interest, should be discharged.; and that there are Glaufes in an Act of che 8th and 9th of King William(intituled, An Act for the more effectual Relief of Creditors, in.Cafes of Escapes; and for preventing Abuses in Prisons, and pretended privileged Places) relating to the said Mortgage.

And the said Sir John Cutler's Executor, Edmund Boulter, Esquire, his Heirs, Assigns, Administrators and Executors, are to have, by that Act, the Nomination of Marshals of the said Prison, till the said Mortgage, and Interest, is paid off; and that the Right of the said Mortgage devolved upon the Earl of Radnor, who, in the Year 1719, fold all his Right therein to Joseph Studley, and others, in Trust, for the present Mortgagees, or those from whom they derive their Title; and that the Sum then charged by che Earl of Radnor upon the More-, gage was upwards of £. 19,000; and that the Sum of £, 10,500 was, bond Jide, paid for the fame.

And the said Mr. Blackwell delivered to your Committee. a General Account of Debtor and Creditor, hereto annexed, in the Appendix, N* 1.; and leaves the Consideration of their Demand to the Judgment of the House.

Upon the strictest Inquiry* your Committee conld not discover where the original Grantor Patent, upon which the Conveyance of the Fee-simple of the said Marshal-ship was made, by Lentball, to Sir John Cutler, was to be found: And,

Mr. Guthrie, being examined, said. That by certain Evidences, on Record, the said Office formerly appertained to the Office of Earl Marshal oi England-, but by Forfeitures, and Failures of Heirs Male, the said Office often reverted to the Crown; and that he apprehended, when the said Marshalship was in the Earl Marshal, he was obliged to maintain and repair the said Prison.

Mr. Owen, Clerk to Lord Chief Justice Lee, being examined, said, That he had heard one Mr. Long, at Per-Shore, in Worcestershire, talk as if a Client of his was in Possession of the Original Patent: And Mr. Owen wrote to the said Long-, and he (the said Long) wrote a Letter in Answer, which is hereto annexed, in the Appendix, N° 2.

Under the Third Head of Evidence, already mentioned, your Committee begs Leave to refer to a Paper laid before them by the said Mr. Owen, with the Authority and Approbation of the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, which is annexed, in the Appendix, (N° 3.) by which it appears to your Committee, That chat Court has long looked upon the present Exercise of the Marlhalship of the said Prison, under a Mortgage, as a Shame and Scandal to the Publick, becaufeof the Hardships and Dangers arising therefrom, not only to the Prisoners, their Creditors, and that Court, but 10 the Subjects in general; and that Application ought to be made to Parliament thereon.

This Representation, from so great and good an Authority, naturally led your Committee to inquire, in the most ftri<ft Manner, into the Conduct and Behaviour of the present Marshal, Mr. Ashton, and likewise into the Fees, Perquifnes, and Profits of his Place.

And First, It appeared, by the concurring and unanimous Testimony of the above Witnesses, and likewise by that of Baron Steine and Mr. John JJpfdale, Prisoners in the said Prison, that the said Marshal's Behaviour and Conduct in his Office, has been very humane, and that he omitted no Opportunity in his Power of alleviating and relieving the Hardships of the Prisoners in his Custody.

Touching the Fees of his Office, he produced a Table of them, by Order of your Committee; which is annexed, in the Appendix, N* 4.

Touching the Perquisites and Profits of the fame, he produced before your Committee his Books of Accounts, and likewise Abstra6ls from the same, distinguishing Year by Year; which Abstradlsyour Committee checked with the Particulars in his Books; and the whole of his said

£ing*sBench APPENDIX, N° 1.

Pnfoh. Sir, Perjhore, 9th 1752.

On Thursday last I went to fVorcefier Assizes, and on "Friday was taken ill with the Gout; which occasioned my not returning till Yesterday in the-Afternoon, when I found yours at my House, of the 5th instant.

I have some Grants and other Deeds, now in my Custody, belonging to the Office of Marshal of the King’s Marshalsea; most of which are wrote in Latin Abbreviations, in the old Court-hand, and most of them contain Three or Four large Skins each; so that it was impossible, had I been at home, when your Letter came, on Saturday, to have lent you up Copies by that Night’s Poll, as you desired, or even by the Post To-night.

And as I am now laid up, exceedingly bad with the Gout, and confined to my Room, I am not at present able to peruse those Deeds, to give you any Satisfaction relating thereto; but 1 hope in a few Days 1 may be in a Capacity for the Purpose.

These Writings was delivered to me by a Client of mine, who claimed the Office of Marshal, with Intent to prefer a Bill in the Court of Chancery against the Mortgagees, inPoffeflion of the Profits of the Office, to account and deliver up the fame; my Client being fully convinced that the Mortgagees had, many Years since, not only been fully paid, but that a considerable surplus Sum of Money was in their Hands to be accounted for; but my Client, soon after I had received the Writings, died, so that the Affair dropt: But the Writings now belong to his Widow, to whom he, by his Will, devised all his Estate, either in Possession, Reversion, Remainder, or Expectancy. I am, Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servant,

Hen. Long.

To Mr. Thomas Owen, Attorney at Law,

over against the End of Plough-court,

Carey-street, Lincoln's Inn, London.

APPENDIX, N° 3.

Thomas Owen, Clerk to the Right Honourable the Lord Chief Justice Lee, pursuant to Order, attended the Committee; and, being examined, declareth as folio we th:

That about Thirteen Years ago, and for several Years before, he was Deputy Marshal of the Court of Kings Bench; and as such, and since he hath been Clerk to his Lordship, hath been acquainted with the State and Condition of the King's Bench Prison.

Saith, The same is a very ancient Building, and was, as he hath heard, and believes, the Stables of King John; and faith, the said Prison is very incommodious for the Purpose to which it is now converted.'

Saith, That Prisoners, from all Parts of the Kingdom, are committed thereto, either for criminal or civil Matters, cognizable in the Court of King's Bench; and, that the said Prison ought to be more commodious than it is at present, for the Reception of the Unfortunate; and a Place of much greater Strength and Security, for the safe Custody of the Guilty; Saith, the Walls thereof are so thin, old, rotten, and crazy, that there hath not been a remarkable high Wind, for many Years past, that hath not blown down many Parts of the Wall of the said Prison; and would have made a general Gaol Delivery of the Prisoners therein, was not the greatest Care and Diligence used, by the Marshal and his Officers, to prevent it.

Saith, That in the Time of the late unnatural Rebellion, when all the Prisons about this Capital were full of Prisoners. the Prison of the King's Bench (the most proper Prison for such a Purpose) was deemed a Place of so little Safety, and ib iniecure, that not One State Prisoner was confined therein.

Saith, He ha:h oftentimes heard the late Marshal, Mullens, ffi-Uare (who w>s a very humane good-natured Man), that when he was first appointed Marshal, he used weekly to order Beef, Pork, Broths, and other Victuals, to be difliffiuted among such of his Prisoners as he thought

were the greatest Objects of Charity; but was soon obliged to leave off those Donations, having found that the annual Rent, Taxes, and Outgoings, which, at that time, amounted to Eight or Nine hundred Pounds per Annum, was actually more than the Fees, Profits, and Perquisites, arising from the said Office.

Saith, He knows, that during the time the late Lord Raymond presided.as Chief Justice of the said Court, that great and many Complaints v/ere then made to his Lordship, of the Inconveniencies arising to the Prisoners, by the Payment of so large an annual Rent, by the Marshal of the said Prison; and, he hath oftentimes heard his Lordship declare, it was a Shame, and a Scandal to the Publick, that the Affairs of the Prison were permitted to remain in such a Situation.

Saith, He is also well afifured, that my Lord Hard-wicke, during the time his Lordship was Chief Justice of the said Court, was of the same Opinion, that the said Mortgage ought to be paid off and discharged.

Saith, That for the Space of Twelve Years last past, he hath been Clerk to the present Lord Chief Justice of the said Court; during which time many Petitions have been presented to the said Court and his Lordship, complaining, that Three, Four, or more Prisoners, were put into One Room; which the Judges (who are always ready to hear the Complaints of the meanest Prisoner) would have prevented, had it been in their Power; but, from the Straightness of the Prison, have found it impossible to redress the Grievance complained of.

Saith, That many Petitions have also been presented to his Lordship, praying, to be discharged without Payment of their Fees; several of whom, on his I.ordship’s Pleasure being signified to the Marshal, have been, accordingly, discharged; as many others would have been, had not his Lordship well known, that by a too frequent Compliance with such Requests, it would be impossible for the MarihaJ, and his Officers, who all purchase their Places, to pay the Rent that is even now paid for the said Office.

Saith, That from the time of this Examinant’s first coming into his Lordfnip’s Service, until now, it hath been his Lordship’s Opinion, that it was very detrimental to the Prisoners, and the Publick, that the Office of Marshal was let to Sale; and the said Court so far interposed with the Proprietors and Mortgagees of the said Office, as he hath heard, and believes, that the Rent is much less now, than was formerly paid for the said Office; and his Lordship was fodefirous that proper Methods should be taken, in relation to the Discharge of the said Mortgage, that he ordered this Examinant, about Three Years ago, as near as he can recoiled as to the Time, to give Notice to the said Proprietors and Mortgagees, to deliver in a dated Account of their Demands on the said Office; which this Examinant then did, on Mr. Langmore, their Attorney or Agent, in the Words, or to the Effect, mentioned in a Paper Writing, signed by this Declaranr, marked with the Letter (A).

Saith, That in pursuance of such Notice, said Mr. Langmore delivered to his Lordship the Account marked Letter (B).

Saith, That since this Examinant’s Order to attend this Honourable Committee, he hath acquainted his Lordship thereof; who hath authorized this Examinant to acquaint the said Committee, that it is with his Lordship’s Consent, Concurrence, and highest Approbation, that Application hath been made to the House to rebuild the said Prison, and pay off the said Mortgage; and that his Lordship hopes it will meet with such immediate Dispatch, as the Nature of the same shall require.

Thos. Gwen.

After which, his Majesty was pleated to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The King's I cannot put an End to this Session of Parliament, Speech. without returning you my hearty Thanks for the great Application and Dispatch with which you have gone through the publick Business: You have not only shewn your just Satisfaction in the Measures I have pursued in foreign Affairs, but have also given me your Support, in carrying them on, with that Zeal and Chearfulness which I had reason to expect from so dutiful and affectionate a Parliament; who are entirely convinced, that those Mea-fores are calculated to maintain their own eflentia! Interests, and to render the present general Peace durable and lading.

The many Laws now passed, will, I hope, attain the good Ends intended by them. Nothing that depends upon me shall be wanting to make them effectual, and particularly to execute, in a right manner, the Provisions made for civilizing and reducing into Order such Parts of the united Kingdom, where the Want of Knowledge, Improvement, and due Obedience to the Laws, had remarkably furnished Opportunities to seduce the People from their Loyalty.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

My particular Thanks are due to you, for the Supplies which you have so readily granted me. Your Care to fopport the Reduction of the national Interest, and to put great Parc of the Debt into a Method more convenient for the Creditors, at Well as for the Publick, is a fresh Instance of your Attention to that important Concern.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Nothing in this World can give me so much Pleasure, as to fee you a flourishing and happy People: Exert yourselves in your several Stations, to do your Parts, and you may depend on my unwearied Endeavours to secure this great B idling to ourselves, and transmic it to Posterity.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers j where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes,obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followed) j viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have received so many Proofs of the good Aife&ions and Zeal of my People for my Person and Government, that every Opportunity of meeting them in Parliament gives me a new Satisfaction. The Maintenance of the general Peace, already happily established, is fodc-firable for all Europe, that all mv Views and Negocia-tions have been incirely calculated and directed to preserve it, and secure its Duration. I am (till proceeding, and shall continue to ad, upon the same Principle; nothing being capable of giving me so much Comfort, as that my good Subjects may long enjoy the happy Fruits of the present Tranquillity/ 1 have the Satisfaction to be allured of a good DilpoGtion ia all the Powers in Alliance with me, to adhere to the same salutary Object; and the Meafurts which have been taken in different Parts of Kurort for that Purpose, cannot fail to give additional Strength and Solidity to the Provisions made by the Treaty of Aix la ChapcUi.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Estimatesfor the current Year shall be laid before you, by my Order. I have no Supplies to a/k of you but what shall be necessary for the ordinary Services, and such as have been already communicated to you, and for the Security of the Nation, and the Support of its Trade and Commerce, on which the ellcntial Interests of this Kingdom depend. 1 mull at the same time earnestly re-V tJL. 26.

commend the Continuance of your Attention to die Re-dudion of xhe Natioual Debt, the Improvement of the publick Revenue, and augmenting chp Sinking Fund.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Whatsoever is fu, ther necessary to perfect so laudable a Work, deserves your serious Consideration 5 that whilst we enjoy Peace abroad,* we may maintain good Order and Regularity at home.. Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any V^itness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be an high Crime and Misdemeanour j and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in auy same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain* for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall fee, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of die House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this Houie do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or 'Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster* do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning, to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and open 1 and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-ball* or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and rhat there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Mr. Charles Torke reported from the Committee, ap- Addrest pointed Yesterday to draw up 3n Address to be presented *hc to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an pecc Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed!; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

Weyour Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, rh£

Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, humbly beg Leave to return your Majesty our hearty Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne; and ta congratulate your Majesty upon your safe and happy Arrival in this Kingdom.

Permit us, Sir, to express our sincere Joy, that the dutiful Conduct of your Majesty’s faithful Commons has been rewarded with your royal Approbation, and to assure your Majesty of the Continuance of that Zeal and Affcdion for your Person and Government, which your Majesty’s constant Attention to the Happiness of your People so justly demands.

We must ever acknowledge your Majesty's Wisdom, as well as Goodness, in pursuing such Measures as may best contribute to maintain, and render permanent, the general Tranquillity in Europe: And suffer us. Sir, at the same time, to declare our Satisfaction at the Affur-ances which your Majesty has received from your Allies, of their good Disposition to adhere to the same falucary Object.

Your faithful Commons, with the trued Zeal and Duty, protuife your Majesty to raise, wiifiT Chearfulness, Unanimity, and Dispatch, such Supplies, as shall be found necessary for the Security of the Nation, and the Support of its Trade and Commerce, so essential to the Well-being of this Country.

We cannot sufficiently testify our grateful Sense of your Majesty’s provident Concern for the Welfare of this Nation, in recommending again to our Attention the Lessening of the National Debt; and do assure your Majesty, that we will take into our serious Consideration the best Means to improve the public Revenue, whereby the heavy Load of our Debts may be put in a Method of being gradually reduced, and the national Credit, already in a flourishing Condition, be firmly established.

We further beg Leave to assure your Majesty, that, whilst we refled: with Gratitude upon the Blessings of Peace abroad, and enjoy the daily Fruits of the Continuance of it, we will not be wanting in our Endeavours to preserve good Order and Regularity at home; happy in this Conviction, that, from the whole Tenor oi youf Majesty’s auspicious Reign, we are sure of youc Majesty’s hearty Concurrence in every Measure, which may tend to promote the true Interests and Prosperity of your People*

The said Address, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty, by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of his Majesty *s rrioft Honourable Privy Council, do humbly know his Majesty’s Pleasure, when he will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That his Majesty’s most gracious Speech to xk* King’s both Houses of Parliament be taken into Consideration Speichtobe Tomorrow Morning. conGderctL

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clocks

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr, William Monkhouse said, That he is well acquainted with the Road from the Town of Penrith, by Hutton, over Skelton, and Castlejowerby Pastures, to Sebergbam Bridge and Chalkbeck, leading to the Market Town of Wigton, which is the Highway between Penrith and Wigton, through the Middle of the said County; and is in a very ruinous Condition, and not capable of being repaired by the ordinary Course of Law: That several Parts of it are very deep, and other Places io narrow as to be scarce passable for Wheel Carriages.

Januarii. A. 1753.

He further said, That the Road leading through Part of the Parish of Castlejowerby, by Hejkett New Market, to Caldbeck, is in a very ruinous Condition, and, in many Places, Coo narrow for Wheel Carriages; and that the Parishes through which the said Road leads are unable, by the ordinary Course of Law, to repair the fame; and that this is th6 nearest and common Highway from Penrith to Cocker mouth.

Lieutenant Colonel John Stephenjon, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Monkhouse, as to chat Part of the Road leading:through Part of the Parish of Castlejowerby, by Hejkett New Market, to Caldbeck, which he said was the common High Road, and the nearest Road cross the Country; thatBy Ktfwick not being passable at all times.

Mr. Charlton, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the Housei which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Ten thousandMen be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year 1753, beginning the First of January 17 53*

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man, per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Ten thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Eighty thousand Two hundred and Six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy, including Half-pay to Sea Officers, for the Year 1753.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, towards the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, for the better Maintenance of the Seamen of the said Hospital, worn out and become decrepit in the Service of their Country.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Popham reported from the Committee, to whom Road. i\jL the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Clothiers, and others, Inhabitants of the Devizes, Seend, Melksham, Atworth, and Places adjacent, in the County of Wilts, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petirion, Henry Colthurjt Esquire, was examined; who said, Thac the Road mentioned in the Petition is the great Road from 1The Devizes to Bath and Bristol, and is Nine Miles long, and most Part of the Soil is a deep Clay, and very ruinous, and in many Places too narrow for Carriages to pass one another: That many Parts of it are liable to be overflowed; and that Two Persons, within the Witness’s Knowledge, have been drowned, in endeavouring to pals the Bridge at Melksham:

He further said, That the Parish of Melksham have performed their Statute-work, and raised a Tax of Six Pence in the Pound, which was laid out upon the said Road; but that Twelve Pence in the Pound, and the Statute-work, would be inefficient to repair the fame.

Mr. RichardBunter Robins, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Colthurst, in regard to the Badness and Narrowness of the Roads.

f bcvon A Petition of the High Sheriff, JustieCs of the Pedce* pointy Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Ctol. Devon, assembled at a General Meeting, held for that Pur-pote, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the high Gaol for Criminals doth not belong to the Sheriff; and that the said County is at present without any Sherife Prison, or Place of Confinement or Security for Debtors; which is a very great Inconvenience to the County in general, and no small Hazard and Expence to the High Sheriff, for the Time being, who is obliged to keep the Debtors in a House on such Terms as the Proprietor has thought fit to impose; which have grown upon the Sheriff for several Years past; and that, for this Year, the High Sheriff was obliged to give him Seventy Guineas; and that the Petitioners have good Reason to think, that the Proprietor of the said House will (till raise his Demands, he having declared, That he will not agree with future Sheriffs, upon the present Terms; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Ward for Debtors was under the more immediate Care of the High Sheriff, for the Time being, the Persons confined there would be better secured, and treated with Tenderness and Humanity: And therefore praying, That Leave may be

fiven to bring in a Bill, for raising a Sum not exceeding 'wo thousand Pounds, by an equal and just Rate on the Lands in the said County of Devon, in such manner as County Rates are raised by the Laws now in being, for erefling or purchasing (as shall be thought most convenient) a County Prison, or Place for Confinement of Debtors, under such Restrictions and Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Richard Valentine said, That he knows the several Roads mentioned in the Petition: That they are very bad, and in many Places extremely narrow and incommodious for Travellers; and that, although the Persons living near the said Roads have performed their Statute-work thereon, and have paid a Race of Six Pence, and sometimes Ten Pence, in the Pound, for the Repair thereof, the same has been found insufficient for that Purpose.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, Small Debts, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Boston, the Di-ftritt called Ski. beck Quarter, and other Suburbs adjoining to the said Borough, lying within the several Parishes of Boston and Skirbeck, in the County of Lincoln, whose Karnes are thereunto set, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Proceedings of the Court of Record, held in the said Borough for the Trial of Civil Actions, being liable to be made dilatory and expensive, the said Court is found to be very insufficient and ineffectual for the Recovery of small Debts; and that several Persons, taking Advantage of the Difficulties which Creditors are thereby laid under, do contract divers small Debts, and afterwards, though very able/refuie to pay the fame, and set their Creditors at Defiance; and.chat the erecting a Court for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the said Borough, District, and Parishes, would greatly conduce to the Furtherance of Justice, the Encouragement of Trade, and the Good of the Publick: And therefore praying for Leave to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the Borough of Boston, and Skirbeck Quarter, and Parishes of Boston and Skirbeck.

Ditto. A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Borough

of Bojlcn, in the County of Lincoln, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Proceedings of the Court of Record, held in the said Borough for the Trial of Civil Adiions, being according to the Forms of the Common Law, and thereby liable to be made dilatory and expensive, the said Court is found to be very infus-ficient and ineffectual for the Recovery of small Debts: And therefore praying for Leave to bring in a Bill for establishinga Court within the said Borough, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts.

That the Harbour of the said Burgh is a very ancient Harbour, conveniently situated, and capable of being made very safe and commodious; but, by reason of the Inability of the said Burgh to maintain the fame, has been for some Years pad, and now is, in a very ruinous Condition; and that the same cannot be sufficiently amended, and kept in good Repair, by the whole present Revenues of the said Burgh: And therefore praying the House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for laying a Duty upon all Beer and Ale which shall be brewed for Sale, brought into, or fold, within the said Burgh and Liberties thereof, and all Places adjacent, lying within Four hundred Yards of the Boundaries of the said Liberties, for repairing, improving, and preserving, the said Harbour, during such Term of Years, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

A PETITION of the Right Honourable Herbert Lord Viscount Winifor, and Baron Montjoy of the Isle of Wight, and of Brigadier General Richard JngJdffy, Churchwardens, the Overseers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants of the Parish of St. George Hanover Square, within the Liberty of the City of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in purfjancfc of divers Statutes now in Force, several and distinct Rates are annually made for the Relief of the Poor, Repair of the Highways, andcleanfing the Streets of the said Parish; and that the Rates so made for cleansing the Streets, ana repairing the Highways within the said Parish, are attended with so much Trouble, Difficulty, and Expence, in collecting and levying thereof as to occasion a confuierable Deficiency in the Sums proposed to be raised thereby? and alleging, That if the several Rates made for the Relief of the Poor, cleansing the Streets, and repairing the Highways, in the said Parish, were consolidated and united into One Rate or Assessment, or to be collected by One and the same Collection, and some further Regulations made for the better and more easy addling and collecting the said Rates, and Employment of the Money thereby raised, the same would be attended with moreEafe and Advantage, and Ids Expence to the Inhabitants of the said Parish, their Poor better provided for, and their Highways and Streets better repaired and cleansed, than by the Laws in being the y can be at present: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to impower the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, Vestry, or principal Inhabitants, to make yearly One or more Rate or

Rates for the Relief of the Poor, repairing the Highways, and cleansing the Streets, in the said Parish, to be collected together by one and the same Collection; with such further and other Regulations relating thereto, and for the better ordering and regulating the Dispofuion of the Money thereby raised, as to the* House shall seem meet*

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to me Consideration of a Committee: And that they doexamine the Matter thereof ? and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Colonel Cornwallis, Mr. Charlton,

Ordered, That the said Accounts and Estimate do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Ealand Mr. Comptroller reported from the Committee, to Road. whom the Petition of several of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed in the 14th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the Road leading from Ealand, to the Town of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House 5 and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for repairing the Road leading from Ealand, to the Town of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, was read: And,

Mr. William Mann, Surveyor and Treasurer to the Trustees for putting the said Act in Execution, said, That the Trustees have borrowed the Sum of Seven hundred Pounds upon the Credit thereof; which, together with the Income of the said Tolls, amounting to about £. 285 annually, after Payment of the Interest of the Money so borrowed, has been duly applied towards the Repair of the said Road; but that the same has been found insufficient for that Purpose.

That the said Road is Sixteen Miles in Length, Seven of which the Trustees have not been able to repair at all; and the Remainder is in a ruinous Condition, and much worn by the many heavy Coal and Lime Carriages passing thereon: That unless the Term and Powers, given by the said Act, be enlarged, and the Tolls thereby granted be augmented, the said Road mu ft be loft.

Mr. Samuel Harpur said. That he knows Part of the said Road, which is much frequented, and is of great Benefit to Trade; that about Three Miles of the same is a Stone Pavement, and kept up at a great Expence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the 14th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for repairing the Road leading from Ealand to the Town of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York: And that Mr. Comptroller, and Mr. Wilkinson, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

High#iteand Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Trustees, appointed to put in w s‘ Execution Four Acts of Parliament, passed in the Third and Eighth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and the Seventh and Eighth Years of his present Majesty, for repairing the Highways leading to Highgate Gatehouse and Hampfteady in the County of Middlesex, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter $f the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: W'here the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The several Acts before mentioned were read; whereby it appeared, that the Term and Powers thereby granted will expire in 1759.

Mr. William Thomas, and Mr. James English, Surveyors of the said Road, said, That great Progress hath been made in amending the lame; notwithstanding which, many Parts thereof in the Winter Season, are very bad, occasioned by the many heavy Carriages travelling along the fame, and cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, without a large annual Expence.

Mr* Humphrey Elmos, Treasurer and Clerk to the Trustees, laid before your Committee, an Account of Receipts and Disbursement? of the said TftUs and Duties for Eight Year* past*by which it appeared,;

And to prove, that Colonel Vernon had been very active and zealous in the Service of King Charles the First and King Charles the Second, from the Beginning of the Civil War to the Restoration, and that he suffered great Hard-ships for such Zeal and Services, certain Depositions in Chancery, taken in the Year 1685, in a Cause then depending between the then Attorney General, Plaintiff, and the said Edward Vernon and others, Defendants, were produced to your Committee, and read; and it appears, by the Deposition of John Greengrafsj thac the Deponent knew the Lands at Sheerness, heretofore the Lands of the said Godfrey Meynell, and purchased of him by Colonel Vernon, and since conveyed to King Charles the Second; and the Deponent further said, that it was about Seventeen or Eighteen Years since that his said Majesty entered there-on, and began to build a Fort ihereori; and the said Fort had been then built aboutTen Years: That he knew, that there was demanded, for the Profits and Damages since his said Majesty's Entry, the Sum of 2,327 I. or thereabouts, by Meynell, or others on his behalf, at the Ordnance Office at the Towet: That the Deponent, being Tenant and Steward to Meynelly a<sted, and was privy to the Transaction of that Affair, on hi* Behalf, and was several times at the Tower about the fame; and the Deponent verily believed, that the Inheritance of the Lands, and Buildings thereon then erected, were worth, to be sold, Forty or Fifty thousand Pounds, his Majesty having laid out a great deal of Money in building the Fore, and erecting the other Buildings thereon, since he entered on the fame.

By the Deposition of the Right Honourable Vere Essex Earl of Ardglaffe, it appeared, That the said Edward Vernon took up Arms for King Charles the First, 164a, and continued in Arms for his Service till the Year 1648, when he raised a Regiment of Foot; and during that time was in several Engagements against the Rebels, and was often in Service to the great Hazard of his Life, and often with good Success.

That he afterwards went into Ireland, and served under the Marquis of Ormond, then Lord Lieutenant, who gave him a Commission for a Regiment of Foot; and Mr. Vernon continued under his Command till the Marquis was forced to leave that Kingdom, and go into France; where Vernon soon followed him, having refused to take Conditions from the Rebels. - ’

That Colonel Vernon* having been commanded by the Duke of York to meet the Royal Army then marching from Scotland, he came to Bologne with the Earl of Ardglaffe and Colonel Nichols, where they were informed of the Defeat at lYorceflen upon which they hastened for England, to assist his Majesty; and the Deponent, Colonel Vernon qpd Colonel Nichols agreed to meet in London, if they escaped the Rebels, which they did; and there finding out Colonel Lane, Lord Ardglaffe, Vernon, and the rest of them, furnished him with Passes, in others Names, to assist his late Majesty and Lord IVilmot to make their Escapes; after which the Deponent and Vernon continued much together, without submitting to, or compounding with, the Rebels, but were always endeavouring to promote several Risings against the Rebels by his then Majesty’s Directions, with very great Hazard of their Lives; in which Vernon, as the Deponent was informed, was taken and made a Prisoner in the Tower, and lay there some Years; and, upon his getting out of the Tower in 1658, carried a considerable Party of Horse to Sir George Booth, out of Derby/hire and Staffordshire, into Cheshire, and continued in that Service till the whole Party separated; when he again went beyond Sea, and there (laid with his Majesty till his Majesty's Return into England', when Vernon landed with him at Dover.

By the Deposition of Henry Earl of Clarendon, Lord Privy Seal, it appeared, That during the Exile of King Charles the Second, whilst he was at Breda, Colonel Vernon brought his Majesty Bills of Exchange to the Value of Two thousand Pounds, which were then looked upon as a considerable P re lent to his Majesty, as his Occasions then flood; which Bills were payable at Answep, and the Money accordingly received; and that his Lord In ip had heard his Majesty Ay, that he looked upon Colonel Vernon to be a very honest Gentleman.

By the Deposition oI John Vernon Esquire ic appeared. That Colonel Vernon had been always loyal, and forward to serve the Crown, from the fetcing up the Standard at Nottingham to the Restoration , and that he suffered many Years Imprisonment in the Tower, in the Usurper's Time, on his Majesty's Account: That, during his Imprisonment, both his Parents, Sir Edward Vernon and Lady Vernon, who was an Heiress, died; Colonel Vernon having prevailed before with his Mother Lady Vernon to fell the Lordships of Hi/kton-and Ejfingtcn, and other Lands, for Four thousand Pounds; which, at the time the Witness was examined, were worth Four hundred Pounds per Annum, besides the Timber and Wood which was then very considerable; the said Lordships and Land.; having been given by ;Lady Vernon to Colonel Vernon; and that the Deponent, being Colonel Vernons. Brother, had good Reason to know and believe, that he laid out and expended most of the Four thousand Pounds, and much greater Sums in his Imprisonment, Sufferings, and Services, for Charles the First and Second.

Then another Petition, presented to his Majesty in December *750, in the Name of the present Petitioner, bating the former Petition, and Proceedings thereon; and that before any Hearing had, pursuant to the said Order of the 31st of May 1726, his late Majesty died, and the , laid Mary Vernon also died in 1729, whereby the Proceedings before the Council abated; and that the Petitioner, having thereupon gone over to Ireland to get into Possession of Colonel Vernon's Estates there, which came to him by the Death of the said Mary Vernon, had ever since been engaged in Law Suits in that Kingdom relating thereto, and an ill State of Health which had detained him from ap-

proaching the royal Presence, for a Revival of the former Reference in his own Name and Right: Therefore, in consideration of the great Services and Sufferings, and of several other equitable and just Demands on account of the former Estates and Interests of Colonel Vernon, then devolved on the Petitioner, and which he hoped fully to prove, he prayed. That the former Reference and Proceedings might be revived in his Name and Right.

A Petition of several Persons employed in the Business of Frame-work Knitcing in the Town of Nottingham, in behalf of themselves, and all other Persons employed in the said Trade, was prefemed to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Company of Frame-work Knitters of the City of London have made certain By-laws, by which, against all Reason, and contrary to the general Liberty of the Subjects of Great Britain, they invest themi'elves with a Power of laying such Taxes upon themselves as may greatly aftift them in carrying into Execution their pernicious Schemes of extending their Jurisdiction over the whole Kingdom, and establishing in themselves a Power of searching all Places belonging to the Members of the said Society, or any using the said Mystery; and moreover endeavouring to monopolize the lending of Frames for Hire; and alleging, That these and other Oppressions, under which the Manufacture labours from this Company, it is feared, will greatly affect the Trade of this Kingdom, unless the poor Manufacturers meet with the Protection and Assistance of the House: And therefore praying the House to take these Matters into ConCderadon, and grant the Petitioners, and the said Trade in general, such Relief as to the House shall icem meet.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, and others. Inhabitants of Godalming, Guildford, and Places adjacent, in the County of Surry, in behalf of the Framework Knitters of their several Towns and Parishes, was also presented to the House, and read; fencing forth. That great Numbers of the Poor are employed in thCTiid Trade, and in preparing Materials for their Use, and great Quantities of Wool, Silk, Thread, and Cotton, are manufactured by (means thereof; and that it appears to the Petitioners, that the Mailer, Wardens, and AGistants, of the Company of Frame-work Knitters of the City of Lrn4on, under Pretence of Authority granted to them by a Charter, 'have afiumed to themselves a Power to make several arbitrary and oppressive By-laws, to the Discouragement of the said Trade; and also to defeat the Intent of the said Incorporation; which, it is preFumed, mud have been designed to promote and encourage, and not tp oppress and injure, the said Manufacture; and that many iaduftrious Persons cannot at this time support themselves and Families w ithout charitable Afliiiance; and alleging. That, if the By-laws of the said Company are binding, it ’will tend to the Decay of the said Manufactory, and thereby bring greater Burthens on the said several Parishes: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and give such Relief as shall appear reasonable.

Were severally presented to the House, and read; fe-veraliy letting forth, That there is a great Decrease in the Exportation of Broad Cloths to Turkey, which the Petitioners apprehend is owing to an exclusive Grant to a Company of Merchants trading thither; and alleging, That this Monopoly hath given our great Rivals the French an Opportunity of supplanc-ing us in this Branch of our Commerce; and that the Petitioners conceive the most likely Method for recovering this once so valuable Branch of Trade, is to lay it open to all his Majesty’s Subjects: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill be brought in for laying open the Trade to Turkey for all his Majesty’s Subjects, under such Regulations as the House shall think proper; and to grant such other Relief to the Petitioners in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of Norwich, in Common Council assembled, was also presented to the House, and read 5 alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, it would greatly contribute to the Encouragement of exporting Woollen Manufactures of this Nation to the several Ports of Turkey, if the Trade to those Places be made open arid free to all his Majesty’s Subjects; and that all Monopolies give our Rivals the French, and other Foreigners, a great Advantage over us in this and many Branches of our Commerce; and that the Petitioners conceive, that, by making the Levant Trade free and open, very great Advantages will accrue, as well to the said City as other trading Places in the Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for laying open the Trade to Turkey for all his Majesty’s Subjects, and give such other Relief to the Petitioners in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Mr. Christopher ricard, being examined, said, That the Woollen Manufacture carried on in the several Towns mentioned in the Petition, and the Villages adjacent, has of late Years considerably increased; and that he apprehends, if the said Road was amended, the said Manufacture might still be further extended, as such Reparations would facilitate the Carriage of the said Manufactures, as well as of Coals and other Provisions necessary for the Manufacturers:

That the said Road is 53 Miles in Length, and very bad, the Soil in general being ftonv, rocky, and uneven: That the greatest Part ofit is very inconvenient, and dangerous for Wheel Carriages, and in many Places too harrow; and he instanced one Part in particular, which he had measured, and found to be no more than Four Feet Eight Inches w ide:

That the Inhabitants are obliged, from the Inconve-niency of the Roads, to use small Carriages drawn by One or Two Horles only; and whenever larger Carriages have been made use of, they have generally been broken or overturned:

That ’tis impossible for the several Parishes, through which the said Road leads, to repair the same by the ordinary Course of Law, there being great Numbers of Cross Roads in the said several Parishes, amounting in the Whole, according to a Calculation the Witness has made, to 176 Miles in Lgngth:

That he had been Surveyor of the Highways for the Township of Settle, when he obliged all the Inhabitants liable to Statute-work (except Two) to perform the fame; but that Work was ineffectual; and that many of the Townships, through which the Road leads, have been several times indicted on account of the said Road; and particularly, that the Town Clerk of Lancaster had, by Instruction of the Merchants of that Town, caused several Parts of the Road to be indicted at the Assizes at York; which Prosecutions had cost a large Sum of Money.

He further said. That, if Turnpikes were crested, the Tolls collected thereat would be sufficienc to amend the said Road, the Country abounding with proper Materials; VOL. 26.

and that the Repair of the same would bt of great and publick Utility.

Mr. fViiliam Bazvdwen said, He was well acquainted with the said Roads; and confirmed the Evidence of Mr.

Picard in every Particular (except so much as relates to Mr. Picard's being Surveyor of the Highways); and added further, That the Road had frequently been indicted at the Quarter Sessions, as well as the Assizes, particularly that Part of it which lies in the several Townships of Skipton, Farnbill> and Keighley.

Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Churchwarden, Overseer of the Poor, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Chrft Church, Middle-/ex, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as foilowerh; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Carter being examined, said, That the Number of Poor in the said Parish are of late greatly increased j and that the Rate in 1745 was only 1,589/.; and in the Year 1751 it amounted to 1,972/.; and the Rate for 1752 will amount to above 2,00c/.; and that if a Work* house was erected, near One-half of the Poor would be employed, which are now relieved by weekly Pensions.

Thomas Jtfrw Esquire said he had lived 79 Years in the Parish, and is a considerable Manufacturer; and if the Pariili was enabled to build a Workhouse, it would not only in a few Years reduce their Race to near One-half, but be the Means of employing several idle People; who, if they were obliged to work, would be very useful to the Community.

George Garret Esquire confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Jarvis; and added, that weekly Pensions rather hurt than assist the Poor; and that the Increase of their Poors* Rate has been so great, from the great Number of Poor, who will not work, that in the Year 1731, when h: iived in a large House of his own, he was rated to the Poor only 2/. 8 j.; that he is since removed to a smaller House; and in the Year 1751 was rated Six Pounds.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, more effectually to enable the Parifoiojiers of the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Middlesex, to purchase, hire, or erect, a Workhouse, for the employing and maintaining the Poor of the said Parish, and for the more effectual Support and Employment of the Poor therein: And that Mr. Cooke, and Sir William Beauchamp Proctor, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Governor and Guardians of the Poor of the City of Gloucester, under their Common Seal,

And the said Petition was read reciting several Provisions in an Act made in the First Year of the Reign of Queeh^wffr (for incorporating certain Persons, for the better providing for, and setting at work, the Poor of the City of Gloucester) and in an Act made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, for repealing Part, and making more efflftual the Residue, of the aforesaid Act; and setting forth. That, according to the Directions of the said Act, the Poor of the Hamlets of Lit tie worth.

Saint Michael's, Saint Mary de Lead, and Saint Katharine's, which are Hamlets lying in the County of Gloucester,hut adjoining to the said City, have been constantly taken in and maintained by the said Corporation, etfer firice the: time of making the lad of the said Acts; 2nd that several Doubts and Difficulties have arisen, whether the Persons that have executed the Offices of Governors, Dcpuiy Go* vernors, Treasurer, or Special Assistants, for Two Years, can be re-chosen into the same Offices; whereas it frequently has happened, and may happen, that the Persons that have executed the said Offices for Two Years, may bd willing, and may be the fitted Persons, to be chosen into the said Offices, for Two further Years; and that several Persons, after they have applied for Relief to the said Corporation,at their full Courts, and after their Circumstances, and the causes of such their Applications have been there fully enquired into, and they have been refused Relief there, as not being proper Objects thereof, have immediately afeer such Courts, and when their Circumstances have not in the lead been altered, applied and got Orders for Relief from private Guardians; whereby frequent Dif-putes have arilen, and the said Corporation have been frequently put to unnecessary Expences in relieving Persons not being proper Objects of Relief; and that the Churchwardens, and Overseers of the Poor, when they have been duly appointed, have, in many Ir»dances,been very remifsin collecting, and paying the Money certified by the said Corporation; insomuch, that the same Money very frequently hath not been paid till Six or Nine Months after the same hath been certified and ordered to be collected; and some Parts of the said Money have been often unpaid for several Months, after the said Officers have been out of their Offices; nor have the Justices of the said County or the said Corporation, by either of the said Acts, or by any Law now in Force, as the Petitioners arc advised, any Power of compelling the said Officers to account for, or pay, the said Money, when the same hath been collected; and that, in some Indances, Officers hath been appointed, who have collected the Money certified, and have thereupon absconded, and never paid the same to the said Corporation; and that sometimes Persons have been appointed Overseers of the Poor of some of the Parishes of the said City, who were not resident therein, and therefore not obliged by Law to serve the same Offices; whereby the Corporation hath been under great Difficulties to get the same collected; and that in t^e Years 1749 and 1750, one Henry Ward was appointed Ovfcrfeer of the Poor of the Hamlet of St.

Mary, Barton Street, being one of the Hamlets of St. Mary de Load, and that the Sum of 5/. 11 s. 2d. Part of the Money by him collected for the Maintenance of the Poof of the said Hamlet for those Years remains unpaid; and that for the present Year the Inhabitants of the Hamlet of *"

St. Mary, Barton Street, have procured a Person to be appointed Overseer of the Poor of the said Hamlet (there being accultomably never more than one appointed to that Office for the said Hamlet) that is not an Inhabitant in the said Hamlet; so that the said Corporation are likely to lose the Sum of 82/. iji. 7 d. being the Money certified to be 7 N raised

Levant ' A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Owners of Trade, ships, of the City of Chester, was presented to the House, and read j setting forth. That the Exportation of British Manufactures to Turkey, is of late greatly decreased; occasioned, as the Petitioners apprehend, by a Company of Merchants having a Gran t to trade thither, exclufi ve ofall the rest of the British Subjects; and that our Rivals the French have greatly increased their Woollen Manufactures, and also their Exportation of them to Turkey, and thereby lessened the Sale of those of Great Britain in that Country; which, as the Petitioners apprehend, is not occasioned only by the Advantage that Kingdom hath over this, in its Situation for that Trade, but also, as they verily believe, by the large Profit which an exclusive Company generally infills on for their Goods: which, though an Advantage to the Company, is a great national Loss; and that the present exclusive Charter, and high Prices of British Goods in Turkey, enable the Merchants of Leghorn to import British Manufactures to that Port, and to reship them from thence to Turkey, also to bring back to that Port the Product of that Country, particularly Cotton, which is re-shipped again, in great Quantities, for Great Britain j and repre-lcnting to the House, that it is the Opinion of the Petitioners, that the most probable Means to enable the , Merchants of Great Britain to vie with their foreign Ri-

vals in this Trade, and to restore it to its former flourishing State, will be, to lay it open to all his Majesty’s Subjects, who, either separately, or in small Societies, can export or import Goods on much lower Terms than a large exclusive Company, under a Charter, will or tan do:

And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for laving open the Trade to Turkey to all his Majesty’s Subjects, under such Limitations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Manufacturers, and others. Inhabitants of the Town of Bradford, and Villages adjacent, in the County of Wilts, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of Woollen Cloths to Turkey is of late Years greatly decreased; which the Petitioners apprehend arises folelyfrom an exclusive Grant to a Company of Merchants trading thereto; and alleging, That the true Cause why the French, our Rivals in Trade, have supplanted us in this important Branch, ariseth from our Monopoly, and not from any superior Excellency in their Commodities; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that this valuable Branch of Trade might be easily recovered, was it laid open: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for laying open the Trade to Turkey i and that all his Majesty’s Subjects may have free Liberty of trading thither, under such Restrictions and Limitations as the House shall think fit; and to grant such other Relief to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the principal Clothiers and Manufacturers of the Town of Shepton Mallet, in the County of Somer-Jet, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That there is a great Decrease in the Exportation of Cloth to Turkey; and that the same is owing to the Trade being carried on by a Company of Merchants, to the Exclusion of the greatest Part of his Majesty’s SuhjeCls; and that, if the same was laid open, it would be a Means to increase the Exportation of Woollen Cloths: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief to the Petitioners, as the House shall judge most meet.

Families, and several Thousands of Persons employed by them, they may be heard in regard to the fame; and that the House will give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in for regulating the said Manufacture, in such manner as ta the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Barrow reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Governor and Guardians of the Poor of the City of Gloucester, under their Common Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and also an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, were read:

That, by the First-mentioned Act, it appeared to your Committee, That certain Persons therein mentioned, are incorporated by the Name of the Governor and Guardians of the Poor of the City of Gloucester, who are to have perpetual Succession, and a Common Seal, and to hold Courts, and are inverted with several other Powers therein mentioned.

And by the said Act, of the 13th of his said late Majesty, a Governor, Deputy Governor, Treasurer, and Six special Assistants, are directed to be chosen every Two Years, to execute the Purposes of the aforesaid Acts; and,

Mr. Yhomas Vernon said, Officers have accordingly been chosen, as by the said Act directed; but that Doubts have arisen whether Persons, who have executed the said several Officers, can be rc-chose into the same Offices for the next succeeding Term.

And he further said, That Persons have frequently applied for Relief to the Corporation Court, and upon a full Enquiry into their Circumstances, have not been deemed proper Objects of Relief; and that those Persons have immediately, upon Application to private Guardians, often obtained from them Orders to be relieved; which has been the Occasion of great Disputes:

And that although a Person, relieved by the said Corporation, is possessed of a fraall Parcel of Land, the said . Vol. 26.

Corporation is not, by either of the said Acts, impowered to dispose thereof;

That the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, the proper Persons to collect the Money for the Relief of the Poor, have been very negligent in the Collection, and have also frequently kept the Money in their Hands feverak Months after they have quitted their Offices; and that the Corporation has not proper Authority to oblige such Collectors to account for the Monies by them so received; and there have been Instances where such Officers have absconded, and the Money thereby loft to the Corporation t

That Persons had been appointed Overseers of the Poor for Parishes wherein they \lid not reside, and therefore refused to officiate, which had laid the Corporation under great Difficulties; and the Witness mentioned an Instance in the present Year, where a Person was appointed for the Hamlet of Saint Mary Barton Street, and, not being resident therein, refused 10 aft; whereupon another Overseer was appointed in his room; but the Inhabitants refuse to pay the Rates to him, as not bring originally appointed; so that the Corporation mull lose the whole Year’s Assessment.

And that, in 17 } % a Person who, although he did collect the Rate, has at this time Partofit in his Hands; for which he refutes to account.

A Petition of the Provost, MagistrateS, and Council Edinburgh of the Ciry of Edinburgh, in behalf of themselves, and Streets, the Community of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the City of Edinburgh is, by its Situation on a Hill, subjected to several Inconveniencies, which are felt not only by the Inhabitants of the said City, but also by the Inhabitants of the other Parrs of Scotland, who are daily under a Necessity of repairing thither; particularly that the Avenues to the said City are difficult, and even dangerous, especially from the Fields on the North, South, and West; and that, by reason of this confined Situation, the Houses have been very much crouded, and raised to an exorbitant Height; by which Means the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, for the most part, are narrow, dirty, and ill disposea, and no proper Space or Area left free and unbuilt upon for an Exchange, or Place of publick Relort, for Merchants and Men of Business; and chat, for the same Reason, there are many publick Buildings wanted within the City, for necessary Purposes; and there are at present no proper Areas upon which they can be conveniently erected; and that neither the Commissioners to the Convention of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland, nor the Magistrates and Council of the City, have any proper Hall for meeting together upon Business; and that there is no proper Accommodation or Offices for the Clerks of the several supreme Courts of Justice, or proper and fare Repositories for the Rolls, Registers, and Records, and ocher publick Archives; which is the more necessary in this Part of the united Kingdom, where all real Estates and Land Rights depend intirely upon the Preservation of the said Records and Registers, &c. against Fire and other Accidents; and that a very considerable Number of Noblemen, Gentlemen, Burgesses, and others, being sensible of the Usefulness and Necessity of remedying these Inconveniencies, and that the proper Funds of the Community of the City of Edinburgh, are in no ways sufficient to answer the Expence chat would be necessary for that Purpose, have opened a voluntary SubscriptionforcontributingcertainlargeSums, and appointed Managers or Trustees to oversee and direct the Application thereof, towards opening and improving the Avenues to the City, enlarging and adorning the Streets, and other Places of publick Resort, erecting proper Edifices for the Preservation of the Rolls, Register9, and Records, and ocher publick Uses, according to a Plan which has been concerted; and chat, in the Execution of this Plan, sundry Difficulties are likely to occur, particularly that certain Lands and Houses, which must necessarily make a Part of the Avenues and Streets proposed to be enlarged, and of 7 X the

the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Berwick upon Tweed, under their Common Seal; and also the Petition of the Justices of Peace, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Shire of Berwick; were severally referred* That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of that Part of the County of Durham commonly called Nor bam and ljland Shires, lying North of the County of Northumberland; and also of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, and others, the Inhabitants of the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Matter of the said Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Berwick upon Tweed, under their Common Seal; no Person appearing on the Behalf of the said Petition of the Justices of Peace, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Shire of Berwick; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Matter of the said Two first-mentioned Petitions, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Mr. Christopher Pattifon was examined; who said, That he is well acquainted with the Roads mentioned in the Petition; particularly those on the North Side the Town of Berwick, the Soil whereof is a deep Clay; and that the said Roads are much frequented by Travellers and Carriages, and are in a very ruinous Condition:

Thar on his going to view the said Roads, about Three Weeks ago, his Horse was (tuck fast in one Part of them, and he obliged to alight in a Place which was over his Boots in Water:

That the Country in general complain of the Badness of the Roads, and desire to have them repaired; and he gave two Instances thereof; the one of a Waggoner, who goes every Six Weeks from Leeds ro Edinburgh, who told the Witness he would rather pay double or treble Toils, than not have the Roads repaired; the other, a Person whom he met on the said Road, who frequently travels the same on Horseback, who told the Witness, he would rather pay a Shilling a time for a Turnpike than want one:

That he was Surveyor of the Highways, for such Part of the said Roads as lies on the North Side of Berwick, in the Year 1742; and at that time, and for Five Years after, the Statute-work was performed, and the Road made pretty good in Summer, but in Winter became as bad as ever; and that, in the Opinion of the Witness, they cannot be made good by the 01 dinary Methods of Law:

That, though he is not so well acquainted with the said Roads on the South of Berwick, yet he knows them to be in a bad Condition; and that he indicted them in the Year 1748; but it was to no manner of Purpose, for the Road has notwithstanding been as bad as ever:

That the Repair of the said Roads would be of general Utility; and that he believes all the Inhabitants would very willingly pay towards it.

Mr. George Lawrie informed your Committee, That he is well acquainted with the Roads mentioned in the Petition, which lie on the South Side of Berwick; which are in a very ruinous Condition: That his Father was Surveyor of the said Roads in the Year 1748; but, being indisposed, the Witness acted for him; that two Parts of the said Roads; viz. Tweedmouth Lane, and Etall Road, were indicted that Year; and the Consequence was, that though they were repaired in Summer, yet in Winter they became as bad as ever, or rather worse:

That the Badness of the Roads is occasioned by the Nature of the Soil, and the many Carriages passing the same: That he believes the Statute-work inefficient to repair them; and that the amending them, in a sufficient Manner, would be of general Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Roads from the Turnpike Road at Buckton Burn, through Berwick upon Tweed, to Lammerton Hill;

DevonCoun- Sir Richard Warwick Bampfylde reported from the tyGiol. Committee, to whom the Petition of the High Sheri ft*, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Devon, assembled at a General Meeting held for that Purpose; and also the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Devon, assembled at a General Meeting held at the Castle of Exeter for that Purpose; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition the following Witnesses were examined $ viz.

William Land Esquire, Under-sheriff, and Edward Collins Esquire; who severally said, That there is no High Gaol for Criminals belonging to the High Sheriff; and that the County is also without a Sheriff’s Prison, or Place of Confinement for Debtors, the High Sheriffs being obliged, from time to time, to hire a private House on the be ft Terms they can, to keep such Debtors; by means whereof many Inconveniencies frequently happen.

And Mr. Lend further said, That, there being no Sheriff's Prison for Debtors, the Proprietor or Keeper of such House obliges the Sheriff to pay for the same what he thinks fit to impose, which hath increased for several Years pad; for, in the Year 1751, there was paid for the said House 70/. and in 175a the Sum of 73/. ioj.: And the Proprietor, who is Keeper of the Prison, has declared, that he would not agree with future Sheriffs on the same Terms, and that, at prefenc, the Under-sheriff and his Officers are obliged to sollicit all Complaints that are preferred at any time against him (by the Prisoners for ill Usage) to the Justices of Assize, either by Motion or Petition; and inlists, for the future, on being indemnified from every such Motion or Petition.

That, in Support of the last mentioned Petition, your Committee were informed, to their Satisfaction, That the Allegations therein contained are true.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in Bill for raising a Sum of Money, by a County Rate, for erecting or p!irchafing a proper Prison for Debtors, in the County of Devon: And that Sir Richard Warwick Bampfylde, Mr. Bullerj Mr. Taylor, and Sir William Tinge, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.
