The Lord Downe reported from the Committee, to Northallertoa whom the Petition of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, Roa<1* assembled at the General Quarter Sessions,holden at Thirsk, the 3d Day o fOBcber, in the Year of our Lord 1752, in and for the North Riding of the County of York, and of the several Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of and in the said Riding, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio wet h; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Mathews, being examined, said, That he lives at Stokejley, and knows the Hoad mentioned in the Petition, which is Fourteen Miles long, and in general very bad, and impracticable for Carriages in Winter; and chat several Parts of it have been indicted; that he thinks the Road cannotbe repaired by the ordinary Course of Law, because the Two Parishes of Tkirtkby and Shipton, through which the said Road leads,have been indicted, and have attempted thereupon to amend the said Road, to no manner of Purpose.

Being asked the Question, he laid, He did not know whether Sixpence in the Pound, if it were to be laid out on the Roads, for many Years together, might not be sufficient to repair the same:

That if the said Road were repaired, it would increase the Trade between the City of York and the Towns of Yarm, Stockton, Stokejley, and Gisburne, and the Country thereabouts, and would be, in particular, a great Advantage to York, on Account of the Conveniency of bringing the Linen manufactured in Cleveland to York, where it is most of it fold; but that he cant’t say what Quantities of Linen come that Way; and if the Road were repaired, he thinks the Inhabitants of Easing would get their Coals carried a nearer Way:

That he believes they carry Coals from Thirsk to North Allerton:

That this Road is much frequented by Carriages in Summer, especially at the latter End of the Year, loaden with Butter, to the City of York.

And being alked the Question, he said, He never heard any Objection made to repairing the said Road.

Mr. Thomas Martin informed your Committee, That he was born at Thirsk, anti knows the Road mentioned in the Petition, which is very bad, the Soil of it being in general very rotten, and a little Tandy about Thirsk; chat / he thinks the Statute-work is not sufficient to repair it in a manner sufficient for Carriages; but that he does not know whether it has been tried.

Mr. Richard Lancaster being examined, laid, He lives at Eafingwould, and is well acquainted with the Road defcished in the Petition, which is in some Places too narrow; and the Soil is a deep Clay and Sand; and no Carriages can pass it in Winter; and that they are very often stuck fast even in Summer; and many Persons on Horse-back have been in Danger of their Lives o nShipton Moor; and that the Road has always' been very bad, buc worse lait Year than ever:

That if the Road were repaired, it would be much frequented by Butter Carriages, as well as Carriages loaden with Linen Manufactures; and that the Butter Trade is 12 carried

Mr. Alderman BetbcU, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Petition of the Society of the Free British Fishery, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is reasonable that the Petitioners, having had in the Bank, within the Term of Eighteen Months next after the Date of their Subscripdon, Money sufficient to answer all their Contracts which were depending during the Six Months allowed after the Expiration of such Eighteen Months, should receive the Interest of Three Pounds per Centum, allowed by the Act of the Twenty-third Year of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of the British White Herring Fishery, in such manner as they would have been intitled thereto, in case so much Money of the Petitioness, as would have been sufficient to answer the said Contracts respectively, had, at the Time of making the same, been in the Bank of England.

a. Resolved, That ir is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Commencement and Duration of the White Herring Fisheries ought to be regulated by the Calendar now in use in these Kingdoms.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners ought to have on board their Vessels, at their Return into Port, the same Number of Hands as they are by the said Act obliged to have at the Rendezvous of such Vessels, unless the Number shall be reduced by Death, Sickness or Desertion.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Vessels employed in the said Fisheries be at Liberty to go into Port, between the Intervals of the Two Fisheries called the Shetland and the Yarmouth Fisheries,. in order to change their Nets, and otherwise to prepare for the Second Fishery.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners be at Liberty to make use of Nets of Five Fathoms deep in the Second Fishery, called the Yarmouth Fishery.

The Three First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second timei were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fourth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time.

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made thereto \ viz.

After " into," to insert " any," and after " Port," to insert " in Great Britain or Ireland "

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That the Vessels employed in the said Fisheries be at Liberty to go into any Port in Great Britain, or Ireland, between the Intervals of the Two Fisheries, called the Shetland and the Yarmouth Fisheries, in order to change their Nets, and otherwise to prepare for the Second Fishery.

The last Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Alderman Bethelly Lieutenant General Oglithorpey Mr. Alderman . Janffen, Mr. Vernon, and Sir Bourchier Wray, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several Merchants, Exporters, and of the Manufacturers, of British Sail Cloth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed,on behalfof themselves, and of several others concerned in* the said Manufacture, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Fund which was established for the Payment of the Bounties upon the Exportation of British-made Sail Cloth, having been found insufficient, a Clause was inserted in an Act in the Year 1750, whereby it was provided, that the said Bounty

should, for the futtire, be paid out of such Part of (he old Subsidy as is applicable to the Payment of Incidents, after satisfying all Payments already charged thereupon by any former Act or Acts of Parliament.^ that behalf, in manner, and under the Regulations and Restrictions which are directed and prescribed by the several Acts of Parliament, for the Payment of such Bounties; and alleging, that the Words " After satisfying all Payments already charged cc thereupon, by any former Act or Acts of Parliament in fi thac Behalf," being inserted in the said Clause, the* Encouragement formerly granted by the Legislature, and by the said Clause intended to be effectually secured, hath been intirely defeated, by reason that several other Bounties are charged upon the said Fund, and the Payment of such Bounties have, by the said Restriction, a Preference to the Payment of the Bounties upon British-made Sail Cloth 5 and as Debentures are continually standing out upon Account of such other Bounties, ’tis impossible to obtain any Allowance upon the Exportation of the said Manufactures; and the Bounties are wholly in Arrear ever since the passing of the said Clause: And therefore praying, That Provisiort may be made for the effectual and regular Payment of the said Bounties, in such' manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, Thac this House will, upon Tomorrow Sevennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

That the said Parish is charged with tiv* larged Quota to the Land Tax of any Parish in the Borough, on account of the Situation thereof, a large annual Sum being assessed and raised on the said Prison for Land Tax, and other parochial Taxes; and that, if any Alteration should be made in the said Prison, to exempt it from such Taxes, the said Parish will be very unable to make up the Deficiency; and representing to the House, That, as the greated Part of the said Parish is within the Liberties of the Rules of the King's Bench, many Persons, in reduced Circumstances, who become Prisoners, and obtain the Liberties of the said Rules, take Houses of the yearly Value of Ten Pounds, or upwards j but, by reason of their Poverty and Imprisonment, never serve any parochial Offices, and pay but very small (if any) Taxes therein; notwithstanding which, they and their Families frequently become chargeable to the said Parish, by virtue of having rented Houses of such Value: And therefore praying. That such Means may be taken to prevent any Loss arising to the said Parish, on account of any Alteration that may be made to the said Prison, as shall be thought most proper; and that such Persons who become Prisoners, or their Families, may not gain a Settlement, or enjoy the Rights and Privileges as Parishioners and Inhabitants, during such time as they remain Prisoners on the Books,although they do inhabit in the said Parish; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sid. and from the 17th June 1751, to the 13th May 1752, being the Year after the Commencement of the said Act, amounted only to 471/. Ti s. S{d.:

That, deduding the interest of the Money so borrowed, and all other annual Expences attending the Trust, there will remain no more than 223/. per Annum to be applied towards repairing the said Roads; which will be insufficient for those Purposes:

That the Road leading from Ardwick Green, through a Ford in the River Mercy, to Wilmslow, being about Nine computed Miles, is a common Highway, and the nearest Road from Manchester to London by Four or Five Miles: That the said River is always difficult to pass; and in Time of high Floods, which frequently happen, is altogether impassable; and that, if a Bridge was erected over the said River, at the said Ford, it would be of great Benefit to Travellers, and to the Trade carried on in those Parts:

That the said Road from Ardwick Green to Wilm-Jlow is, in many Places, very narrow, and almost im-pastable in Winter, and Materials for repairing the same are very scarce, and lie at a great Distance; and that the same cannot be repaired, iior such Bridge erected, by the ordinary course of Law.

That, by an Act of the First of King William and Queen Mary, for encouraging the Exportation of Corn, it is enacted, That when Malt or Barley should be at Twenty-four Shillings, and Wheat at Forty-eight Shillings, per Quarter; or under; in any Port or Ports of this Kingdom, every Merchant who should put on board of any Engiish-built Ship, the Master, and Two-rbirds of his Mariners at least, being their Majesty's Subjects, any Sores of the said Corn, with an Intent to export the fame, every such Person, upon a Certificate, and Proof, upon Oath, of the Quantity and Quality lb shipped, and giving such Bond to export, and not reland the fame, as in the said Act is mentioned, should have paid them by the Commissioners* Farmers, or Collectors of his Majesty’s Customs, of the Port from whence such Corn was exported, a Bounty of Five Shillings for every Quarter of W hear, Three Shillings and Sixpence for every Quarter of Rye, and Two Shillings and Six Pence for every Quarter of Barley, or’Malt; so shipped; which Money so paid by the Commissioners, Farmers or Collectors, should be accepted of in thtif Accounts, as so much paid to their Majeliies.

Then an Act, of che 12th and 13th Years of King William the Third, was read; which enadls, That if the Collector of the Customs of any Port on the Coasts of this Kingdom should not have sufficient in his Hands to satisfy and pay such Sum and Sums of Money which were or should be due to any Exporters, by virtue of the first-mentioned Act, that then such Collectors should give to the Person, demanding such Sum or Sums of Money, a Certificate, under his Hand, of what should be due to such Person for the Corn exported from such Porr; certifying to the Commissioners of the Customs in London, that he had not Monies in his Hands sufficient to pay the fame; which Certificate being affixed to the Debenture for the Corn so exported, and being produced to his Majesty's Commissioners of the Customs in London, they the said Commissioners of the Customs are thereby authorized and required, on Demand, by the Person that shall bring the fame, to cause the Money thereby due to be paid wiihin Three Months, by the General Receiver or Cashier of the Customs, out of such Monies as should be in his Hands, arising out of such Customs or Duties in the Port of London, as were chargeable with die Payment of any Money for the Exportation of Corn.

come; and that he does not doubt, but, by his diligent ComBoafcty. Attendance, he has got Debentures paid, when others, of an older Date, have remained unpaid.

Being asked, Whether a Person who has a Debenture, dated the last Day of November, may not be paid before one dated the first ? he said, He has been told, upon applying to the Custom-house, That they had Money to pay Debentures, of the first Part of a Month, when they had not to pay the last; and he added, that the Debentures for Corn exported from the Port of London were usually paid about Two Months-after the Exportation; and the Debentures from the Out-ports not under 15 or sometimes 18 Months:

That if the Debentures for the Corn exported from the Out-ports were as well paid as those from London, it would be a great Inducement to export more Corn; as the Discount of 7£ per Cent. is, in effect, so much added to the Price of the Corn; and must prevent the Exportation of some; and the locking up such a Sum of Money is a still greater Disadvantage, as a Man must have a much larger Capital to carry on the Business; and that the Reason of the Discount being so great, is the Uncertainty of the Time of Payment, and the great trouble in attending at the Custom-house for the fame; for that the Witness believes he has sent thither 30 times for every Debenture that has been paid him this last Year.

Mr. Robert Wilson said, That he had several Certificate Debentures in his hands, for Corn exported; some of which were due the 3d of December 1751; that Three or Four Months ago it was not usual to pay the Country Debentures in less Time than 18 Months; but that the Exportation has lately decreased; and they are now paid in about 15 Months; and that he has Debentures of his own, and hisCorrcfpondents, in his hands, to the Amount of 17,000l.; which have all been due above Six Months, and some as long as Fifteen.

Being asked, How Jong the London Debentures commonly remained unpaid ? he said, The time of Entry made some Variation as to that; for if the Entry was made the latter-end of a Month; for Example, the latter-end of December, the Debenture would come round by the 6th or 7th of February, when they should get their Money; but if the Entry was made the first of January following, they should, by that means be delayed a Month longer; that the Reason of this he supposes to be, the manner of keeping their Accounts at the Custom-house, which they do in Months; but after they have got the London Debentures, *tis generally paid in about a Week’s Time; though several Hundreds of London Debentures had passed through his hands; and that he never had one Three Weeks without Payment.

Mr. Ellis reported from the Commitree, to whom the Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, Surveyors of the Highways, and other Inhabitants, of the Pari lb of East Greenwich, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto fubl’cribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition 5 and had direClcd him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act passed in the 43d Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, and also an Act passed in the 2d and 3d Years of the Reign of King Philip and Queen Mary, were read: And,

Mr. John Everejl said, That the Streets of the said Parish are almoll wholly paved; and that the Parish contains about 1,500 Houses.

Mr. Samuel Driver said, That there has been Sixty-one Pounds a Year, for Six Years pad (communibus An-tiis) expended in paving the said Streets: That not above Forty of the Inhabitants do their Statute-work yearly: That there are many Poor people who do not pay: That the Money arising from the Forfeitures of those who do not perform their Statute-work, amounts to (One Year with another) about 1281, which, if the whole could be collected, would amount to upwards 400l.: That he knows these Fadls from the Books and Accounts which have passed through his Hands: And that the Highways within the said Parish are very ill paved, and are at present in a very bad Condition.

Mr, Hayward Baker said. That there are several Roads within the said Parish (exclusive of the Pavements) to repair which would amount to upwards of ico/. a Year to keep in Repair; and that the said Roads and Streets are in a very ruinous Condition, and very dirty in the Winter Season.

Mr. Hayward Baker, Mr. George Joade, and Mr. David MiDowell, severally said. That if there was a Power to raile an additional Rate of Sixpence in the Pound, for repairing the Highways, and cleansing the Streets, to be added to, and collected with, the Rate or Rates made for the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish, the said Rates would be collected with more Ease and Certainty, and less Expence to the Inhabitants.

And upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Relief and Employment of the Boor in the Parish of East Greenwich, in the County of Kent; and for repairing the Highways, and cleansing the Streets thereof.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants Qf England, trading to the Levant Seas, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That in the Bill now depending before the House, for enlarging and regulating the Trade into the Levant Seas, there are several Clauses, which, should they pafsinto a Law as they now stand, will deprive the Petitioners of several of the Privileges granted by their Charter, very much affect them in their Properties, endanger the Ruin of their Establishment in Turkey, and greatly distress, if not occasion the total Loss of, the Turkey Trade to this Nation: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against such Clauses in the said Bill.

King’s Bench , Sir William Calvert reported from the Committe ap-PriTon. pointed to enquire into the State of the King's Bench» prison, and of the Office of the Marshal of the Marfialjea of the Court of King's Bench; and to report the fame, as it > ftfouid appear to them, to the House; That the Committee had enquired accordingly, and h^d directed him to report; a State of the Matters to them referred, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together wirh> an; Appendix thereto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read.

The said Report and Appendix are as followeth; viz.

It appeared by the concurrent Testimony of Mr. Steers and Mr. Poulteney, Surveyors, That the said Prifori is in a very decayed Condition, and extremely insecure for the safe-keeping of Prisoners 5 and that it ought to be rebuilt — No-body would repair it, the Expence would be so great:

That the Tide flows frequently Two Feet in the Yard of the Prison; and that the Apartments for the Prisoners, on the common Side* are below the Surface of the Ground.

Mx. William Soame confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Steers and Mr. Poulteney; and added. That not long-ago he observed, that in Two Rooms, in che upper Part of the Prifori, on the common Side, the Water appeared to be Two Feet high j and that, at lead, Four People lay in each Room, that did not exceed 7 Feet by 6.

John Ashton Esquire, the prefenc MarfHal, said, That of lace 1,200 Feet of the Prison Wall is blown down; and that the Whole is much cracked, and in Danger of falling; which obliges him to keep the Prisoners more closely confined than usual.

The Reverend Do6lor Howard said, That the greatest Distress he ever saw in his Life was in this Prison: That the common Side is most deplorable, and the Masters Side very bad, and that the Cells in Newgate are more comfortable:

, That he visited a Tick Woman.on the common Side the lad Year; and in his Opinion (he wanted Air more than than any thing: That the Maftef is willing:to afford all the Relief in his Power; and that, finee. a Lazaret was_ built, it is of great Benefit to the Prisoners, who are removed thither whfcn Tick.

Mr. Isaac Stap'eton, Surgeon, said, He had, by Appointment, condantly attended the Prisoners on the com* men Sideior 20 Years; and that scarce ever a Summer

passes without an Infectious Didemper there; which, the Witness said, he attributed to the great Number of Per- ‘ Tons being obliged to lie together in small Rooms, and to the common Sewer flowing into their Rooms:

That, in the Opinion of the Witness, the Marshal is a Man of great Humanity; and he has often heard the Prisoners say as much; and that as far as in his Power, no care is wanting to relieve their Distresses; but, in the present State of the Prison, it is impossible:

That the Mader’s Side, as well as the common Side* is so extremely close, that, whenever any infedlious Distemper happens there, 'tis very difficult to remove; and that the Sick on the Mader’s Side suffer extremely for want of a Person (killed in Physick appointed to attend ‘ them, as on the common Side. — In Confirmation of the foregoing Evidence,

Mr. Charles Moore, a Turnkey of the Prison,. said. That, on the common Side, great Part of the Rooms where the Prisoners lie are sometimes a Foot and a half under Water:

That he had known 18 or 19, and at this time 16 or 17, Persons lie in one Room, that does net exceed 16 Feet by 16, and not 12 Feet high; and that the Beds dand so ciofe together (in each of which 3 or Persons lie) that they have but just room to turn round in their several Apartments; and that the whole Building is so de-, cayed, that the Rain frequently comes in at the Roof; of which frequent Complaints have been made by the Prisoners to the Marshal; and they have been relieved as far as has been in his Power.

Mr. John Chapman, Under-marshal, said, He had knowm the Prison between 20 and 30 Years; and he confirmed* the Evidence given by Mr. Moore.

Then the Committee enquired into the Office of the Marshal of the Marshalsea of the Court of King’s Bench; and it appeared.

That King Jamest the id, by Letters Patent, dated the 15th Day of May, in the 14th Year of his Reign* granted to Sir William Smith Knight, the aforesaid Office,* to hold to him, his Heirs and Assigns, to be exercised by him or themselves, or sufficient Deputy or Deputies, for ever; and also granted to him all Fees and Profits belonging to the said Office, together with the Custody of the Prison, and of the Prisoners committed, and to be committed there:

That by Indenture, dated the 26th June 1618, reciting the aforesaid Letters Patent, the said Sir William Smith declared his Name to be used therein, in Trust for Sir David Wood; and he and Sir David Wood did thereby grant the said Office to Sir Edward Gorges and others, in Fee-simple, subject to a Proviso for making void the fame, on Payment of 1,100/ as therein is mentioned:

That by Deed-poll, dated 27 th June 1618, the said Sir William Smith, by Direction of Sir David Wood, released to the said Sir Edward Gorges, and others, the aforesaid Proviso, and all Equity of Redemption in the aforesaid Office;

That by Indenture, dated the 30th March 1630, reciting, that the aforesaid 1,100l. had been duly paid, the said Sir Edward Gorges and others, at the Requestof Sir Henry Wood, Brother and Heir of the said Sir David Wood, re-granted the Office to David Wood, Son and Heir apparent to the said Sir David Wood, in Fee;

That by Indenture, dated the i6ch of May 1631, in Consideration of 1,550L paid and secured to the said David Wood, and 1,100l. to be paid to him, as therein and herein after is mentioned, the said David Wood granted the said Office to Sir John Roaje, in Fee, under a Proviso, to be void if the said Sir John Roaje did not pay to the said David Wood, 1,100l. at a certain Day’ therein mentioned:

Colonel Abercrombie reported from the Commitreee, to whom the Petition of the Heretors, Fewars, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Parish of Preston Pans, in the Shire of East Lothian, alias Haddingtoun, thereunto subscribing, on behalf of themselves, and others the Proprietors of Houses or Land within the said Town and Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

George Drummond, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Town of Preston Pans is situate at tli* Bottom of a Bay, about Six Miles East from Edinburgh, and as many West from Haddingtoun, and is a principal Port; and has divers Creeks and Members belonging to it:

Thar, before the Union, the Town carried on a considerable foreign Trade; for which they were rated by the General Convention of Boroughs at Five Shillings Scots Money:

That, for some Years after the Union, the Inhabitants of the said Town employed several Ships; but their Trade continued gradually to decay; insomuch, that in the Year 1743, upon Proof made of the Deere'afe thereof, before the Convention of the Royal Boroughs (of which the Witness was Prades) the said Convention granted the Town an Abatement of their Proportion of the Tax Roll, by reducing it from Five to Three Shillings; and, in the Year 1752, the said Proportion was further reduced from Three to One Shilling Scots Money.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners produced to your Committee, an Act of Parliament, passed in the 7th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for repairing and improving Morrifons Harbour, and the Fort there, in the Shire of East Lothian, alias Haddingtoun; whereby it appeared, that certain Duties were laid on Merchandizes imported and exported at the said Harbour, for repairing the fime, for the Term of 31 Years; which Act expired in the Year 1739. — -Then,

Mr. Drummond further said. That the said Harbour, which is the only one of the Town, is in a very ruinous Condition, the Stone Pier being broken down, and the Harbour itself almost filled up with Sand; and that the Decay of Trade in the said Town has occasioned a great increase of Poor therein; and that the Town is ill fop-plied with Water, that which they are forced to use being brackilh:

That he apprehends the best Methods to recover and extend the Trade of the said Town, would be the effectual repairing of the said Harbour, and erecting a Workhouse, for employing and maintaining the Poor (which would be an Advantage not only to the said Town, but the adjacent Country) and the supplying the said Town with lweec Water, which might be effectually done from the rising Grounds in the Neighbourhood; but that the said Town is not poffrfled of a Revenue sufficient to complete those Works; nor can a Sum sufficient for that Purpose be raised, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for laying a Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or a Sixth Part of a Penny Sterling, upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer, which shall be brewed for Sale, brought into, tapped, or fold, within the Town and Parish of Preston Pans, in the Shire of East Lothian, otherwise Haddingtoun, for repair-

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants of the several Counties of Flint, Denbigh, Carnarvon, and Ar.glefey, on behalf of themselves, and others travelling through the said Counties, was presented to the House, and read; reciting the Provisions in Two Acts made in the 6th and 17th Years of his present Majesty’s Reign, for obliging the Undertakers of the Navigation of the River Dee to appoint, and keep Two Ferry Boats, for conveying PaflTengers and Carriages over the said River; and also Provision made in the said Act of the 6th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, to oblige the Commissioners therein named, to let out and maintain a convenient Road or Roads over the Sands, Soil, and Grounds, within the Limits of the Works of the said Navigation; and also in the said Act of the 17th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for impower the said Commissioners to set out convenient Roads over the Sands, Soil, and Grounds, vested in the said Undertakers, lying on the North Side of the new Channel, to and from the said Ferries, to the City of Chester, and other Places in the County of Chesterwhich Roads are to be maintained by and at the Charge of the said Undertakers; and setting forth, That no Provision is made by either of the said Acts, for setting out or main-tainingany Road on the South Side of the said new Channel over the Salt Marshes, lying between the said Ferries and the Town of Flint; and thar, by reason of the River being brought through the said Marshes, and for want of the South Bank being kept up, the Tides have walbed and worn several of the Gutters, running through che said Marshes, so deep, as to render them impafiable for any

Carriage, and dangerous for a Horse; and that the same cannot be repaired by the Parishes or Townships in which they lie, nor by the County, it being no High Roid before the making of the said Works; and that, for want of such Road, the Petitioners, and all who have orcasion to travel that Way, are forced to go several Miles round, and through very deep Roads; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that, in case an Act shall pass, as desired by the Petition of the said Company, to explain and amend the said former Acts, and for other Purposes, the same Provision may be thereby made, for setting out, maintaining, and repairing a necessary and convenient Road, or Roads, on the South Side of the said new Channel, over the said Marshes, leading to and from the said Ferries, to the Town of Flint, as is by the former Acts made, for setting out, maintaining, and repairing, the Road or Roads on the North Side of the said new Channel, leading to and from the said Two new Ferries to the said City of Chester.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Undertaking for recovering and preserving the Navigation of the River Dee, in General Court assembled, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as ic shall appear to them, to the House.

Sir Hutchins Williams Baronet, and Perkbam Williams Esquire, were examined, and said. The City of Chichester is burdened with a very numerous Poor; and that it would be of great Advantage if a general Workhouse was established for their Reception and Employment.

Thomas Steele Esquire, Recorder of the said City, was examined, and said, That the Corporation of Chichester acknowledge to have received 2001, in the Years 1664 and 1672, from the Right Reverend Doctor Henry King, and Doctor Peter Gunnings Bishops of Chichester, for the Purposes mentioned in the Petition.

And he produced Two Deeds; whereby it appeared, that the said Corporation did, in 1681, convey a House,

called Cawley s Almshouse, to be used for ever, as a Workhouse for the Poor; and also Two Fields to Trustees, to levy a Fine of the Premises, which should enure to the said Corporation for ever, upon Trust, that they should let the said Lands for any Term, not exceeding 21 Years, and apply the Rents thereof in the Repair and Maintenance of the said House, and the Surplus of the said Rents towards establishing a Manufactory to set the Poor to work; and if that should not be found practicable, then to be employed towards such other like charitable Use, for the Poor, as the Mayor, Recorder, and Aldermen, should appoint; and that, in pursuance of the said Deed, a Fine was accordingly levied.

And the said Mr. Steele said, That the Parishes of St.

1 Peter the Great, St. Bartholomew, and St. Pancrajs, lie partly within the Liberties of the City, and partly without; and that the Close is not within the Jurisdiction of the said Corporation; and that if Provision was made for maintaining and employing the Poor of such Parts of the said Parishes aa lie out of the City, and also of the said Close, in a general Workhouse, it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants:

That the said Almshouse might be made, at a small Expence, a Workhouse for all the Poor of the City, and such Parts of the said Parishes as lie without the City, and of the said Close; and that if the Rents of the said Two Fields were to be appropriated to the Use of the Poor in f such general Workhouse, and Power was given, if there was Occasion, to mortgage or fell the said Fields, and to . apply the Produce of such Sale or Mortgage to the like ‘ ! A Petition of Charles Amcotts Esquire, High Sheriff of Fxportadoi the County of Lincoln, the Right Honourable the Lord of Wool Vere Bertie, and the rest of the Gentlemen upon the fr°®kdandj Grand Jury, at the Assizes held for that County, at the Castle of Lincoln, on the Twelfth Day of March 1753, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That a Bill is depending for permitting the Exportation of Wool, and Woollen or Bay Yarn, from any Port in Ireland, to any Port in Great Britain; and setting forth, That the Petitioners, for several Years past, have been not only encouraged, by a tolerable ready Sale for Wool, but also necessitated, by the Distemper of the Cattle (not yet ceased) to flock their Lands extraordinarily with Sheep; insomuch, that at this Time there is not only much more Wool than usual growing, but great Quantities of the last Year lying upon the Hands of the Farmers unfold; and if still more was wanted, more would naturally be produced; and alleging, That the Importation of Wool from Ireland is prejudicial; and that the Petitioners have been informed, the Caules of dur late supposed flourifljing Trade for Woollen Goods were accidental, and are, in a great measure, ceased; and that therefore, considering the aforesaid BillI. to be calculated for increasing the Growth of Wool in Ireland, and for the Importation of it in larger Quantities, the Petitioners judge the same to be most, unseasonable, at this Juncture especially: And therefore praying, That either the Importation of Wool, or Woollen Yarn, from Ireland, may be totally inhibited for the present; or for such other Relief, as to the House shall Teem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for permitting the Exportation of Wool and Woollen or Bay Yam from any Poyt jn Ireland, to any Port of Great Britain, be read the Third time.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the7^ by a deficient Importation (all foreign Sugars being ex-Ships mentioned in the Petition were properly fitred out for ’ eluded, by Duties which amount to a Prohibition) may Jbe a Voyage to the Greenland Seas, and there unavoidably loft, a Temptation to them to forbear breaking up more Land

and that the Planters are greater Gainers by a small Importation, than a large one; but the Navigation, the Revenue, the Petitioners, and the Conveners of Sugar, are great Sufferer's; and that the foreign Markets are supplied with Sugar from the French at less than half the Price it is here fold for, exclusive of all Duties paid here; and the Price of Sugars at the British Sugar Colonies is more than double the Price of what it is at the French SugarColonies; and alleging, That theexceffive Gain of the British Planters,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That the Petitioners be paid the Bounty which they would have been intitled to, in case the Ships had performed their Voyages, and all Matters required by the A£Vs of Parliament had been performed.

A Petition of the Sugar Refiners, Grocers/ arid other Dealers in Sugar, in the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Borough of Southwark, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Price of Muscovado Sugar is become excessive high, owing to a deficient Importation from our Sugar Colonies in America; notwithstanding the Assurances given by the Planters in the Year 1739, of a much greater Supply, when the Legislature indulged them the Xiberty of fend ing their Sugars directly to ahy foreign PortSouth of Cape Finisterre; and that, ever Once Lady-day 1749, the Sugar Planters have received for their Sugars a much higher Price than what they did for many Years before the Commencement of the late War; and notwithstanding these Encouragements, instead of increasing their Plantations, and fending home a larger Produce, they have decreased in their Importation ever since the Year 1739, upon an Average, very considerably;

VOL. 26.

which our other Sugar I Hands are subject, have, notwithstanding, forborn to cultivate them; bjat, instead thereof have pradbifed the Trade of refining Sugar there;' and, in order to encourage it, have imposed #, Puty of no less than 6 d. per Pound on al) refined Sugary imported from Great Britain, to the great Detriment of the Navigation and Revenue of this Kingdom, as wellas of the Petitioners; and that, in some of the other British Sugar Islands, Refineries are likewise fee jjp; which Pradtic<? *i$ injurious to the Navigation and Revenue, by diminUhing, the Quantity of Muscovado Sugar, which would otherwise be imported; and interferes with the Manufacture of refining Sugar here: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and make it the interest of the British SugarColonies to produce, and fend home, a large Quantity of Sugar to Great Britainin order to ’ become more useful to their Mother Country, its Trade, Navigation, and Revenue; or to grancany ocher Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Prayers.

A PET IT I ON of the Sugar Refiners, Grocers, and Importation other Dealers, in Sugar, in the City of Bristol, whose of Sugar. Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the present excessive Price of Muscovado Sugar is principally owing to a Deficiency in the Importation of that Commodity from the British) Sugar Colonies in America; and that, notwithstanding the Planters have been indulged by the Legislature with the Liberty of fending their Sugars directly to any Port South of Cape Finisterre, on their Assurances that their Colonies made a larger Produce than could be vended in this Kingdom, yet, instead of fending Home a larger Quantity of Sugar, they have (upon an Average) considerably decreased in their Importation ever since die Year 1739, although they have made no use of such Indulgence, finding the Prices at our Markets to be higher than at ail others; and that, although the Planters themselves may be greater Gainers by a small Importation than a large one, yet the same is, and will be, very detrimental to the Navigation, the Revenue, and the Dealers in, and Consumers of Sugars in this Kingdom; and that the excessive Gain of the British Planters by a deficient Importation (whilst all foreign Sugars are excluded by Duties nearly amounting to a Prohibition) may* probably induce, if it has not already induced, many of them to forbear extending the Cultivation of their Lands for SugarPlantations, especially in the Island of Jamaica, wherein there are large Tracts of Land fit for that Purpose, which dill remain uncultivated; and that the foreign Markets arefuppiied with Sugar from the French at half the Price the same is fold for in England; and the exporting either Muscovado or refined Sugar to any Port in Europe is greatly prejudiced by the high Prices, even to Ireland, where they use the Liberty they have of importing all the Portugal Sugars they can, and White clayed Sugar from Lisbon are received there (as the Petitioners are credibly informed), which in a great Measure defeats the wife Design of the Legislature in granting the Bounty on refined Sugars, which used to be exported from hence in large Quantities; and that the Deficiency in the Exportation of Sugars, and the high Price to which the same are raised in consequence thereof, is not only very detrimental to the Manufacturersofrefining ofSugars, wherein great N umbers of Persons are employed, who depend entirely upon it for the Support of themselves and Families, but the Revenue will thereby be greatly injured, and all his Majesty’s Subjects, who now look upon the L fe of this Commodity asone of the Conveniences of Life, pvt to extravagant and unreasonable Expence; and that the Inhabitants and Proprietors of the Island of Jamdicah avc lately pruftifed the Trade of refining Sugar there; and, in order to encourage it, and farther to dtftrefs their Mo-8 S ther

710 / £3 Martii.: A% 1753.

ther Country, have imposed a Duty of Sixpence in the Pound on all refined Sugars imported from Great Britain, to die great Prejudice of Navigation, his Majesty’s Revenue, and the Manufacturers here; and that, in some of the other British Sugar [(lands, Refining Houses have been fe.t up, and Sugars refined, which is, in the like manner, prejudicial: And therefore praying the Houseto take the % Premiles into their Consideration, and, by a salutary Law

for that Purpose, make it the Interest of the British Sugar Colonies, to extend the Cultivation of their Lands, in order to enable them to raise a larger Produce, and to fend greater Quantities of Sugar to Great Britian, and thereby become niore useful to their Mother Country, its Trade, Navigation, and Revenue; or to grant such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Petition of the Sugar Refiners, Grocers, and other Dealers in Sugar, in the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Borough of Southwark, whose Names are thereunto subscribed.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, passed in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for repairing the Road from Catberick Bridge, in the County of York, to Stockton, and to the City of Durham, was read; by which Act several Tolls and Powers were granted for the Repair of the said Road.

Mr. Benjamin Chip was examined; and said, That' all the said Road is 42 Miles in Length; and that all the said Road (except about One Mile) has been repaired; but, as the Trustees have not been able to keep the same in Repair, several Parts thereof are now in a very ruinous Condition:

That the said Road is the common Highway to the Ports of Yarm and Stockton; and is also, in many Parts, for a considerable Way together, the common Road to several Coal Mines, Coal Pits, and Lead Mines.

And it appeared by the Treasurer’s Book, That 6000l. had been borrowed, and was now remaining due, upon the Credit of the Tolls, besides iqo /. for Interest; and that the Tolls collected had amounted, upon a Medium per Annum, to between 5<:oand 600l.

And the said Mr. Chip said, That there are many Hills and Bridges upon the said Road; and that Materials, proper for the Repair of the fame, lie at a considerable Distance; and that the Interest upon the said Sum of 6000 /. and the Expences of keeping the Road in Repair, and of carrying the Act into Execution, will amount to 955 /. \$s. od. per Annum.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had diredbed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House j and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Storey, being examined, laid, That the Town of Paisley carries on a considerable Manufacture of Thread and Linen Cloth, and thin Lawns:

That the said Town is Gtuate on the River Cart, which falls into the Clyde, about Four Miles below Glasgow* but that there are so many Obstructions to the Navigation of the said River, by Fords, Banks, and Rocks, that Vis very difficult for a Boat ro get up to the Town; and that the Witness himself has failed down the said River in a small Boat; but that he and the rest of the Passengers were obliged frequently to get on Shore, on account of the said Obstructions:

That there is not a sufficient Prison, Court-house, or House of Corrt&ion, in the said Town, nor any School-house; and that the Shambles, which are in the Middle of the Town, are a great Nuisance: That the Inhabitants of the said Tpwn have, by Subscription, built, a new Church, but have not a sufficient Fund for the Stipend of a Minister to officiate therein.

Then the Witness produced to your Committeean Account of the annual Revenue of the Funds of the said Town, together with the present annual Expences payable out of the fame, signed by the proper Officer; whereby it appeared, that the Expence of the Town exceeded their Income yearly 3/. 4s.

And he added. That the several necessary Works before mentioned could not beperfe&ed without the Aid of Parliament.

Mr. Bacon reported from the Committer, who were appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them arc fit to be revived or continued, That the Committee had enquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Clause contained in an Act, made in the 9th and 10th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third (intituled, An Act to settle the Trade to Africa) for allowing, during a limited Time, a Draw-back of the Duties upon the Exportation of Copper Bars imported, and which Clause, after the Expiration thereof, was, by an Act made in the 12th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, revived and continued for Fourteen Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and also the Proviso in the said last Act contained. That no Drawback shall be allowed on the Exportation of any Copper, but such as had been, or should be, imported from the East India and the Coast of Barbary only; and which said Clause and Proviso, by another Act made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, were further continued for Fourteen Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which said Clause and Proviso, by another Act made in the 15th and 16th Years of his present Majesty’s Reign, were further continued for Fourteen Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Sei-Con of Parliament; are near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 19th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign intituled, An Act for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on foreign-made Sailcloth imported into this Kingdom; and for charging all foreign-made Sails with a Duty; and for explaining a Doubt concerning Ships being obliged, at their first letting out to Sea, to be furnished with one complete Set of Sails made of British Sail-cloth; which was to continue in Force from the 24th Day of June 1746, for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the further Punishment of Persons going armed, or disguised, in Defiance of the Laws of Customs or Excise; and for indemnifying Offenders against those Laws upon the Terms in this Act mentioned; and for the Relief of Officers of the Customs, in Informations upon Seizures; which Act was to continue in Force for the Space of seven Years, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament; as relates to the further Punishment of Persons going armed, or disguised, in Defiance of the Laws of Customs or Excise; and for the Relief of Officers of the Vol. %6.

Customs, in Informations upon Seizures; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 19th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to enable his Majesty to make Rules, Orders, and Regulations, more effectually to prevent the Spreading of the Distemper which now rages amongst the horned Catde in this Kingdom; which was to continue in Force for the Space of Eight Months, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act made in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was explained, amended, and continued, and to be in Force, with the said last mentioned Act, for the Space of pight Months, from the 10th Day of Jamary 1746,.and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which said Acts, by an Act made in the 21st Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, were further continued until the 24th. Day of September 1748, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act made in the 22d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, werr further continued until the 24th Day of September 1749, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and also several Clauses in the said Act, made in the 22d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, foe amending, explaining, ind enforcing, the said Acts, made in the 19rh and 20th Years of his present Majesty’s Reign; and for preventing the Spreading of the Distemper amongst the horned Cattle; and for impowering his Majesty to prohibit the killing of Cow Calves; and which, by an Act made in the 23d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, were further continued until the 29th Day of September 1750, and from thence to the End of the rhea next Session of Parliament; and also several Clauses in the said Act, made in the 23d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, and which, by an Act made in the 24th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, were further continued until the ift Day of September 1751* and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and also several Clauses in the said Act, made in the 24th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for explaining and enforcing the said Acts; and which, by an Act made in the ljth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, were further continued until the 1 ft Day of September 1752, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and also several Clauses in the said Act, made in the 25th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, for explaining and amending the said Acts; are near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Clauses contained in an Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom; and for taking off several Duties on Merchandizes exported; and for reducing the Duty upon Braver Skins, Pepper, Mace, Cloves, and Nutmegs, imported; and for Importation of all Furs of the Product of the British Plantations into this Kingdom only; and that the Two Corporations of Assurance, on any Suits brought on their Policies, shall be liable only to Angle Damages and Costs of Suit, relating to the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom; and for taking off several Duties on Merchandizes exported; which were to continue in Force for Three Years, from the 25th Day of March 1722, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which said Clauses were, by an Act made in the 11th Year of his said late Majesty’s Reign, continued from the Expiration thereof for Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and by another Act, made in the ad Year of his present Majesty's Reign, were further continued, from the Expiration thereof, for Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and by another Act, made in the Second Year of his present Majesty 's Reign, were further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the AjdV

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others of his Majesty’s Subjects, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act lately passed, for encouraging the White Herring Fishery, all Vessels intended for tSe Utter Fishing in the Western Seas are required to rendez-

vous at the Port of Campbeltoun, in order to their being intitled to the Benefit of that Act; and alleging, That the said Port of Cajnpbeltoun.is very incommodious for all Vessels which go on the said Fishery, from any Part of the Eastern Shore, being obliged to fail a great Way beyond ' the Fishing Grounds, and back again, through a dangerous Sea, which is attended sometimes wich no (mail Risque, and always with great Loss of Time, besides Charges; and that all Vessels going on the said Fishing from the East-ward, pass dole by the Orkneys; and there being at Kirkwall, in the Orkneys, not only a Custom-house, but also a good and safe Harbour, it would be very beneficial if all Vessels going from the Eastward, to the said Fishing, were permitted to rendezvous there; and that, as the Nature of the said latter Fishery requires no more than one Fleet of Nets, it would be a Saving and a Benefit both to the private Adventurers and to the Publick, if the Law required no more; and that the time appointed by the said Act, for the Rendezvpus of Fifiiing Vessels, for the latter Fishing, should be altered conformable to the Stile now in use: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and do therein what to them shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act made in the 23d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of the British White Herring Fishery, and for regulating the said Fishery, according to the Calendar now in use; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed. That they have Power to receive a Clause or Clauses for verifying the Account of Salt delivered, or to be delivered, to the said Society, or their Agents, for curing of White Herrings, under the Acts of the Fifth and Eighth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and the Eighth Year of his present Majesty, which have been, or shall be, sent to foreign Markets immediately from Sea, without being first brought into Port.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to gr*l6k resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon Fishefy. the said Bill, be now read:

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

Being asked, if Wepra Gutter, which lay in the.old Road, was not dangerous before the new Navigation? He said, he believed it was always so 2 and that be believed People might go over the Marshes before the Navigation, when the said Gutter was very bad; but that the Road from the Ferries to Chester, on the North Side* is very good.

Being asked, whether any particular Parifne&or Town-jOiips are obliged to repair the said Road on the South Side of the River? He said, That Application would have sheen made ro compel the repairing thereof, if the Road could have been proved to he a publick High Road.

And being further asked, whether the Commifilcners are obliged to make the Road, on the North Side the River, any further than the Company’s Lands extend ? He laid, he thought not; and tjiat, he believes the Company have no Lands on the‘South Side of the Riyer.

That, for the better Payment of the Bounties allowed by Law, upon the Exportation of Com from that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, the Commissioners of the Customs at Edinburgh be authorized and required, upon a Certificate from the Collector of the Customs at any Port in Scotland, that he has not fuflteient in his Hand to pay the Bounty on Corn exported from such Port,^irifing out of the Customs and Duties out of which it ought to be paid; to cause the Monies thereby due to be paid in Three Months by the General Receiver or Cashier of the Customs in Scotland, out of such Monies as shall be in his Hand arising out of such Customs and Duties as are chargeable with the Payment of such Bounty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That, from and after the T wency-fifth Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred Fifty-three, Interest after the Kate of Three Pounds per Centum per Amum, be allowed upon every Debenture, for the Bounty on the Exportation of Corn from any Port within that Parc of Great Britain called Scotland, payable by die General Receiver or Caftiier of the Customs at Edinburgh, which, after the End of Six Months next following the Day on which the same shall be produced to the Commissioners of the Customs at Edinburgh, shall remain unsatisfied, to be computed from the End of the said Six Months, until the Principal, with such Interest, shall be paid, or until Money sufficient shall be reserved for that Purpose, and proper Notice shall be given thereof; such Interest, together with the Principal, to be paid out of such Customs or Duties as are chargeable with the Payment of any Bounty fof the Exportation of Corn.

Good*) and other Things, so sent by the Petitioners, and other Traders of this Kingdom, in single Letters, not being whipped up in another Piece of Paper, but inclosed in, or affixed to,lhe Piece of Paper whereon the Letters containing the same were wrote, the said Letters arc (as the Petitioners are advised) by the said Act, only chargeable with the Portage of single Letters; or if charged by Weight, in case such Letters should weigh less than Half an Ounce they are chargeable only with the Weight of a Quarter of an Ounce, which is the same as the Portage of a single Letter; and taking Notice, That, in the Bill depending in the House, for the more effectual preventing the fraudulent Removal of Tobacco by Land or Water, and for the Ease of the fair Trader in Tobacco, and for ascertaining the Rares payable for the Portage of certain Letters, and for amending and explaining the Laws relating to the Sale of Spirituous Liquors by Retail, there is a Clause inserted. That for every single Letter, or Piece of Paper, containing One or more Pattern or Patterns of Cloth, Silk, or Stuff, or One or more Sample or Samples of any other Sort of Goods, or One or more Piece or Pieces of any other Sort of Thing inclosed or affixed thereto, though not Paper, if the same together do not weigh an Ounce Weight, the Rates payable by the said Act for a double Letter, shall be paid, and no more; and alleging, That the said Clause, in case the same should pass into a Law, will bringan additional Burthen upon the Petitioners, and others the Traders of this Kingdom, by subjecting them to double v Portage, in the Cafes above-mentioned; which will be of great Prejudice to the Trade of this Kingdom, and the Manufactures thereof: And therefore praying, That the said Clause may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Complaint being made to the House, That the Publishers of several News Papers had taken upon them to give Accounts therein of the Proceedings of this House;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That it is an high Indignity to, and a notorious Breach of the Privilege of, this House, for any News Writer, in Letters, or other Papers (as Minutes, or under any other Denomination) or for any Printer or Publisherof any printed News Paper, of any Denomination, to presume, under any Pretence whatsoever, to insert in the said Letters or Papers, or to give therein any Account of the Debates, or other Proceedings whatsoever, of this House, or of any Committee thereof, as well during the Recess, as the Sitting of Parliament 5 and that this House will proceed with the uemost Severity against such Offenders.

In Support of the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Thomas Paulin said, That he had made observa^ tions of the several Streets of the said City and Liberty, and

A. 1753-

that in general the Pavements are in a very ruinous Condition; and he particularized several Places, which he said were very dangerous for Carriages, not only upon Account of the Pavement being broke up,but from thcDeepness of the Kerinels, which are dangerous for Carriages to cross:

That the Pavement in general is not fa good, nor doe* it last so long, as if the whole was pitched with Stones of a moderate Size.: and that the Proprietors of the Waterworks do great Damage to the Pavement, as they never repair the Places they break up so well: as they ought to do.

Mr. Franklin said, That he had observedthe Pavements, in different P^rts of the Town, to be very bad; that he had seen a Coach broke down, and another overturned, which he attributed to the Deepncfs of the Kennel.

He then mentioned several Streets in the Parish of Si. Martin, the Pavements whereof he said were very bad; andi in general, that whole Pariflv is very ill lighted, cleansed, and paved.

Thomas Smith Esquire confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Paulin; and added, Thatthe Acftof the 2d of King William, relating to the lighting and cleansing the Streets in the City and Liberty of Westminster, is greatly defective, and very ill executed; and he mentioned to your Committee, several Streets of the said Ctcy and Liberty, and the Number of Houses and Lamps "in each Street, a particular Account whereof he said he had took; and that many of the Lamps are lighted at the Expence of the Crown; and cnoft of the others are lighted only from Michaelmas to Lady-day i and that the Streets in general are very ill cleansed.

Thomas Lediard Esquire laid. That he does not think the Laws for paving, lighting, and cleansing, the Streets in the said City and Liberty, sufficient to answer those Purpose*:

That in respect to Lighting, the A6fc dife&s no more than from Michaelmas to Lady-day, and, in that Period, not after Twelve o’Clock at Night, and that only extends to Houses in the open Streets; and should the Owners of those Houses neglect to hang out Lights, he Ihoukl be afraid to execute the Laws to compel them:

That he is equally afraid of enforcing the Laws against Persons neglecting to keep their Pavements in Repair, or indeed any penal Law whatsoever.

And being alked, If a regular Information was to be brought against any Person, for not keeping his Pavement in Repair; Whether he would not put the Law in Execution ? he said, If that was to be the Cafe, he could not refuse it; but that he should not think himself safe in doing it; and laid, He had never known any such Information brought.

Stuff, or One or more Sample or Samples of any other Sort of Goods, or One or. more. Piece or Pieces of any . other Sort of Thing inclosed therein, or affixed there;-to, though not Paper, if the same together do not weigh an Ounce Weight, or Half^ an Ounce Weight, the Rates payable by an Act of the 9th Year of Queen Anne for a double Letter shall be paid for the Port of every such Letter, will, in cale the same should pass into a Laws. bring an additional Burthen upon the Petitioners, and;, others, the Traders of this Kingdom, by fubjccting them to double Portage in Cafes mentioned in the Petition, which will be of great Prejudice to the Trade of this, Kingdom, and the Manufactures thereof: And therefore praying, That the said Clause may not pals into a Law; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from and after the Expiration of the Term for which the Bounties on the Exportation of British and Irish coarle Linens by several Acts of the Fifteenth, Sixteenth, and Eighteenth Years of the Reign of his present Majesty, were granted, and by several Acts of the Twentieth and Twenty-second Years of the Reign of his present Majesty, continued and made payable, the Sum of Three thousand Pounds, be paid yearly and every Year, for the Space of Nine Years, to the Commissioners and Trustees for improving Fisheries and Manufactures in Scotland, to be charged and chargeable upon, and payable out of, any of the Customs, Duties, Excises, or other Revenues, in Scotland, introduced by virtue of the Treaty of Union, or to which the Subjects of Scotland are, or shall be liable, and to be applied by the said Commissioners and Trustees, forencouraging and improving the Manufactory of Linen in the Highlands of Scotland only.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Prison of the Marfoalfea of the Court of King's Bench is, in its present Condition, unsafe for the Custody, and dangerous to the Health, of the Prisoners; which Inconveniencies cannot be remedied unless the Prison be rebuilt.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Office of Marshal of the Marflmlfea of the Court of King's Bench, is an Office of great Trust and Importance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the granting in Fee by King James the First, and the subsequent Mortgaging of the Office of Marshal of the Marshalsea of the Court of King's Bench, by Persons claiming Title under the Crown, has been a very great Obstruction to the due and proper Exercise of the said Office, highly detrimental to the Authority and Jurisdiction of the said Court, and to the Safety of the Prisoner9 committed to the Prison of the Marfiafea of the Court of King's Bench.

A PETITION of the Merchants and Traders of the Removing Town of Macclesfield, in the County of Chefiery was Tobacco, presented to the House, and read} alleging, That the Alterations intended by the Bill, depending in the House, for ascertaining the Rates payable for the Portage of certain Letters will be a great Clog upon Trade, and contrary to the original Intent of erecting the General Post Office, which was to preserve and encourage Commerce, not to burthen it: And therefore praying, in case the House should think proper to make any Alterations in the present Laws relating to the Portage of Letters by the General Post Office, That (for the Encouragement of Trade) it may be to ascertain the Rates payable for the Portage of all Letters inclosing Patterns (under an Ounce Weight) to be the same as for Single Letters.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Upon the Petitions of the Manufacturers of the Town and County of Nottinghamr

Mr. John Page, a Frime-work'Knit ter, at Nottingham, said. That the Company had Deputies at Nottingham, from 1718 to 1730, and appointed others the latter end of 1751, who now continue there; and that from 173010 1751 the trade of that Place greatly increased; and, in his Opinion, the Trade had decreased in London in that Period, because at least 800 Second-hand Frames came from London to Nottingham lince that time, and were fold for £. 100.per Cent, less than their Value:

That all the Deputies at Nottingham are Stocking-makers, and employ Persons not free of the Company, both Women and Children, in common with their Neighbours) and if that was not the Practice, it would be very injurious to Trade, as Hose arc made so low priced as i d% a Pair; in which Branch of Trade no Person will work who has served an Apprenticefhipof Seven Years.

That he never knew the Deputies apply any Money for the Benefit of the Trade, or refulc any rerfon his Freedom, who was willing to pay for it; that, upon binding an Apprentice, they never desire to fee the Proof Piece, but receive the Money for it:

781

That he never heard that the Company endeavoured Frame-work to prevent Frauds in the Manufacture; and believed the Knitten. foie Reason of putting their By-laws into Execution was to raise Money:

That the Court at Nottingham summoned whom they thought proper to attend them, and be admitted; that when the Company came to Nottingham, several of the ftibftamial Hofiers met the Master and Wardens at the Crown Inn s where their Clerk made a Speech, shewing the Utility of the Court; to which the principal Hofiers intirely disagreed; whereupon the Master and Wardens proceeded to threaten them with Proceedings at Law; but they were so far from being affrighted with their Threats, that if they could then have tried the MatteF, they would have joined Issue:

That 3 of the principal Hofiers, who keep ioo Frames each, desired it might be tried with them, and not with the poor Manufacturers 5 to which the Company answered, they would begin with whom they pleased:

And that when the Company was told, that as the Town of Leicester, and Country adjacent, had never acknowledged the Company, it was very hard to begin with Prosecutions against the People of Nottingham, who bad stood by the Company until the Manufacture had like to have been loft; to which the Company again replied, they would begin with whoiq, and where, they pleased:

That the Company acquainted the Manufacturers, that their By-laws were Sgned by the Lord Chancellor, and the Two Chief Justices and that this (as he apprehends) was the Company’s foie Pretence for creating their Court:

And he produced to your Committee a printed Paper, dated 14th October 1752, many of which he saw dispersed by the Beadle giving Notice that a Court would be held on the 26th of that Instant, at the Crown Inn, in the Long RowNottingham, for admitting all Matters and Journeymen, who were desirous to take up their Freedom; which Paper is annexed in the Appendix, N°. 3.

And, to shew that the Company themlclves have been of Opinion, that the By-laws, by them made, cannot affect any but their own Members, the following Paragraph, in a Letter wrote by the then Clerk of the Company, by Order of the Master, and a Committee of the Company, to the Deputies at Nottingham, dated aoth May 173 a, was read.

44 1 am also directed to say somewhat as to the unadmitted Members} it would surely never be apprehended by you, that such would be effectually brought into Subjection by any By-laws made, or to be made 44 (the By-laws of any Corporation only afftdling their own Members) and therefore the Unadmitted are not compellable to be admitted by virtue of any By-law; 44 but that must be done by Authority of Parliament; 4‘ which, after the Establishment of our By-laws, we in- tend to apply for; and a Abort Clause in an Act will effectually do that BuGness: And I do allure you the Court hath that Point at Heart, as much as you possibly can; but the Work we are about was thought to be most necessary, in order first of all to repair the Breach nude by the late Trials at Law,

And to shew the great Increase and State of the Manufacture for several Years part,

Mr. William Woolley, Mr. Samuel Handley, Mr. Wil-

liam Davey, Mr. John Hook bam, and Mr. "Timothy Hem-all of the City of London, and considerable Dealers in the aforesaid Manufactures, and who employ great Numbers of Manufacturers in different Parts of England were examined; and by whose Evidence it appeared to your Committee,

That the said Manufactory had, from the Year 1730, greatly increased, both in the Consumption at home, and in the Quantities exported; and that, at present, there is a want of Hands to carry on the same:

That from 1720, to 1730, when the company were in a more flourishing Condition, and when more Trade centered in their Hands, than at present, worfc Goods were iu general made than at this time; and One of the Wicnesses said, that, the more any Trade is laid open, the better it is for that Trade, and for the Nation in general: That it would be a great Disadvantage ter the Manufacturers, if Persons, who are not free of the Company, were not frittered to let out Frames, as there are several Persons who keep Frames constantly to let by the Year: That several of the present By-laws are prejudicial to the Manufacturers 5 and that the Company acting under them are so far from being an Advantage to the Trade, that it is a Burthen and Incumbrance to it: that Frauds are committed in the Marking of Hose, as well byPeribns free of the Company, as by those who are not free; and that Regulations, under proper Persons, might be of Advantage to Trade, if it could be done without putting a Burthen upon the Manufacture; but that the laying any Burthen upon the Manufacture would over-balance the Regulations.

Upon the Petition of the Manufacturers of Leicester, Mr. Richard Garle said, he is a Manufacturer of Stockings at Leicester; and that the Trade has greatly increased there within these 20 Years, and if they had more Hands, they might have employment: That he had fecn the Company’s By-laws, in Print, and apprthended them to be injurious to Trade:

That he did not think it necessary, that a Person should serve Seven Years Apprenriccship to learn the Trade: That the Witness had 100 Frames at present; and apprehended, if he could not let them to Hire without being free of the Company, it would be a great Injury to him; and that, by a printed Table of Fees, he had seen the Fee for Admittance is 15 Shillings, and he had been told so by several People.

And, being croL-examineJ, he said. That the Company had never exerc;fcd any Juriiuiction at Leicester these 20 Years; and tin: he knew nothing of the Company, or their Powers, but by report.

Then to shew the general Behaviour of the Company,

Mr. Matthews was examined; and said. He had been Clerk to the Company from 1728 to 1742: That during that tim^h? never knew the Company guilty of One hard Act, buHjfe contrary:

That,*perhaps, in that Period, 8 or 10 Actions might be brought, but not above One tried; the rest were discontinued, either on Submission of the Party, or on account of their Poverty.

Being asked, if the Company had ever took any Measures to improve the trade? He said, That, in London, they used to go to examine Work', and to detcCl frauds: and that, he believed, they had done it in the Country § for that he had been with the Company, as Clerk, at Godalming, and had attended them in their Searches; and that they there bound Apprentices and made Freemen, and visited the Workmen and examined their Work.

And he said, he apprehended, it was owing to the Company's

party's inspecting Goods, that made Persons cautious what Goods they manufactured: Thac he had seen them examine Proof Pieces before the Persons were admitted; but that no bad Goods were ever produced before them.

And being asked, if he did not remember Persons summoned, from distant Parts, to attend the Company in London? He said he did not.

Then to shew the Motives for the Company’s appointing Deputies at Nottingham, and their Conduct there;

Mt. James Holland and Mr. Viliters laid. That the Company’s Motives for making Deputies at Nottingham were the Good of the Trade, and at thet Desire of a Majority of the Trade, at a great Meeting in the Country; at which Meeting the Wicnesses were present.

And being asked, why the Manufacturers applied for a Court there ? They said, because they thought it would be for the Benefit of Trade; and that the Gentlemen, at the Meetings, behaved with great Candour, and no Threats were used to any present: And Mr. Villiers,being alkcd in what manner the Employers and Mailers were called together at the said Meeting, laid, that publick Notice was not given of such Meeting; but that the Persons, who met, assembled upon private Invitation; and thac there were Objections made to the 14th By-law, and the Deputies proposed to alter such By-laws as the Trade thought ufeltfs.

Being cross examined, he said, That, 15 Months ago, he was an Opponent of the Company, because he had heard that they rellrained the Trade; but upon considering the thing maturely, he found the Arguments made Use of against the Company to be falsely grounded; for that the Company V Rules rather tended to increase, than restrain the Trade:

Tha«, with regard to the 14th By-law, the Witness is of the same Qpiniori he always Was^ that it is a bad one; and that, in general, he did not fee much Complaint to be. roaide against any of the others.
