Mr. Bacon reported from the Committee, who were appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, or continued; That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for prohibiting the Importation of Books reprinted abroad, and Arft composed or written and printed in Great Britain; and for repealing so much of an Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, as impowers the limiting the Prices of Books; which Ad was to continue in Force, from the 29th Day of September 1739> for the Space of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act made in the 20th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the 29th Day of September 1754., and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; as relates to the prohibiting the Importation of Books reprinted abroad, and first composed or written and printed in Great Britain; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the better Encouragement of the Making of Sail-cloth in Great Britain, which was to continue in Force for Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which was, by an Act made in the 5th Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, further continued for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 10th Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was further continued for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 8th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued until the 25th Day of March 1742, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 15th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued until the First.-Day of June 1747, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the First Day of June 1754, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act, made in the 7th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Revival of an Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for the free Importation of Cochineal during the Time therein limited, and also for the free Importation of Indico, which was to continue in Force, from the 24th Day of June 1734, for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 14th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the First Day of June 1747, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the First Day of June 1754, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 5th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act, passed in the First Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for punishing such Persons as shall wilfully and maliciously pull down and destroy Turnpikes for repairing Highways, or Locks, or other Works erected by Authority of Parliament for making Rivers navigable; and also an Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for rendering the Laws more effectual for punishing such Persons as shall wilfully and maliciously pull down or destroy Turnpikes for repairing Highways, or Locks, or other Works erected by Act of Parliament for making Rivers navigable, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, which said Acts expired, and were afterwards, by an Act made in the 15th and 16th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, revived, and were to be in Force, for the Purposes therein mentioned, from the First Day of June 1742, until the First Day of June 1747; and which, by another Act made in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the First Day of June 1754, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

A PETITION of John Bonnell Esquire was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Bill, now depending in the House, for discharging the Corporation of the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Company of the Conservacors of the Great Level of the Fens, commonly called Bedford Level, from a Debt due to the Duke of Bedford and Earl of Lincoln-, and for enabling the Proprietors of Lands in the North Level, Part of the said Great Level, to raise Money to discharge the Proportion of the said North Level in the Debts of the said Corporation; and for ascertaining and appropriating the Taxes to be laid on the said North Level; and for the more effectual draining and preserving the said North Level, and divers Lands adjoining thereto, in the Manor of Crow!and; will greatly prejudice the Petitioner, if the same should pass into a Law as it now stands, the Petitioner having a considerable Estate in South Holland\ in the County of Lincoln: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by himself, or Counsel, against the said Bill, or to such Part thereof as affects and relates to the Property of the Petitioner; and that he may have such further and other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordaed, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioner be heard, by himself, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fir.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That Mr. Torke of Higham Ferrers do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

That, before the said Bill is read a Second time, Copies thereof may be delivered to the Solicitor or Agents of the Petitioners, to be sent to the Petitioners and the Owners of such Lands and Estates (several of whom are at a remote Distance) as the said intended Canal is to be cut through, to examine and consider how and in what manner the said Bill may affect the Publick, or damage the Owners of the Lands it is to concern; and that such Efficient Time be allowed for the fame, as to the House shall seem meet and proper for a Matter of such Moment and Consequence to that Country; and that if any Obscurities shall appear in the said Bill, that the said Persons concerned in the said Scheme shall fully and clearly reveal and discover their said Scheme in its full Extent, and in every Light and Branch thereof; and that the Petitioners may be heard by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, touching such Objections as they may have to the said Scheme,

Your Committee then proceeded to examine Mr. Leheup; and, being asked what Method he pursued in taking in Contributions, he gave the following Account.

At the time the Aft and Scheme were known, 1 thought it my Duty to promote the Subscription as much as I could, and more so as every Body seemed todefpair of the Success — I did endeavour to accommodate Gentlemen as much as 1 could. I took down the Names in the original Book; which was the only Entry — As soon as any Name was in that Book, I looked upon it as condusive in me to give those Tickets.

No Person, who was put down in that Book to have Tickets, was afterwards refused to my Know ledge, if the First Payment was offered me before the 25 th of July — 1 think the Names before the Name of George Fox Laney Page 54, were taken down without Money before the

14th June, unless some few to accommodate them — I acted according to my Judgment, I took no Money before Bonds were given — I had no Interest but ro accommodate Gentlemen — It has been the constant Method in the Lotteries I have been Manager in, to deliver Certificates in Exchange for Tickets the Day before advertised, in order, to take off Hurry the next Day.

I frankly own I was told by the Speaker of the House of Commons, That no-body was to have above soTickets, and that there must be no Lifts — I represented the great Difficulties it would put the Receivers to; and that Foreigners could not come in, if no Lifts; nor People from Ireland, nor People in the Country — I represented very strongly this Lottery would want all Manner of Encouragement to be given to Subscribers — Speaker told me, " Sir " John Barnard and I have warranted to the House no-<c body shall have more than 20" — I was going away, and the Speaker saw I was dispirited with respect to the Success of the Lottery (this was the Day the Act passed, or the Day before): Speaker said, <c I tell you for your " Comfort, I hear, Mr. Nejhilt from Ireland has Commission for 1,000 Tickets." 1 then did tell People about Offices I was under Difficulties about taking in Lifts, and desired several People not to bring me any; some People then gave m'e Names without any List at all, so many for one, and so many for another, and brought different Names upon different Slips of Paper; the great Bankers who applied, I thought might have Occasion for a great Number of Tickets by Commissipn.

When I found there were these Subterfuges, I thought one thing became the Speaker of the House of Commons and another thing became a Clerk. It gave me inexpressible Concern not to be able to comply strictly with Mr. Speaker’s Declaration to me of the Intention of the Act — Upon which I read the Act — I thought I was exposed to Complaints on both Sides; but there was no going back, I had accepted the Office, for which I was very sorry — I thought the safest Side was to secure ioo,ooooh to the Publick: I was told so by most of my Friends — As to the Intention of the Act, I thought the Intention of the Preamble to the Lottery Part declared no other Intention in Parliament than raising the Money — I thought by the Act I was obliged to receive Money from any Contributors, for as many as they asked, not exceeding 20 for any one Person — There was nothing I thought could dispence me from it, but Orders, Rules, and Directions, from the Archbishop, Chancellor, Speaker, or Two of them; and I had no Opportunity to apply to them jointly from the Hurry and Confusion that followed — And I thought it would be an indelible Reproach to me to lose the Filling of such a Lottery, by putting Contributors under Difficulties which I knew every one could evade: I thereupon did tell People they were to have but Twenty for themselves, and the common Answer was, " What they asked for more was for Friends and Rela^ " tions." — I had no Power to oblige them to take an Oath — On the 14th, when the Crowd came on, there was an End of all Order and Quefiions of every Sor: — I was exceffivtly eager to lay hold of the Opportunity; too eager — I worked beyond my Strength, in taking Money and signing Receipts. It was the First time I was so employed, and could not bear to fee People fainting from the great Crowd without giving all the Assistance 1 could — I found the Office was too final!; but was too late to remedy it — If I would ask Quefiions, it was only augmenting the Crowd, and endangering the filling the Lottery; for I must observe that i knew at that time, that there were a great many Irish Lotteries going on. 1 was apprehensive in Holland and France Lotteries would be grafted on ours; and though I saw a Crowd Today, I doubted we ffiouid have it the morrow — At about One of the Clock that Day, no Gentleman would have wished himself in my Place for 150/. which was my Parliamentary Allowance — People broke in upon me, above me, behind me, ancj before me, and in at the Windows with Ladders; the Partitions of my Dcfk were broke down, while I lay exposed to be plundered of all my Money, which was quit$

Lottery for The Exchange of the Receipt Is the Delivery of the purchasing Ticket: And then being asked, How Tickets could &c exchanged, and not claimed at the same time ? he

Ietitions. said, That, from the Beginning, he entered every body’s Name in his Book, who bespoke Tickets, in the Course they bespoke them and when the Quota was settled, that each Receiver was to answer, he looked upon himself as answerable to the Publick for all the Tickets set down in that Book, and bound to pay £.3 to the Publick for each of them and had paid for them beforehand, to accommodate Gentlemen.

That when the 25th of July came, he no longer looked on himself as answerable to those who bespoke them: That he exchanged them for Tickets, and kept them in his Custody, till he found out he had signed more Receipts than he knew of, and then he kept the Tickets to answer such Surplus.

Being asked, If he could assign any Reason why so many Tickets were not claimed? he again mentioned what had passed with regard to Lord Barrington, &c. as before mentioned, but gave no other Reason: Said, He put down no Names as Contributors, without being applied to for that Purpose: Being asked, If Sir Charles Mordaunt had applied for Tickets ? said, He believed he mult have applied to some Friend of his: Being asked the Meaning of the Circumflexes in his Book ? said. He apprehended it was to refer to the Personswho had bespoke Tickets.

Admitted that the Advertisement in the Gazette was put in by his Order, as One of the Four Receivers — Upon this the Committee read the Advertisement in the Gazette of the 9th of June which is as follows:

" Lottery-Office at the Exchequer, June 9, 1753.

u The Receivers of the Contributions to the Lottery <€ for 300,000l. granted by Act of Parliament passed Anno u 1753> ^ve Notice, That thrv have appointed this <c Office wherein to receive, pursuant to the said Act, the f€ Contributions for the Purchase of Tickets in the said <c Lottery, of Three Pounds each Ticket, whereof One <c Pound to be paid down, and the Remainder on or <c before the 26th Day of Oftuber 1753; and that At-cc tendance will be given here on the 14th Inflanr, from c< Nine till Ojie in the Forenoon, for that Purpose, and c< so continue constantly every Day, Sundays and Holi-<c days excepted.’’

And also Two Clauses in the Lottery Act, Page 246 and Page 355.

Whereupon Mr. Leheup being nfked, Whether the Advertisement was repeated in the Gazette? said, He did not know, but that it was repeated in other Papers several times: That he thought the Advertisement of the particular Day a Work of Supererogation, the Act of Parliament not directing that any certain Time should be fixed* and the Reason of his fixing a Time, was, because he thought it for the Benefit of the Service* yet imagined, that by the general Words of the Act, that fays <c at w any time or times after Bond given/* he was justified.

And being asked. Whether he considered himself as an Officer under the Act, who was to obey the Directions or Regulations of it? he said. That he did look upon himself as such an Officer* but thought, that when an Act of Parliament is passed, and unforeseen Cafes and Events happen, which might defeat the whole declared Intention of the Act, it was the Duty of an Officer to comply, as much as was possible in the nature of Things, with the Directions of the Act.

And being asked. What unforeseen Accidents happened, to make him take in Subscriptions before the Time mentioned in the Gazette ? said, Because he knew the Receivers were confined to a very small Place, the Lottery-Office near the Exchequer, where it would be impossible to do the Business without Confusion and Hurry, if the Lottery was to fill.

Being then asked, How the Lottery-Office came to be named ? said, He was sorry ic was wished it had been at the Bank or the South-Sea House: That it was necessary to have a secure Place, and thought being near the Exchequer was some Security: That the Lottery-Office was fixed on soon after the Act passed: That he did not remonstrate against it, because he thought the Security of publick Money was the first: and primary Consideration.

Being asked, How many Subscriptions he took ift before the Day, in order to moderate the Crowd ? said. He did not take any Subscriptions before he had given Bond, and his Commission was signed but that he took down a great many Names before the Day.

And being asked. Whether he had any Admonition, with respect to the Intention of the Act, from any Gentlemen employed in drawing ic up ? said. He had already acquainted the Committee what a certain great Personage had cold him, and was extremely sorry ic was not in his Power to comply with all his Directions.

Being next asked, Whether he was consulted about the Act while it was framing ? said, he was employed as a Clerk, in writing out the Bill: That he never attended the Committee of Gentlemen — Admitted he did make a Draught of a Bill but was no ways originally privy to private Persons being appointed, instead of the Bank, to receive the Money.

Being asked, Whether the exceptionable Parts of this Act are not the same as in his Draught ? said, he really could not tell, but knew the Bill underwent some Alterations.

Being then asked. Whether he took in no Subfqrip-tions before the Day, but from particular Gentlemen, to accommodate them ? said, He was extremely glad when any body offered to subscribe and, if the Lottery had not filled, should have made a bad Figure here, if any Gentleman said he had not taken his Subscription: That he believes in general* after he had given Bond, he took in Subscriptions from every body that offered before the 14th of June and added, That, relying upon the Candour of the Committee, he very freely declared, that he lent a Letter to the Bank of England, to acquaint them, that he would attend the Day before the Day fixed in the Advertisement, to receive such Subscriptions as the Gentlemen of the Bank should desire within the Description of the Act: That he desired a Clerk of the South-Sea House to acquaint the Gentlemen of that Company to the like Effect and told him the Reason was, to avoid the Hurry of the next Day: That the Directors of the Bank said, They would have none at all.

And being asked, Whether he did this as his Duty, or as the bed Expedient to fill the Lottery? said. That what he did, he apprehended to be his Duty.

And being asked. Whether he did not think the Intention of the Act was to raise the Money by an open Subscription ? said, He did think so: That the Advertife-mentcould only mean till the Subscription was completed: That he attended the First Day not only from Nine to One o’Clock, which was the Time advertised, but also from Morning to Night, the whole Day publickly.

And being asked, Whether, by taking Contributions previous to the Time fixed, he did not turn what was intended to be an open Subscription into a private one? said, That he knew there would be as many Tickets left as could be possibly demanded by an open Subscription on the Day advertised.

That, from the Smallness of the Office, and the unpreA vided Cafes in the Act, this was the best Means of furthering the Intention of Parliament: That he thought, if a Gentleman came to ask for Twenty Tickets before the Day appointed, that was an open Subscription within the Intention of the Act, especially as there was enough to supply every body who demanded them the Day advertised: Said, that he took down Names of Contributors before the Act passed, for furthering the Service, and as a private Transaction of his own as an Agent: That he saw no Persons demanding Tickets the First Day within the Hours advertised, that were not served: That, on the Second Day, there were some, to be sure.

Your Committee being desirous to be informed who those large Lifts delivered in by Williams, the Exchequer Porter, came from, he was ordered to attend.

And being called in, and examined as to the Lifts distinguished in Mr. Mujfo's and Mr. Monypenny's Books as Exchequer Lifts ? said. They were delivered to him by Mr. Martin and Mr. Eades, Two Clerks of the Bank, who, from coming every Day to the Exchequer, are called Exchequer Clerks: That at the same time he had a List of Names from Mr. Clift the Banker for about 490 Tickets, and about 50 from Acquaintances of his own; and that the Lifts the Clerks brought from the Bank were rolled up, and he (Williams) did not know what they contained; only the Clerks told him, that the Gentlemen of the Bank had sent them J That, upon his carrying them to the Receivers, he was asked from whence they came: That he answered, " From the Gentlemen of the " Bank/' Wilson, (Mr. Mu/fo*s Clerk) said, There was Work for Two Hours: Upon which Mr. Lebeup said, f< I will take Part, I am willing to oblige every-body;" and that he had not the Receipts till the Saturday or Monday after the 14th of June: That the Receivers asked him no Questions, as they saw the Money agreed with the Lifts.

Williams having referred to Mr. Martin and Mr. Eades, as the Persons he had the Lifts from, your Committee ordered them to attend.

Your Committee, desiring a further Explanation of the Bank Account, ordered that a List of the Bank Notes paid in by Peter Lebeup Esquire, on the 21st of June, should be laid before them; which Lift is annexed in the Appendix, N* 5.

Mr. Henry Martin and Mr. Joseph Eades, being called in, severally said, That they gave Lifts for about 2,500 Tickets to William, and told him they came from the Bank, and at the same time gave him Money and Bank Notes to pay for them: That they chiefly had them from the Bank Clerks, or Gentlemen that kept Cash there.

Mr. Eades further said, That he subscribed for 20 Tickets for himself on Saturday before the 14th of June, and paid his Money to Mr. Lebeup, but had not the Receipts till the Tuesday following.

Your Committee being informed, That Mr. Lebeup attended, and desired to make some Amendments to his former Evidence;

He was called in; and, having produced a Paper of the Amendments, the Minutes were made agreeable thereto.

After which, being asked to explain the Rasure in the Margin, Fo. 1. to Miss Lightfoot* Name, said. The Letters rased were PL; the Meaning of which Note was only a Memorandum to himself to deliver Eight of the Fifteen (put down to Miss Lightfoot) to other People; and named Three Persons for Four of the Eight Tickets: That Miss Lightfoot had only Seven.

As to the Rasure in Fo. 11. to the Name of Benjamin King, he could not say any thing to it. — It was only a little Memorandum of his own.

Mr. Peter Calmel, being again called in, was asked by Mr. Lebeup (with the Leave of the Committee) whether

he did not think that he (Mr. Lebeup) meant the Furtherance of the Service by letting him have the Tickets? — said. He knew he meant it as a Civility to him.

Peter Lebeup Esquire, being examined in regard to the Receipts for 260 Tickets delivered by him to Mr. Calmel, was asked* Why, when a Gentleman applied to him for 260 Tickets in his own Name, he did not give him Twenty, as the most he could have under the Ad, instead of telling him, that if he would give a List that would include the Whole at 20 for each Person, he should have the whole 260? To which he answered, That he did not remember that the Gentleman applied to him for 260 Tickets in his own Name; but believes he might say in general he wanted 260 Tickets, and believes his answer might be, " You can have but Twenty <c for yourself," or of Twenty in your own Name;" and at the same time cold him. If he would have any more, he must set down the Persons Names.

And being asked, When any Gentleman came to ask him for 26b Tickets, whether lie did not think they were for himself? said. He might think so, but he was not sure.

Being asked, Whether he did not tell Mr. Heje, who applied to him on the 13th of June for Receipts, that he had already taken in 5,000 more than his Department I he said. He verily believed he did not: That he might say he could take no more at that time, for that the Subscription he then proposed to take was full.

Mr. Peter Calmel, being again examined, was asked. How he apprehended Mr. Lebeup understood him when he asked for the 260 Tickets ? said. That he believes Mr. Lebeup understood them to be for himself and Friends: That he might say they were for himself and Friends* but will not take upon him to affirm that he said so: That he is not sure Mr. Lebeup said, " Make out a 4< Lift j* he said, I must have a List of Names made <c out;" but the Witness afterwards said. That he thought his first Evidence was to the Purport of whaf passed.

Your Committee then ordered Mr. John Hejfe, Mr. William Turner, and Mr. Joseph Jones, to attend.

And Mr. John Hejfe, being examined, informed your Committee, That he was applied to by Mr. Calmel to get some Tickets from Mr. Lebeup', to whom he applied for that Purpose on Wednesday the 13th of June: And Mr. Lebeup asked him, How many he wanted ? To which the Witness answered, As many as he could spare. Mr. Lebeup replied, cc 1 cannot let you have more than €€ Twenty;" and took the Witness’s Name down for Twenty Tickets, and gave him Two Receipts for Ten each.

Upon the Whole of which Examination, your Committee find the following Fads material to be laid before the House:

That Peter Leheup Esquire, One of the Receivers of the Contributions to the late Lottery, did takedown the Names of several Persons, who desired to be Contributors, a good while before the Act passed, and those to a very considerable Amount.

That Mr. Leheup took upon himself the Management, Order, and Direction of the Lottery, providing all the Clerks, preparing Books and printed Receipts, and fixing the Place for receiving Contributions at, before any Meeting or Board of Receivers.

That the First Meeting of the Four Receivers was on Saturday the 9th of June 175 3, when the Advertisement was produced, appointing the Thursday following, and the subsequent Days, at the Lottery-Office at the Exchequer, for taking in Contributions; and One of the Clerks sent it to the Printer of the Gazette, to be inserted that Evening.

That Mr. Leheup then advised and directed the other Receivers to begin taking Contributions immediately 3 and that Mr. Leheup, and the other Receivers, did thereupon take in Contributions on that and the following Days preceding the 14th of June [Sunday excepted) to a very great Amount.

That the Receipts are all dated on the 14th and 15th June, several of which were issued in Mr. Leheup*s and Mr. Monypenny's Department before the Day advertised.

That on the Day advertised (the 14th of June 1753), and the subsequent Day, Mr. Leheup took in Contributions in a very hasty and irregular Manner, receiving Lifts for large Numbers of Tickets, without any Questions; taking the Lifts and Contribution-money, and putting both into his Drawer, without making any Entry in his Book at the time, or in the Office, of the Contributors Names contained in such Lifts.

That the Answer from the Bank to Mr. Leheup*sLet-Vol. 26,

and that the Receivers would attend on the 13th June Pur^|arin£

1753, to accommodate them), was, that they would have &c# Collec. none. — And this Answer was afterwards confirmed to Mr. tions. Leheup by One of the Directors.

That on the nektDay, the 14th June, Lifts for 2,500 Tickets were brought by Williams the Exchequer Porter, which came, as he said, from the Gentlemen of the Bank:

That Mr. Leheup recommended it to the other Receivers to take in the Lifts, and that he would take some hirn-self.

That a very great Crowd pressing to contribute on the said 14th of June, Mr. Leheup, about One o’Clock, caused Proclamation to be made out at Window, That no more Contributions would be taken that Day.

That all the Receivers, on the said 14th of June, took in Contributions after One o’Clock, and some till near Eight at Night, not only of such as were in the Office at the Time the Doors were (hut, and Proclamation made, but of several others, who got in by means of the Mef-' fengers, and others.

That Contributions were taken in by Mr. Leheup, at the Treasury, on Monday or Tuesday the nth or 12th, and Wednesday the 13th, of June 1753, particularly One Lift from Mr. Calmel for 260 or 270 Tickets, which was made out by him at the Treasury, on Mr. Leheup’s informing him he could have but Twenty Tickets in One Name.

That Mr. Leheup*s Department contains near One,

Half of the Contributors to the whole Lottery.;

That Mr. Leheup d\d not make good his First Payment at the Bank within Three Days after the Lottery was full, as the other Receivers did, and as the Act di-red! s.

That Mr. Leheup issued Receip^ for 705 Tickets more than he had entered in his Book, occasioned by his irre- gular Method of taking in Contributions. .:

That Mr Leheup bought no Tickets, but supplied that Deficiency of 705 out of the non-claimed, double-charged* and forfeited Tickets.

That, in consequence, the non-claimed Tickets, as marked in the Account delivered to the House, does not contain the whole Number of non-claimed Tickets.

That no Contributor’s First Payment became forfeited till after the 26th of October.

That Mr. Leheup disposed of 60 forfeited Tickets on. or before the 26th of Ohober,

That Mr. Leheup has not accounted for the Premium such Tickets bore, as the other Receivers have done.

That it has not appeared to your Committee what Right any Receiver had to dispose of non-claimed Tickets.

That Mr. Leheup has admitted himself answerable for all the First Payments on the non-claimed Tickets;

That no Evidence has been laid before your Committee, to shew why the non-claimed Tickets (hoqld not be deemed forfeited ones.

That Receipts for Tickets bore a Premium before the Day fixed in the Gazette for receiving Contributions to the Lottery, and continued rising for near a Week after.

That above Six thousand Tickets were fold in Exchange Alleys within a few Days after the Lottery was full, for Samjon Gideon Esquire, at a very considerable Premium.

That Samjon Gideon Esquire was gone to Paris before your Committee had the Opportunity of Examining him as to those Tickets.

That a Draught of the said Mr. Gideon*s on Mr. Brajfey and Company, and payable to Mr. Leheup for £ol. was paid into the Bank by Mr. Lebeupy as Part of his First Payment, and brought from the Bank to Mr. Brajfeys on the 19th June 1753.

That a Sum of 1,666/. 5r. is charged as paid at Mr. Brajfey*s the same Day, by Order of Mr. Gideon, to Peter Leheup juniorr Esquire, 1,550/. whereof was paid in Bank Notes i which individual Bank Notes were paid into the Bank, by Mr. Leheup the Receiver, on the 21st of June 1753, towards making good his First Payment.

Then several Clauses in the Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Purchase of the Mufiseum or Colledlion of Sir Hans Sloane, and of the Harleian Collection of Manuscripts; and for providing One general Repository for the better Reception, and more convenient Use, of the said Collections, and of the Cottonian Library, and of the Additions thereto; were read.

Resolved, That Peter Lebeup Esquire did enter the Names of several Persons, as Contributors to the Lottery established by an Act passed last Session of Parliament, in the Book prepared by his Order, and for his Use, as One of the Receivers of the Contributions to the said Lottery; and that Contributors Names for above Five thousand Eight hundred Tickets were entered by him in the said Book before the First Meeting of the Receivers, on Saturday the Ninth of June 1753.

Resolved, That the said Peter Lebeup took upon himself the Management, Order, and Direction, of this Branch of the Lottery, appointing the Place to receive Contributions at, and preparing the Advertisement for that Purpose, naming Clerks lor the other Receivers, providing Books and printed Forms of Receipts, and directing the other Receivers how to proceed.

Resolved, That the Lottery Office at the Exchequer was the Place appointed to receive the Contributions to the said Lottery; whereof Norice was given by the Receivers, in The London Gazette of the Ninth of June 1753, purporting, That the said Receivers would attend, on the then 14th Instant, at the said Office, from Nine till One of the Clock in the Forenoon, and so continue constantly every Day; Sundays and Holidays excepted.

Resolved, That the said Receivers, without Regard to the above Notice, did take in many Contributions on the said It inch of June, and on several other Days preceding the Time appointed by them in ‘The Gazette for that Purpose.

Resolved, That Contributions were taken in by the said Receivers, on Thursday the said 14th of June, before and alter the Hours appointed, and after Proclamation was made that no more would be taken that Day, and after the Doors were ordered ro be shut, in pursuance of such publick Notice.

Resolved, That Contributions were taken in by the said Mr. Lebeup, at the Treasury, on Monday or Tuesday the 1 ith or 12th, and on Wednesday the 13th of June last; parti*-cularly from Mr. Caimel, who alked for 260 or >70 Tickets.

Resolved, That the said Peter Lebeup, after telling the said Mr. Caimel there could be only Twenty Tickets in his own Name, bid him take Paper, and Pea and Ink, and lit down in the Office and make out a List: That after Mr. Caimel had so made out a List of Names for the Number of Tickets he proposed taking, Mr. Lebeup made no Objection to the Names, but delivered him Receipts for that Number of Tickets.

After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

IOI9

My Lords, and Gentlemen*

Nothing could have given me greater Satisfaction The King’* at this time, than the Unanimity and Dispatch, with Speech, which you have gone through the Business of this Session:

Though no particular Point of extraordinary Moment hath offered itself to your Consideration, yet you have shewn the most attentive Regard to every Branch of the publick Service. As to foreign Affairs I shall say nothing at present; except, that it is my fixed Resolution to do every thing in my power to maintain the general Tranquillity, and to adhere to such Measures for that Purpose, as 1 have hitherto pursued in Conjunction with the Powers in Alliance with me.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my hearty Thanks for the Supplies which you have so chearfully granted; and which are the more acceptable to me, as they have brought no new Burthen upon my good Subjects.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Time draws near when the present Parliament mud determine by Law, and it is my Intention very speedily to call a new one; but it would be unjust to this, not to give It a publick Testimony of my Approbation. The many eminent Proofs which you have given of your Duty and Affection to my Person and Government, of your Zeal for this excellent Constitution, and for the Security of the present Establishment, can never be forgotten by me.

By your vigorous Assistance, under the Protection of the Divine Providence, I was enabled to put an End to an expensive, though neceflaryWar,byan honourable Peace; which you have greatly contributed to preserve, by readily and uniformly supporting my Measures. You have gone further, and whilst the Difficulties arising from the War were scarce over, seized the first Opportunity to per-fest one of the greatest Works of Peace, by concurring in the most proper Means for a gradual Decrease of the National Debt, and at the same time raising the Publick Credit. You have also, by several new Laws, laid a Foundation to strengthen and advance the Trade and Commerce of my Kingdoms. Such a Series of wife and Ready Conduct cannot fail to recommend you to the Good-will and Esteem of your Fellow Subjects, as well as mine. For my own Part, I securely rely upon the Loyalty and good Affections of my People, and have no other Aim but their lading Happiness.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, said j

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the 25th Day of this instant April, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the 25th Day of this instant April.

6° Aprilis.
